exp.0:3:
Ezekiel sees a strong storm coming from the north. It is a great cloud with a fire that folds in upon itself, surrounded by a brilliance. At the center of the fire something shines like amber, a bright metal, though some scholars think it refers to an alloy such as electrum.

Ezekiel was a priest and was exiled in Babylon, beside the river Chebar, with other Israelites taken captive. He himself tells what he saw. God appears to him in a vision, and it is notable that this happens far from the temple in Jerusalem. This prepares his calling as a prophet to speak to a wounded and rebellious people.

For today: God is not limited to one place or to our circumstances. Even when you feel far from home, without strength, or in a time of crisis, He can make Himself present. Seek Him with reverence and listen to His voice, for His glory is greater than any situation you face.
exp.0:7:
Under the wings of these living beings, on all four of their sides, there were human hands. Each of the four had faces and wings, and the vision shows them turned in every direction. Human hands suggest service and action, ready to carry out what God wills.

The prophet Ezekiel, a priest who was exiled in Babylon with the people of Judah, is the one speaking here. He describes a vision of God that he received beside the river Chebar. These beings surround the divine throne. Scholars interpret them in various ways: as angels, or as an image of God's glory and power. God revealed himself to his people even in exile.

For today: God is not far away when we feel exiled or without a way out. Just as those beings had hands ready to act, we can ask God how we might serve today with our hands, even in difficult times.
exp.0:8:
This verse describes the living beings that Ezekiel saw in his vision. Their wings touched one another, forming a joining between them. As they advanced they did not turn their bodies, but each one went straight forward, in the direction it faced.

Ezekiel speaks, a priest who lived exiled in Babylon. He tells of the vision of God's glory that he received beside the river Chebar. These beings bear up the throne of God. Many understand that they show God's power and his perfect order. The exact details of their symbolism are interpreted in various ways.

For today: we can learn to serve God with unity and with focus. The living beings went together and without being distracted. Today we can ask God to help us walk alongside other believers, moving forward with firmness toward what he has entrusted to us, without going off course.
exp.0:9:
It says that each living creature had four faces: the face of a man in front, the face of a lion on the right, the face of an ox on the left, and the face of an eagle (probably at the back).

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here, a priest exiled in Babylon. He describes a vision of God's glory among the exiles. The four faces are often understood as symbols of the noblest parts of creation: intelligence, strength, service, and speed. Their exact meaning is not explained here, and there are several interpretations.

For today: even when you feel far from home or from God, He remains on His throne and is not limited to any place. You can worship Him with confidence, even in difficult times, because His glory reaches you wherever you are.
exp.0:10:
This verse describes the living beings that Ezekiel saw in his vision. Each one had four wings: two were stretched upward and joined the wings of the being beside it, and with the other two they covered their bodies.

"Such were their faces" refers to the faces he has just mentioned: man, lion, ox, and eagle.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest who lived in exile in Babylon by the river Chebar. He tells of the vision God gave him when God called him to be a prophet. Many understand that the covered wings express reverence, and that the vision shows the glory and majesty of God, although the details of the faces are interpreted in various ways.

For today: God deserves our respect and awe. Before asking him for anything, we can pause for a moment to worship him with humility, knowing that he is present even when we feel far from home or in difficult times.
exp.0:12:
The living creatures Ezekiel saw looked like burning coals of fire, like torches blazing. The fire moved back and forth among them, shone brightly, and lightning came out of it.

The prophet Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon with the people of Judah, tells of the vision God gave him by the river Chebar. The living creatures are beneath God's throne, and the fire shows his holiness and his power. God revealed himself to a people who felt far from their land and their temple.

For today: God remains holy and present, even when we feel far away or in the midst of trials. We can draw near to him with reverence and confidence, and pray today: "Lord, help me to remember that you reign."
exp.0:15:
This verse says that the wheels Ezekiel saw beside the living creatures shone with a color like beryl, a precious stone with a golden or greenish tone (it is not known with certainty which exact color was meant). The four wheels were all alike. Each appeared to have one wheel inside another, crossing through it, which may explain why they could move in any direction without turning.

The one who speaks is Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, who describes a vision of the glory of God. God prepares him this way to call him as a prophet to a people in exile. Interpreters differ about the meaning of the wheels, but many see that they show God present and active everywhere.

For today: even when you feel far from home or without direction, God is not limited by your place. He moves with you and continues to rule. Trust in Him today.
exp.0:18:
This verse says that the wheels moved together with the living creatures. When they walked, the wheels walked beside them; when they rose up from the earth, the wheels also rose up.

The prophet Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, speaks here. He describes a vision of God's glory that he received by the river Chebar. The verses that follow explain that the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels, so everything moved in perfect unity. Interpreters explain the meaning of the wheels in various ways, but many see in them that God is not limited to one place.

For today: even if you feel far from everything, as Ezekiel did in exile, God remains present and in motion. Trust that He accompanies you and directs your path.
exp.0:20:
This verse says that the wheels moved in exact step with the living creatures. When they walked, the wheels walked; when they stopped, the wheels stopped; and when they rose from the ground, the wheels rose with them. The reason given is that the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels. Here the word "creatures" refers to living beings, not ordinary animals. And "spirit" can be understood as their drive or inner force that guided them.

The passage is spoken by the prophet Ezekiel, who describes a vision of God that he received by the river Chebar while he lived in exile in Babylon. Many understand that the vision showed God's glory present even far from the temple in Jerusalem. The exact meaning of each detail is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God is not confined to one place. If you feel far from home or in a difficult season, you can trust that he moves with you, and you can ask him to guide your steps.
exp.0:21:
Over the heads of each living creature there was what looks like a vast expanse, a kind of sky or arched dome stretched out, gleaming like an astonishing crystal. Here the word for the creatures refers to living beings in general, not to ordinary animals. The description of what was seen is about how it looked to the observer.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon along with other Jews. He describes a vision of God. Beneath that dome are the living creatures and their wings, and higher up, in the verses that follow, the throne of God appears. Interpreters differ on the exact meaning of each detail, but all of them see the greatness and holiness of God.

For today: even in times of exile, pain, or uncertainty, God continues to reign above all things. We can draw near to Him with reverence and confidence, remembering that no circumstance is beyond His reach.
exp.0:23:
Ezekiel tells us that he heard the noise of the wings of the living creatures as they moved. It sounded like great waters, like the voice of the Almighty (God, the all-powerful one), like the noise of a crowd or an army. When they stopped, they let their wings down, that is, they lowered them and let them rest.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. He is describing a vision of the glory of God that he received beside the river Chebar. The living creatures carry God's throne, and the loud noise shows his greatness. Some think the phrase "the voice of the Almighty" is only a comparison; others see in it an echo of divine majesty. Either way, the text gives no further detail.

Even in the midst of difficulties, God remains great and reigns. When everything seems noisy or confused, pause for a moment to listen to him and to worship him.
exp.0:27:
Ezekiel compares the brightness around the throne to the rainbow, which appears in the clouds when it rains. He says that this was the appearance of "the likeness of the glory of the Lord", that is, something resembling God's glory, not the glory itself. When he saw it, he fell on his face to the ground, and he heard a voice speaking.

The one speaking is Ezekiel, a priest who was living in exile in Babylon with other Jews. Beside the river Chebar he saw this vision of God above a throne, before receiving his call as a prophet. God revealed himself to him even far from the temple in Jerusalem. The bow evokes beauty and, for many readers, the faithfulness of God, although the text does not explain this.

For today: before we speak, God deserves our reverence and attention. Today you can begin your prayer in silence, acknowledging who God is, and then listen to his voice in the Bible with humility.
exp.1:1:
When God spoke to Ezekiel, a spirit entered into him and set him on his feet. The verse says the spirit entered him as God spoke, and that Ezekiel was lifted to his feet so that he could hear the one speaking to him. After he stood up, Ezekiel was attentive to hear what God was telling him.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. He has just seen the glory of God and had fallen face down on the ground. God addresses him as a human being and lifts him up to give him his mission: to speak to a rebellious people. Some understand the spirit to be the Spirit of God; the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: when God calls us to something difficult, He himself gives us strength to rise. First let us listen to His voice with humility, and trust that He sustains those whom He sends.
exp.1:5:
God tells Ezekiel not to be afraid of the people he will be sent to. "Son of man" is a way of addressing him as a human being. The "briers and thorns" and the "scorpions" are images of a hurtful and dangerous setting. A "rebellious house" means a people who refuse to obey God.

God speaks at the moment he calls Ezekiel as a prophet. The people of Israel were in exile in Babylon. God warns him in advance that many will not want to listen to him, but that his task is to speak faithfully. According to the text, even if they do not heed him, they will know that a prophet had been among them.

Today, when you want to speak with truth and love but fear rejection or criticism, remember that God asks you for faithfulness, not for everyone's approval. Pray, speak with respect, and leave the results in his hands.
exp.1:8:
It says that Ezekiel looked up and saw a hand stretched out toward him, holding a roll of a book. In that time books were rolls of leather or papyrus, rolled up for storage. The hand holds the message that God wants to give him.

God, who has just called Ezekiel as a prophet to the people of Israel, whom he calls rebellious, is speaking. Before showing him the roll, he asks him not to be rebellious like them and to open his mouth to receive what he gives him. It will be seen afterward that the roll contains laments and painful warnings.

For today: before speaking of God to others, we need to receive his Word with humility and obedience. We can begin the day by reading the Bible with an open heart, ready to listen even to what costs us.
exp.1:9:
God shows Ezekiel a scroll spread out before him, written on both sides. On it were dirges (sad songs sung over a dead person), lamentation (weeping) and woes (cries of pain and anguish). In other words, the message contained judgment and sorrow.

Ezekiel is a priest living in exile in Babylon. God calls him to speak to Israel, a rebellious people who do not want to listen. Before sending him, God asks him not to be rebellious like them, but to listen and receive the word. The scroll written on both sides suggests a complete message, although some interpret it in other ways.

Today, God invites us to receive his whole word, even when it is uncomfortable. We can ask him for a heart willing to hear his truth with humility, not choosing only what comforts us, trusting that his correction seeks our good.
exp.2:0:
God tells Ezekiel that he is called "son of man," that is, simply a human being. He orders him to eat what he finds, a scroll, and then go and speak to the people of Israel.

The one speaking is God, who has just shown Ezekiel his glory and called him as a prophet. The people of Israel were living in rebellion, and Ezekiel was among the exiles in Babylon. Eating the scroll is a picture: the prophet must receive and take in God's message before announcing it. Scholars agree on this general sense, though not all of them agree on every detail of the symbol.

For today: before speaking about God to others, let yourself be fed by his Word. Read it calmly, meditate on it, and obey it, so that what you share comes from a heart that has already received it.
exp.2:3:
God tells Ezekiel to go to the house of Israel, that is, to the people of Israel, and to speak to them with God's words, not his own. "Son of man" is a way of addressing him as a simple human being.

God is speaking. Shortly before, Ezekiel had eaten a scroll containing the divine message, and it tasted as sweet as honey. This shows that he first had to receive God's word and make it his own, and only then pass it on. God sends him to his own people, who spoke the same language as he did, though later it is said that they would not listen to him easily.

For today: before speaking about God to others, let yourself be fed by his Word. Read it calmly, pray with it, and let it transform you. In this way you will be able to speak with sincerity, without adding your own ideas to what God says.
exp.2:5:
God tells Ezekiel that he is not being sent to foreign peoples, whose speech is strange or hard to understand, and whose words he could not comprehend. And He adds something surprising: if He had sent him to them, they would have listened to him.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel when He calls him to carry His message to Israel, His own people. Ezekiel shared a language and culture with them, so there would be no excuse of misunderstanding. God points out that the problem would not be communication, but Israel's hardness of heart, since they were already rejecting Him.

For today: sometimes we believe people do not respond to God because of a lack of clarity or of arguments. This verse reminds us that the heart also has an influence. We can speak with love and simplicity, and trust that God is the one who opens ears.
exp.2:7:
It says that God himself made Ezekiel firm and unyielding to face those who would oppose him. "Face" and "forehead" speak of a person's attitude and determination. Just as the people had hard foreheads, God gives his prophet a forehead just as strong, so that he will not bend.

God speaks here, having just called Ezekiel as a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. He warns that Israel will not listen to him, not because the message is difficult, but because they do not want to hear God. For this reason he prepares him with a special firmness, so that he can carry out his mission without fear.

For today: if God asks you to speak or live with truth in an environment that resists it, do not depend on your own character. Ask God for the strength that he gives, and stand firm with kindness, without letting fear or rejection silence you.
exp.2:14:
Ezekiel arrives at a place called Tel-abib, beside the river Chebar, where the Jewish exiles were living. He sits down where they were sitting, and he stays there seven days, stunned, overwhelmed, and speechless.

Ezekiel is both a priest and a prophet, and he writes in the first person. He has just seen an overwhelming vision of God's glory and has received the call to speak to his people. He goes with bitterness and anger in his spirit, but with God's firm hand upon him. Those seven days of silence prepare him before he receives his mission as a watchman.

Before speaking, it is often wise to sit beside those who are suffering. Listen, accompany them, and keep patient silence. In this way God prepares your heart to offer words that are true and compassionate.
exp.2:16:
God tells Ezekiel that he has made him a watchman, someone who stands guard from a high place and gives warning when danger approaches. His task is to listen to what God says and to warn the people of Israel clearly on God's behalf.

The LORD speaks. Ezekiel was living among the Jewish exiles in Babylon, beside the river Chebar. After seven days of being overwhelmed and silent, he receives this call. God reminds him that he will be responsible for delivering the message faithfully, no matter how the people respond.

For today: if God gives us the opportunity to speak of Him to someone, let us do it with love, truth, and humility. First let us listen to His Word, and then share it with respect, leaving the outcome in God's hands.
exp.2:17:
God tells Ezekiel that if He announces that a wicked man will die for his evil way and Ezekiel does not warn him, that man will die for his sin, but God will hold Ezekiel accountable.

Scripture here speaks of Jehovah speaking to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. God appoints him as a watchman, one who gives warning of danger. His task was to pass on faithfully what God said, and the purpose of the warning was that the people would turn and live.

For today: if you know someone who is turning away from God, do not stay silent out of fear or comfort. Speak to him with love, humility and truth, and leave the results in God's hands. Many believers understand that this calling applies in different ways to each person.
exp.2:25:
God says he will make Ezekiel's tongue stick to the roof of his mouth, meaning he will be unable to speak. He will be silent and unable to rebuke or correct the people, because they are a rebellious house, that is, a stubborn people who resist God. A reprover is someone who warns or corrects.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier he told Ezekiel to shut himself up in his house, and it was said that he would be bound with cords. His silence was a sign to a people who would not listen. Scholars debate whether all of this was literal or symbolic. God would only open his mouth again when he had a message from God to deliver.

For today: we do not always need to speak much; sometimes it is wise to stay silent until God shows us what to say. Before correcting someone, let us ask God to give us his words and not only our own.
exp.3:0:
God tells Ezekiel to take a tile, that is, a brick of clay still soft, set it in front of him, and draw the city of Jerusalem on it. "Draw" here means to carve or sketch. "Son of man" is the way God addresses Ezekiel, reminding him that he is an ordinary human being.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon, together with other Jews. God asks him for a symbolic action, like a play with a message, to announce that Jerusalem would be besieged because of its sins. The verses that follow explain the siege in detail. Many of the exiles believed the city would not fall, and this gesture challenged that false hope.

For today: God speaks to us with clarity, even though at times we find it hard to accept. We can ask him to give us humility to hear his correction in time, instead of clinging to what comforts us but is not true.
exp.3:2:
God tells Ezekiel to take an iron plate, a kind of pan or sheet of metal, and set it up as a wall between himself and the city drawn on the clay tablet. Then he must turn his face toward it, as one who lays siege to it. A siege means a blockade of a city, and a sign is a warning that can be seen with the eyes.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon, and sends him to act out this message before the people. Jerusalem had not yet fallen, and the people believed they were safe. Many understand the plate to represent a barrier between God and the city, though some see it as the force of the siege.

For today: God speaks to us with seriousness because He loves us. When something in your life pulls you away from Him, do not ignore it; listen to it and return to Him with humility.
exp.3:3:
He says that God commands Ezekiel to lie on his left side and to lay upon it the wickedness, that is, the sin, of Israel. He would bear that guilt for a certain number of days. Here the verb "lie" means to lie down, not so much to sleep at night.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. With this action, which was a sign for the people, God showed that Jerusalem would be besieged because of its rebellion. The verses that follow explain that each day represents a year of sin. Scholars discuss how to understand those 390 years, and not all of them interpret it the same way.

God takes sin seriously, but he also communicates clearly and patiently before he acts. Today we can listen to his warnings in time, recognize our faults, and return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.3:5:
God tells Ezekiel that, when he has finished lying on his left side, he is to lie on his right side for forty days. There he will "bear the iniquity" of the house of Judah, that is, the sin and its consequences. Each day stands for a year.

God speaks, and the prophet Ezekiel is living in exile in Babylon. Through this strange action, God announces the judgment that is coming upon Jerusalem. Ezekiel acts as a sign that everyone can see. Interpreters do not agree on which exact years the forty days represent, and it is better not to claim a certain figure.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also speaks to us clearly before the consequences arrive. If you sense his call to change today, do not put it off; answer him with humility and trust in his mercy.
exp.3:7:
God says to Ezekiel that he has placed cords on him, that is, bonds, so that he cannot turn from one side to the other. He was to remain this way until the days of the siege were complete, the siege of Jerusalem that he was representing.

God is speaking, and Ezekiel is his prophet among the exiles in Babylon. Through this symbolic action, God announces the judgment that would come upon Jerusalem and shows that the people would bear the consequences of their sin. Scholars debate whether the cords were literal or an image of his restriction; the text does not make this clear.

For today: God speaks in earnest, but he also draws near. Ask him to show you if there is something you have minimized, and respond to him with sincere repentance, trusting in his mercy.
exp.3:8:
God tells Ezekiel to mix six kinds of grain and legumes (wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt, or another grain), to store them in a single pot, and to make bread from them. That will be his food during the 390 days he lies on his side.

God himself speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He is commanded to portray the siege of Jerusalem with his own body. This scarce, rationed bread shows the shortage the people would suffer during the siege. Scholars debate how the 390 days should be understood, and there is no single certain explanation.

For today: God speaks with seriousness, but he does not leave his people without warning. If today we feel that God is correcting us, we can listen to him with humility and return to him without delay, trusting that his purpose is to restore us.
exp.3:10:
God tells Ezekiel to drink water that is rationed, only a sixth part of a hin, and to take it at fixed intervals during the day. A hin was a Hebrew measure of liquids; a sixth part comes to a little over half a liter, although exact calculations vary.

The LORD speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet exiled in Babylon. Through this symbolic act, God announces what will come upon Jerusalem during the siege: a shortage of bread and of water, as a consequence of the people's rebellion. Ezekiel lives out the message in his own body so that everyone can see it.

For today: learn to value what God gives you, like the daily bread and water, and to live with gratitude and moderation. Also remember that God warns in love before correcting; listening to him in time spares us much pain.
exp.3:12:
This verse says that God explains to Ezekiel the meaning of his symbolic action: just as the prophet will eat bread that is unclean, the people of Israel will eat food that is impure when they are scattered among the nations. The nations are foreign peoples, and unclean means ceremonially impure, not fit according to the law of Moses.

The Lord speaks to Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. God had commanded him to portray before the people the siege of Jerusalem and the scarcity that would come because of their disobedience. Bread baked with dung was a sign of humiliation. Ezekiel protests because he had always kept himself pure, and God allows him to use cow dung instead.

For today: sin has real consequences, but God still speaks with mercy. If you feel today that you are living far from what God wants, listen to his voice and return to him with humility, knowing that he hears our complaints.
exp.3:13:
Ezekiel protests before God. He says that he has never been defiled: he has not eaten an animal that died on its own (a carcass), nor an animal torn apart by beasts, nor any impure meat. He has kept himself pure from his youth until now, and no impure flesh has ever entered his mouth.

The prophet Ezekiel was a priest. God had commanded him to perform a symbolic act: to cook his bread with human waste, to show that Israel would eat defiled food among the nations. Ezekiel is distressed because he had guarded ritual purity his whole life. God answers with compassion and allows him to use cow dung instead, though the message of scarcity and anguish still stands.

For today: you can be honest with God about what it costs you to obey. He listens with patience, and sometimes He answers with mercy in the midst of a hard task.
exp.3:15:
God says to Ezekiel that he will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem. This means he will take away the supply of food. The people will eat their bread rationed, by weight, with anxiety, and they will drink the water measured out, with dread, that is, with great fear that it will run out.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who acts as a sign for the people. Through symbolic actions, he announces the siege of Jerusalem. Earlier, Ezekiel asked not to eat something unclean, and God allowed him to change the fuel. The cause is the people's wickedness, as the following verse says.

For today: God invites us not to take for granted what we have. We can thank him each day for bread and water, share with someone who lacks them, and humbly examine whether there is anything in our lives we should repent of.
exp.4:0:
God tells Ezekiel to take a sharp knife, like a barber's razor, and run it over his head and his beard. Then he must weigh the hair on a scale and divide it into parts. "Son of man" is the way God addresses Ezekiel throughout the book.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet and priest who lived in exile in Babylon. This is a symbolic action, a kind of acted-out message: the hair represents the people of Jerusalem, and what follows announces judgment for their disobedience. Shaving the head was also a sign of mourning and shame, and for a priest it was a very strong thing to do.

For today: God takes our disobedience seriously, but he also warns before he acts. Today we can listen to his voice with humility and correct our course in time.
exp.4:1:
God tells Ezekiel to use his own hair, cut off, as a sign. A third part he is to burn with fire in the middle of a drawing of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled. Another third he is to strike with the sword all around the city. The last third he is to scatter into the wind. God says that he will draw out a sword after those who are scattered.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet in exile, and asks him for a visible action. The text indicates that it represents Jerusalem and the judgment for its rebellion. Many understand it as death by fire, by the sword, and by dispersion.

For today: God is in earnest when he warns, but he does so so that we will return to him. Today we can ask him what things we should leave behind, and answer him with humility before the harm grows.
exp.4:3:
He tells that Ezekiel must again take a few hairs from those he had tied up in his garment, and throw them into the fire until they are burned. From that fire another fire would come out that would reach the whole house of Israel.

God speaks, giving a command to his prophet Ezekiel. He uses Ezekiel's hair as a sign to show what would happen to Jerusalem: siege, death, and scattering. The following verse gives the reason: the people despised God's laws and lived worse than the surrounding nations. Even the few who were spared were tested again by fire.

God takes our disobedience seriously, but he also cares for his own. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are listening to his Word or setting it aside, and return to him with humility.
exp.4:4:
Here God says that Jerusalem is the city he himself placed at the center, surrounded by other nations and lands.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Earlier, Ezekiel had performed a symbolic act with his hair, which represented the judgment on Jerusalem. Many understand that its central location shows that God wanted the people to be a visible witness to the others. But they rejected his commands, and that is why punishment comes.

God gives us places, gifts, and opportunities so that others may see his goodness in us. Today we can ask ourselves: does the way I live in my family, my work, and my neighborhood reflect God, or does it contradict him? Let us ask him for help to obey him sincerely.
exp.4:7:
This verse says that God himself sets himself against Jerusalem. The repeated "I" adds emphasis: it will not be just any enemy, but God himself who acts.

The word "judgments" refers to punishments or just sentences. The phrase "in the sight of the nations" means that all the surrounding peoples will see what happens.

Speaking through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon, God says that Jerusalem had received God's law and lived in the midst of the nations, but rejected it, and according to the text, did not even keep the standards of the neighboring peoples. For this reason God announces a public and serious punishment.

For today: God takes seriously the way we live, especially if we claim to belong to him. We can humbly ask ourselves where we have ignored his word, and return to him without excuses, trusting in his mercy.
exp.4:8:
God says he will punish Jerusalem in a way he has never done before and will never do again. The reason is "all your abominations," that is, its detestable practices, above all idolatry.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God accuses Jerusalem of being worse than the nations around it: it had received his law and his temple, yet it despised them. The verses that follow describe a terrible siege, and interpreters connect it with the fall of Jerusalem.

For today: the more we have received from God, the more responsible we are to live faithfully. Instead of excusing ourselves by what others do, we can ask him to show us where we need to return to him sincerely.
exp.4:9:
God says that the city will suffer a famine so terrible that fathers will eat their sons and sons will eat their fathers. Furthermore, God will bring punishments upon it and will scatter the few who are left in every direction, to all the winds, that is, in all directions.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing Jerusalem. She had sinned with idols and abominations, even inside the temple. This warning announces the siege by the Babylonians. Moses had already warned of something similar if the people broke the covenant (Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53).

For today: God speaks seriously about sin, but his warnings are a call to return to him. Let us not ignore his voice; if anything in our lives has taken his place, let us repent today and trust in his forgiveness.
exp.4:11:
God's judgment on Jerusalem will have three parts: a third of the people would die of disease and hunger inside the city, another third would fall by the sword all around it, and the last third would be scattered in every direction, and even there the sword would pursue them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Earlier, Ezekiel had acted out a sign with his hair, divided into three parts. God explains that Jerusalem had defiled his temple with idolatry and detestable practices. It is a harsh message, announcing what would happen when the city was conquered.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also warns before he acts. Today we can hear his call to turn back to him without delay, instead of growing used to what we know displeases him.
exp.4:12:
It says that God will carry his judgment through to the end. Where the source speaks of his fury being fulfilled, that means his anger will be brought to completion. Where it speaks of his wrath coming to rest on them, that means his anger will be satisfied once the punishment is finished. The word about his zeal refers to his demanding love, which will not tolerate his people betraying him. In the end, they will know that God meant what he said.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, before the fall of Jerusalem. The people had defiled the temple with idols and sinful practices. God had warned them, and now he announces the consequences: famine, war, and scattering. Scholars understand this zeal as the pain of a faithful God in the face of betrayal.

For today: we should not take God's warning lightly. If anything in our lives competes with him, it must be corrected soon. His discipline seeks to bring us to recognize him and return to him.
exp.5:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel.

The one speaking is the Lord, the God of Israel, and the one receiving the message is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The verses that follow show that God asks him to speak against the mountains of Israel, where the people had set up places of worship to other gods. God wants to warn them about the consequences of their idolatry.

For today: God still speaks, above all through his Word. Before asking him for anything, take a moment to listen. Read the Bible calmly and ask yourself: "Lord, what do you want to say to me today?"
exp.5:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," a way of reminding him that he is simply a human being. He tells him to set his face toward the mountains of Israel, that is, to look at them with a firm gaze, and to prophesy against them, that is, to announce a message of judgment.

The LORD speaks through Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The mountains were places where the people had built altars and idols. By addressing the mountains, God is in fact confronting the people who worshiped there. The message is harsh, but its purpose is to make them recognize who the Lord is (v. 7).

For today: ask yourself what things in your heart are occupying the place that belongs only to God. He speaks to us with truth because he wants to bring us back to himself. Listen to him with humility.
exp.5:2:
God commands Ezekiel to speak to the mountains, the hills, the streams, and the valleys of Israel, as if they could hear him. He announces that God himself will bring a sword, that is, war, and that he will destroy the high places, the elevated sites where the people worshiped idols.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. The mountains represent the land and its people, who had filled those high places with idolatry. God warns of judgment because his people had abandoned him.

For today: God does not overlook what takes the place that belongs to him alone. We can honestly ask ourselves what things we love or trust more than God, and ask him to help us return to him before those things harm us.
exp.5:3:
God says that he will destroy the places where the people worshiped idols. The altars were places for offering sacrifices, and the sun-images were figures or pillars used in pagan worship (the exact meaning of the Hebrew term is debated). Desolate means ruined or destroyed. Moreover, the bodies of the dead would lie scattered in front of those same idols, which could not save them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God announces judgment on Israel because his people had stopped worshiping him and were practicing idolatry on the mountains. The judgment would come by the sword, that is, by war.

For today: examine what things occupy in your heart the place that belongs to God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. None of that can save you, but God can. Return to him with sincerity.
exp.5:5:
In all the places where the people live, the cities will be left empty and in ruins. The "high places" were raised sites where false gods were worshiped. Those altars will be destroyed, the idols broken, and the sun pillars (probably columns or altars used to worship the sun) will be cut down. Everything they made with their hands will disappear.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God announces judgment on Israel because his people turned away from him to worship idols. But the next passage shows that not everything ends in destruction: some will escape, and so they will know that the LORD is God.

For today: examine which things in your heart have taken the place that belongs to God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Hand them over to him before they collapse on their own.
exp.5:6:
It says that, when God's judgment comes, there will be dead people in the midst of the people of Israel. "Fall" means that they will die, above all in war. And the final result is that they will know, by experience, that the Lord is God.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people had filled the land with idols and false altars. God announces that those idols will not be able to save them. But the passage does not end in destruction: God promises that some will escape and, while far away, will remember him with repentance.

For today: what we put in the place of God, such as money, success or pride, cannot sustain us when a crisis comes. Examine what gives you security and turn your heart back to God before a difficulty forces you to do so.
exp.5:7:
God says that, in the midst of the punishment, he will not destroy everyone. Some of the people will escape the sword and will live among the nations, when they are scattered through various lands. Here "sword" means war.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Israel, who had fallen into idolatry. He announces judgment on their altars and idols, but leaves a promise: a remnant will survive. The verses that follow explain that these survivors will remember God and will repent.

For today: even when we face the consequences of our mistakes, God remains merciful. His discipline seeks to bring us back to Him, not to destroy us. If today you feel far away, you can remember Him and return with sincerity.
exp.5:13:
God says he will stretch out his hand, that is, he will act in judgment against the people. Their land will be left desolate, meaning ruined, and empty of people, more than the wilderness toward Diblath. This will happen in all the places where they lived. In the end, they will know that the Lord is God. As for Diblath, it is not known with certainty which place it was; some believe it is a variant of Riblah, but this is uncertain.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. The people of Israel had filled the land with idols and altars on the hills and under the trees. God announces the consequences of that idolatry, so that they may recognize who the only true God is.

For today: examine what things are taking the place of God in your heart. God calls you to return to him before those things leave you empty.
exp.6:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel, called "son of man," that is, a simple human being. He commands him to announce to the land of Israel that the end is coming. The word "the end" is repeated to stress that it is certain and urgent. The "four corners" are the edges or extremes of the land; here it refers to the whole territory of Israel, leaving no place free.

Ezekiel was a prophet and priest among the exiles in Babylon. God speaks through him because the people had fallen into idolatry and wickedness, and judgment was already near. The verses that follow explain that God would act according to his ways, so that they would know that he is the Lord. Some scholars see here the fall of Jerusalem, and there is no doubt that this is a historical judgment.

Today we can take God's warnings seriously and not postpone repentance. If something in your life does not please him, bring it to him today with sincerity; his patience is an invitation to return, not an excuse to stay the same.
exp.6:12:
This verse says that whoever sells a property will not be able to get it back again, even while still alive. It also says that the vision of judgment over the whole multitude will not be overturned, and that no one can save their life through their wickedness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Judah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. He announces that violence and ungodliness have reached their limit. According to the law, land that had been sold could return to its owner in the year of jubilee, but now the judgment will be so complete that this hope will be lost. Many understand this as a sign that the exile would be harsh and long.

For today: do not place your security in possessions, businesses, or plans, because all of that can be lost. Seek God with humility and correct today what you know is wrong.
exp.6:13:
It says the people will blow the trumpet to call for war and will have everything made ready, but no one will go out to fight. The reason is that God himself has poured out his wrath on the whole multitude.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem and Judah for their idolatry and injustice. The trumpet was the usual sign of alarm, but this time it will not help, because the people will have neither courage nor strength. It is a judgment already decided.

For today: let us not trust in our preparations, plans or resources as if they were enough without God. It is wise to examine the heart in time, to turn back to him with humility, and to seek his mercy before the consequences arrive.
exp.6:14:
It says there will be no way to escape. Outside the city waits the enemy's sword, and inside, plague and famine. Whoever is in the field will die by the sword; whoever is in the city will be consumed by famine and plague. The sentence that explains one of the phrases is rewritten as follows: the word translated "sword" here means the sword itself, that is, war.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem for its idolatry and its injustice. The people kept trusting that nothing serious would happen, but God says that his wrath is already determined and that no one will be able to save themselves by their own means.

For today: do not take lightly the patience of God. If He shows you something you need to correct, do not put it off. Return to Him with humility, remembering that in Christ there is forgiveness and refuge for whoever repents.
exp.6:17:
They will dress themselves in mourning clothes, made of rough cloth called sackcloth. Trembling will cover them like a blanket, and their faces will show shame and confusion. They will also shave their heads, which was a sign of deep grief.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem for its idolatry and injustice. The people had trusted in their riches and idols, and now they would see that none of that could save them.

For today: let us not wait for a crisis to return to God. We can examine what we truly trust in, whether money, success, or security, and give that place to Him today, for He is the one who can truly sustain us.
exp.7:0:
Ezekiel tells us that one day, on the fifth day of the sixth month of the sixth year, he was sitting in his house. The elders of Judah were with him. Suddenly, the hand of the Lord fell upon him. This expression means that the power of God seized him and gave him a vision.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who lived in exile in Babylon with other Jews. The elders had probably come to seek a word from God. According to the calendar of the exile, this happened around 592 B.C., although the exact date is calculated in different ways. Here a vision begins in which God shows him what was happening in Jerusalem.

God can speak in the midst of everyday life, even in a house and an ordinary conversation. It is good to be alert and willing to listen to him, even when we think we are only sitting and waiting.
exp.7:1:
Ezekiel sees a figure that looks like a man, made of fire. From the waist down it is fire, and from the waist up it shines like amber, a gleaming metal.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, speaks from exile in Babylon. He is in his house with the elders of Judah when he feels the hand of the Lord, a phrase that indicates God has taken hold of him to give him a vision. Soon he will be carried in vision to Jerusalem to see the people's idolatry.

Many think this figure is connected with the glory of God he saw earlier, although the text only says it has the appearance of a figure.

For today: God is holy and shows himself as he is, not as is convenient for us. Ask him to show you honestly what is in your heart, and listen to him with humility.
exp.7:2:
It says that a figure with the appearance of a man, made of fire and brightness, stretched out his hand and took Ezekiel by the hair. The Spirit lifted him up between heaven and earth and brought him, in visions of God, to Jerusalem. There, at the north gate of the inner court, stood the image of jealousy, an idol that provoked God to jealousy.

Ezekiel, a prophet and priest, lived in exile in Babylon. While the elders of Judah listened to him, God showed him in a vision what was happening in the temple. He wanted Ezekiel to understand why judgment was coming. It is not known for certain what that image was, but it was clearly idolatry within the holy place.

For today: God sees what happens in the hidden places of our hearts. We can ask Him to show us what things occupy the place that belongs to Him alone, and turn back to Him with sincerity.
exp.7:5:
God asks Ezekiel whether he sees what the people are doing: great abominations, that is, things God detests, committed in the temple. These actions drove God away from his sanctuary, his house. And he warns him that he will see things even worse.

He speaks, in a vision that shows the prophet Ezekiel what was happening inside the temple in Jerusalem. Near the gate there was an idol that provoked the anger of God. Scholars do not agree on exactly what the figure was. God shows the cause of his judgment: his people had abandoned true worship.

For today: ask God to show you which things in your life are occupying the place that belongs to him. With humility, set them aside, and return to worshiping him sincerely, for he desires to dwell near his people.
exp.7:6:
It says that the Spirit of God brought Ezekiel to the entrance of the court, the courtyard of the temple in Jerusalem. There he looked and saw a hole in the wall.

Ezekiel was a prophet who was exiled in Babylon. In a vision, God took him to Jerusalem to show him the hidden sins of the people, above all their idolatry. God speaks with him step by step, and each scene is worse than the one before. The hole in the wall is the beginning of a discovery: what was being done in secret would come to light. Scholars do not offer a single explanation for the detail of the hole, but the general meaning is clear.

For today: what we hide is not hidden from God. Let us ask him to show us, in love, what is in our hearts, so that we may confess it and be healed.
exp.7:7:
God tells Ezekiel to dig through the wall. As he does, he uncovers a hidden doorway.

God addresses the prophet as "Son of man" and speaks directly to him. The verse shows Ezekiel obeying right away, digging through the wall and finding what was concealed behind it.

God speaks, and Ezekiel describes what he saw in a vision. He is in the temple in Jerusalem, and God shows him, step by step, the idolatry the people were practicing in secret. The hidden doorway leads to a place where they worshiped images. God wants Ezekiel to understand why judgment is coming upon Jerusalem.

For today: nothing hidden is hidden from God. We can ask Him to show us what we have kept silent about or hidden in our hearts, and confess it with confidence, knowing that He forgives those who turn back to Him.
exp.7:10:
It says that seventy men, leaders of the people of Israel, were standing before the painted images of idols on the wall. Each one held a censer, that is, a vessel in which incense is burned. Among them was Jaazaniah, son of Shaphan. The smoke of the incense is fragrant, and from it rose a thick cloud.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who in a vision is brought to the temple in Jerusalem. God shows him that the leaders were worshiping images in secret, while saying that God did not see them. That is why the judgment coming upon Jerusalem has a clear reason. Some think that this Jaazaniah is different from the Jaazaniah of Jeremiah 35, but this is not certain.

We can ask ourselves whether there is something we do in the dark, in secret, that we would not do in front of others. God sees the heart. Having one public life of faith and another hidden one does not please him. Today we can honestly confess to him what is hidden and ask him to be the only Lord of our worship.
exp.7:14:
God asks Ezekiel whether he is seeing what is happening, and tells him to turn again, because he will see things that are even more serious and offensive. "Abominations" are practices that God detests, above all idolatry.

God speaks with Ezekiel in a vision, around 592 B.C., while Judah was living in sin. He takes him through the temple in Jerusalem to show him how the people mixed the worship of God with false cults. In the nearby passage, women are seen weeping for Tammuz, a pagan god. God shows this to explain why judgment is coming.

Today we can ask ourselves whether there is something in our hearts that competes with God, even though we keep going to church. Ask him to show you it, and open that area to him with sincerity.
exp.7:15:
He brought me into the inner court of the Lord's house, and there, at the entrance of the temple of the Lord, between the porch and the altar, I saw about twenty-five men. They had their backs to the temple of the Lord and their faces toward the east, and they were bowing down to the sun as it rose.

God speaks, showing Ezekiel in a vision what is happening in Jerusalem, while the prophet is among the exiles in Babylon. This is the third abomination in a series. These men were in the most sacred place and yet they were worshipping something created instead of the Creator. God explains in this way why judgment is coming. Some think the twenty-five were priests, but the text does not say so clearly.

Today we can ask ourselves what good thing has taken the place of God in our hearts. A person can be in church and yet, inwardly, have their back turned toward Him. Let us look to Him again with sincerity.
exp.7:17:
He says God will respond in anger to what he has seen. He will show no pity and will not spare with his gaze. Even if the people cry out loudly asking for help, God will not listen to them.

God speaks in a vision that he shows to Ezekiel. Inside the temple, about twenty-five men, with their backs to the sanctuary, were bowing down toward the rising sun, that is, they were worshiping creation and not the Lord. In addition, the land was full of violence and injustice. God announces here the judgment on Judah, which had rejected his covenant.

For today: God takes sincere worship and justice seriously. It is not enough to be in a religious place if the heart turns toward other things. Today we can examine what holds first place in our lives and return quickly to God with humility, knowing that he offers forgiveness to those who repent.
exp.8:1:
This verse describes a vision that Ezekiel receives: six men come from the gate facing north, and each one carries a weapon for destruction. With them comes a seventh man dressed in linen, with a writing case with ink and pen at his waist. They all stop beside the bronze altar, in the temple.

God shows Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon, the judgment that would come upon Jerusalem because of its idolatry and its detestable practices. The men who come are carrying out God's judgment. Some think they are angels; the text does not say so with certainty. The man in linen will mark those who grieve over the sin of the city.

God is just and judges evil, but he also sees and cares for those who suffer because of the sin around them. Today we can ask him for a sensitive heart, one that does not grow used to injustice, but that prays and trusts in his mercy.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that the glory of God, which had been over the cherub in the temple, rose up and moved to the doorway of the house. From there, the LORD called the man dressed in linen, who carried at his side a case for a scribe, that is, a container with ink and a pen for writing.

Ezekiel, a prophet living in exile in Babylon, sees in a vision how God judges Jerusalem for its idolatry. Here the glory of God begins to withdraw from the temple. Before sending the punishment, God orders those who grieve over the city's sin to be marked. Some understand that the scribe represents God's care for his own people.

God sees who laments the evil and does not forget them. Today we can ask him to give us a heart that is sensitive to sin, without growing used to what grieves him, and to trust that he cares for those who are faithful to him.
exp.8:3:
The Lord tells the man dressed in linen to go through Jerusalem and put a mark on the foreheads of those who grieve and cry out over the evil done in the city. Those words speak of deep pain, and the abominations are practices that God detests, such as idolatry.

The prophet Ezekiel receives this vision from the Lord while the people are living in rebellion, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. God is going to judge the city, but first he sets apart, with a sign, those who are still faithful to him and who feel sorrow over sin. The judgment begins at his own sanctuary.

Today we can ask ourselves whether the evil around us still hurts us or whether we have grown used to it. God sees those who are grieved by sin and cares for them. We can pray for our family, our church, and our community with a sensitive heart.
exp.8:7:
Ezekiel reports that, while the executioners were doing their work, he was left alone. He fell face down on the ground and cried out to God. With grief he asks whether God is going to destroy all the remnant of Israel by pouring out his fury on Jerusalem.

God has shown Ezekiel a judgment on Jerusalem for its idolatry and violence. Those who had the mark were protected. Ezekiel, who was both a prophet and a priest, speaks here as an intercessor for his people. God answers that the wickedness is great, since the people were saying that he did not see, but that he would not overlook their sin.

For today: when you see injustice or sin around you, do not stop at criticizing. Pray with grief and humility for your family, your church, and your country, trusting that God is just and that he also sees.
exp.8:8:
God answers Ezekiel's complaint. He says that the sin of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great. The land is full of bloodshed, that is, of violence and unjust killing, and the city is full of injustice, meaning the twisting of what is right. The people justified themselves by saying: "The Lord has forsaken the earth, and the Lord does not see."

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision where Jerusalem is judged. Ezekiel had just fallen face down, distressed, asking whether God would destroy all that remained of the people. God explains that the judgment is not arbitrary: the violence was widespread, and the people had abandoned faith in a God who sees and judges.

For today: it is dangerous to live as if God were not watching. When we think no one sees our choices, we can excuse wrongdoing. Remembering that God sees, and that he is also just and compassionate, invites us to live with honesty and to seek his forgiveness.
exp.9:0:
Ezekiel tells us that he looked again and saw, in the firmament or vault above the heads of the cherubims, something like a sapphire stone. It had the appearance of a throne. The firmament is that stretched-out vault, and the cherubims are heavenly beings who serve God and surround his presence.

The one speaking is the prophet Ezekiel, exiled in Babylon. He is seeing a vision of the glory of God, similar to the one in chapter 1. Here the throne appears just before God orders that burning coals be scattered over Jerusalem, as a sign of judgment for the sin of the people.

For today: God still sits on his throne, even when everything seems confused or unjust. This invites us to take him seriously, to live with reverence, and to trust that he governs with justice. Today you can pray, acknowledging his authority over your life.
exp.9:1:
He spoke to the man clothed in linen, and told him to go in between the wheels, under the cherub, and fill his hands with coals of fire from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city. He went in while Ezekiel watched.

Here God is the one speaking, in a vision Ezekiel receives among the exiles in Babylon. His glory is preparing to leave the temple, and the burning coals are an image of judgment on Jerusalem for its persistent sin. Scholars discuss exactly what the fire symbolizes, but the general message is clear: God acts with justice.

For today: God is holy and takes sin seriously, but he also warns us before he acts. Today we can respond to him with humility, acknowledge what we need to correct, and return to him without delay.
exp.9:2:
This verse describes a scene in Ezekiel's vision. The cherubim, heavenly beings who serve God, stood on the right side of the temple when the man clothed in linen went in. A cloud filled the inner court, that is, the inner courtyard.

Ezekiel speaks as a prophet, from exile in Babylon. God is about to judge Jerusalem for its sin, and the man clothed in linen is commanded to take burning coals and scatter them over the city. The cloud points to the holy presence of God. Scholars see it as a sign of his glory and also of his judgment.

For today: God is holy and deserves our reverence. Live with a sincere heart, and when you fail, return to Him in humility. His presence corrects us, but it also invites us to come back to Him.
exp.9:3:
Ezekiel 10:4 says that the glory of God, which had been above the cherub (a heavenly being that supports God's throne), moved toward the threshold of the temple. Then the house was filled with a cloud, and the court was full of the brightness of that glory.

Ezekiel, a prophet living in exile in Babylon, recounts a vision. God is preparing judgment against Jerusalem for its idolatry and sin. That his glory moves toward the threshold seems to indicate that God is beginning to withdraw from the temple, though some understand it as a preparation for judgment.

God is holy and deserves to be taken seriously. We cannot give him a place of decoration while we live in sin. Today we can ask him to cleanse our hearts so that his presence may remain with us.
exp.9:6:
It says that one of the cherubim reached out his hand toward the fire that was between them, took coals, and put them into the hands of the man clothed in linen. That man received them and went out.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he had among the exiles in Babylon. God had commanded the man clothed in linen to take fire to scatter over Jerusalem (10:2). This represents judgment for the sin of the people. Some scholars see here a symbol of purification, others of punishment; the text itself speaks of judgment upon the city.

For today: God is holy and acts with justice, but also with order and purpose. We can trust that none of his judgments is arbitrary. This invites us to live with reverence, to examine our hearts, and to turn to Him with sincerity.
exp.9:7:
This verse says that, under the wings of the cherubim, something resembling a man's hand could be seen. "Form" means shape or appearance. Ezekiel does not say it was a real hand, but that it had that form, and he uses it to describe what he saw in his vision.

Ezekiel, a prophet and priest exiled in Babylon, recounts a vision of the glory of God. God is about to display his judgment against Jerusalem, and that is why a man clothed in linen takes fire from among the cherubim. Many understand the hand as a sign that the heavenly beings act in obedience to God, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: God acts with order and purpose, even when we do not understand everything. Trust that he knows what he is doing, and offer him your hands to serve him in obedience.
exp.9:8:
Ezekiel says he saw four wheels beside the cherubim, one next to each of them. Their appearance shone like a precious stone, a term from older usage that many understand as a gem of golden or sea-green color, though it is not known for certain which stone was meant. The word "beryl" in the verse above refers to this same kind of stone.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, speaks from exile in Babylon. He is seeing a vision in which the glory of God is preparing to leave the temple in Jerusalem because of the people's sin. The wheels and the cherubim recall the vision of chapter 1, where God appears in motion and with complete freedom.

For today: God is not confined to one place or to our circumstances. Even when everything seems lost or distant, he still rules and is present. Today you can trust that he is with you, and live with reverence, never taking his presence for granted.
exp.9:9:
This verse describes how the four wheels beside the cherubim looked. All four had the same form, and each one seemed to be set crosswise in the middle of another, like a wheel within a wheel. Many understand that this is how they could move in any direction without having to turn.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting what he saw in a vision from God. He was exiled in Babylon with his people. In this scene, the glory of God is getting ready to leave the temple in Jerusalem because of the people's sin. The exact meaning of the wheels is understood in several ways.

For today: even when it sometimes feels like everything is moving without direction, God is not limited or bound to one place. He sees everything, moves with perfect order, and continues to govern. Trust Him and seek His presence wherever you are.
exp.9:10:
It says that the creatures with wheels moved in any of the four directions, forward, backward, or to the sides, without needing to turn. Wherever the head went, the one at the front, the others followed it.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who was in exile in Babylon, speaks here. He tells again the vision of God's throne, which he had already described in chapter 1. Here he sees it in the temple, when God's glory is about to leave Jerusalem because of the people's sin. The image shows order, unity, and free movement. Interpreters understand it in several ways, but almost all see in it the power and presence of God.

God is not bound to a place or to our plans. You can trust that He goes with you and guides you, even when the direction changes suddenly.
exp.9:13:
Every living being that Ezekiel saw had four faces: the first was the face of a cherub, the second the face of a man, the third the face of a lion, and the fourth the face of an eagle. A cherub is a heavenly being who serves God and guards his holiness.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest and prophet who was living in exile in Babylon. He describes a vision of the glory of God, which leaves the temple in Jerusalem because of the sin of the people. In Ezekiel 1:10 the first face is the face of an ox, not of a cherub. Scholars explain that difference in several ways, and there is no certain answer.

For today: God is not confined to one place. His glory moved with his people, even in exile. If you feel far from everything, remember that God can find you wherever you are. Seek him with humility and reverence.
exp.9:15:
This verse says that the wheels moved together with the cherubim. When they walked, the wheels went beside them. When they lifted their wings to rise from the earth, the wheels did not turn away from them. Everything moved in perfect harmony.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting a vision. He is among the exiles in Babylon, and he sees the glory of God leaving the temple in Jerusalem because of the sin of the people. Ezekiel recognizes that these beings are the same ones he saw by the river Chebar. The next verse explains that the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.

For today: God is not bound to one place, and his direction is perfect and coordinated. We can trust that he continues to work even when everything seems lost. Seek to move in step with his guidance.
exp.9:18:
This verse says that the cherubim lifted their wings and rose from the ground while Ezekiel watched. The wheels moved along with them. They stopped at the entrance of the east gate of the temple, and the glory of God was over them.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who was exiled in Babylon, speaks here. He is seeing in a vision how the presence of God is leaving the temple in Jerusalem because of the sin of the people. This departure is a judgment, but it also shows that God is not bound to a building. Later, the glory stops at the east gate, and other passages speak of its return.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he does not abandon his own forever. We can examine our hearts, turn back to him with sincerity, and remember that his presence goes with us wherever we are.
exp.9:20:
It says that each of the cherubim had four faces, four wings, and something resembling human hands under the wings. The cherubim are heavenly beings who serve God and accompany his presence.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting a vision. He sees the glory of God leaving the temple in Jerusalem, because the people had fallen into idolatry. Ezekiel recognizes that these are the same beings he had seen earlier by the river Chebar. The exact meaning of the four faces is interpreted in several ways, and the Bible does not fully explain it here.

For today: God is holy and above all things, but he is also present and attentive. Today we can take his presence seriously, live with reverence, and not give anything else the place that belongs to him alone.
exp.10:15:
God tells Ezekiel to announce to the exiles: although He Himself sent them far away, among the nations and through many lands, He will be with them as a little sanctuary in the places where they arrive. A sanctuary is a place where one is near to God. Some understand that God Himself would be their refuge; others, that He would be a place of worship in place of the temple. The verse allows both ideas.

Ezekiel is among the exiles in Babylon. Those who stayed in Jerusalem looked down on them and said that the land belonged to them alone. God answers with comfort: the exiles have not been abandoned, and later He promises to gather them and bring them back to their land.

For today: even if you feel far from your home, your church, or your safe place, God does not depend on a location to be with you. Seek Him in prayer right where you are.
exp.10:17:
This verse says that the Israelites would return to their land and there remove all their detestable things and all their abominations. These are old words for speaking of the idols and the impure practices that had defiled their worship of God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people live in exile in Babylon. Earlier, in Jerusalem, the city had become filled with idolatry. Even so, God promises to gather them, give them back the land, and be with them as a little sanctuary in the place of exile. The next verse shows that the cleansing would not be only outward, for God would give them a new heart.

For today: God does not only want us to leave behind what separates us from Him, but also wants to change us from within. You can ask Him to show you what things have taken His place in your life, and trust that He helps you let them go and gives you a heart that is sensitive to Him.
exp.10:19:
This verse says that God wants to give his people a new heart so that they will live according to what he commands. "Statutes" and "ordinances" are his commands and his just decisions. "Keep" means that they put them into practice. At the end appears the central promise of the covenant: "they shall be my people, and I will be their God," a relationship of belonging and closeness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Many in Jerusalem had filled themselves with idolatry. Even so, God promises to gather the scattered, to cleanse them, and to give them a soft heart, not one of stone. Obedience is the fruit of that inner change, not the starting point.

For today: instead of obeying only by your own effort, ask God to transform your heart. Pray sincerely and let his Word shape you from within.
exp.10:20:
This verse says that there are people whose heart goes after what their unclean desires want and their detestable practices. God says that He will bring their way down on their own heads, meaning they will receive the consequences of what they have chosen.

God Himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, to the people of Jerusalem shortly before the city fell. Just before this, He promises one group a new and tender heart. Here He contrasts them with those who remain attached to idolatry. Right after this, the glory of God leaves the city.

For today: ask God to heal your heart and do not let yourself be carried away by what only pleases you. What we sow with our decisions, sooner or later we reap.
exp.10:21:
The cherubim, heavenly beings who support God's throne, lifted up their wings. The wheels beside them moved as well. Above everything was the glory of God, that is, his visible and majestic presence.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here, recounting a vision he received among the exiles in Babylon. God shows him that his presence is departing from Jerusalem because of the people's idolatry. Even so, God first promises a renewed people who will walk in his commands. Scholars agree that the departure is a judgment, but they also see that God is not bound to a temple.

For today: God is not limited to one place, but he invites us to live close to him with an obedient heart. Ask him today to remove whatever pulls you away from him.
exp.10:23:
Afterwards the Spirit lifted Ezekiel up and brought him back, in a vision given by the Spirit of God, to the exiles in Chaldea. The phrase about those carried away refers to people taken into exile. The phrase meaning he was brought back again is rendered in the verse as "brought me in a vision by the Spirit of God into Chaldea." When it ended, the vision left him.

Ezekiel was a priest and a prophet, and he lived as an exile in Babylon. In the vision, God took him to Jerusalem and showed him the sins of the people and the judgment that was coming. Then he saw the glory of God leave the city and stop on the mountain to the east. Now the vision ends, and Ezekiel returns to his fellow countrymen. According to the next verse, he told them everything God had shown him.

For today: what God shows us in his Word is not only to be kept to ourselves, but to be shared with humility and faithfulness, even when the message is difficult to say or to hear.
exp.10:24:
This verse says that Ezekiel told the exiles, the people who had been carried away and were living in Babylon, all the things that God had shown him in the vision. The name of God is the LORD, and the exiles are the Jews who had been taken away into captivity.

Ezekiel speaks here as a prophet and priest who was himself in exile. In the vision he saw the glory of God leave Jerusalem because of the people's sin. When the vision ended, he returned to his fellow exiles and faithfully passed on the message, even though it was hard to hear. Some believe this also pointed ahead to the hope that God would remain with the exiles.

For today: when God teaches us something in his Word, we should share it honestly and with love, adding nothing and taking nothing away. Let us speak faithfully, even when the message is not easy.
exp.11:1:
God tells Ezekiel that he lives in the middle of a rebellious people. They have eyes, but they do not see; they have ears, but they do not hear. It is not that they are blind or deaf in body, but that they refuse to understand and to obey.

The Lord speaks, and Ezekiel is his prophet among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. God prepares him for a sign: he will act out a departure in front of everyone, so that they may see with their own eyes what is coming. God holds on to the hope that they might take notice, although he knows how hard their hearts are.

For today: we can hear the Bible many times and still not change. Ask God for a willing heart, and when you understand something of his Word, obey it today in a concrete action.
exp.11:4:
God tells Ezekiel that, while the people watch him, he is to dig a hole through the wall of his house and go out through it. The word "dig through" means to break open or make a hole. It is an instruction for Ezekiel to act like someone who leaves his house secretly.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. God asks for these actions as a visible sign, since the people were a rebellious house and did not want to listen. Through them he announced that the inhabitants of Jerusalem would be taken into exile. Many understand that Ezekiel represented the people fleeing from the city.

For today: God takes seriously reaching our hearts, even through unusual methods. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are listening to his voice with humility, or whether we are hardening ourselves against what he shows us through his Word.
exp.11:5:
God tells Ezekiel that, while the people watch him, he is to load his belongings onto his shoulders and go out at night. He must cover his face so that he cannot see the ground. His belongings are his baggage or luggage, and his act is meant as a sign or example for the people.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who was living among the exiles in Babylon. The Israelites refused to believe that Jerusalem would be judged. God uses this visible action, like a prophetic drama, to show that the king and the people would go into exile. Many understand that the covered face shows shame and the loss of their land, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: do not ignore God's warnings just because you do not like them or they seem distant. Listen to His Word with humility and respond in time, while there is still an opportunity to return to Him.
exp.11:8:
God speaks to Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man", that is, a simple human being. He asks whether the people of Israel, whom he describes as a rebellious house, have asked him what he was doing.

Ezekiel had just acted out, in plain view of everyone, a person going into exile: he carried out his belongings by day, and at night he dug a hole through the wall. The people were curious, and God uses that question to explain the message to them: Jerusalem and its prince would be taken captive. God speaks this way because he wanted them to understand the consequences of their rebellion.

For today: when God shows us something clearly, let us not take it merely as curiosity. Let us ask what he wants to change in us, and respond with humility and obedience.
exp.11:11:
He says the prince of Jerusalem will be carried on his shoulder, that is, borne upon the shoulders, and will go out in the dark. They will make an opening in the wall to take him out secretly. He will cover his face so that he does not see the ground he is leaving.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Ezekiel had acted out the flight and the exile with his own actions. God warns that the ruler will try to escape from Jerusalem, but he will not succeed. Many understand this to refer to King Zedekiah, and the following passages show that he would be captured and taken to Babylon.

For today: we cannot hide our decisions or escape the consequences through cunning. It is better to listen to God humbly and in time, to trust Him and obey Him, rather than depending on our own plans.
exp.11:12:
God says he will catch the prince like an animal in a net. The word for the net's trap is not used here; the verse simply speaks of the net. He will be brought to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans, but he will not see it, and there he will die.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who was living in exile among the captives. He acted out the exile that was coming upon Jerusalem. Nearly everyone understands the prince to be King Zedekiah. According to 2 Kings 25, he was captured, had his eyes put out, and was taken to Babylon. In this way what was said came true, that he would not see it.

For today: God's warnings are serious, but they aim to bring us to recognize him. It is not wise to trust our own plans when God calls us to obey. Today you can ask him to help you listen to him in time.
exp.11:15:
God says that from the judgment coming on Jerusalem, he will leave a few people alive. They will be spared from the sword, from famine, and from plague.
