These survivors will tell, among the nations where they go, all the wicked deeds of his people, that is, their serious sins, above all their idolatry. In this way they will come to know that God is the Lord.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Before the fall of Jerusalem, God announces the fate of the king and his people, who will be scattered. Even in judgment, God leaves a group that bears witness to the truth.

For today: when we honestly acknowledge our mistakes, without hiding them, we make room for God to correct us and teach us. We can ask him for the courage to admit our failures and learn from them.
exp.11:16:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel once again. "Moreover the word of the Lord came to me, saying" means that a message from the Lord came to him. It is the phrase the prophet uses to introduce a new message. What God will say comes in the following verses.

Here speaks Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. God uses him to warn the people that Jerusalem will be judged. Earlier, God said that some would survive and would recognize who He is. Now He gives Ezekiel a new sign: to eat and drink with trembling, to show the fear that would come upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

For today: God still speaks, above all through His Word. Before beginning the day, take a moment to read the Bible and ask Him to speak to you, with a heart ready to listen and obey.
exp.11:17:
God tells Ezekiel to eat his bread trembling and drink his water with shaking and anxiety. That is, he must eat and drink like someone who is afraid.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. This action is a visible sign, a message acted out. As the verses that follow explain, it represented how the inhabitants of Jerusalem would eat in fear when judgment came and the land was left desolate because of the violence of its people. God wanted them to understand the consequences of their wickedness.

Today we can remember that God speaks in earnest, but also that he warns so that we will turn back to him. Ask yourself: is there something God is pointing out to me that I have ignored? Answer him today with humility and obedience.
exp.11:21:
God speaks to Ezekiel and asks him about a popular saying that was going around in Israel. The people were saying, "The days pass and no vision will be fulfilled." A saying is a common expression, and a vision refers to the messages God gave through his prophets. It was a way of mocking the warnings.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people saw that the judgment announced was taking a long time, and they concluded it would never come. With that excuse, they ignored the call to turn back to God. That is why the Lord says he will put an end to that saying, because his word will indeed be fulfilled.

For today: when God's response seems slow, do not mistake his patience for absence or indifference. His word still stands. Use the time to listen to him, correct your path, and trust that what he says is true.
exp.11:22:
God orders Ezekiel to tell the people that He is going to put an end to a popular saying: "The days go on and on, and no vision ever comes true." A saying like this is a phrase everyone repeats. Instead, God announces that the days are now near when every vision He has given will be fulfilled.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Many mocked his warnings and believed the judgment would take a long time or would never come. God answers that attitude of doubt and excuse.

For today: let us not take God's word lightly just because it seems slow to come true. His patience is an opportunity to turn back to Him, not a sign that His words don't matter. Today we can obey what we already know He asks of us.
exp.11:24:
God says that what He speaks will come to pass, and that there will be no more delay. He says it to Israel, whom He calls a rebellious house, and He assures them that everything will happen in their own days.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people were repeating a saying that the visions took a long time or never came to pass, and others thought they were meant for distant times. In this way they justified themselves for not taking the warning of judgment seriously. God answers that His word is neither empty nor far away.

For today: do not use God's patience as an excuse to put off your obedience. If you sense that God is speaking to you through His Word, respond today with humility, because He is faithful both in His promises and in His warnings.
exp.11:27:
This verse is God's answer to a mocking saying. God tells Ezekiel to tell the people that there will be no more delay: what God has spoken will be fulfilled.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people are in exile in Babylon. Some in Israel were saying that the warnings of judgment were for a very distant future, and so they felt at ease and had no need to change. God corrects that idea: his word is not a distant or doubtful matter. Scholars understand this as referring to the judgment on Jerusalem that was drawing near.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are putting off something God has already shown us, such as asking forgiveness, giving up a bad habit, or obeying clear guidance from his Word. Today is a good day to take that step with humility and trust that God does what he says.
exp.12:9:
They say that the false prophets deceived God's people by announcing "peace" when there was no peace. He uses an image: someone builds a weak wall, and others, instead of strengthening it, cover it with loose mortar, that is, a thin mixture that only makes it look good.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people live under the threat of judgment from Babylon. The false prophets were saying what the people wanted to hear, without calling them to repentance. That is why God rebukes them and announces that their wall of lies will fall in the storm.

For today: let us not look only for words that comfort us. Let us ask God to speak to us with truth, even when it corrects us, and build our lives on his Word and not on appearances.
exp.12:10:
He says God commands that warning be given to those who plaster it with loose mortar, that is, those who cover a weak wall with a thin layer of mud so it looks solid. That wall will fall. A heavy rain will come pouring down, along with hailstones and a stormy wind that will tear it down.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The false prophets said there was peace when there was no peace, and the people built a weak wall, the wall of false security. They decorated it with pleasant lies. God warns them that their deception will be exposed when judgment comes.

For today: it is not enough for something to look good on the outside. Ask yourself whether your life, your decisions, and what you believe are built on the truth of God, even when it hurts, and not on comforting words that only soothe for a moment.
exp.12:12:
God says he will send a very strong wind, a flood of rain, and hailstones. These storms represent his anger against something that has been badly built. The verse's wording about the wall being plastered over and the mixture being loose and unable to hold anything is explained by the picture of a wall covered with a thin coat of mud or plaster, and a weak mortar that holds nothing together.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. There were false prophets who announced peace when there was no peace. They were like people who cover a weak wall with paint so that it looks firm. God says that wall will fall, and it will be seen that the foundation was rotten.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are building our lives on the truth of God or only covering up what is wrong. Pretty words do not hold up a house; obedience and truth do. It is worth examining our foundation before the storms arrive.
exp.12:13:
God says that he will tear down the wall that the false prophets plastered over with loose mud, that is, with a weak mixture. When it falls, its foundation will be laid bare, and those who built it will be destroyed along with it. The result is that they will know that the Lord is God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a time of crisis for Jerusalem. Some prophets announced peace when there was no peace. They were like someone painting a fragile wall so that it looks solid. God shows that their lies will not survive judgment, like a storm that brings down what was badly built.

For today: it is not enough that something looks good on the outside. Let us examine whether our faith and our decisions are firm in God's truth, even when that truth is uncomfortable. Let us build on his Word, not on pleasant words.
exp.12:14:
God says he will finish pouring out his anger on the wall and on those who covered it with loose mortar, that is, with a weak mixture that holds nothing up. Covering a wall with a coat of plaster is what the mortar was for. In the end, God says that neither the wall nor its builders will continue to exist.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The wall represents the false security that the false prophets offered, since they promised peace to Jerusalem when there was no peace. They decorated a weak wall instead of calling the people to turn back to God. For that reason the judgment would come like a storm and would tear down everything.

For today: let us not build our lives on pretty but empty promises. Let us seek words that are true, even when they make us uncomfortable, and let us build on Christ and his word, which do withstand any storm.
exp.12:15:
This verse says that there were prophets in Israel who spoke about Jerusalem and claimed to have seen a vision of peace. But there was no peace. God declares that those messages were false. The phrase about prophesying concerning Jerusalem means that they spoke on God's behalf to the city. The part about seeing visions refers to what they claimed to have seen from God.

God speaks through Ezekiel shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. The false prophets reassured the people with pleasant words, like someone covering a cracked wall with loose mud. God says that wall will fall, because it had no firm foundation.

For today: let us seek God's truth, even when it is uncomfortable, and not only what makes us feel at ease. Let us compare what we hear with the Bible, and when we speak with others, let us try to be sincere and kind.
exp.12:17:
God speaks against certain women who claimed to be prophetesses. They sewed bands for the wrists and made head coverings, which were probably veils or head wraps for people of every height and age. With these they hunted people, that is, they trapped and manipulated others. God asks whether they do it to save their own lives, that is, to earn their living.

God speaks through Ezekiel, during the time when Jerusalem was falling. Many false prophets promised peace when judgment was coming. These women deceived the people with practices that seem like divination or magic. Scholars do not know exactly what those objects were like.

Today we should be wary of anyone who uses spiritual things to gain advantage or to control others. And if we speak on God's behalf, let it be with truth and not to gain money, fame, or power.
exp.12:18:
This verse is an accusation from God against certain women who claimed to speak on his behalf but were in reality making up messages. God says they dishonored him among his people for a few handfuls of barley and pieces of bread, that is, for small payments. With their lies they declared innocent people doomed to die, and promised life to guilty people who would not live. And the people believed them.

It is God, speaking through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. These women practiced forms of divination with cushions and veils, whose exact use is not known with certainty. God confronts them because they deceived his people to earn their living.

Today it invites us not to trade in the truth, and to examine what we hear in the light of the Bible, without being carried away by comfortable words.
exp.13:6:
It says that anyone at all, whether an Israelite or a foreigner living among them, who has turned away from God and set up idols in his heart, and then goes to the prophet to ask something on God's behalf, will receive a direct answer from the Lord himself. The stumbling block of their wickedness is what causes them to fall into sin. Turning away from following after me means ceasing to follow God.

God speaks through Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some elders of Israel came to consult him, but God saw that their hearts were still attached to idols. First he calls them to turn back. The answer he promises is not one of comfort but of judgment (in the verses that follow). Some scholars understand the phrase about answering by himself in this way.

Today: before seeking direction from God, let us examine what occupies first place in our heart. God invites us to return to him sincerely, not merely to ask him for advice.
exp.13:11:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel again.

The one speaking is God, and the prophet Ezekiel receives it. Earlier, God had spoken about false prophets and those who sought answers from idols, and about his desire that the people stop defiling themselves and be his again. Now God begins another teaching, addressed to Ezekiel and to the people exiled in Babylon.

For today: God still speaks, and we need to listen. We can set aside time each day to read the Bible carefully, asking God to speak to us through it.
exp.13:12:
God speaks to Ezekiel and tells him that when a land is unfaithful to him and rebels against him, God will act in judgment. The first quoted word is not in the verse, so I will simply state the idea: the land turns against God by breaking faith and betraying the trust between them. The second quoted phrase means taking away the means of support, the thing people rely on to eat. It speaks of famine and of the loss of people and animals.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel. Some of the people's leaders kept blaming others and trusting in idols. God warns that his judgment is not arbitrary but a response to persistent unfaithfulness. His aim, according to the previous verse, is that the people stop straying and return to belonging to him.

For today: let us not take for granted our daily bread or our peace, as if they were secure without God. Let us ask him for a faithful heart, and examine in what things we are placing our trust in place of him.
exp.13:15:
Noah, Daniel, and Job are said to be in the midst of a land under judgment, but even if they were there, they would save only their own lives. Neither their sons nor their daughters would be spared, and the land would be left in ruins. "Deliver" means save; "desolate" means destroyed; "men" are people; "as I live" is an oath of God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the leaders of Israel, who were in exile. Many believed that Jerusalem would be saved because of the righteous people within it. God answers that the judgment for the people's persistent wickedness would be so firm that not even the most righteous could save others by their righteousness. About the details of these three men, the Bible says nothing more here.

For today: do not live confident in the faith of others, such as your parents or your church. Seek God yourself, with repentance and sincere trust, and pray for your own.
exp.13:16:
It says God could send war ("sword") upon a land and command it to pass through. The result would be that people and animals die. Here "cut off" means to cut down or remove, the way a tree is cut down.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. God explains that Jerusalem had fallen so deep into idolatry that not even the prayers of righteous men like Noah, Daniel and Job would save the city. Those men would save only themselves. This is the third of four warnings: famine, wild beasts, sword and pestilence.

For today: the faith of others is valuable, but it does not replace my own. Each person must turn to God personally and not trust in the spiritual reputation of parents or friends. God also always invites us to return to Him.
exp.13:19:
It says that even if three men famous for their righteousness, Noah, Daniel and Job, were in a land, they could not save their sons and daughters. They would only save themselves by their righteousness.

God speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, to the exiles in Babylon. Some were thinking that Jerusalem would not be destroyed, because there were good people in it. God answers that the people's sin was so serious that neither the prayer nor the righteousness of others would prevent the judgment. Scholars debate who this Daniel was, but the text does not make it clear.

For today: faith is neither inherited nor lent. We can pray for our family, but each person must trust God for themselves. Take care of your own walk with Him.
exp.14:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man", that is, a simple human being. He asks him a question: in what way is the wood of the vine better than any other piece of wood? The branch of the vine has no special value for building anything among the trees of the forest.

Here the LORD speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God uses this comparison to speak about Jerusalem and its inhabitants. The vine is good for bearing fruit, not for making furniture or tools. If it does not bear fruit, it is almost worthless. The verses that follow develop this.

For today: our worth before God does not come from our strength or our appearance, but from remaining in him and bearing fruit. We can ask ourselves with humility: am I united to God, and do I live in a way that bears fruit?
exp.15:2:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to Jerusalem. He reminds her that her origin and her lineage come from the land of Canaan, and that her father was an Amorite and her mother a Hittite.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God wants to show the people their abominations. Many understand that this is not speaking of a literal biological inheritance, but that Jerusalem, before belonging to Israel, was a Canaanite city. In this way she is humbled, to remind her that everything she had was a gift from God.

For today: do not boast of what you are or what you have, as if it were your own merit. Remember where God took you from, and live with gratitude and humility.
exp.15:3:
This verse describes a newborn whom no one cared for. Her navel cord was not cut, she was not washed with water to clean her, she was not rubbed with salt (an ancient custom for caring for a baby), and she was not wrapped in swaddling cloths to keep her warm.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an abandoned girl to represent Jerusalem. Her origins, the Amorite and the Hittite, show that she had nothing that made her special. God wants the people to remember that everything they came to have was by his grace, not by their own merit.

For today: when you are tempted to feel proud or self-sufficient, remember that everything good in your life is a gift from God. That leads us to live with gratitude and humility, and also to care for those who today are alone and helpless.
exp.15:4:
It says that no one felt pity for this newborn girl. No one did for her the basic care of a baby, such as cutting the cord, washing her, or wrapping her in cloth. They left her lying out in the open field, meaning on the open ground, because her life mattered to no one. The phrase about her life being despised means that they looked down on her and scorned her.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem. He uses the image of an abandoned girl to show the humble and fragile beginnings of the people. By saying that their roots were Canaanite, He reminds them that they had no merit of their own. Everything they became came from God's mercy, which continues in the verses that follow.

For today: if you have ever felt ignored or worthless, remember that God looks on you with compassion. And if He has lifted you up, respond with gratitude and humility, never forgetting where He brought you from.
exp.15:6:
It says that God made Jerusalem grow like a girl left abandoned: he multiplied her like the plants of the field, made her grow, and made her beautiful. Even so, she was still bare and exposed, that is, without covering or dignity of her own, still in need. The phrase about coming to adornment speaks of reaching maturity, and the phrase about her breasts growing shows that she was already a young woman.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an abandoned baby, whom He rescues, to remind Jerusalem of her humble origin and the grace she received. Then He covers her and makes a covenant with her. Many understand that the account sets up an accusation about her unfaithfulness.

For today: do not forget where God took you from. Everything good you have is His gift, so respond with gratitude and faithfulness, not with pride.
exp.15:8:
He says that God washed the young woman with water and removed the blood that was on her. Then he anointed her with oil. The word "blood" here refers to the filth of her birth described earlier in the chapter. The verb used in the original, which means to anoint or to perfume, was a way of caring for someone and honoring them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an abandoned girl whom He rescues, cares for, and takes as a wife. That girl represents Jerusalem and the people of Israel. God reminds them how much He loved them and how greatly He favored them, to show how serious their unfaithfulness is, which is denounced later on.

For today: nothing good we have came from ourselves. God cleansed us and cared for us when we could not do it alone. Today you can thank Him for one specific way He has cared for you, and respond to Him with faithfulness and gratitude.
exp.15:9:
God says that he clothed the woman in fine garments: embroidered cloth, footwear of leather, and linen and silk. The leather he mentions is uncertain. Some think it was a fine, strong hide, and it is not known for sure what animal it came from. The same is true of the fine cloth in the verse, which may have been a fine fabric.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He describes Jerusalem as an abandoned girl whom he rescued, cared for, and took as his wife. The clothing shows his care and generosity. Later in the chapter, it shows how she forgot that love and was unfaithful to him.

Today we can remember that all the good we have comes from God's grace, not from our own merits. Ask yourself: what has God done for me? Respond to him with gratitude, humility, and faithfulness.
exp.15:11:
It says that God, like someone caring for a beloved person, adorned her with jewels. He put a ring or jewel on her nose, earrings in her ears, and a beautiful crown on her head. The jewels and earrings are the ornaments mentioned in the verse, and the crown is the royal band worn on the head.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an abandoned girl whom He found, cared for, and helped grow up, and with whom He later made a covenant, as in a marriage. That woman represents Jerusalem, that is, God's people. The passage first shows how much He gave them, and then points to their unfaithfulness. What they had came from God, not from themselves.

For today: remember that everything good we have is a gift from God. That leads us to live thankful and humble, and to be faithful to Him, instead of boasting or trusting in our own strength.
exp.15:12:
God says that he adorned Jerusalem with gold and silver, and with fine clothing of linen, silk, and embroidered work. She ate the best food: finest flour, honey, and oil. She was exceedingly beautiful and became like a queen.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the picture of an abandoned girl whom He took in, cared for, and clothed as a wife. It represents Jerusalem and her history with God. He reminds her of everything He gave her, because she later trusted in her beauty and went after other gods and alliances. The verses that follow say this plainly.

For today: all the good we have, whether talent, success, or blessings, is a gift from God. Remembering this keeps us grateful and humble, and keeps us from trusting in ourselves more than in Him.
exp.15:20:
It says that Jerusalem took the children who belonged to God, killed them as an offering, and gave them over to idols. The phrase about causing them to pass through the fire refers to burning them as a sacrifice. The part about giving them over speaks of the images of false gods. The words about her children show that God regarded them as His own.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He describes Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife who received everything from Him and used it to worship idols. Sacrificing children was a practice of neighboring peoples, and God condemns it harshly. His accusation aims to show how serious the people's sin was.

For today: everything we have, family, time, and talents, comes from God. Let us ask ourselves whether we are sacrificing what is most precious, such as the care of our children, for things that promise success or security but are not God.
exp.15:25:
This verse says that Jerusalem, pictured as an unfaithful woman, gave herself to the Egyptians, who were her neighbours. The image of being unfaithful is the picture of her infidelity. The phrase about the Egyptians being large and strong speaks of their physical vigour and abundance, and the wording is an old and very blunt one. The word "provoke" shows that by doing this more and more, she stirred up the anger of God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile. The whole of chapter 16 is a parable: God cared for Jerusalem from when she was young, but she left him. Here the unfaithfulness stands for the alliances with Egypt and for idolatry, in place of trusting in God.

For today: let us examine where we look for security apart from God, such as money, fame or other people. Let us return to trusting in him, who is faithful and forgives the one who comes back.
exp.15:26:
God says that he stretched out his hand against Jerusalem and took away part of what she needed each day. He handed her over to the daughters of the Philistines, who despised her. Even they were ashamed of her conduct. The phrase about her daily provision means her food and her daily sustenance. The way of her shameful living is a disgraceful life.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He describes Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife who went after other peoples and their idols. It is strong language, used as an image of idolatry and of alliances with pagan nations. God corrects his people because he loves them and wants them to return.

For today: when we look for security or satisfaction in things that are not God, they never fill us. If we feel that something is missing, we can ask ourselves what we have clung to and return to God with humility.
exp.15:40:
This verse says that the enemies of Jerusalem will burn her houses and carry out judgments against her in the sight of many women, meaning the other nations. The figure of a prostitute is used to speak of unfaithfulness. The verse says God will make her stop her unfaithful ways, and that she will no longer give gifts to her lovers.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he compares Jerusalem to a wife who, after being cared for and blessed by God, abandoned him to follow other gods and alliances. Scholars understand this judgment as a reference to the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. God does not speak lightly: he shows grief and justice before a very serious betrayal.

For today: let us not take God's blessings for granted. If we notice that our heart is going after other things, let us return to him quickly and with humility. His correction seeks to awaken us.
exp.15:41:
He says that when God finishes punishing, his anger will be satisfied. The phrase about his anger coming to rest means that his anger calms down. The phrase about his jealousy departing from you means that his jealousy, his pain at having been betrayed, is withdrawn. The phrase about no longer being angry means that he will no longer stay angry.

He speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem, whom he presents as an unfaithful woman who forgot the love and care he gave her in her youth. The image of a prostitute describes idolatry and alliances with other nations. The punishments announced speak of judgment through enemy peoples. Even so, the chapter ends further on with a promise of restoration.

For today: God grieves when we forget him, but his anger is not eternal. Today you can remember what he has done for you and return to him sincerely before seeking comfort in other things.
exp.15:46:
It says that Jerusalem did not merely follow the wickedness of her neighbors Samaria and Sodom. She went far beyond them. Walking in their ways means living the way they lived, and the practices God detests are the things He calls abominations. The sentence about it being a very little thing is ironic: copying their sin was already serious, but Jerusalem outdid them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter He compares Jerusalem to an unfaithful woman whom He cared for and loved. She responded with idolatry and alliances with other nations. By comparing her to Sodom, known for its wickedness, God wants to show the seriousness of her sin and call her to acknowledge it.

For today: the more we have received from God, the more responsible we are. Let us avoid comparing ourselves with others to feel better; rather, let us examine our own hearts with humility and return to God, who is merciful.
exp.15:47:
God swears by his own life, a very solemn oath, and says that Sodom, together with her dependent towns, did not sin as much as Jerusalem and her villages. It is a comparison that surprises and hurts. Here "sister" is used as a figure for cities related through their conduct.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. In this chapter he accuses Jerusalem of unfaithfulness, like a wife who abandons the one who cared for her. The following verses explain Sodom's sin: pride, plenty, comfort, and failing to help the poor. Jerusalem had received more light and yet did worse.

For today: let us not compare ourselves with others to feel righteous. God looks at how much we have received from him and how we respond. Let us ask him for a humble heart and open hands to help the needy.
exp.15:49:
It says that Sodom and her daughters (the nearby cities) became full of pride and did detestable things before God. The reference to becoming proud means they grew haughty, and the word for "abomination" is something God hates. The phrase about God taking them away as he saw good means that God removed them from the scene according to his just judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem. She thought herself better than others, but God shows her that her sin was even worse than Sodom's. The previous verse highlights pride, abundance without generosity, and failing to help the poor.

For today: when we have comfort and well-being, it is easy to forget those in need. Let us ask God for a humble and grateful heart, and this week let us look for one concrete way to help someone who needs it.
exp.15:52:
He says that God will bring back, that is, return or restore, the captives of three groups: Sodom with her daughters (her villages or nearby cities), Samaria with her daughters, and the captives of Jerusalem, to whom he is speaking. The captivity refers to the situations of ruin and slavery into which they had fallen.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he compares Jerusalem to an unfaithful woman who turned away from God and committed more wickedness than Samaria and Sodom. Before announcing restoration, he shows her her shame. Scholars understand in different ways how this promise would be fulfilled for Sodom, but it is clear that God promises mercy after judgment.

For today: do not compare yourself with others to make yourself feel better. Acknowledge your failures with humility, and trust that God, who corrects, also restores those who return to him.
exp.15:54:
God says that He will restore Sodom and Samaria, together with their daughters, to their former condition. He will do the same for Jerusalem and her daughters. Here "daughters" means the nearby cities and villages.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem, whom this chapter accuses of unfaithfulness, comparing her to a wife who betrayed her husband. Sodom and Samaria are called her "sisters," and Jerusalem turns out to be worse than they are. Scholars debate whether this restoration is literal or symbolic. Even so, punishment is not God's final word.

For today: when we honestly acknowledge our own failures, and not only those of others, God can restore us. We can draw near to Him with humility, trusting in His mercy.
exp.15:55:
It says that Judah (Jerusalem) did not even mention Sodom, her sister, while she was living in pride. The word "sister" in this sentence means a close relative, and "pride" here means arrogance or self-importance. Jerusalem thought itself better and did not want to speak about Sodom's fall.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he compares Jerusalem to an unfaithful wife who fell into idolatry and wickedness, even more than Sodom and Samaria. God reminds her of her pride so that she will feel shame and repent. Later he promises to restore her, so the message does not end only in judgment.

For today: when you feel that you are better than others, remember that all of us need the mercy of God. Before pointing out the faults of others, examine your own heart and ask God for humility.
exp.15:58:
God asks Jerusalem a serious question: should He treat her the way she treated Him? She despised the solemn promise she made to God, and she broke the covenant as if it meant nothing. God announces that there will be consequences for that unfaithfulness.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapter 16, God describes Jerusalem as a woman He cared for and made a covenant with, but who betrayed Him through idolatry and alliances with other nations. This verse connects the judgment with what follows: God will remember His covenant and offer an everlasting one.

For today: God takes promises seriously, and we should too. When we fail, we should not harden ourselves or despair, but return with humility, trusting that His mercy is greater than our failure.
exp.15:59:
It says that God will not forget the covenant he made with Jerusalem when she was young, that is, at the beginning of her history as a people. Although she broke it, God promises to establish with her a covenant that is eternal, without end. The word that is rendered as "everlasting" here is what the reader needs to understand, so it is enough to note that the covenant lasts forever.

The words are spoken by the Lord through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16, God describes Jerusalem as a woman he rescued and cared for, but who was unfaithful to him through idolatry. After announcing the punishment, God declares that his faithfulness is greater than her unfaithfulness. Many Christians see here a sign of the new covenant, though interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: even if you have failed, God does not reject you forever. Return to him with humility and trust in his faithfulness, not in your own.
exp.15:60:
It says that Jerusalem, the people of God, will remember her bad conduct and feel shame. On that day she will receive her other sisters, that is, other cities or peoples, both the greater and the lesser. God will give them to her as daughters, but not because Jerusalem has kept the covenant.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier he has compared Jerusalem to an unfaithful wife who broke the covenant. Even so, he promises to remember his covenant with her and to give her an everlasting one. Scholars understand in various ways who the sisters are (Samaria and Sodom, mentioned earlier), but all of them see here a restoration that comes from the grace of God.

For today: when we remember our failures, shame can lead us to repentance and not to despair. God restores us through his mercy, not through our merits. We can return to him with humility and gratitude.
exp.16:5:
It says that the seed that was planted grew and became a leafy vine, but a low one, not a tall one. Its branches leaned toward the eagle that had planted it, and its roots stayed beneath it. The new shoots of the vine are the tender growths that spring from it, and the branches that take root and produce new plants are the ones that spread its life further.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who presents a parable about two eagles and a vine. Almost everyone understands that the first eagle represents Babylon, and that the vine is Judah under the king whom Babylon placed on the throne. Its growth was humble and dependent. God uses this image to show the need to remain faithful to a covenant, and the foolishness of Judah in seeking help from Egypt.

Today we can ask ourselves on whom we truly depend. Growing under God's blessing is good, but seeking security in human powers, instead of trusting in Him and keeping what has been promised, leaves us fragile.
exp.16:8:
God tells Ezekiel to ask whether the vine will prosper. The answer is no: its roots will be pulled up, its fruit cut off, and all its fresh leaves will wither. Without great power or many people, it will be plucked up by the roots.

God speaks through Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon, using a parable. The vine represents King Zedekiah of Judah, who broke his covenant with Babylon and sought help from Egypt, the other great eagle. Many interpreters see in this a judgment for that disloyalty.

For today: trusting in allies, money, or human plans rather than in God may seem safe, but it does not give lasting life. Ask yourself today where you are resting your roots, and bring it to God in prayer.
exp.16:9:
It says the vine was planted in good soil, yet God asks whether it will prosper. The answer is no: the east wind, a hot, dry wind from the desert, will dry it up completely. Even in the furrows where it had grown green, it will wither.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Israel, who was in exile. This is a parable: the vine represents Judah and its king Zedekiah, who rebelled against Babylon. As the following verses say, the king of Babylon had already taken the earlier king and his officials captive. God shows that trusting in human alliances and breaking the covenant would not bring success.

Being in a good place does not guarantee a fruitful life if we turn away from God. Today we can ask ourselves what we trust more: our circumstances or the Lord.
exp.16:11:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to the rebellious people of Judah. He asks them whether they do not understand the meaning of the parable of the eagles and the vine that Ezekiel has just told. Then he gives them the verse: the king of Babylon (Nebuchadnezzar) came to Jerusalem, took its king and its princes, and led them away as captives to Babylon.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. The people did not want to accept that their situation was the consequence of their disobedience, and God explains clearly what had happened and why. This took place when King Jehoiachin was taken captive, around 597 B.C.

For today: sometimes God speaks to us plainly, and we do not want to understand. We can ask him for humility to recognize our mistakes, to listen to his correction, and to trust him again, instead of hardening our hearts.
exp.16:13:
It says that Babylon left the kingdom of Judah brought low and unable to lift itself up. But there was a way out: if it kept the covenant it had made, it could remain standing under it. The words "brought low" and "covenant" are not used in the verse above, so I will not explain them here.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar carried off King Jehoiachin and placed Zedekiah on the throne, and Zedekiah swore loyalty. Afterward Zedekiah rebelled and sought help from Egypt. God holds him to account because he broke an oath made in God's name. Some understand this as a call to humility under punishment.

For today: keeping one's word is a serious matter before God. Even when we go through times of humiliation, faithfulness and humility are worth more than seeking shortcuts or misplaced support.
exp.16:15:
God says, with an oath by his own life, that the king of Judah will die in Babylon. There lived the king who had placed him on the throne. This king despised his oath and broke the covenant he had made with him. "Despised" means he took it lightly, without giving it any value.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had placed Zedekiah on the throne, and Zedekiah pledged loyalty before God. Afterward he rebelled and sought help from Egypt. God regards this as a serious offense, because the oath had been made in his name. Scholars often identify the king with Zedekiah.

For today: our word matters to God. Strive to keep your promises, in marriage, work, or agreements, even when it costs you. And when you fail, turn to God with humility instead of looking for ways out on your own.
exp.16:16:
This verse says that the pharaoh of Egypt will not truly help the king of Judah in the war. Even with a great army and many people, he will not save him when Babylon raises mounds and builds siege towers to cut off many lives.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The king of Judah, Zedekiah, had sworn loyalty to Babylon, but he rebelled and asked Egypt for help. God calls him to account because he broke an oath made in God's name. Some scholars believe the passage also shows the uselessness of trusting in human powers.

For today: before seeking support in money, influence, or powerful people, ask yourself whether you are being faithful to your word and to God. Keeping what you have promised and trusting in Him gives more security than any army.
exp.16:21:
It says that God himself will take a tender branch from the top of a tall cedar and plant it on a high and lofty mountain. The tender top of the tree is what the verse calls the shoot taken from its highest twigs, and the new growth is the fresh sprouts. God does not leave the future in the hands of human kings; he acts himself.

The Lord speaks through Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Before this, King Zedekiah rebelled and was judged. Now God promises a new beginning. Many Christians see here a promise of the Messiah, a descendant of David, although the text speaks directly of the restoration of Israel.

For today: when you feel that everything is over, remember that God can bring life out of what seems cut off. Trust that he knows how to begin again.
exp.16:22:
God says he will plant a tender shoot on the high mountain of Israel. That young branch will grow, put out boughs, bear fruit, and become a magnificent cedar. Birds of every kind will make their home in its shade.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier, he told a parable about kings and an eagle, and he announced judgment on Judah. Now he offers hope: God himself will raise up something new. Many Christians see here a prophecy of the Messiah, Jesus, and his kingdom that gives shelter to all peoples. Others see it first as a promise of restoration for Israel. Both readings have been held.

When everything seems lost, God can begin something small and make it grow. Trust him, even if today you see only a weak shoot in your life or your family.
exp.16:23:
God says that all the trees of the field, that is, all the nations and peoples, will recognize that He is the Lord. He brings down the one who is very high and lifts up the one who is low. He dries up the green tree and makes the dry tree flourish. He ends by saying that what He has said, He will do.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel at a time when Judah was in crisis and many were in exile in Babylon. The kings of Judah had trusted in political alliances and not in God. God promises to take a tender shoot from a cedar and plant it on the high mountain of Israel. Many Christians see here a hope that points to the Messiah, although the text speaks first of the restoration of God's people.

For today: even if you feel small or dry inside, God can give you new life. Trust in Him, not in your own strength, and do not think of yourself as more than you are.
exp.17:1:
God asks the people what they mean by a saying they kept repeating in Israel. They said, "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge." With this saying they were suggesting that the children were paying for the sins of their parents.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were suffering and used the saying to complain, as if the punishment were unfair and they bore no responsibility. God corrects that idea and, in the verses that follow, teaches that each person answers for their own life.

For today: do not use your family's past as an excuse, and do not sink into guilt over other people's mistakes. Recognize your own steps, return to God with sincerity, and trust that He offers you a new beginning.
exp.17:2:
God swears by his own life, something very solemn, and says that the people will no longer use a popular saying: "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge." Sour grapes are unripe green grapes, and having your teeth set on edge is that unpleasant sensation in the teeth. With that saying they meant that the children paid for their parents' sins.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, when part of the people were living in exile in Babylon. Some used the saying to claim that their suffering was the fault of earlier generations and not their own. God corrects that excuse and teaches that each person answers for their own decisions. The verses that follow make this clear.

For today: do not use your family's past as an excuse for not changing, and do not condemn yourself for other people's mistakes. Recognize your own responsibility, ask God for forgiveness, and walk with Him from today.
exp.17:4:
This verse begins to describe a righteous man. A "righteous" person is one who lives well before God. Acting with uprightness and treating others in a fair and honest way is what the verse points to. The sentence is left open, because the description continues in the verses that follow.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was in exile in Babylon. The people kept repeating a saying that blamed their parents for their suffering. God answers that every person belongs to him and answers for himself. So he gives concrete examples of a righteous life: not following idols, not oppressing others, and helping the poor.

For today: God's justice shows up in everyday life. This week, look for one concrete act of honesty or generosity, such as paying what is fair, keeping your word, or sharing your food with someone in need.
exp.17:6:
The man who is righteous does not oppress anyone. If someone gave him something as security for a debt, he returns it to the debtor. He does not commit robbery, but gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with clothing.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people are in exile in Babylon. The people were saying that they suffered for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person is responsible for his or her own life, and he describes how someone who is righteous lives. This verse is part of that list: righteousness includes honest and compassionate treatment of others.

For today: look this week for someone you can help in a concrete way, with food, clothing, or your time. And check whether you should return anything or pay what you owe. Obeying God also shows in how we treat those in need.
exp.17:7:
He says that the righteous man does not lend money at interest and does not take any profit from it. Those old words refer to charging abusive interest, especially to a needy brother. He also withdraws his hand from wickedness, that is, he turns away from doing evil. And "executes true judgment between man and man": he settles disputes with justice and honesty, without favoring anyone.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person is accountable for his own life. Here he describes how a righteous person lives: it is not merely keeping rituals, but treating one's neighbor well.

For today: review how you handle money and agreements. If you lend, do not take advantage of others' need. If you have to decide something between people, be just and honest, even when no one is watching.
exp.17:9:
This verse begins a second example. Earlier, a righteous man who lives well was described. Now it says: if that man has a son who is a robber, a shedder of blood (that is, a murderer), or who does any of the wicked things that follow, that son will be judged for his own actions.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. They were repeating a saying: "the fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge." With it they claimed they were suffering for their parents' sins. God answers that each person is accountable for his own life.

For today: do not use your family past as an excuse, and do not lean on your parents' faith. Today you can choose to obey God, and He receives you with mercy.
exp.17:11:
He oppresses the poor and needy, commits robbery, and does not return the pledge (something the poor person left as security for a loan). He also looks with longing at idols and does detestable things in God's sight.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were saying they were suffering for the sins of their fathers. God answers with an example of three generations: a righteous father, a wicked son, and a grandson who decides not to follow that evil path. Each person answers to God for their own choices.

For today: do not use your family past or your circumstances as an excuse. Today you can choose to treat with justice and kindness those who have less than you, and to break with bad examples.
exp.17:20:
If a wicked person turns away from all the sins they have committed, keeps everything God commands, and acts with justice and righteousness, they will surely live and not die.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people complained that they were suffering for the sins of their ancestors. God answers that each person is responsible for their own life, and that the way of repentance is always open. Many understand that "live" here speaks of life and favor before God.

For today: you are not condemned by your past or by the mistakes of your family. If you turn back to God today, you can start over, and He welcomes you gladly.
exp.17:30:
God tells the people to cast away all the wrongs they have committed, the ones by which they rebelled against Him. He asks them to make themselves a new heart and a new spirit, that is, a life renewed from the inside. And he ends with a painful question: why will you die, house of Israel?

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Some of the people, in exile, were saying that the way of the Lord was not fair, meaning that God was unjust. He answers that each person will answer for their own actions, and he invites them to turn back to Him. At the end he makes clear that he does not desire the death of anyone.

For today: if there is something in your life that pulls you away from God, do not hide it or excuse it. Acknowledge it, leave it behind, and ask God to renew your heart. He offers this because He wants you to live.
exp.18:0:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel: "Take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel." A lamentation is a sad song, the kind that was sung at funerals. To "take up" a lamentation means to begin singing it aloud. The princes are the kings or rulers of Judah.

The speaker is God, and he gives the task to Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. What follows is a poem with images of lions and a lioness. Many scholars think it refers to the last kings of Judah and their fall, though not all agree on exactly which kings are meant. The poem does not celebrate; it mourns a loss.

For today: God grieves over the fall of leaders, even when they have failed. We can pray and lament with sincere sadness, without mocking, for leaders who go wrong, and ask God to give us just rulers.
exp.18:4:
This verse tells how the lioness, seeing that her hope in her first whelp had been lost, chose another of her whelps and made him a strong young lion. The phrase "made him a young lion" means that she set him up as a young lion, that is, as a king. The idea of a long wait is shown by her long time of waiting.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over the princes of Israel. The lioness is usually understood as the nation or the mother of the royal line of Judah, and the whelps as kings, such as Jehoahaz, who was taken to Egypt. The second whelp is identified in several ways: as Jehoiakim or Zedekiah. Scholars do not agree on this.

When a hope falls apart, it is wise to seek God's direction before placing trust in another human solution. A new plan made only on impulse can repeat the same mistakes.
exp.18:5:
He walked among the lions, that is, among the other powerful kings and nations. He became a strong young lion, he learned to catch and seize prey (he learned to hunt and trap victims), and he devoured men (he destroyed and abused people).

God speaks through Ezekiel and asks him to make a lament over the princes of Israel. The lioness represents Judah or its royal line, and the cubs represent its kings. Many believe this second cub is Jehoiachin or Jehoiakim, but this is not certain; some think of Zedekiah. The clear point is that he ruled with violence and fell.

Whoever holds power can learn to use it to harm. Today we can ask God to teach us to lead, work, and direct with justice and compassion, not with abuse.
exp.18:8:
They caught this young lion, put him in a cage with chains, and brought him before the king of Babylon. They shut him up in strongholds, that is, in well-guarded places, so that his roar would no longer be heard on the mountains of Israel.

God speaks through Ezekiel and composes a lament about the princes of Israel, using the image of lions. Many understand that it refers to kings of Judah taken captive, such as Jehoahaz, who was taken to Egypt, or Jehoiachin, who was taken to Babylon. Interpreters do not fully agree on which king is described here. The central message is that the pride and violence of the rulers ended in downfall.

For today: power and fame are not secure forever. If you have authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, use it with humility and justice, and remember that you answer to God.
exp.19:0:
It says that in the seventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day, certain leaders of the people of Israel came to inquire of the Lord. They sat before Ezekiel to hear what God would say.

Ezekiel speaks here as a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The "seventh year" is usually understood as the seventh year since the exile of King Jehoiachin, that is, around 591 B.C. The elders come looking for a word from God, but the following verse shows that God does not answer them as they hoped, because their hearts were not sincere.

For today: it is not enough to draw near to God in appearance. Before asking Him for direction, we should examine whether we are truly willing to obey Him. He looks for an honest heart, not merely a religious visit.
exp.19:1:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel. The phrase "the word of the Lord came to me" is the way the prophet announces that what follows is not his own ideas but a message received from God. It is how he signals that the words that come next are a message from God.

Ezekiel was among the exiles in Babylon. Some elders of Israel came to seek the Lord, that is, to ask for a word through the prophet, and they sat down in front of him. Before Ezekiel says anything to them, God speaks first. His answer will be surprising: he will not listen to them, because their hearts were not right.

For today: before asking something of God, it is good to examine the attitude with which we approach him. He desires a sincere heart willing to obey, not only words or rituals.
exp.19:8:
God says that, despite Israel's rebellion, he brought his people out of Egypt for the sake of his name, that is, for his honor and reputation. He did not want his name to be dishonored before the nations where the Israelites lived, since those nations had seen that he made himself known to his people.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to some elders of Israel who were consulting him. He reminds them of their history: from Egypt onward the people rebelled and followed idols. Even so, God acted out of faithfulness to his own name and his promise, not because of anything they had earned.

For today: our salvation rests on God's faithfulness, not on our good performance. Trust his grace, acknowledge your failures with humility, and live in such a way that his name is honored, not dishonored, by your conduct.
exp.19:10:
God says that, after bringing Israel out of Egypt, he gave them his ordinances and explained to them his rights, that is, his laws and righteous decrees. He promises that whoever keeps them will live by them, meaning they will have a good life under his care. The words "gave them" are the meaning of the phrase, and "made known to them" is what the same phrase means in this context.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who recalls the history of Israel. God rescued them for the sake of his name and led them into the wilderness. There he showed them how to live as his people. But the text goes on to say that they rebelled. Some understand "live" as a full life in this present world; others understand it also as spiritual life.

Today, God's instructions are not a burden but a path toward a healthy life. Ask yourself: what teaching from the Bible can I put into practice this week, trusting that God guides me for good?
exp.19:11:
God says that he also gave the Israelites his sabbaths. The sabbath would be a sign between him and them, a visible reminder of their relationship. His purpose was that they would know that the Lord is the one who sanctifies them, that is, the one who sets them apart as his people and makes them holy.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some leaders of Israel came to consult him, and he reminds them of their history: he brought them out of Egypt, gave them his law and the sabbath. But they rebelled and profaned the sabbaths, that is, they treated them as something common. Even so, God acted for the sake of his name and did not destroy them.

Today we can set apart a regular time to rest and remember that God sustains us and makes us his own. Resting is trusting that our life does not depend only on our own effort.
exp.19:12:
God says that Israel rebelled against him in the wilderness. They did not follow his statutes, they despised his judgments (his righteous rules), and they profaned his sabbaths, that is, they treated them as ordinary days. That is why God said he would pour out his fury to consume them, that is, to destroy them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel who are in exile. He reviews their history to show that the rebellion did not begin today, but from the time they left Egypt. God had given them his law so that they would live and know that he sanctifies them. But the next verse shows that, for the sake of his name, God did not destroy them.

For today: do not see God's commands as a burden, but as a path to life. Today you can set aside a time of rest to be with God and remember that he is the one who sustains you.
exp.19:17:
God says that, while the people were in the wilderness, he spoke to the second generation, the children. He asked them not to follow the customs and the rules of their parents, and not to make themselves unclean with their idols. "Ordinances" are rules or customs; "defile" means to become spiritually dirty.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The leaders of the people come to consult him, and God reminds them of their history: their parents rebelled in the wilderness, but God was patient and did not destroy them. Now he calls the children to choose another path, the path of obeying him.

For today: not everything we inherit is good. We can be thankful for the good in our family, but we can also examine, with humility, the harmful habits or customs that pass from generation to generation. With God's help, we can decide to walk differently and to follow his Word.
exp.19:18:
God presents himself as "the Lord your God", that is, the Lord who has a relationship with his people. He tells them to walk in his commands (his instructions), to keep his decrees (his just rules), and to do them, that is, to practice them and not only to hear them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel during the exile in Babylon. He reminds them of the history in the desert: he forgave the generation of their fathers and asked the next generation not to follow the idols and customs of those before them. Even so, the children also rebelled.

For today: God invites us to truly obey him, not only to know his Word. Today you can choose one clear command from the Bible, such as forgiving or being honest, and put it into practice, without copying without thinking what others do.
exp.19:19:
God asks his people to set the sabbaths apart as holy days, that is, days dedicated to him. The sabbath would be a sign between God and Israel, a reminder of the relationship they shared. To make something holy means to set it apart for sacred use. The Lord is God's name, the Lord himself.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel, during the exile in Babylon. He reminds them of what he told their ancestors in the desert, after bringing them out of Egypt. He asked for faithfulness and that they not follow idols. But they rebelled and profaned the sabbaths, and even so God showed patience for the sake of his name.

For today: set aside a regular time to rest and remember who God is. Turn off the noise, pray, give thanks, and trust that he sustains your life, not only your effort.
exp.19:20:
This verse says that the children of that generation, who came out of Egypt, also rebelled against God. They did not follow his ordinances (his commands), nor did they keep his rights (his righteous laws). Those laws gave life to whoever practiced them. They also profaned the sabbaths, that is, they treated them as common. For this reason God said he would pour out his wrath on them in the wilderness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel during the exile in Babylon. He recounts their history to show that their rebellion is not new. Even so, the following text says that God held back his hand for the sake of his name.

For today: obedience to God is not an empty burden but a path of life. Today you can ask him for help to obey him in something specific, trusting in his patience and his mercy.
exp.19:22:
It says that God, while the people were in the wilderness, lifted up his hand, that is, he made a solemn oath. He promised that, if they kept rebelling, he would scatter them among the nations. The word "scatter" in the verse refers to this: it means to spread something out, as grain is tossed in the air so the wind carries away the chaff.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes to the exiles in Babylon. God reviews the history of Israel to show that the rebellion did not begin then. From the wilderness, after leaving Egypt, the people despised his commands and turned to idols. The exile was no surprise: God had warned them of the consequences. Scholars debate how best to understand this passage, but it shows that God is just and also patient.

For today: God warns out of love because he wants us to live. If you feel that he is calling you to correct something, do not put it off; respond today with humility and simple obedience.
exp.19:23:
This verse explains why God decided to scatter Israel. The people did not keep his commandments, rejected his laws, and dishonored the day of rest, and their eyes went after the idols their ancestors had worshiped.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes among the exiles in Babylon. He reviews Israel's history to show them that their punishment was not unjust: from the wilderness onward, generation after generation repeated the rebellion. The verses that follow are difficult and have been understood in several ways; many think God handed them over to the consequences of their own choices.

For today: what we look at with persistence ends up guiding our hearts. We can ask God to help us fix our eyes on him and to take care over what things occupy our attention.
exp.19:24:
Here God says that, because Israel rejected his good laws, he gave them statutes that were not good, rules by which they could not live.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel, during the exile. He reminds them of their long history of rebellion, going back to the wilderness. The verse is hard, and it is interpreted in several ways: some believe God handed them over to the punishment of following pagan customs, such as sacrificing firstborn children; others think it refers to laws that showed the hardness of their hearts. God does not approve of those practices; the next verse says they were a defilement.

For today: when we turn our backs on what God says, we can end up tied to burdens that do not give life. Let us return to his Word with humility.
exp.19:29:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to the house of Israel. He asks them a question that sounds like a rebuke: are you not defiling yourselves in the same way your fathers did? Going after their abominations means being unfaithful to God, chasing after idols and detestable practices, the way a person betrays a spouse.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing the leaders of the people in exile. He reminds them that since they entered the promised land, they worshiped on the high places. The high places refers to the shrines on hilltops where they worshiped. God shows that the children were repeating the sins of their fathers, and yet they still wanted to consult him.

For today, it is worth asking ourselves what harmful customs we have inherited without questioning them. God invites us not to repeat what is wrong simply because it has always been done that way, but to turn back to him with sincerity.
exp.19:31:
He says God knows what Israel has in mind: wanting to be "like the nations," that is, to live like the pagan peoples who worshiped idols of wood and stone. But God declares that this shall not be. It will not happen; he will not allow it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to some leaders of Israel who were in exile in Babylon. They were still following idols, as their ancestors had, and yet they wanted to consult God. He rejects this double life and announces that, with a strong hand, he will reign over them and gather them together again.

For today: let us not copy what most people do just to fit in. It is worth asking ourselves which things are taking God's place in our hearts, and giving them over to him with sincerity.
exp.19:32:
God says, swearing by his own life, that he will indeed reign over his people. He will do it with a mighty hand (power), a stretched-out arm (decisive action), and fury poured out (his anger expressed with firmness). These are words that recall the exodus from Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the leaders of Israel, who were in exile. They wanted to be like the other nations and to serve idols of wood and stone. God answers that this plan will not succeed. He will not let them go: he will bring them out from among the peoples and confront them to correct them. His anger seeks to bring them back to himself.

For today: we cannot mix God with other gods, such as money or success. If he corrects us, it is not to destroy us, but because he loves us and wants to be our Lord. Today you can give him something that is pulling you away from him.
exp.19:36:
He says that God will make His people pass "under the rod" and will bring them into the bond of the covenant. Passing under the rod was an image of shepherds who counted and inspected the sheep one by one as they entered the sheepfold. The phrase about the bond of the covenant means the tie or obligation of the covenant, that is, the commitment between God and His people.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. Israel had rebelled and kept following idols. God promises to examine His people, separate out the rebels, and draw the faithful back into His covenant. Some understand the rod as discipline, others as the shepherd's counting; both ideas fit.

For today: God knows us one by one, and sometimes He corrects us to bring us back to Himself. We can ask Him to examine our hearts and sincerely renew our commitment to Him, setting aside whatever has taken His place.
exp.19:39:
God promises that one day all of Israel will worship him on his holy mountain, in the land he gave them. There he will receive them with favor and ask for their offerings, the firstfruits (the first and best of the harvest) and everything set apart, that is, dedicated to him.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to an exiled and rebellious people who mixed the worship of the Lord with idols. First he rebukes them and says he will separate out the rebels. Then he announces hope: he will gather his people and restore them, so that they worship him sincerely and it is shown that he is holy.

For today: God does not want divided worship but a whole heart. Think about what idol competes with him in your life, and give God the best of your time, your strength, and your possessions, trusting that his grace accepts you and restores you.
exp.19:43:
God says that his people will come to recognize who he is when he deals with them for the sake of his own name and not according to their wicked ways and corrupt deeds. In other words, Israel did not earn what God does for them. He acts out of his own reputation and faithfulness, which stand firm even when his people do not.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel. The chapter reviews the people's constant rebellion from the time of Egypt onward. Even so, God promises to bring them back to their land. There they will feel shame for their sins and understand that their restoration was an act of grace, not a reward.

For today: when you fail, remember that God treats you according to his faithful character and not according to your mistakes. That grace is not an excuse to sin, but a reason to repent with humility and to give thanks for his goodness.
exp.19:46:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to the forest of the south, that is, to the south. God says he will kindle a fire that will burn every tree, both the green and the dry, and that no one will be able to put it out. The phrase about faces refers to the surface, or to everything there is, from the south to the north.

God speaks, and Ezekiel is his messenger. Many understand that the forest is an image of Jerusalem and Judah, and the fire is God's judgment for their disobedience. The idea of green and dry trees suggests that the judgment would reach everyone. Then Ezekiel says that the people take him for someone who speaks in riddles, and so they do not understand the warning.

For today: let us not take God's warnings lightly or think they are simply stories. If something in your life needs to change, respond soon and with humility, because God corrects us to invite us to return to him.
exp.20:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," that is, simply a human being. He tells him to set his face toward Jerusalem, meaning to look toward the city with firmness, like someone about to deliver a serious message. To pour out a word means to preach with force. The holy places were the sites of worship, and to prophesy means to announce what God says.

The LORD speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people had fallen into idolatry and injustice. This message opens an announcement of judgment: God will compare his judgment to a sword that will come out of its sheath.

For today: God does not delight in remaining silent before sin, but he always gives warning first. If you hear his correction today, do not harden your heart; draw near to him in humility, and change in time what he shows you.
exp.20:5:
God tells Ezekiel, called "son of man," to groan in public. He must do it with the breaking of his loins, that is, with his body bent over by deep pain, and with bitterness, before the eyes of the people. It is not a quiet weeping but a sign that everyone can see.

God speaks to his prophet. Jerusalem was under judgment, and God announces that his sword, an image of destruction by war, will come against everyone. Ezekiel must groan so that, when people ask him why, he can announce the news that is coming and the people will understand how serious it is. Scholars agree that it is a symbolic gesture.

For today: when God shows us the pain of sin and its consequences, let us not speak with coldness. Let us ask him for a sensitive heart, one that feels compassion for others and warns them with love and sincerity.
exp.20:6:
God tells Ezekiel to groan openly, and when the people ask him why, he will answer that it is because of the news that is coming. That news will bring terror: every heart will melt with fear, every hand will grow weak, every spirit will faint, and every knee will become weak as water. God assures them that it is coming and will be fulfilled.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. In this chapter he announces judgment on Jerusalem, pictured as a sword that God draws from its sheath. The prophet's groaning is a dramatized sign so that the people will understand how serious what is coming is. The exact details of how this was experienced are known only from what the text says.

For today: when God warns us, it is wise to take it seriously and turn back to him in time, rather than ignoring the sign. His word also invites us to feel the weight of sin with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.20:8:
God commands the prophet Ezekiel to announce a message: a sword is ready to act. The sword is described as having a sharp edge and being polished and bright, prepared for use. It is an image of judgment that is already about to fall.

The Lord God speaks through Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God announces judgment on Jerusalem and its people because of their disobedience. Many understand that the sword represents the army of Babylon, although the text presents it as an instrument in God's hands. The people would feel fear and discouragement when the news arrived.

For today: God is serious, but He also warns before He acts. If there is something in your life that He has pointed out to you, do not put it off. Respond with humility and change today.
exp.20:18:
God tells Ezekiel, called "son of man," to draw two roads along which the sword of the king of Babylon can advance. The two roads start from the same country and are drawn where the way toward the city begins. The phrase about casting lots seems to refer to the king deciding his route by means of chance or divination.

The Lord speaks, and He does so through a symbolic action that Ezekiel is to act out. According to the following text, one road led to Rabbah of the Ammonites and the other to Jerusalem. The king of Babylon consulted idols and the livers of animals, but the passage presents God as the one who directs the outcome and announces judgment on Judah.

For today: even though we sometimes feel that our lives depend on luck or on the decisions of powerful people, we can trust that God still governs. Today you can bring your decisions to Him in prayer.
exp.20:20:
He says that the king of Babylon stopped at a fork in the road, where the way divides in two, to find out which direction to take. He used three kinds of divination: he shook up and mixed marked arrows and drew one out, he consulted the household idols, and he looked at the liver of a sacrificed animal.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. One road led to Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, and the other to Jerusalem. The lot pointed to Jerusalem. God uses this pagan decision to show that judgment on Judah for its sin was already coming.

For today: no one decides by chance or by superstition. God governs even the decisions of the powerful. Before choosing a path, let us seek his guidance in prayer and in his Word, and not in horoscopes or doubtful signs.
exp.20:21:
He says that the king of Babylon cast lots to decide where to attack, and the sign fell into his right hand: he would go against Jerusalem. Then he makes all his preparations: he appoints captains, gives the order to kill, raises the war cry, sets battering rams against the gates, and builds up ramps and siege towers. Divination is the attempt to learn the direction of events through signs.

Here God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. God explains that, although the pagan king uses arrows, idols, and the liver of animals to decide, God is the one directing events to judge the sin of Jerusalem. Some scholars see here God using Babylon as his instrument.

For today: do not look for guidance in superstition or doubtful signs. Seek God with humility, in his Word and in prayer, and let him correct your heart before the consequences arrive.
exp.20:27:
God tells Ezekiel to prophesy against the Ammonites, who mocked Israel. The message is that the sword of judgment is already drawn from its sheath. It is polished and sharpened, ready to slay, that is, to kill, and to destroy with a glittering flash like lightning.

The Lord God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier he had announced that the sword of Babylon would fall on Jerusalem. Now the judgment also reaches Ammon, a neighboring people who rejoiced at Israel's pain. Scholars discuss some details of the scene, but the central message is clear: God judges the nations.

For today: do not rejoice when others fall, and do not mock their suffering. God sees pride and mockery, and he also calls you to treat others with humility and compassion.
exp.20:31:
God says that this people will be like wood for the fire. Their blood will be poured out in the middle of their own land, and no one will remember them anymore. The Lord himself, who speaks here, declares that this is his word.
