God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this passage the judgment is directed at the Ammonites, who mocked the fall of Judah. God's sword, used by cruel men, would also fall upon them. Some scholars see here a general warning against the pride and violence of nations.

For today: do not rejoice when others suffer, and do not think yourself untouchable because of your success. God sees every injustice and every pride. With humility, let him correct you in time, and trust that his justice is true.
exp.21:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," a way of addressing him as a simple human being. He asks him, insistently, whether he will not judge the city that sheds blood, that is, full of violence and unjust deaths. He also charges him to show her all her abominations, that is, her practices that are detestable in God's eyes.

The one speaking is the LORD, and the city is Jerusalem, as seen in the rest of the chapter. Ezekiel was a prophet and a priest, and he lived among the exiles in Babylon. God sends him to declare clearly the guilt of the city: violence, idolatry, and corruption, which would bring consequences.

For today: God expects us to call things by their name, with truth and humility. Let us ask him to show us first our own faults, and to help us speak with courage and love when there is injustice.
exp.21:3:
God tells Jerusalem that she is guilty because of the innocent blood she has shed and the idols she has made, which have made her unclean. In this way she herself has hastened her judgment, and now the end of her years has come. That is why God allows the nations to mock her. Disgrace and mockery both mean public shame and ridicule.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God commands him to confront the city, that is, to show her clearly her sins. The verses that follow point to the leaders of Israel, who abused their power. God does not act without warning: first he declares the wrong.

For today: sin is never small or private when it harms others or when we put something in the place of God. Ask him to show you which idols have taken his place in your heart, and return to him with humility while there is still time.
exp.21:7:
It says that Jerusalem has treated with contempt what God regarded as holy. "Holy things" refers to the temple and to the things dedicated to God. "Despised" means that you took away their value, treating them as something of no importance. "Profaned" means that what was holy was treated as common. The sabbaths were the day of rest that God set apart for his people.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, during the time of exile in Babylon. He is accusing Jerusalem of serious sins: violence, injustice against orphans, widows and foreigners, and immorality. This verse shows that their wickedness was not only against people, but also against God, since they despised his worship and his day.

For today: let us ask ourselves whether we take what belongs to God seriously, such as his Word, prayer, and the time of rest and worship. And let us notice that loving God and caring for the weak go together.
exp.21:10:
It says that in Jerusalem the people were committing serious sexual sins within their own families and with their neighbors. Doing something detestable in the eyes of God describes what the phrase means. Shamefully dishonoring a daughter-in-law is what is meant by the sin of defiling her. Taking sexual advantage of someone by force refers to abuse. It also mentions abusing a sister, a daughter of the same father.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, before the fall of Jerusalem. He accuses the city of violence, injustice, idolatry, and sexual wickedness. These behaviors broke the law given to Israel (Leviticus 18 and 20). The people had forgotten God, and for that reason judgment would come.

For today: God is concerned with how we treat our family and our neighbor. We can guard purity, protect the vulnerable, and not stay silent in the face of abuse. If we have failed, there is forgiveness in Christ, who calls us to change.
exp.21:13:
God asks Jerusalem whether her heart will hold up and whether her hands will stay strong when He acts against her. These are rhetorical questions: the answer is no. At the end, God affirms that He has spoken and that He will carry it out.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Jerusalem had given herself over to violence and theft, had taken unjust gain from loans, and had forgotten God. Therefore He announces that He will scatter her among the nations and purge her uncleanness, so that they will know that He is the Lord.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are living with honesty and justice, without taking advantage of anyone. Let us not trust in our own strength; it is better to turn back to God in time, with humility, and let Him cleanse our hearts.
exp.21:19:
God says he will gather his people inside Jerusalem, the way someone puts metals (silver, iron, lead, tin) into a furnace and lights the fire to melt them. "Anger" and "wrath" speak of his righteous displeasure. "Leave you there" means he will keep the fire burning over them until they melt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He says Israel has become dross, meaning the worthless waste left behind when silver is refined. That describes their injustice, their idolatry, and their violence. The judgment on Jerusalem would be severe, and its purpose was that they would come to recognize that the LORD is Lord.

For today: let us not take sin or God's patience lightly. If he corrects us, let us listen quickly, repent, and return to him in humility, trusting in his justice and his mercy.
exp.21:20:
God says that he will gather his people inside Jerusalem, the way someone puts metals into a furnace. Then he will blow the fire of his anger on them, and there they will be melted down. To be melted means to become liquid from the heat. Anger like this is very intense.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was writing to the exiles in Babylon. Earlier he had said that Israel had become like dross, meaning the worthless remains left behind when metal is refined. The people were full of injustice, violence, and idolatry. Jerusalem would be the furnace where judgment would arrive.

For today: let us not take sin or God's patience lightly. If there is something in our lives that we know does not please him, we can acknowledge it today, ask for forgiveness, and change direction. God calls us to return to him before the consequences reach us.
exp.21:23:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to Jerusalem. He says she is not a land that has been made clean, meaning a land that is pure and healthy. Nor has she received rain in the time of God's judgment. The image speaks of a land that is dry and polluted, with no freshness or cleansing.

The Lord is speaking, and the message is directed to the people of Jerusalem. Shortly before, God compared them to impure metals melted in the furnace. Then the text points out the sins of prophets, priests, and rulers: injustice, abuse, and contempt for what is holy. Scholars understand the image in different ways, but all of them see a city without repentance.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are letting God cleanse our hearts or whether we are hardening them. When God corrects us, it is better to respond with humility and return to Him soon.
exp.21:25:
Her priests have broken my law and profaned my holy things. They have made no distinction between what is holy and what is common, and they have not taught the difference between the unclean and the clean. They have ignored my Sabbaths on purpose, and so I have been dishonored among my people.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, shortly before or during the fall of Jerusalem (around 590 B.C.). He is accusing the city's leaders: prophets, priests, and princes. The priests were supposed to teach the people to distinguish the sacred from the ordinary, but they did the opposite. That is why God announces judgment.

For today: if you teach or guide others, be faithful to God's Word and do not bend it to your own convenience. All of us can ask ourselves whether we give God the place that belongs to him.
exp.21:28:
This verse says that the common people of the land also took part in the injustice. They practiced oppression and robbery, mistreated the poor and the needy, and treated the foreigner badly without any justice.

God speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, during the time when Judah was about to fall to Babylon. Earlier, God had accused the princes, the priests, and the prophets. Here he shows that the guilt reached down to the people. Then he says that he looked for someone to stand in the gap, and found no one.

Today we can ask ourselves who near us is in a disadvantaged position: an underpaid worker, an immigrant, a poor neighbor. God calls us to treat them with justice and not to remain silent in the face of abuse.
exp.21:30:
This verse says that God let his anger fall on the people and destroyed them like a fire. The phrase "poured out" is like emptying out a container, and "consumed" means to finish off completely. The phrase "I have recompensed their way upon their heads" means that he gave back to them the consequences of what they had done.

God himself speaks here, through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. Before this, the passage explains the people's sins: they oppressed, they stole, and they mistreated the poor and the foreigner. God looked for someone who would stand in the breach of the wall, that is, who would intercede and defend the land, and he found no one. In this way, the judgment is presented as a fair response to injustice that had spread widely.

For today: God pays attention to how we treat the weak. We can ask ourselves who near us needs justice or help, and be someone who prays and intercedes for others and acts with kindness.
exp.22:1:
This verse begins a parable. God calls Ezekiel "son of man," a way of addressing him as an ordinary human being. He speaks of two women who were sisters, daughters of the same mother. Later the passage makes clear that they represent two cities.

The one speaking is God, who gives his message to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. The verses that follow explain that the sisters are Samaria (Aholah) and Jerusalem (Aholibah), that is, the northern and southern kingdoms. With this vivid story, God shows his people that they had been unfaithful to him by seeking help and gods from other nations.

For today: God desires our whole heart. We can ask ourselves in what things we are placing the trust that belongs only to him, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.22:5:
This verse says that the Assyrians, the lovers of Oholah, were men of impressive appearance: clothed in blue (a deep blue or violet cloth, a luxury fabric), captains and rulers, attractive young men, and horsemen riding on horses. "Desirable young men" means young men who were attractive.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses a harsh parable about two sisters: Oholah represents Samaria (the northern kingdom) and Oholibah represents Jerusalem. Their unfaithfulness symbolizes the spiritual infidelity of Israel, which sought alliances and foreign gods instead of trusting in God. The verse shows what dazzled them: power, beauty and prestige.

For today: the glitter of what the world admires can draw us away from God without our noticing. Before trusting in something, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to God or takes God's place.
exp.22:6:
It says that Oholah, who represents Samaria (the northern kingdom of Israel), gave herself to the Assyrians, the most select men of that people. The word for her acts here refers to spiritual unfaithfulness, not only sexual sin. The phrases about her being infatuated and about her defiling herself with all their idols show that she sought political alliances and also took on their false gods.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, using an allegory of two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah (Samaria and Jerusalem). Israel had made a covenant with God, but sought security in foreign powers and in its idols. Therefore God handed her over into the hands of the very ones she had clung to, and Assyria ended up destroying her.

For today: examine the things in which you seek security or worth apart from God, such as money, prestige, or relationships. Return to trusting Him first, because whatever takes God's place ends up enslaving us.
exp.22:9:
This verse says that the Assyrians, Aholah's former lovers, left her in shame: they uncovered her nakedness, took away her sons and daughters, and killed her with the sword. She became famous among women, because judgment was carried out against her.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he tells a parable about two sisters: Aholah represents Samaria (the northern kingdom of Israel) and Aholibah represents Jerusalem. The sexual unfaithfulness in the parable stands for faithlessness toward God, through seeking alliances and idols from other nations. Samaria fell to Assyria, and here it is presented as a warning for Jerusalem.

For today: trusting in what is not God may seem attractive, but in the end it betrays us. Today we can ask ourselves where we look for security apart from Him, and return our trust to God.
exp.22:11:
She says that Oholibah, the younger sister, fell in love with the Assyrians, her neighbors: captains and princes dressed in fine clothes, horsemen on horses, all of them very attractive young men. The second part of that description means young men worth desiring, and the phrase about their clothing refers to uniforms or very fine clothes.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria, the northern kingdom) and Oholibah (Jerusalem, Judah). With this picture of marital unfaithfulness, God denounces that his people sought political and religious alliances with foreign powers instead of trusting in him. Samaria had already been destroyed, and Jerusalem did not learn the lesson.

For today: examine what things dazzle you and where you place your security: money, power, fame, or influential people. What shines on the outside can draw you away from God, so ask him to keep you faithful.
exp.22:14:
He says that the men Oholah saw painted on the wall wore belts of leather around their waists and colorful turbans on their heads. All of them looked like military leaders, dressed like the Babylonians, born in the land of the Chaldeans. "Belts" are straps worn at the waist, and "turbans" are tall caps or headpieces.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he tells a parable about two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem. Here the focus is on Oholibah (Jerusalem), who let herself be impressed by the power and appearance of Babylon instead of trusting God. God uses very strong language to show how painful the unfaithfulness of his people is.

For today: be careful about what dazzles us. Power, image, and success can attract us more than God does. Before you admire something, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to him or pulls you away.
exp.22:21:
Here God speaks to Aholibah and announces a punishment. He says he will rouse up the very lovers she has grown weary of, and bring them against her from every side. These lovers are the nations she allied herself with in search of security.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Aholibah represents Jerusalem and Judah, described as an unfaithful woman who gave herself to Assyria, Babylon and Egypt instead of trusting God. It is strong, symbolic language, meant to show how serious her idolatry was. The judgment came through Babylon.

For today: whatever we place our trust in instead of God, such as money, reputation or people, can end up hurting us. Today we can return to Him sincerely and rest in His care.
exp.22:23:
This verse describes a great army that comes to attack Aholibah. They arrive with war chariots, carts, wheels, and many peoples. The shields are large, and the helmets are head coverings. They surround the city fully armed. God says he will set judgment before them, and they will judge her according to their own laws.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter, Aholibah represents Jerusalem, which turned away from God and sought alliances with Assyria and Babylon instead of trusting him. God uses those same nations as an instrument of judgment. Scholars understand this as a strong and poetic image of unfaithfulness.

For today: when we place our trust in things that are not God, sooner or later they fail us and hurt us. Today is a good day to return to him with sincerity.
exp.22:24:
God says he will set his jealousy against Jerusalem, meaning the anger of a wounded husband. Her former lovers will attack her with fury. The verse says they will take away her nose and ears, a cruel punishment of ancient warfare. Whoever survives will fall by the sword, they will take her sons and daughters, and what remains will be consumed by fire.

God speaks through Ezekiel. He uses the story of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem), to describe the people's unfaithfulness, which sought alliances and foreign gods instead of trusting in him. Babylon, once admired, becomes the instrument of judgment. The language is strong and symbolic, but it reflects God's grief over betrayal.

For today: examine the things in which you place your trust apart from God. What now seduces you may wound you later. Return to him sincerely; his discipline seeks to restore us.
exp.22:25:
This verse says that the enemies will strip Jerusalem of her clothing and take away her valuable possessions. The fair jewels are the ornaments and beautiful goods that she took pride in. In other words, she will lose her honor and her wealth.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapter 23 he tells the story of two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem. They gave themselves to other nations, looking for security in alliances and foreign gods instead of trusting in God. Now he allows those same allies to punish them.

For today: what we rely on to feel secure or important, such as money, reputation, or human support, can disappear. Let us put our trust in God, who does not fail us, and ask him to free us from depending on other things.
exp.22:26:
God says he will put an end to the impurity and the sexual unfaithfulness that Jerusalem brought with it from Egypt. Here the word for unfaithfulness is an image of spiritual infidelity. The people will no longer look back toward Egypt with longing or remember it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he tells the story of two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem. They sought alliances and the gods of other nations instead of trusting the Lord. The punishment announced is severe, and it aims to bring an end to that unfaithfulness. Some scholars also see here a desire for the people to wake up.

For today: ask yourself in what things you place your trust instead of in God. Ask him to free you from whatever pulls you away from him, and do not keep idealizing a past that harmed you.
exp.22:28:
Ezekiel 23:29 says that Aholibah's former lovers will deal with her in hatred, take away everything she worked for, and leave her stripped bare, exposed to shame. The sentence that explains the old wording is rewritten to fit the verse: the words "naked and bare" mean she will be left with nothing and open to shame. Her wrongdoing, both her shameful conduct and her unfaithfulness to God, will be brought fully into the open.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter He uses the picture of two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, to show how His people turned away from Him by forming alliances with other nations and by worshiping idols. The allies she trusted will turn against her. This is a judgment, but it is also meant to wake the people up.

For today: whatever we put in place of God, whether money, approval, or power, eventually fails us. Today you can ask yourself what you trust more than God, and return to Him with humility.
exp.22:30:
It says that Jerusalem (called Oholibah) followed the same path as her sister Samaria (Oholah), that is, idolatry and alliances with other nations. That is why God says he will place in her hand the same cup as her sister's. The cup was a vessel that represents the judgment and suffering she would have to drink.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He uses a story about two sisters to show the unfaithfulness of Samaria and Jerusalem. Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom, had already been destroyed. God warns that Jerusalem, by repeating her sin, would receive a similar consequence.

For today: learn from the mistakes of others. If we see that a certain path leads to pain, there is no need to walk it. Today you can ask God to show you where you need to return to him, before the consequences arrive.
exp.22:31:
It says that Jerusalem, called by the name of Oholibah, will drink the same cup of punishment that her sister Samaria drank. The cup is a vessel for drinking, and here it stands for God's judgment. It is deep and wide, a huge cup full of suffering. The words that say the nations will mock her and scorn her mean that the peoples will laugh at her and bring her down to humiliation.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Ezekiel uses the image of two sisters to speak of Samaria (the northern kingdom) and Jerusalem (the kingdom of Judah). Both turned away from God and sought alliances and idols from other nations. Samaria had already fallen, and God warns that Judah, by following the same path, would face the same end.

For today: let us learn from the mistakes of others. If we see that someone suffered the consequences of turning away from God, let us not think that it will not happen to us. Today we can return to God with humility, because He offers forgiveness to those who repent.
exp.22:32:
It says that Jerusalem will be filled with drunkenness and sorrow, like someone who drinks a bitter cup. "Cup" here is a cup that stands for God's punishment. The cup of astonishment and desolation means being left alone, empty and destroyed. It is the same cup that her sister Samaria drank.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he tells a story about two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, who represent the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. Both turned away from God and sought help from other nations and their idols. Since Samaria had already been destroyed, God warns that Jerusalem will meet the same end if she follows the same path.

For today: learn from the mistakes of others. If we see that turning away from God brings ruin to other people, we can return to Him in time, before suffering the same consequences.
exp.22:39:
This verse says that the two women, Oholah and Oholibah, sent for men from distant lands, and when those men arrived, she bathed, painted her eyes with a dark powder used for makeup, and put on jewelry. She did all of this to please them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of two sisters, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem, to show how his people sought alliances and foreign gods instead of remaining faithful to him. The passage presents this as a very painful betrayal, since they were also mixing their idols with worship in the sanctuary.

For today: let us ask ourselves what things we arrange and prepare with the most care to win the approval of others, while we neglect our faithfulness to God. He invites us to return to him with sincerity.
exp.22:40:
She is described as sitting on a splendid couch of honor, with a well-prepared table set before her. The word translated as "couch" here refers to an elegant seat or divan. On that table she placed the incense and the oil that belonged to God. In other words, she used for shameful purposes what rightfully belonged to Him.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In a parable, He compares Samaria and Jerusalem to two unfaithful sisters, Oholah and Oholibah. Through this, He denounces that His people sought foreign alliances and idols, and even mixed that idolatry with worship in the temple. Some scholars think the incense and oil recall sacred offerings, although the text does not fully explain this.

For today: examine whether you are using for other purposes what God has given you, such as your time, your talents, or your possessions. Place them again at His service with gratitude and sincerity.
exp.22:45:
God says that he is going to bring against Aholah and Aholibah a large crowd of enemies. He will hand them over to terror and to plunder, which means violent robbery. It is the announcement of a punishment that has already been decided.

Here God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter, Aholah and Aholibah represent Samaria and Jerusalem, that is, the people of God who were unfaithful to him by seeking alliances and idols from other nations. God uses the image of adultery to show the pain of a betrayed promise, and also the injustice of his people. Scholars agree that this is symbolic language.

For today: God takes the faithfulness of the heart seriously. Examine the things you place your trust in before him, and return to him with sincerity, because his desire is to restore, not only to correct.
exp.22:47:
He says God will put an end to the wickedness and immoral behavior that was in the land. The women, that is, those who hear or see this punishment, will learn the lesson (learning by punishment is what it means) and will not imitate that shameful conduct, which here speaks of disgraceful and immoral behavior.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter, Samaria and Jerusalem appear as two sisters, Ahola and Aholiba, who represent the unfaithfulness of Israel and Judah, since they joined themselves to other nations and their idols instead of remaining faithful to God. The judgment is a warning for other peoples.

For today: let us not take faithfulness to God lightly. If we see the consequences of idolatry and sin, let us learn in time and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.23:2:
God tells Ezekiel to speak a parable to the rebellious house, that is, to the people of Israel who had turned against him. He is to put the pot on the fire, set it on, and pour water into it. The picture is simple and vivid, and it is meant to be understood right away.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. On that very day the king of Babylon began the siege of Jerusalem, and God reveals it to Ezekiel in advance. The pot represents the city, and what follows in the chapter shows the judgment that would come because of its persistent rebellion.

For today: God speaks clearly before he corrects, and his warnings are a sign of his patience. If you sense that he is calling you back to his way, do not harden your heart. Listen, acknowledge your error, and return to him, who is willing to forgive.
exp.23:4:
He says to take the best sheep from the flock, to build a fire with the bones under the pot, and to let everything boil well, until the bones are also cooked inside it. "Choice" means the best, and "boil" is the same as "cook" in the verse above.

God speaks to Ezekiel and tells him to tell this parable to the rebellious house, the people of Judah. The pot represents Jerusalem, and the good pieces represent its inhabitants. Then it says the city is full of blood, that is, of violence and injustice. The fire announces God's judgment through the siege by Babylon.

For today: God sees injustice and does not overlook it. Let us ask that he examine our hearts, let go of what harms others, and seek repentance before sin consumes us.
exp.23:7:
God says that, because Jerusalem has provoked his anger, he will do justice. The blood she spilled will not stay hidden: he will set it upon a smooth, hard rock, where no one can cover it. Here "vengeance" means justice that answers evil, not a whim of anger.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. He compares Jerusalem to a dirty pot, full of violence and injustice. In the law, spilled blood was covered with earth (Leviticus 17:13). But Jerusalem left her blood in plain sight, as if defying God, and he leaves it in plain sight so that her guilt may be seen.

For today: God sees what we try to hide. Instead of covering our faults, we can confess them honestly and seek his forgiveness, for he is faithful to cleanse us (1 John 1:9).
exp.23:13:
God says that what he has announced will come to pass and that he himself will carry it out. He will not change his mind, will not feel pity, and will not relent.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem, which is compared to a rusty, dirty pot. For years the people rejected the cleansing God offered them and kept on in their wickedness. That is why judgment is coming, and shortly afterward Ezekiel will lose his wife as a sign of that grief.

For today: do not take God's warnings lightly. If he shows you something you need to change, respond quickly with humility and repentance, because his forgiveness is offered, and it is better to accept it today than to harden your heart.
exp.23:16:
God tells Ezekiel not to show his grief in public: he is to sigh quietly, not to observe the customary mourning, to keep the headpiece on his head and his sandals on his feet, not to cover his lips, and not to eat the bread of men, that is, the food that neighbors would bring to those who were grieving.

The LORD speaks to his prophet. He announces that his wife, the delight of his eyes, will die suddenly. His behavior would be a sign for the people, who would soon lose the temple and Jerusalem. The verses that follow show that the people asked him what it meant.

For today: God can use even our most painful moments, and sometimes obeying him costs us a great deal. If you are suffering today, do not keep your pain silent before God; he understands you and walks with you.
exp.23:18:
The people ask Ezekiel what his actions mean. He is acting in a very strange way: his wife has just died, and he does not carry out the customary mourning. The old words are explained this way: the first is a turban or headdress, the second is a cloak that covered the face, and the third was the food that friends brought to those who were grieving.

The speakers are the people of Israel, who are in exile in Babylon. God had commanded Ezekiel not to weep openly for his wife, so that he would be a living sign. His silence showed what the grief of Israel would be like when Jerusalem and the temple fell: a blow so great that there would not even be strength for weeping.

For today: sometimes God speaks to us through difficult situations. When something puzzles us, we can humbly ask what it teaches us, and listen to his Word sincerely before the pain arrives.
exp.23:19:
This verse is a transition phrase. Ezekiel answers the people's question and says that God spoke to him.

Ezekiel was a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God had told him that his wife would die and that he must not mourn for her in public. The people, puzzled, ask him what this means. His conduct was a sign: this is how they would react when the temple in Jerusalem fell. Scholars agree on the basics of this symbolism, although they debate some of the details.

For today: before giving answers to those who suffer or ask questions, it is wise to pause and listen to God. Praying and seeking his word helps us speak with truth and humility, not only with our own ideas.
exp.23:20:
God tells Ezekiel to announce to Israel that He is going to let His sanctuary be defiled, that is, allow the temple to be dishonored and destroyed. That place was their pride, the thing they trusted in, the thing they loved most, and the thing they wanted most. Their sons and daughters they had left behind in Jerusalem would also fall by the sword.

God speaks through Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. People asked him what it meant that he did not mourn the death of his wife. That sign announced the grief that would come with the judgment on Jerusalem, caused by the people's persistent rebellion.

For today: let us not place our security in places, customs, or religious achievements, but in God himself. What we love most must be under his lordship.
exp.23:22:
The people will do the same as Ezekiel: they will leave their turbans or headdresses and their shoes in place, normal signs of everyday life, instead of the signs of mourning. They will not make public laments or weep aloud. Their grief will be internal: they will waste away because of their sins and groan among themselves.

God speaks through Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. God had just commanded him not to mourn the death of his wife, so that he would be a sign. In this way the people would understand that the fall of Jerusalem and the temple would be so painful that they could not even express their grief openly.

For today: let us not wait until the pain is so great before we recognize our faults. A sincere repentance, made in time before God, is better than mourning late over consequences we could have avoided.
exp.23:23:
God tells Ezekiel that he will be a sign to the people. What he did, they will do too. When what has been announced comes to pass, they will know that God is the Lord.

The phrase "will be a sign" means that Ezekiel serves as a living example. The phrase "you will know that I am the Lord God" means that they will recognize that God had truly spoken.

God speaks to the exiles of Judah through Ezekiel. The prophet's wife suddenly dies, and God forbids him to mourn in public. By this, He shows that Jerusalem and the temple would be destroyed, and the grief would be so great that the people would not even be able to express their mourning. Interpreters see here a judgment for their sins, but also a warning so that they would respond.

For today: let us not wait until the crisis arrives to take God's voice seriously. If He warns us through His Word, let us listen in time, acknowledge our failures, and return to Him in humility.
exp.23:25:
He says that on that same day someone who managed to escape from Jerusalem will reach Ezekiel. That person will bring the news of what happened.

God speaks, addressing Ezekiel, who was in exile in Babylon. Jerusalem had been besieged, and the Lord announced that the temple, the delight of their eyes, would be taken away. Ezekiel was not to mourn publicly for the death of his wife, so that it would be a sign to the people. When the survivor arrived, Ezekiel would speak again, and the people would recognize that God had fulfilled his word.

For today: God keeps what he says, even when his warnings hurt. If there is something he has shown you and you have been ignoring, take it seriously with humility and return to him before the difficulty arrives.
exp.23:26:
God tells Ezekiel that when a survivor (the one who "escaped") arrives with news from Jerusalem, his mouth will be opened and he will no longer be mute. Ezekiel will be a sign to the people, and so they will know that God is the Lord.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. He had announced that Jerusalem would fall, but many did not believe him. His silence as a prophet seems to have lasted until the news of the fall arrived (Ezekiel 33:21-22). Scholars debate exactly what that silence was like, but the message is clear: God keeps his word.

For today: God remains faithful even when his word takes time or we do not take it seriously. Today you can trust him and listen to his voice with humility, before circumstances force you to do so.
exp.24:1:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and commands him to turn his face squarely toward the Ammonites, a people neighboring Israel, and to deliver a message from God concerning them. "Son of man" is how God addresses Ezekiel, and it simply means a human being. Setting one's face toward someone means facing them with firm resolve. To prophesy is to speak what God says.

The LORD speaks. Ezekiel was among the exiles in Babylon. The Ammonites had rejoiced when the temple was defiled and Judah was taken captive. For this reason God, who cares for his people, announces judgment against them. This is the beginning of a series of messages against neighboring nations.

For today: rejoicing in another's pain displeases God. When someone suffers, even someone with whom we have differences, God calls us to compassion and not to mockery.
exp.24:5:
This verse explains the reason for God's judgment against Ammon. Clapping the hands and stamping the feet are gestures of mockery and joy at another's misfortune. Rejoicing from the heart, with all their scorn toward the land of Israel, means they were glad within themselves, with complete contempt for Israel's land.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Ammon, a neighboring people of Israel, mocked when Jerusalem and the temple were struck by Babylon. God did not overlook that attitude. The judgment that appears before and after this passage follows from this accusation: God takes contempt for his people seriously.

For today: when someone stumbles or suffers, even someone with whom we have had problems, let us avoid rejoicing in secret. Better to pray for that person and help if we can, remembering that God looks at the heart.
exp.24:6:
God says he will stretch out his hand against Ammon to punish it. He will hand it over to other nations, who will plunder it. He will cut it off from among the peoples and wipe it off the earth. In the end, Ammon will know that the Lord is God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The Ammonites rejoiced and mocked when Jerusalem and the people of Israel suffered. God takes that contempt seriously. This message is part of the oracles against neighboring nations, and it shows that God rules over all peoples.

Today we can learn not to rejoice in the pain of others, even when we have been wronged by them. God sees the heart. If someone is suffering, it is better to pray for that person, help them, and treat them with compassion and humility.
exp.24:7:
This verse begins a message from God against Moab and Seir (another name for Edom). They were saying that Judah was like all the other nations, meaning that it had nothing special and that its God did not protect it in any way different from other nations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Judah had already been struck by Babylon, and its neighbors were mocking it. By saying this, they despised God's covenant with his people. That is why God announces judgment on Moab, which would lose its border cities. Note: the text names Seir together with Moab, but the punishment that follows focuses on Moab.

For today: when others mock faith or those who are suffering, do not join them. God sees the contempt and cares for his own, even in difficult times. Respond with humility and compassion.
exp.24:10:
God also says that he will carry out his judgments against Moab, the neighboring nation of Israel. To "execute judgments" means to apply his justice and punish wrongdoing. The expected result is that they will know that he is the Lord, meaning they will recognize that the God of Israel is the true Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile of Judah in Babylon. Moab had looked down on Judah, claiming that it was just like the other nations (v. 8). For this reason God announces that Moab will lose its border cities and will be handed over to the people of the east. The passage shows that God does not overlook contempt toward his people.

We can trust that God sees every injustice and that he will bring about justice in his own time. So we do not need to take revenge or mock anyone. Instead, we leave judgment in his hands and live with humility.
exp.24:14:
God speaks here against the Philistines. They acted out of revenge, with a hateful, spiteful heart, and they brought ruin on others out of an old enmity that had lasted for generations. The word for ruining others means harming or destroying them without mercy.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he judges several nations that bordered Israel, including Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia. The Philistines were enemies of Israel for a long time, and here God calls them to account for their vengeance and hatred. The text gives no further details about each specific event.

For today: a grudge held for years can become destructive. Ask God to heal old wounds and help you forgive rather than take revenge. He is the righteous judge.
exp.25:2:
God says to Tyre, a great trading city by the sea, that he is against her. He announces that he will bring many nations against her, one after another, like the waves of the sea that rise and rise without stopping. Here "nations" means nations or peoples.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the eleventh year of the exile. Tyre had rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking she would now have more business, since Jerusalem was a gateway for the nations. God answers that mockery and that greed. Scholars often connect the fulfillment with Babylon and, later, with other armies, although there is debate about how each detail came about.

For today: let us not rejoice in the misfortune of others or seek to gain at the expense of someone else's pain. God sees the heart and calls us to compassion, not pride.
exp.25:8:
He says that the army of Nebuchadnezzar will attack the city of Tyre with battering rams, which were thick tree trunks used to strike and bring down the walls. He will also break down its towers with axes, that is, with iron tools or weapons made for demolition. It is a siege scene: the city that thought itself safe will be torn down piece by piece.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich and proud city, and it rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking it would gain from it (Ezekiel 26:2). God announces that Babylon will come against it. It is known that Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for years; the details of how that siege ended are interpreted in various ways.

For today: no human wealth, fame, or strength gives us true security. We are also called not to rejoice in the misfortune of others. Let us place our trust in God, who humbles the proud and cares for the humble.
exp.25:11:
This passage describes how the invading army will plunder the city of Tyre. They will carry off its riches and merchandise, break down its walls, and destroy its houses, which were pleasant to look at. Even the stones, the timber, and the dust from the rubble will be thrown into the water, that is, into the sea.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel against Tyre, a city rich and proud through its trade, which rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem. The text names Nebuchadnezzar as the invader (v. 7). Many understand that verse 12 was also fulfilled later, when the rubble of the coastal city was thrown into the sea, although some interpret it only of Nebuchadnezzar and others of several conquerors.

For today: riches and success are not a secure foundation. Let us place our trust in God, and treat those who suffer with humility, without rejoicing in their fall.
exp.25:12:
God says he will silence the music of the city of Tyre. The noise of its celebrations and songs will come to an end. The stringed instruments that accompanied them, which were something like ancient harps or lutes, will be heard no more.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a very rich trading city, and it had rejoiced over the fall of Jerusalem, thinking it would profit from it. God announces that Tyre too will be torn down by an invading army. The verses that follow say it would become like a bare rock where fishing nets are spread out to dry.

For today: riches and festivities may seem secure, but they do not last. Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in, give thanks to God, and live with humility, without mocking the suffering of others.
exp.25:15:
This verse says that the rulers and leaders of the coastlands and the cities of the sea, who were allies of Tyre, will come down from their thrones. They will take off their robes and their embroidered garments, that is, their signs of power and wealth. Instead, they will clothe themselves with trembling: they will sit on the ground, shaking, and be astonished, that is, greatly amazed, as they see the fall of Tyre.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich and powerful city of maritime trade. God announces its judgment, among other reasons because of its pride. The rulers who depended on it are frightened because they see that their security is collapsing.

For today: wealth, position, or prestige are not a firm foundation. We can be thankful for what we have, but we should place our trust in God and live with humility.
exp.26:1:
God says to Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man," that he should take up a lamentation over Tyre. A lamentation is a funeral song, a mourning that is sung for someone who has fallen or is about to fall. Tyre was a great trading city by the sea.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes during the exile in Babylon. God announces judgment against Tyre for its pride and its wealth. What follows shows that Tyre boasted of its perfect beauty. The lamentation is ironic: it mourns a city that believed itself invincible.

For today: let us not place our security in money, success or appearance. All of that can disappear. We can receive with humility what God gives us and trust in him, who endures forever.
exp.26:6:
It says that Tyre's ship was of great luxury. Its sail, called here a "sail" in the verse, was of fine linen with embroidered work, brought from Egypt, so that everyone could see it from afar. Its awning over the deck was of blue and purple cloth, and of scarlet, from the isles of Elishah. It is thought that Elishah was in the Mediterranean, but where exactly is not known for certain.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and composes a lament over Tyre, a trading city famous for its wealth. He describes it as a beautiful ship, made with materials from many nations. Behind that image there is a warning: such beauty and pride would not save it from the judgment that was coming.

For today: enjoying what God gives us is not wrong, but we can place our trust in success, money or image. Today you might ask yourself: what is my security resting on? Rest in God, who does not sink.
exp.26:8:
Tyre is compared to a great ship, and it received help from other cities. The elders and wise men of Gebal, a coastal city near modern Byblos, were in Tyre to repair its cracks and leaks, so that no water would get in. Large oared ships came to Tyre with their sailors to trade.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a city rich and proud of its trade. The poem describes its beauty and power, but it does so to show how much Tyre trusted in itself before its announced fall.

For today: everything we have, our work, our reputation or our success, depends on the help of many people. Let us thank those who support us and not place our security in what we have achieved, but in God, who is the only one who never wears out.
exp.26:9:
It says that Tyre had foreign soldiers from distant places: Persia, Lud and Phut (probably a region of Africa, though it is not known exactly). They hung their shields and helmets on the city's walls. With this, according to the text, they gave Tyre fame and splendor.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and composes a lament over Tyre, a rich and trading city. He describes it as a great, beautiful ship, full of riches and of people from many nations. The poet highlights its pride and its confidence in its power, before announcing its fall.

For today: it is not wrong to have resources, preparation or good allies, but we should not place our security or our identity in them. Let us put our trust in God, who sustains everything we have and gives us true worth.
exp.26:11:
It says that Tarshish traded with Tyre. Because of the great abundance of riches that Tyre had, Tarshish brought it silver, iron, tin and lead to sell in its fairs, that is, in its markets. The word "merchant" means a trader or dealer. Tarshish was a distant place; no one knows for certain where it was, though many think it lay in the western Mediterranean.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and raises a lament over Tyre, a seafaring city that was very rich and proud. He compares it to a beautiful ship loaded with goods from many nations. This list of trading partners shows its enormous wealth, but it also prepares the announcement of its fall.

For today: riches and success are not bad in themselves, but they are not a secure foundation. Ask yourself what you are really trusting in, and ask God for a grateful and humble heart that uses what it has to bless others.
exp.26:22:
This verse lists cities and peoples of the ancient Near East who did business with Tyre. Haran, Canneh and Eden were places in Mesopotamia or nearby. Sheba and Asshur also appear as trading partners. Chilmad is a little-known place, and no one knows for certain where it was. The word "merchants" in the verse means that these peoples traded or dealt with the city.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and raises a lament over Tyre, a rich and proud seaport city. The long list of partners shows how much wealth and fame it had. But God presents it this way to announce that, however powerful it was, its fall would come.

For today: money, connections and success can give a sense of security, but they are not firm. We can be thankful for what God gives us and work with integrity, but we should place our trust in Him and not in what we have.
exp.26:23:
The passage says that merchants from various peoples came to the city of Tyre to sell goods of great value: cloaks of deep blue-violet, embroidered work, bundles of fine clothing tied with cords, and cedar wood. Merchants are traders, and to trade means to carry on business.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a great trading city by the sea. This list of goods shows its enormous wealth and influence. But the text that follows announces that this glory will sink like a ship broken by the wind. God warns against the pride that grows out of prosperity.

For today: We can enjoy and work with what God gives us, but without setting our hearts on money or success. Ask yourself: is my security in my possessions or in God?
exp.26:25:
They say that Tyre's rowers brought her into deep, open waters, and there the east wind, the wind from the east, broke her to pieces in the middle of the sea. Tyre appears as a great ship.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and raises a lament over Tyre, a city rich from its sea trade. Earlier the text describes her as full of pride and wealth. Now it announces that her power will not save her. The east wind is often strong and destructive, and here it represents God's judgment. Interpreters see it as an image of the city's fall, not as a literal storm.

For today: we may have success, plans and resources, but none of that gives us final security. Let us trust in God more than in what we have achieved, and live with humility.
exp.26:28:
This verse describes the sailors of Tyre: the rowers and the pilots who guided the ships. They come down from their vessels and stand on dry land, as people who can no longer continue sailing. The rowers are those who handle the oar, and the pilots are those who directed the ship.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who composes a lament over Tyre, a city made rich by its sea trade. He announces its fall because of its pride and its trust in riches. The sailors appear as witnesses of the disaster: they see what seemed unshakable sink, and they weep bitterly.

For today: examine where you place your security. Money, success, or reputation can disappear quickly. Trust in God first, and use what you have with humility and generosity.
exp.26:29:
They who lived from the sea and from trade with Tyre, such as sailors and pilots, cry out their grief aloud. They weep bitterly, throw dust on their heads, and roll in ashes. These were common signs of deep mourning in that time.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a very rich port city, and here the prophet describes it as a great ship that is sinking. Those who profited from it now mourn its loss. The passage shows that its power and its trade could not save it. Some also see in it a warning against Tyre's pride.

For today: wealth and success can disappear quickly. It is worth examining where we place our security and trusting in God, who remains. Let us use what we have with humility and generosity.
exp.26:32:
It says that when Tyre's ships returned loaded with goods, many peoples were satisfied. Its wealth and its trade even made the kings of the earth rich.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament over Tyre, a city famous for its sea trade. The nearby verses describe other peoples mourning over its fall. Here its past glory is remembered, to show how great it was and how hard its ruin would be. The text does not say that trade is bad; the underlying problem in the chapter is pride.

Today we can be thankful for what God gives us, but without trusting in money or success. If you work or own a business, try to make sure your profit also blesses others, and remember that what matters most is not lost in a storm.
exp.27:1:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, calling him "son of man," and tells him to deliver a message to the ruler of Tyre, that is, the leader of that city. He accuses him of having a heart that has been lifted up, meaning he had become proud. He claimed to be a god and to sit in the seat of God in the midst of the seas. But God reminds him that he is only a man.

Tyre was a rich and powerful city on the Mediterranean coast, famous for its trade and its ships. Here the Lord speaks through Ezekiel, in a prophecy of judgment against that ruler. His wealth and success led him to think himself greater than he was. The verses that follow mention his wisdom and his riches.

For today: achievements and money can make us forget that we depend on God. Today you can thank Him for what you have and acknowledge that every gift comes from Him.
exp.27:7:
This verse says the king of Tyre will be brought down to "the pit," a phrase that means the grave or the place of the dead. He will die "the deaths of those who are slain in the midst of the seas," that is, with a violent death and without honor, like someone who dies far from his homeland and without a proper burial.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The king of Tyre, a rich and powerful city built on sea trade, thought himself a god because of his wisdom and his riches. God announces to him that foreign nations will defeat him. Some see in this passage also a broader allusion to pride and the fall of Satan, though not everyone interprets it this way.

For today: pride deceives us and makes us believe we do not need anyone. Today you can thank God for what you have and recognize that everything is a gift from him.
exp.27:9:
It says that the ruler of Tyre will have a shameful death, like that of the uncircumcised, that is, the death of those who did not belong to God's people. He will die at the hands of strangers, that is, at the hands of foreigners. And this is not simple chance: God says he has already declared it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the king of Tyre, who believed himself to be a god because of his wealth and wisdom. The verses before remind him that he is only a man. Some think the passage speaks only of a human king; others also see a broader background about pride. Scholars interpret it in different ways.

For today: pride deceives us and makes us feel untouchable. We can be thankful for what we have, recognize that everything comes from God, and live with humility before him.
exp.27:14:
It says that this figure was created perfect, without fault in his conduct, until wickedness appeared in him. "Created" means made by God. The verse says that wickedness was found in him, meaning it came to light in him. The words do not say that God made the evil, but that the evil arose afterward.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament against the king of Tyre, a proud ruler. The language uses images of Eden and of a cherub, and for this reason some believe it also alludes to Satan, while others see it only as a poetic portrait of the king. Christians interpret it in both ways.

For today: what God gives us, such as talents, success, or beauty, can become pride if we are not humble. Let us ask him for a grateful and watchful heart.
exp.27:17:
He says the king of Tyre filled his life with wickedness through his injustice and his dishonest dealings, and so he defiled his holy places. Therefore God brought out a fire from within him that consumed him and left him reduced to ashes in the sight of all.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament against the king of Tyre, a city rich from its trade. The language uses images of Eden and of a guardian cherub. Some see only the human king; others also see an allusion to Satan. It is debated, and the text does not fully settle it.

For today: wealth, beauty, or success can make us proud. Let us examine with humility how we earn and use what we have, and ask God for an honest heart.
exp.27:20:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to set his face toward Sidon, a city neighboring Tyre, and to speak a message against it. "Set your face" means to direct your attention firmly.

"Son of man" is the way God addresses Ezekiel throughout the book, reminding him that he is an ordinary human being.

The LORD speaks. Earlier he had already announced judgment on the king of Tyre for his pride. Now the message extends to Sidon, another Phoenician city that had also mistreated Israel. The purpose God declares is that they will know that he is the LORD.

For today: God sees all nations and all people, and he does not ignore injustice. We can trust that he is just, and also examine whether our pride is pulling us away from him.
exp.27:22:
God says that he will send deadly disease (pestilence) upon Sidon, and violence in its streets. There will be dead people inside the city, and the sword will surround it on every side. The final result is that they will know that he is the LORD, the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Sidon was a neighboring city of Israel, and the passage mentions it among the nations that looked down on Israel. God announces judgment on it to show his holiness and his justice. Then he promises that Israel will no longer have anything that pierces and hurts them, and that it will be gathered back into its land. The passage does not say here how or exactly when the judgment on Sidon happened.

For today: God sees injustice and is not indifferent. You can trust that he cares for his people and will have the final word, so do not seek revenge; give your pain to him in prayer.
exp.28:1:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man," to set his face against Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, and to deliver a message from God against him and against all of Egypt. To set one's face against someone means to confront them with determination. Here, to prophesy means to declare what God says.

The Lord speaks, and the message comes in the tenth year of Ezekiel's exile, while Babylon was pressing on the region. Egypt was a proud power. Later, Pharaoh appears as a great dragon who boasts: "My river is my own, and I made it for myself." God answers that pride.

Today we can remember that everything we have comes from God, not only from our own effort. We can thank him this week for something specific and avoid the attitude that everything depends on us.
exp.28:4:
God tells Pharaoh that he will be left thrown out in the wilderness, along with all the fish of his rivers. He will fall on the open field, and no one will gather him up or bury him. He will be food for the wild animals and the birds of the sky. The phrase "the open field" refers to the surface of the field, and the word "gathered" means brought together for burial.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Pharaoh is called the great dragon of the rivers, a picture of the power of Egypt and the Nile. He had thought himself the owner of everything and said: "My river is mine, and I made it for myself." Moreover, Egypt had been a fragile reed on which Israel leaned, and it failed.

For today: everything we have, such as health, work, or achievements, is a gift from God. Trusting in our own power or in human supports ends up failing. We can thank God every day and rest in him.
exp.28:5:
It says that all the inhabitants of Egypt will know that the Lord is God. The reason is that Egypt was like a staff of reed to Israel. A staff is a stick for leaning on, and a reed is weak and breaks. Egypt seemed like firm help, but it failed.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile. Judah had sought support in Egypt instead of trusting God. God compares Pharaoh to a great monster of the Nile and announces judgment on his pride. The verses that follow explain that Egypt broke when Israel leaned on it.

For today: review the things you lean on more than God, such as money, a position, or a person. They can help you, but they are fragile reeds. Rest first in the Lord, who never breaks.
exp.28:7:
God himself declares a punishment against Egypt: he will bring a sword, that is, war and invasion, and he will cut off both people and animals. It is strong language to describe a great destruction.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing the pharaoh and Egypt. Egypt had been like a fragile reed on which Israel leaned when seeking help, and it failed them. In addition, the pharaoh felt he owned the Nile, as if everything were his own doing. Scholars often connect this prophecy with the invasions of Babylon, though the text does not give all the details.

For today: trusting in power, money, or human alliances as if they were the safest things can leave us wounded. We can be thankful for what we have, but place our final trust in God, who does not fail.
exp.28:11:
God says he will leave the land of Egypt desolate, just like other lands that have been ruined. Its cities will remain in ruins for forty years. He also says he will scatter the Egyptians among the nations.

Speaking through the prophet Ezekiel, who was in exile in Babylon, God addresses Egypt. Egypt considered itself powerful and had been a deceptive support for Israel. God judges it for its pride. The forty years can be understood literally or as a symbolic period of punishment; scholars interpret them in different ways, and there is no certainty about how this was fulfilled historically.

For today: let us not place our final trust in human powers, whether money, fame, or governments. Only God is secure. And even in judgment, the following text shows that he leaves a door open to restoration.
exp.28:12:
God says that, when forty years have passed, He will gather the Egyptians again, the very people He had scattered among the nations. The verse's wording for "gather" means to bring together, and the word for scattered means spread out, dispersed to different places.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Egypt had thought itself very powerful and had been a source of false confidence for Israel. For this reason God announces judgment on its pride. But the punishment has a limit: afterward restoration will come, although Egypt will remain a humble kingdom. Scholars debate whether the forty years is a literal or symbolic figure, and it is not known with certainty how it was fulfilled.

For today: God corrects, but He does not destroy without hope. If you are going through a difficult season, remember that He sets limits on punishment and can restore. Learn humility and trust in God, not in your own power.
exp.28:15:
This verse says that Egypt will no longer be a place where Israel puts its trust. In the past, when Israel looked to Egypt for help, that reminded them of their lack of faith in God. Looking back to the Egyptians for support was a sign of turning away from God. In the end, Israel will know that the Lord alone is God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Egypt had been an ally that Israel turned to instead of trusting God. Here God announces that Egypt will be humbled and weakened, so that no one will see it as a source of salvation.

For today: it is worth asking ourselves where we place our security, such as money, people, or plans. All of these can fail. God invites us to trust Him first, for He does not change and does not disappoint.
exp.28:20:
He says that God will cause the horn of Israel to bud forth again. In the Bible, the horn is a symbol of strength and power; to bud forth again means to sprout anew, like a plant coming back to life. He also promises Ezekiel that he will be given an opening of the mouth: that he will be able to speak with confidence among them. In the end, everyone will know that the Lord is God.

God speaks through Ezekiel, a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier, he announced that Egypt would be handed over to Nebuchadnezzar. This is the only message of hope in the chapter: while Egypt falls, Israel will receive renewal. Many believe that "that day" points to a future restoration of Israel, though it is not known with precision what moment is meant.

For today: when you feel your strength has dried up, remember that God can make new life spring up. Trust that he keeps his promises, and when the moment comes, speak of his faithfulness with courage.
exp.29:6:
It says that Egypt and its allies will be destroyed and left empty. The word "desolate" means ruined, left in ruins. Their cities will be just like other cities that are already deserted, that is, without people and without life. Nothing will set them apart from the other fallen nations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people of Israel are living in exile. He announces judgment against Egypt and the nations that supported it. Egypt was proud and trusted in its strength. God shows that no human power, not even its allies, can stop what he has decided. Scholars debate exactly who some of those peoples were, such as Chub.

For today: do not place your ultimate security in money, power, or human alliances. All of that can fall. Trust first in God, who remains firm.
exp.29:12:
God says he will take away from Egypt the things it trusted in. The "images" and "idols" are the religious figures they worshiped, and Memphis was one of their most important cities. He also says there will no longer be a ruler of their own, that is, a leader born in that land, and that he will put dread, meaning fear and awe, on the whole country.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. The message is a judgment against Egypt for its pride and its idolatry. The text connects it to the Babylonian invasion, but how exactly it was fulfilled is interpreted in several ways.

For today: nothing we put in place of God, whether money, power, or fame, can sustain us forever. Today you can examine what you trust in most and surrender it to God in prayer.
exp.29:14:
He says that God will pour out his anger on Sin, which was a strong city of Egypt, a kind of defense on its frontier. He also says that he will cut off the multitude of No, that is, that he will destroy it or cut it down, as one cuts down a tree. No was not the ancient city of Thebes.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. Egypt considered itself secure and had given Israel false hope. God announces judgment on its cities, its idols and its pride. Many understand that Babylon would be the instrument of that judgment, as the nearby context of the chapter says.

For today: let us not place our security in how strong something seems, such as money, power or fame. Only God is a true fortress. We can ask ourselves what we are trusting in and return to rest in him.
exp.29:15:
God says he will send fire, that is, destruction, upon Egypt. Sin (probably a fortified city in the northeast) will suffer great pain. No (the city of Thebes) will be invaded, and Memphis will live under constant distress. The phrase about the city not being torn apart is hard to translate, and other versions render it as being broken open through breaches.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, around the time when Babylon dominated the region. Egypt was a power in which Judah had placed its trust. God announces that this human security will fall, and that he is Lord over all nations.

For today: examine where you are placing your security, whether in money, work, influence, or your own strength. All of these can fail. Rest first in God, who does not change, and ask him for wisdom to use well what you have.
exp.29:17:
God says that in Tehaphnehes, a city of Egypt, the day will be darkened. There he will break the yokes of Egypt, that is, its power and its defenses, like someone breaking the bars of a door. The pride of its strength will come to an end. A cloud will cover it, a cloud of judgment, and the people of its villages will be taken away as prisoners.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Egypt trusted in its power, and Judah sometimes sought support from it. God announces judgment on that nation so that it will be known that He is the Lord. Some scholars connect this with the Babylonian invasion, although the text gives no further details.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether money, work, reputation, or your own strength. All of these can fail. Entrust your plans to God with humility and trust Him first.
exp.29:20:
God tells Ezekiel, called "son of man," that he has already broken the arm of Pharaoh, king of Egypt. That arm was not healed: no one applied medicine or a bandage to hold it together. So Pharaoh does not regain strength to take up the sword again, that is, to fight.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the eleventh year of the exile (around 587 B.C.). Egypt seemed a secure power, and some hoped it would help Judah against Babylon. God announces that this power will be broken. The "arm" symbolizes military strength. The verses that follow show that the judgment will continue.

For today: let us not place our ultimate trust in human powers, such as money, positions, or alliances. All of these can be broken. Let us rest in God, whose care truly sustains and never fails.
exp.29:21:
God says he is against Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. He announces that he will break his arms, both the one that is still strong and the one that was already broken, and that he will make the sword fall from his hand.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile of Judah in Babylon. Egypt seemed like a possible ally, but God announces that its power will come to an end. The "arms" represent military strength. Pharaoh had already been struck down, and now a greater blow would come, while Babylon would be used by God as an instrument of judgment.

For today: let us not place our ultimate security in money, power, or human alliances, because all of these can fail. Trusting in God gives us a support that does not break.
exp.29:23:
This verse says that God will strengthen the hands of the king of Babylon and put his own sword in the king's hand. But God will break the arms of Pharaoh, king of Egypt. The "arms" stand for power and the ability to fight. The phrase about groaning like a man mortally wounded means that Pharaoh will cry out like someone seriously injured.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Egypt was a great power, and Judah had put its trust in Egypt instead of trusting in God. God announces that Egypt will fall and that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, will be the instrument of that judgment. The final purpose is that they will know that He is the LORD.

For today: no human strength, whether money, work, or influence, can give us complete security. God rules over all powers. Today you can hand Him your fears and lean on Him before anything else.
exp.29:25:
God says that he will scatter the Egyptians among the nations and drive them from one country to another, the way someone throws grain into the wind. The verb rendered "scatter" means to spread them out, and the image is of throwing them far away. The final purpose is that they will know that the Lord is God.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Egypt had trusted in its power and in its king, Pharaoh, and God announces judgment against it. In this passage, Babylon appears as the instrument God uses. The Bible presents this as God's judgment on the pride of the nations.

For today: nothing we use to feel secure, whether money, power, or prestige, can stand if God does not hold it up. Today you can ask yourself what you are really trusting in, and turn your trust back to God, who is faithful and above all things.
exp.30:0:
This verse marks the moment when God speaks to Ezekiel. The text says it happened in the eleventh year, in the third month, on the first day of the month. It is the exact date of a new message.

The one speaking is the prophet Ezekiel, who receives God's message. It is generally understood that the eleventh year corresponds to the exile of the people in Babylon, around 587 B.C., although the text gives no further detail. The message that follows is for Pharaoh and Egypt, and it warns them with the image of a great cedar, the one of Assyria, which fell.

For today: God speaks at concrete and real moments in history. We can approach his Word with confidence, knowing that he is interested in our time. It also reminds us that no human power is eternal; only God remains.
exp.30:5:
This verse describes a huge, leafy tree. In its branches all the birds of the sky made their nests, under its boughs the beasts of the field gave birth to their young, and in its shade many peoples lived.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and tells him to speak to the pharaoh of Egypt. With the image of this tree, compared with Assyria, God shows the greatness of a powerful empire. Scholars understand the passage in several ways, but all of them see a warning: the tree grew proud, and for that reason it would be brought down.

For today: everything we have, such as strength, success, or influence, comes from God. If we use it to give shelter and help others, and do so with humility, we honor the Lord. Pride, on the other hand, makes us fall.
exp.30:6:
It says this great tree became very beautiful because of its size and its long, spreading branches. The reason is that its roots reached a great deal of water, and this fed it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and addresses the Pharaoh of Egypt. He uses the image of an enormous tree, comparing it to Assyria, to warn him that his power will also fall. Many understand that the tree represents Assyria as an example, though some see it as a direct image of Egypt. God makes clear that the tree's greatness was a gift from him.

Everything good we have, such as talents, success, or influence, comes from God. We can thank him for it and use it to bless others, without becoming filled with pride.
exp.30:12:
It says that when the great tree falls and lies in ruins, the birds and the beasts of the field will settle on its fallen trunk and its broken branches. Before, they sought shelter in its shade; now they live only off what remains.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He compares Assyria, or perhaps Egypt (interpreters understand it in different ways), to an enormous and proud cedar. Because of its arrogance, God allows strong nations to bring it down. Its fall serves as a warning to other powerful ones.

For today: power, success, and prestige do not last if the heart is filled with pride. We can be thankful for what God gives us, live with humility, and remember that all our strength depends on Him.
exp.30:17:
God asks Pharaoh: who is like you in glory and greatness among the trees of Eden? And He answers that you will be brought down along with them, down to the underworld, the place of the dead. You will lie among the uncircumcised, that is, pagan peoples, and among those who died by the sword. All of this refers to Pharaoh and his people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout the chapter He compares Egypt to a huge cedar, like those of Assyria, which filled itself with pride and fell. The "trees of Eden" are images of powerful nations. It is poetic language, and scholars debate the details of this picture of the place of the dead.

For today: power, success, and fame do not make us invincible. God opposes the proud, so it is wise to be thankful for what we have and to live with humility, remembering that everything comes from Him.
exp.31:1:
God tells Ezekiel to raise a lament over Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. He compares him to a young lion among the nations and to a sea monster, which in Hebrew is a large creature of the water, perhaps a crocodile. This creature stirred up the rivers with its feet, muddied the waters, and trampled the banks.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is among the exiles in Babylon. Egypt believed itself powerful and untouchable, but God announces its fall. The image shows a proud ruler who stirs up everything in his path.

For today: power and success do not give us the right to trample on others. If God gives us influence, let us use it to care for others, not to muddy their lives. Examine today how you treat those who depend on you.
exp.31:2:
It says that God himself will catch the pharaoh of Egypt the way one catches a large animal in the water. The net and the throw-net (a round fishing net thrown by hand) show that he will not be able to escape. God will use many peoples, that is, gathered nations, to drag him up onto the shore.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is to sing a funeral song of lament over the pharaoh. The pharaoh was like a monster that stirred up the waters, and his pride and power harmed others. God announces that his fall will come.

For today: No one is so powerful that God cannot humble him. We can trust that He sees injustice, and we can also examine our own pride before He has to break it.
exp.31:3:
God says he will leave Pharaoh lying on dry land, abandoned out in the open field. There the birds of the sky and the wild animals will feed on him. The phrase about the surface of the field is explained as the ground's surface, and the word for filling him completely means he will be satisfied with them completely. It is a strong image of total defeat.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and commands him to raise a lament over Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He is compared to a crocodile or sea monster that stirred up the rivers. Scholars understand this as announcing God's judgment against the pride and violence of Egypt, which believed itself invincible. The image is poetic, not a literal description.

For today: no human power or success is above God. If we ever feel tempted to trust in our own strength or to treat others badly, let us remember that God resists the proud. We can rest in Him with humility.
exp.31:7:
