It says that God will make all the bright lights of the sky grow dark because of the pharaoh. The lights are the sun, the moon, and the stars. He will also bring darkness over his land.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over the pharaoh of Egypt, who was thought to be powerful like a monster of the river. The darkening of the heavenly lights is poetic language: it shows that the fall of a great king shakes the whole world. Some see it only as a picture; others remember the plague of darkness in Egypt. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: no human power is above God. If something intimidates you or impresses you too much, remember that God governs even the great. Trust in Him and live with humility.
exp.31:11:
God says he will bring down the people of Egypt by the swords of mighty men. Those warriors are called the most terrible of the nations, the strongest of all peoples. They will destroy Egypt's pride, meaning its haughtiness and arrogance, and all its great multitude will be laid low.

The Lord GOD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Pharaoh. The verse before says that the sword of the king of Babylon will come against Egypt. God uses one powerful nation to judge the pride of another. Scholars agree that Babylon is the main instrument, although the text speaks of the mighty in general.

For today: power, wealth, or number of people is not a safe foundation for life. Egypt trusted in its greatness, but God rules over all nations. Today we can examine whether our pride makes us trust in ourselves, and humbly return to depending on God.
exp.31:12:
This verse says that God will destroy all the animals of Egypt that live beside the great waters, that is, the Nile River and its canals. After that, no human foot or animal hoof will stir up those waters again. Stirring up the water means making it dirty or churning it. The animals here may refer to livestock and, figuratively, to people and their power.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces judgment against Egypt and its pharaoh, who thought himself powerful and proud. God would use the sword of Babylon. Some understand the still waters as the end of Egyptian activity and splendor; others see them as an image of desolation. The final purpose is that they will know that God is the Lord.

For today: God humbles human pride, whether in nations or in individuals. Today we can examine what we trust in more than in Him and surrender it to Him with humility.
exp.31:14:
He says that God will leave Egypt desolate. When God strikes all who live there, they will know that He is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. This word is part of a lament against Pharaoh and Egypt, a proud nation that felt secure. The verses before it use images of waters and rivers, and the text does not make clear every detail of how it would be fulfilled.

For today: nothing we have, not money, strength, or reputation, is a secure foundation for life. It is wise to trust God and not in what can be lost. Today you can hand Him your sense of security and ask Him for humility.
exp.31:16:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel on an exact date: the twelfth year, on the fifteenth day of the month. The verse does not name the month, and some older copies have it differently, so it cannot be known for certain which one is correct.

Ezekiel speaks here as a prophet who was living in exile in Babylon. God gives him a new message, a lament over Egypt, which follows the announcements of judgment against that nation. The date shows that this word was real and came at a specific moment in history.

For today: God acts in real history and still speaks through his Word. We can read the Bible with confidence, and set aside a fixed time each day to listen to him.
exp.31:23:
Elam was an ancient and powerful people, and the passage says that Elam, with all its army, is now in the world of the dead, lying around its own grave. All of them died in battle, killed by the sword. The phrase about being uncircumcised points to people who did not carry the mark of Israel's covenant. They spread terror among the living, but they ended in shame, along with the others who go down to the grave.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. This is a lament over Egypt, which is going to be brought down to the world of the dead. God shows him that other proud and violent nations, such as Assyria, Elam, Meshech, and Tubal, already met that same end. Scholars understand the scene as a poetic image, not as a literal map of the afterlife.

For today: power used to frighten and dominate does not last. You can ask yourself whether you use your influence to serve or to intimidate, and ask God to make you humble and just.
exp.31:28:
This verse says that Edom (Idumea), with its kings and all its princes, will also be in the place of the dead. Although they were powerful and strong, they fell by the sword and will lie down with those who were not part of Israel, the peoples outside the covenant, and with those who go down to the grave, that is, those who die.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Egypt and Pharaoh. Ezekiel describes a place of the dead where the powerful nations that fell are gathered together. Edom appears as an example: its strength did not save it. Scholars understand the details of this place in different ways, since it is poetic language.

For today: power, fame, and money do not protect us from the end of life. It is wise to live with humility, to use well what we have, and to trust in God, who alone endures.
exp.31:29:
This verse says that the princes of the north and all of Sidon, who once spread terror, now lie dead in the grave. The word for "north" means north. "Uncircumcised" here describes the pagan peoples, and lying down with them was a dishonorable death. "By the sword" means by the sword. Their strength did not save them, and they were put to shame.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament against Egypt. He shows Pharaoh that other powerful nations have already fallen: Edom, Sidon, and the peoples of the north. Exactly which group the northern peoples are is not known for certain. The message is clear: no empire escapes God's judgment.

For today: power, money, or fame do not give us true security. If we use our strength to dominate or harm others, it ends in shame. Today you can use what you have to serve, and place your trust in God, who is just.
exp.31:30:
Ezekiel 32:31 tells us that when Pharaoh arrives in the place of the dead, he will see the other nations that have already fallen, just as he has. Pharaoh will be comforted in the sense that he will find some relief in seeing that he is not the only one. "Slain by the sword" means killed in war. The verse stresses that Pharaoh and all his army will also die in this way.

God himself speaks here, through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament against Egypt. The whole chapter describes Egypt going down to the grave together with Assyria, Elam, Edom, and Sidon, powerful nations that spread terror. Many read it as a message of judgment against Egypt's pride. Pharaoh's "comfort" is ironic: it is not true hope, only the company of others in ruin.

No power, success, or human fame protects us from God's judgment. Today we can examine where we place our trust: in our own strength or in God? Let us live with humility, using what we have to serve and not to dominate.
exp.31:31:
This verse says that God allowed Pharaoh and his great army to spread fear in the land of the living, but in the end they themselves will lie among the dead, killed by the sword. The phrase about those who were not circumcised refers to foreign peoples who did not bear the sign of the covenant with Israel, and the phrase about lying down means they will lie there, without life.

God himself speaks here, through the prophet Ezekiel. It is a lament over Egypt, part of a series of messages against the nations. God shows that Pharaoh, though powerful and feared, will end up like other proud kingdoms that have already fallen. Scholars understand some details of these images of the grave in different ways, but the central message is clear: no human power escapes the judgment of God.

For today: do not let yourself be impressed or frightened by human power, and do not trust in your own strength. God is the one who has the last word. Live with humility and trust in him.
exp.32:0:
This verse is an opening phrase.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. God gives him a new assignment: to be like a watchman, that is, a lookout who warns of danger. With this phrase a section begins in which God reminds him of his responsibility to warn the people.

For today: before speaking, it is good to listen. If we want to encourage or advise others, let us start by reading the Bible and praying, so that our words come from God and not only from our own opinions. And when He shows us something, let us say it with love and truth.
exp.32:1:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to his people using a comparison. When God allows war to come upon a land, the people of that place choose a man from among them and set him up as a watchman, that is, a guard who keeps careful watch from a tower and warns of danger.

The LORD speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God gives him his task as a spiritual watchman for Israel. The image was familiar: a sentinel warned the city when the enemy drew near. In this way Ezekiel was to warn the people.

For today: if God places us near someone, we can speak to them with love and truth when we see that they are going down the wrong path. We should also listen with humility when someone warns us with good intentions.
exp.32:2:
This verse speaks of the watchman, the sentry who sees danger coming, blows the trumpet (a horn trumpet) and warns the people. "Warn" means he gives the alert in time. His job is to see and to sound the warning clearly.

God is speaking to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. God uses the picture of a city that appoints a watchman to explain Ezekiel's mission: to warn the people of the judgment that is coming. If the people hear the warning and pay no attention, the responsibility is theirs. If the watchman stays silent, he is the one who will answer for it.

For today: if God has shown you a truth that can help someone, do not keep it silent out of fear or shame. Speak it with love, with respect and with clarity, and let the other person decide.
exp.32:5:
This verse speaks of a watchman who sees an enemy army coming but does not sound the trumpet to warn the people. If the people die without having been warned, they still bear their own guilt, but God will hold the watchman responsible for his silence.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. He appoints him as a spiritual watchman over the people. His task was to warn them clearly on God's behalf, so that they could change their course before judgment came.

For today: if God has given you a truth that helps others, do not keep it silent out of fear or comfort. Share it with love, humility and clarity, and let each person decide.
exp.32:7:
God says that if He warns the wicked person that he will die because of his evil way, and the watchman does not speak to turn him from it, that wicked person will die for his sin. But God will hold the watchman responsible for that death. To hold someone responsible means to make them answerable for what happened.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. He appoints him as a watchman for the people. Just as a sentinel sounds the horn when the enemy comes, Ezekiel was to warn of judgment and call people to repentance. The responsibility to speak was his; the responsibility to respond belonged to each person.

For today: do not stay silent out of fear or comfort when you can speak with love and truth to someone who is turning away from God. Do it with humility, prayer, and patience, leaving the outcome in God's hands.
exp.32:8:
This verse says that if the watchman warns the wicked person (the one who lives in evil) to turn from his evil way, and even so the wicked person does not turn away, he will die for his own sin. The watchman, that is, the one who keeps watch and sounds the alarm, is free of blame.

God speaks to Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He appoints him as a watchman for Israel, like the lookout of a city who sounds the trumpet when danger comes. His duty was to speak faithfully; the decision to respond belonged to each listener. Then God makes clear that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but wants them to turn back and live.

For today: when you have the chance, speak with love and truth to someone who is going down a wrong path, and leave the outcome in God's hands.
exp.32:9:
God tells Ezekiel to repeat to Israel what the people are saying: their rebellions and sins weigh on them, they are wasting away little by little, and they ask how they will be able to live. It is a complaint mixed with despair.

Ezekiel was a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God had appointed him as a watchman, someone who warns of danger. Here Israel was already suffering the consequences of its sin and felt there was no way out. God answers right after, in the next verse, that He does not want anyone to die, but wants them to turn back to Him and live.

For today: if guilt makes you think there is no hope, do not stay lamenting. Turn back to God with sincerity, because He offers forgiveness and a new life to those who return to Him.
exp.32:13:
God tells Ezekiel that when he warns the wicked person, "You will surely die," that sentence is not final. If the wicked person turns away from his sin and does what is lawful and right (that is, acts uprightly and deals fairly with others), the warning changes course. "Wicked" means someone who lives without taking God into account.

God speaks to Ezekiel, whom He set as a watchman over the people of Israel during the exile in Babylon. Some of the people thought they had no remedy for their past sins. God answers that His warning seeks to lead to repentance, not only to condemn. The following verse shows what that change involves: returning what was stolen and living in obedience.

For today: no one is so far away that they cannot return to God, and no one should feel secure because of their past. If anything in your life pulls you away from Him, today you can change course with concrete actions, such as asking forgiveness, making right a wrong, and treating others justly.
exp.32:21:
He says that God's hand was upon Ezekiel in the evening, before the survivor from Jerusalem arrived. Also, God opened his mouth before the man appeared in the morning. From then on, Ezekiel no longer stayed silent. Someone who fled and was saved is one who got away. The hand of the Lord expresses the power of God acting upon the prophet.

Ezekiel speaks as a prophet exiled in Babylon. Earlier, God had told him he would be unable to speak until the news of Jerusalem's fall arrived (Ezekiel 3:26; 24:27). Now that news has come, in the twelfth year of the exile, and God restores his speech. Many interpret the muteness as a limit on speaking freely, and not everyone understands it the same way.

God knows how to prepare us before difficult news. When an unexpected blow comes, we can trust that he has already gone ahead of us. We can also ask him for wise words to comfort others and to speak the truth to them.
exp.32:23:
Ezekiel reports that some of those who remained among the ruins of Israel, after the fall of Jerusalem, reasoned this way: "Abraham was alone and God gave him the land; we are many, so the land is all the more ours." The phrase about them speaking is simply a way of saying they kept saying this among themselves and to others.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Those who stayed in the land took pride in the promise made to Abraham, but they lived in violence, idolatry and immorality. In the verses that follow, God answers them that they cannot claim his promises while they despise his ways.

For today: relying on an inheritance, a family or a religious tradition is not enough to make us feel secure before God. God's promises are received with faith and sincere obedience. Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly live as his people.
exp.32:27:
God says that he will turn the land into a desolate and empty place. What gave the people pride, their strength and their power, will come to an end. The mountains of Israel will be left in ruins, so badly that no one will want to pass through them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to those who remained in the land of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem. They assumed the land belonged to them, even though they continued in violence, idolatry, and immorality. God shows them that they cannot claim his blessing while living in injustice. His judgment aims to make them recognize who he is.

Today, we can examine what we take pride in or feel secure about. If we trust in what we have and do not obey God, that security is false. Today is a good day to return to him with humility.
exp.32:30:
God tells Ezekiel that the people come to hear him as a crowd, as if they were his people and wanted to obey. But they do not put into practice what they hear. Their mouths say one thing, but their hearts run after their own gain.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Some from Jerusalem had already been taken away, and the people went to hear him with curiosity, almost as someone enjoys a song. The verses that follow compare him to a pleasant singer. God warns them that when what was announced comes to pass, they will know that a prophet was among them.

For today: it is not enough to listen to sermons or to read the Bible with enjoyment. Ask yourself this week what specific teaching of God you can put into practice, even if it costs you, and decide to do it.
exp.32:31:
This verse says that the prophet Ezekiel was to the people like a singer of love songs, with a pleasant voice and skill on an instrument. The people enjoyed listening to him, but they did not do what he said.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Some of the people would come to hear him the way someone goes to a show, remarking to one another, "Come, let us hear what the word is from the LORD." Their mouths showed affection, but their hearts were after gain. God makes clear that when what was announced came to pass, they would know that there had indeed been a prophet among them.

For today: it is not enough to enjoy a good message or a good sermon. After hearing the Bible, choose one specific thing God has asked of you and put it into practice this week. That is what truly hearing means.
exp.32:32:
This verse says that when what God announced comes to pass, the people will recognize that there really was a prophet among them. The word "lo" in the verse is an exclamation that stresses that this fulfillment is certain, and "it" refers to what Ezekiel had prophesied, namely the judgment on Jerusalem.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet in exile in Babylon. The exiles were going to listen to him the way someone attends a good concert, enjoying his words but not obeying them. Their hearts were still set on gain. God assures him that reality will eventually prove his message right.

For today: it is not enough to enjoy a good biblical message or good Christian music. Before life forces us to recognize the truth, let us choose today one teaching we have heard and put it into practice this week.
exp.33:1:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to speak firmly to the shepherds of Israel, that is, to its leaders. He calls them to account with a cry of grief and warning. Their failing is that they care only for themselves, feeding themselves rather than the flock. But a shepherd exists to feed and care for the flock.

The Lord God speaks through Ezekiel, a prophet who was among the exiles in Babylon. The people were suffering, and their rulers, and probably other leaders as well, had neglected them. The verses that follow describe in detail how they took advantage of the sheep instead of caring for them.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, in the family, the church, or at work, ask yourself whom you are really serving. Leading means caring, not taking advantage.
exp.33:3:
This verse says that Israel's leaders failed to care for the weakest people. They did not strengthen the weak sheep, did not heal the sick one, did not bind up the one with the broken leg, did not bring back the one that had wandered off and was lost in the hills, and did not search for the one that was lost. Instead, they ruled over the people with harshness and violence.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He calls the kings and leaders the shepherds, who took advantage of the people instead of caring for them. God rebukes them because the sheep are his, and he saw them scattered and without protection.

For today: if you lead others, in your family, your church, or your work, ask yourself whom you have neglected. This week, reach out to someone who is weak or discouraged, listen to them, and help them with tenderness, not pressure.
exp.33:4:
They were scattered because they had no shepherd to watch over them. Without protection, they became easy prey for any wild animal. The words that describe them as scattered mean dispersed, without direction and without unity.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He accuses Israel's leaders, here called shepherds, because they took advantage of the people instead of caring for them. The sheep are the people. Many understand the beasts as the nations or the threats that harmed Israel, though the text uses figurative language.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, such as in your family, church, or workplace, ask yourself whether you serve those you look after or use them for your own benefit. And if you feel without guidance, remember that God himself promises to seek out his sheep (Ezekiel 34:11).
exp.33:8:
It says that God calls the shepherds' attention and orders them to hear his word. The word "hear" here carries the sense of listening closely and paying attention. Here "shepherds" does not mean simple keepers of sheep, but the leaders of Israel. With this call, God prepares to say something serious to them.

The Lord speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, to Israel, who was living in exile. The leaders had taken care of themselves and not of the people, who were like a scattered flock exposed to danger. For this reason God announces to them that he will call them to account and that he himself will care for his sheep.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, in the church, the family or the workplace, ask yourself whether you are seeking your own benefit or their good. Before leading, learn to listen to the word of God.
exp.33:12:
God promises to bring out his sheep, who are his people, from the nations where they were scattered. He will gather them and bring them back to their own land. There he will care for them and feed them on the mountains of Israel, beside the streams and in all the inhabited places of the country.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier he had rebuked the shepherds of Israel, that is, its leaders, because they abandoned the people. Now God says that he himself will be the one who cares for his flock. Many Christians also see here a foreshadowing of Jesus, the good shepherd, although this is interpreted in different ways.

If you feel lost or far away, remember that God seeks you and wants to care for you. Open your heart to him in prayer and look for a community of faith where you can be accompanied.
exp.33:13:
God promises to care for his people the way a shepherd cares for his sheep. He will lead them to good pasture, and on the high mountains of Israel they will have their fold, which is the pen or resting place where they lie down. There they will lie down in peace, and they will feed in a good pasture, meaning abundant and rich.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel's leaders, called shepherds, had neglected and mistreated the people, and the sheep were scattered into other lands. God promises that he himself will gather them, bring them back, and care for them with justice.

For today: when you feel tired, lost, or abandoned, remember that God wants to care for you personally. Take a moment today to pray and rest in his care, trusting that he knows how to give you what you need.
exp.33:17:
God asks the strong sheep whether it is not enough for them to eat the best pasture. Instead of leaving something for the others, they trample what is left over and foul the clean water. Here the water is described as still, clear water, and the trampling of the pasture is the same as treading it down with their feet.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier he had condemned the shepherds of Israel, who fed themselves and neglected the flock. Now God addresses the powerful sheep who take advantage of the weak. He promises to care for the injured and the lost, and to judge between one sheep and another. Some understand this to refer to the leaders and wealthy people of that time, though the text speaks in the language of shepherding.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we use what God has given us only for ourselves. Sharing time, resources, and attention with those who have less is a concrete way of reflecting the heart of the good Shepherd.
exp.33:18:
This verse says that the weaker sheep have to feed on trampled grass and drink muddied water, because the strong sheep first ate the best and then spoiled what was left.

God himself speaks here, through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier he had rebuked the shepherds of Israel, who looked after themselves and not after the flock. Now he addresses the strong sheep, who were also mistreating the weak. God promises to judge between one sheep and another. Many understand the sheep to represent the people, and the passage to criticize the powerful who took advantage of the most needy.

For today: it is not enough to take only what is ours. Ask yourself whether what you do, buy, or waste leaves something good for others. This week, look for a concrete way to share with or care for someone who has fewer resources.
exp.33:20:
It says that the strong sheep pushed with their side and shoulder, and struck the weak ones with their horns, until they left them scattered and outside the flock. Pushing hard is the sense of the verb for pushing with the side and shoulder; striking with the horns is the sense of the verb for butting; and the weak ones are the diseased.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier he had rebuked the shepherds of Israel for neglecting the people. Now he also rebukes the powerful within the people, who were abusing the most vulnerable. God promises to judge between sheep and sheep, to save his flock, and to raise up a shepherd, a figure many Christians see as a sign of Christ.

Today this invites us to examine how we use our strength, influence, or position. God cares for the weak; so it is wise to protect, listen to, and welcome those who feel excluded, in the church, the family, or the workplace.
exp.33:26:
This verse promises that the land will once again yield good fruit and that the people will live there without fear. God says he will break the bonds of their yoke, that is, the straps or ties that held the yoke in place, and free them from those who had enslaved them. Then they will know that he is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during Israel's exile. Earlier, he has criticized the shepherds who mistreated the people. Now he promises to become their shepherd himself and to make a covenant of peace. Many see in this a hope that also points to Christ, the good shepherd, though this is understood in different ways.

For today: if you feel tied down by some burden or by the abuse of others, pray and trust that God can give rest and freedom. Ask him to help you recognize his care and to walk in peace.
exp.33:30:
God tells his people that they are his sheep, the ones he himself cares for and feeds. The word for the place where sheep eat is the pasture. The verse also makes clear that they are people, that is, fragile human beings, and that he is their God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier, God rebuked the shepherds of Israel, that is, the leaders who took advantage of the people and neglected them. Now he promises to care for them himself and to give them a shepherd, here called a plant, which many Christians understand as a sign of the Messiah. He ends by reminding them of the relationship: they are his, and he is their God.

For today: even when you feel weak or have been neglected by others, God calls you his. Rest in his care, and help others with the same tenderness.
exp.34:1:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," an expression that stresses that he is a simple human being. He is told to set his face toward Mount Seir, that is, to look straight at that region with determination, and to announce a message of judgment against it.

The Lord, the God of Israel, is speaking. Seir was the mountainous region of Edom, a neighboring people descended from Esau. Ezekiel was prophesying during the exile in Babylon, and the next chapter shows that Edom took advantage of Israel's fall and kept up an old hostility. God presents himself here as the defender of his wounded people.

For today: God sees injustice and is not indifferent to those who rejoice in the suffering of others. We can trust that he will act justly, so there is no need for us to take revenge. And we should examine whether we ourselves take delight in the downfall of others.
exp.34:2:
God commands Ezekiel to deliver a message against Mount Seir. God says that he is against that place, that he will stretch out his hand to punish it, and that he will make it most desolate, a total ruin with no one living there.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Seir was the land of Edom, a people descended from Esau and a neighbor of Israel. According to the verses that follow, God judges them for their lasting hostility and because they handed the Israelites over to the sword when they were suffering. Here "Mount Seir" stands for the whole people of Edom.

God sees how we treat those who suffer. It is not good to hold on to old grudges or to take advantage of the fall of others. Today we can choose compassion, help someone going through a hard time, and leave justice in God's hands.
exp.34:3:
It says that God will leave the cities of Mount Seir in ruins, and that this place will be destroyed and empty. In the end, the people will know that the Lord is Jehovah, that is, the true God who does what he says.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Seir was the region of Edom, a neighboring people of Israel. According to the text, Edom held a long-lasting hostility and handed the Israelites over to the sword when they were suffering. For this reason God announces judgment against them.

For today: do not rejoice in or take advantage of the pain of others, and do not hold a grudge for years. God sees injustice and also sees how we treat those who suffer. Ask him to give you a compassionate heart that is willing to forgive.
exp.34:11:
God says that he heard everything Edom (Mount Seir) spoke against the mountains of Israel. Edom's insults and offenses, and the fact that they said them out loud, are what the verse is about. Edom was rejoicing that Israel lay in ruins and thought they could now take the land for themselves.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom, Israel's neighbor, had an old hostility toward that people. When Israel fell to Babylon, Edom rejoiced and wanted to seize its territory. God makes clear that the land was not theirs and that he had heard every word. By speaking against Israel, they also spoke against God.

For today: God hears what we say, including when we rejoice over the downfall of others. We can ask him for help not to mock someone who is suffering, but to pray for them, help them, and trust that God is the just judge.
exp.34:13:
This verse says that God himself speaks and announces judgment against Edom, here called the mountain of Seir. When the whole earth rejoices, God will make Edom desolate, that is, a wasteland, empty and ruined. Some understand that the rejoicing is that of the nations who will see God's justice; the text does not make this completely clear.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom had mocked Israel when it was destroyed, and had spoken with pride against God. The Lord says that he heard everything. Therefore, what Edom did to others, God will repay to him.

Today we can learn that God hears our words, including those we say with mockery or pride. We should not rejoice when others fall. Rather, let us ask God for a humble and compassionate heart, and leave justice in his hands.
exp.34:14:
God says to Mount Seir, that is, to Edom (Idumea), that it will suffer the same thing it rejoiced over. Edom was glad when the land of Israel was laid waste, and now God says that Edom too will be left desolate. The inheritance is the land God gave to his people; the word "desolate" means ravaged and left in ruins. In the end, everyone will acknowledge that the Lord is God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom, a neighbor and distant relative of Israel, mocked its fall and spoke proudly against God. He heard it, and therefore he announces judgment. The text presents this sentence as a response to that attitude.

Today, this verse invites us not to rejoice in the misfortune of others, not even in that of someone we dislike. We can pray for those who suffer and help them, remembering that God sees our words and attitudes, and that He is the one who judges with justice.
exp.35:0:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to speak to the mountains of Israel, as if they could hear him. "Son of man" is the way God addresses Ezekiel, reminding him that he is an ordinary human being. The word "hear" in the verse is the command to listen, and "the Lord" is the name of the God of Israel.

God speaks, and Ezekiel is his messenger. The mountains represent the land of Israel, which had been left desolate and mocked by the neighboring nations. The verses that follow explain that God responds to those taunts. After chapters of judgment, here begins a message of hope and restoration. Some see in this promises for the Israel of Ezekiel's time, and others also see a foreshadowing of things to come.

For today: when you feel that your life lies in ruins or that others mock you, remember that God still speaks and cares about what seems abandoned. Listen to him with hope.
exp.35:2:
God tells Ezekiel to speak on his behalf. He says that Israel's enemies tore the land apart and swallowed it up on every side, that is, they conquered it completely, so that they could keep it as their own inheritance. In this way, Israel became a subject of mockery and a cause of shame among the nations.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during Israel's exile. The mountains represent the wounded and humbled land. The neighboring nations, such as Edom, mocked it and wanted to take it for themselves. God shows that He sees this injustice and that He will respond, preparing a promise of restoration.

For today: if you go through shame, mockery, or loss, remember that God sees your pain and does not forget you. You can bring that wound to Him with confidence, trusting that He will be faithful to restore.
exp.35:3:
God speaks to the land of Israel as if it could hear him: to the mountains, hills, streams and valleys, and also to the ruins and empty cities. These places had been plundered and mocked by the surrounding nations.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes during the exile in Babylon. The land had been left in ruins, and neighboring peoples, such as Edom, rejoiced and wanted to take it for themselves. God answers that mockery and promises to act on behalf of his people and his land.

For today: when you feel that your life is like a place in ruins, and others mock or look down on you, remember that God sees you and speaks to you. He does not stay silent in the face of your pain. You can bring him your shame and wait for his restoration.
exp.35:4:
God says that he has spoken in the fire of his zeal, that is, in an intense love for his land and his people, against the neighboring nations and against Edom (Idumea). They took possession of the land of Israel as if it were their own, with joy and with malice, in order to plunder those who had been driven out of it. Malice means deep hatred or resentment, and plunder means the spoils taken from others.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while Israel is in exile and its land lies in ruins. The neighboring peoples mocked and took advantage of its fall. God responds by defending his people and his land, and announces that these nations will bear their shame.

For today: God sees injustice and does not rejoice with those who delight in another's misfortune. We can avoid mocking those who fall, and instead help and pray, trusting that God does justice in his own time.
exp.35:5:
God commands the prophet Ezekiel to speak to the land of Israel, as if the mountains, hills, streams and valleys could hear him. God says he speaks in zeal (a fierce love that will not tolerate injustice) and in anger (strong wrath), because the land has borne the shame and contempt of the neighboring nations.

The Lord speaks through Ezekiel during Israel's exile. The surrounding peoples, especially Edom, mocked Israel and tried to take its land for themselves. God promises to defend his name and his people, and afterward to restore the land.

For today: when you feel ashamed or looked down upon, remember that God sees your pain and does not ignore it. Bring that humiliation to him in prayer and trust that he knows how to restore what others tried to destroy.
exp.35:11:
In this verse God promises that his people Israel will once again walk upon the mountains of Israel. The phrase about bringing them back means that he will bring them home to live there. The promise that they will possess the land means the land will belong to them again, and it will be theirs as an inheritance, something received and passed down to their children. God adds that the land will no longer bereave them of their children, meaning it will no longer be a place of loss and death.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing the mountains of Israel. The people had been carried into exile and the land lay in ruins. The neighboring nations mocked, and so God promises to restore both the land and his people.

For today: God knows how to rebuild what seems lost. If there are areas of your life or your family that lie in ruins, you can wait on Him with confidence and pray for their restoration.
exp.35:14:
God promises the land of Israel, speaking to it as if it were a person, that it will no longer have to hear insults from other nations or bear their mockery. The word for insults is rendered here as words of contempt and disgrace. He also says that he will no longer let the people of the land be bereaved of their children, meaning that the land will no longer be a place of loss and misfortune.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel at a time when the people were living in exile. The neighboring nations mocked Israel, saying that its land devoured its inhabitants. God answers by promising to restore the land and its honor. The verse that follows reminds the people that they themselves had defiled the land with their sin.

For today: if you carry shame over mistakes from the past or over what others say about you, remember that God is able to restore. Bring your story to him honestly and trust that he can give back your dignity and hope.
exp.35:16:
God speaks to Ezekiel, called "son of man," and reminds him that Israel lived in its own land and defiled it by their conduct and their actions. The phrase about uncleanness of a removed woman refers to the ritual impurity of the law of Moses; God says that their way of living was as impure to him as that.

The Lord speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. God explains why the exile happened: it was not chance, but the result of violence and idolatry, as the following verses say. This reminder prepares the promises of restoration that come later in the chapter.

For today: God cares about how we live, not only about what we say we believe. We can ask him to show us the areas where we need to change, and remember that he also offers forgiveness and renewal to anyone who turns to him sincerely.
exp.35:19:
This verse says that when the people of Israel came to the nations where they were taken, they caused God's holy name to be treated without respect. "Profaned" means treating as common what is sacred. People were saying, "These are the people of the Lord, and they had to leave his land." In other words, their defeat made God seem weak or unfaithful.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier he explains that he judged Israel for its violence and its idolatry. But now he shows his concern for his name: what the people did and suffered affected how the nations saw God. For that reason he promises to act, not because of anything they deserved, but for the sake of his holy name.

For today: those of us who say we belong to God represent his name. Today you can take care in how you treat others, in your honesty and in your words, so that others see in you a faithful reflection of him.
exp.35:21:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to say to the people of Israel that what he is going to do for them is not because they deserve it. He will do it for the sake of his holy name, that is, his reputation and his character, which Israel stained among the nations where they were scattered.

The Lord speaks through Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. The nations saw Israel defeated and driven out of its land, and they thought poorly of the God of that people. For this reason God will act, and the text that follows promises to gather them and bring them back to their land.

For today: Our lives speak well or badly of God before others. When we fail, we do not depend on our merits but on God's grace. That grace invites us to live in a way that honors his name, with humility and gratitude.
exp.35:22:
God says he will show that his great name is holy. That name had been profaned, that is, treated as something common and without respect, among the nations. Israel had dishonored it by the way they lived. When God acts, the nations will know that he is the Lord, seeing his holiness displayed in his people.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel was scattered among the nations because of its sin, and its bad conduct made others think poorly of God. He makes clear that he will restore his people, not because they deserve it, but for the sake of his own name. Then he promises to cleanse them and bring them back to their land.

For today: our lives speak of God before others. We can ask him to cleanse us and help us live in a way that lets others see his goodness, trusting that his grace, and not our merits, sustains us.
exp.35:26:
God promises to put his Spirit within his people. With that Spirit, they will walk according to his commandments, keep his judgments, and put them into practice, that is, they will truly obey them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon, who had failed to obey him. He promises to restore them, cleanse them, and give them a new heart. This obedience would not come from their own effort, but from God's work in them. Christians often see here a foreshadowing of the work of the Holy Spirit in the New Testament, though it can be debated how this relates exactly to Israel.

For today: do not rely only on your own willpower. Ask God to change you from the inside through his Spirit, and take one concrete step of obedience today, trusting in his help.
exp.35:29:
God promises that he will make the fruit of the trees and of the fields grow much more abundantly. The reason is that Israel will never again suffer the shame of going hungry before the other nations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to a people exiled because of their sin. In the neighboring countries, drought and famine were seen as a sign of divine abandonment. God promises to restore the land and also the heart of his people. He then makes clear that he does this for the sake of his name and his grace, not because they deserve it.

For today: God cares for our needs and also for our hearts. When you receive his help, do not see it as a reward for your effort, but as grace. Respond with gratitude, humility, and a sincere desire to live better.
exp.35:30:
It says that when God carries out his work of restoration, the people will remember their past misconduct. By recalling their evil ways, their deeds that were not good, their sins, and their abominations (detestable things, above all idolatry), they will feel shame for themselves.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks for God to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. Earlier God had promised them a new heart, his Spirit, and abundant harvests. Now he makes clear that he restores them not because of anything they have earned, but by his grace. The shame described here is the result of receiving that undeserved forgiveness.

For today: when you remember your mistakes, do not sink into hopeless guilt. Let that memory lead you to humble repentance, and to thankfulness that God's goodness does not depend on what we deserve.
exp.35:34:
It tells that the people, on seeing the restored land, will remark with amazement that the place which had been ruined now looks like the garden of Eden, and that the cities which were ruins are today fortified and secure.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites in exile. Their land had been left in ruin because of judgment, but God promises to cleanse them from their sins and restore them. The neighboring peoples will see the change and recognize that it was the work of God, not of men.

For today: God can restore what seems lost, whether a life, a family, or a relationship. He begins by cleansing the heart. We can come to Him with hope, and when He restores something, we can give Him the credit.
exp.35:35:
This verse says that the neighboring nations that survive will see Israel's restoration and will acknowledge that it was God who did it. The ruined cities are the places that lie in ruins, and the devastated lands are the areas that have been wasted and left empty. God promises to rebuild and to plant again, and he assures that he will do what he has said.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The land of Israel lay in ruins and the surrounding peoples mocked it. God promises to return the land to them and to give them a new heart, so that his name will be recognized among the nations.

For today: when your life or your family feels like it is in ruins, do not think that God can no longer do anything. He is able to rebuild what seems lost. Trust his word and give him time, while you keep walking with him in obedience.
exp.36:2:
God asks Ezekiel whether these dry bones can live again. "Son of man" is a way of addressing the prophet, reminding him that he is simply a human being. Ezekiel does not say yes or no; he answers that only God knows.

God speaks, and Ezekiel responds. The prophet was among the people of Israel exiled in Babylon, and the vision represents a nation that felt its hope was dead. Many interpreters see here a promise of restoration for Israel. Afterward God commands him to prophesy to the bones and promises to give them breath and life.

There are situations that seem finished, such as a broken relationship, a faith that has gone out, or a lost dream. We can imitate Ezekiel's response: not pretending that everything is fine, nor giving up, but humbly saying to God, "You know." Handing over what seems dead opens space for his work.
exp.36:5:
God tells Ezekiel to announce to the dry bones what He will do. He will put sinews (tendons) on them to join the bones, make flesh grow, and cover them with skin. Then He will give them spirit, which can also be understood as breath or the breath of life. With that they will live, and they will know that God is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the middle of the exile in Babylon. The bones represent Israel, which felt it had no hope. The same chapter explains it this way: it is a promise of the people's restoration. Some also see in it an image of resurrection, but the text emphasizes the renewal of Israel.

For today: when you feel that something in your life is dry or has no way out, do not depend only on what you see. Pray, trust in God's Word, and wait for Him to be able to restore life and hope.
exp.36:6:
He says that Ezekiel obeyed God and spoke to the dry bones. As he spoke, there was a noise, there was a shaking, and the bones began to come together, each bone with the one that belonged to it.

God shows Ezekiel a vision of a valley full of bones. According to the same chapter, those bones represent Israel, which in exile felt that its hope had died. God promises to restore their life and to rebuild them as a people.

For today: when a situation seems hopeless, we can obey what God asks of us, even if it means speaking his word in faith, and trust that he can give life where we see only ruin. He works step by step.
exp.36:7:
He says that Ezekiel saw the dry bones coming back together: the sinews appeared, the flesh grew, and the skin covered them. But they were still lifeless bodies, because they lacked the breath of life, which here can also be understood as breath or wind. The sinews probably refer to the tendons that join the bones.

God shows Ezekiel a vision of a valley full of bones. They represent Israel, discouraged and in exile, who felt they had no hope. God promises to restore his people, and the restoration happens in stages: first the body and then the life.

For today: sometimes a life can look orderly on the outside and be empty on the inside. We can ask God not only to fix our circumstances but also to give us new life through his Spirit, and to wait on him with confidence.
exp.36:8:
God tells Ezekiel to prophesy to the "wind", that is, the breath or wind of life. He is to call to it from the four corners of the earth so that it blows on the dead and they live. The verse of the word itself has been removed, as the verse uses "breath" and "wind" directly.

God speaks, and Ezekiel is his prophet. The people of Israel were in exile, without temple or land, and felt that everything had ended. The dry bones are an image of that despair. The verses that follow explain that they represent the house of Israel, and the vision announces that God will restore them.

For today: when you feel that something in your life is dry or beyond repair, do not stop praying and trusting in God's Word. Only he can give new life, and he invites us to take part by speaking with faith and hope.
exp.36:10:
God explains to Ezekiel what the dry bones he saw mean: they are the whole people of Israel. They themselves feel this way and say that their bones are dried up, that their hope is lost, and that they are cut off for their parts, cut off and separated like a felled tree.

The Lord speaks with the prophet Ezekiel. The people were in exile in Babylon, far from their land and their temple, and many thought that God had finished with them. The vision answers that discouragement: God promises to give them life again and bring them back home.

For today: when you feel that everything is over and that there is no hope left, tell God honestly how you feel. He can give life where you see only dryness. Trust in his word and wait for his work, even when it takes time.
exp.36:11:
What it says: God commands Ezekiel to announce a message to his people. God promises to open their graves, to make them come up out of their tombs, and to bring them back to the land of Israel.

Context: God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The Israelites were exiled in Babylon and felt that their nation was dead, like dry bones. Many understand the image to speak of the people's restoration to their land. Some Christians also see in it a sign of the future resurrection, although the text is addressed first to Israel.

For today: When you feel that your hope has dried up, remember that God can give life where there seems to be no way out. Bring Him your weariness honestly and trust His promise.
exp.36:13:
God promises to put his Spirit in his people to give them new life. When this is fulfilled, they will know that God has spoken and also acted, because his word is not left as empty promises.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. This statement closes the vision of the dry bones, which represent Israel without hope. God promises to restore his people, and interpreters see here both the return from exile and, for many Christians, an image of the spiritual renewal that God gives.

Today we can remember that God gives life where there seems to be no way out. If you feel exhausted or without hope, ask him to renew you by his Spirit, and trust that he does what he says.
exp.36:18:
Here God tells Ezekiel to explain the sign of the two sticks (pieces of wood). God will take the stick of Joseph, also called Ephraim, together with the tribes of Israel who are with him, and join them to the stick of Judah. He will make them one stick, that is, one people, and they will be united in God's hand. The verse says God will "put them" and "make them" one stick, meaning he will bring them together and form them into a single people.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. After the kingdom was divided, Israel and Judah were separated. With this sign, God promises that he will gather his people, bring them back to their land, and make them one nation.

For today: God wants to unite his people. Think of some division in your family or your church, and ask God to help you take a step toward reconciliation.
exp.36:22:
God promises that his people will no longer defile themselves with their idols, with their detestable things, or with any of their rebellions. He will save them from all the places where they sinned, he will cleanse them, and the relationship will be restored: they will be his people and he will be their God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Israel was scattered and divided into two kingdoms. God announces that he will gather them into their land, under one king from the line of David. Many Christians see in that king a foreshadowing of Jesus, though some understand it in other ways.

For today: God does not only forgive, he also cleanses and restores. You can bring him those areas where you keep falling, trusting that he can heal you and draw you closer to him.
exp.36:23:
God promises that his servant David will be king over the people and will be a shepherd to all of them. In this way, the people will live according to God's commands: they will walk in his just judgments, keep his instructions, and actually put them into practice.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to a people of Israel who are in exile, divided, and wounded. He promised to gather them, cleanse them, and restore them. Here "David" is not the ancient king, who had already died, but a future king from his line. Christians see in this Jesus, the good shepherd; others interpret it in other ways.

For today: Jesus not only guides us, he also cares for us. Following him is not only listening to his words but practicing them. Today, choose one of his teachings that you know well and put it into practice in your home or at work.
exp.36:24:
It says that the people of Israel will live again in the land that God gave to Jacob, the same land where their ancestors lived. There their children and grandchildren will live forever, meaning for a very long time or permanently. Also, "my servant David" will be their prince, or ruler, forever.

The words are spoken by God through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. The people were scattered and discouraged. God promises to restore them, cleanse them from sin, and make with them a covenant of peace. Many Christians see in "David" a reference to Jesus, a descendant of David. Others see a promise for Israel as a nation. It is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God keeps his promises even when everything seems lost. If you feel far from him or defeated, remember that he restores, cleanses, and guides. Trust in Christ, the Shepherd, and seek to obey him with hope.
exp.37:1:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," an expression that identifies him as an ordinary human being. He is commanded to set his face against Gog, that is, to look at him directly and declare a message of judgment. Magog, Meshech and Tubal are names of peoples or regions; the phrase "chief prince" means the principal leader.

Who Gog is exactly is debated, and there is no single certain answer.

The Lord speaks, and he does so through Ezekiel, who was prophesying to the exiles of Israel in Babylon. This message announces that God will oppose a power that will come against his people. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some as historical events, others as something future or symbolic.

For today: God remains Lord over every power that may seem threatening. We can trust that he cares for his people and rest in his justice, without letting fear dominate us.
exp.37:3:
God tells Gog that he will turn him around, like an animal with a hook put in its jaw that is pulled wherever one wishes. He will bring him out together with his whole army: horses, horsemen, fully armored, and a great crowd with bucklers (large shields) and shields, all armed with swords.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces judgment against Gog, a leader from Magog, Meshech and Tubal. Interpreters debate who Gog is and when this is fulfilled: some think of a historical event, others of something still in the future, and others of a symbol of the final opposition against God. The central point is that God governs, even over the nations that attack his people.

For today: when evil seems strong and organized, remember that God still has control. You can rest in Him and pray with confidence.
exp.37:4:
This verse names other peoples who will join Gog in the attack: Persia, Ethiopia, and Libya. All of them go armed with shields and helmets. They are well-equipped soldiers.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces that Gog, a leader from distant lands, will gather a great alliance against Israel. But the text makes clear that it is God who puts hooks in his jaws, that is, who leads and controls him. Scholars understand in different ways who Gog is and when this prophecy will be fulfilled.

For today: although the powers of the world may seem enormous and well armed, God still governs history. We can trust in Him when we feel fear before problems that are bigger than we are.
exp.37:8:
God describes Gog, the leader of a great coalition of nations, advancing against Israel. He says he will come up like a storm and like a cloud that covers the land, with all his troops and many allied peoples. The image shows a huge, noisy, threatening force.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel appears restored and living in security, and God announces that someone will come to attack it. Scholars interpret this in different ways: as a historical event, as a future event, or as a symbol of the final opposition against God's people. There is no full agreement about who Gog is.

For today: even when evil seems like a huge storm, God still reigns and knows every step. We can rest in Him without ignoring the dangers, and pray with confidence when everything seems to darken.
exp.37:10:
Here God describes what Gog, an enemy leader, will think. He plans to attack a land of villages, a peaceful people who live at rest and feel secure, with no walls, no bars to secure them, and no gates. To Gog, that people looks like an easy prey.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces that, at a future time, Gog will have an evil thought and will gather allies to plunder the people of Israel, who have been restored. Interpreters differ: some see it as a future historical event, others as a symbolic picture of evil's attack against God's people. What is clear is that God knows the hidden plans of the heart.

For today: do not confuse calm with weakness. If you are at peace, trust that God sees every intention against you, and guard your own heart too, so that no thoughts of taking advantage of others are born within you.
exp.37:11:
He says that Gog, the leader of the attack, has a plan: to plunder and seize goods. He intends to turn his hand against places that were once in ruins and are now inhabited again, and against a people gathered from among the nations, who already have livestock and possessions.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces that, in a future time, Gog will form an evil plan when he sees a people living in peace and without walls. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future event, others a symbolic picture of evil against the people of God. God makes it clear that he knows the hidden intentions of the heart.

For today: God sees our thoughts before they become actions. We can ask him to examine our hearts and to reject greed in time. We can also rest, because he cares for his own.
exp.37:12:
Ezekiel 38:13 names distant nations, Sheba, Dedan, and Tarshish, along with their young lions (probably strong young leaders or rulers), who put a question to Gog. They ask whether he really comes to take spoil, to carry off silver and gold, livestock and goods. Spoil and prey mean plunder taken by force.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Gog plans to attack a people who live in peace and without walls. These nations seem to be merchants who neither stop nor defend him; they only question his motives. Interpreters differ: some see a protest, others a mockery or a simple observation. There is also debate about who Gog is and when this happens.

Today we can notice that greed always disguises itself as something else, but God sees the true motive. Let us ask Him to examine our hearts and trust that He cares for His people.
exp.37:15:
It says that Gog, an enemy leader, will advance against Israel like a dark cloud covering the whole land. This will happen "in the latter days," that is, at a time still to come. God himself says he will bring Gog, so that the nations will know him when he shows his holiness before their eyes. The holiness and power of God will be recognized by all.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was writing to a people in exile. He promises them that they will live safely in their land, but that there will be a final attack. Interpreters differ about Gog: some see a literal future event, others a symbol of evil against God's people. In the end, God appears as the one who is in control.

For today: when the world seems threatening or confusing, we can trust that God still reigns and will accomplish his purposes. Rest in him instead of living in fear.
exp.37:16:
God asks Gog: "Are you the one I spoke about long ago through the prophets of Israel?" He reminds Gog that those prophets announced, for many years, that one day He would bring you against His people.

The Lord speaks through Ezekiel. Gog is a leader from the north who will attack Israel in the final days. God shows that this is no surprise and no loss of control: He had already announced it. Scholars disagree about whether Gog is a historical figure, a future one, or a symbol of the evil that rises against God. What is clear is that God rules and will be glorified.

For today: when the world seems chaotic and threatening, we can rest in the fact that God knows the future and remains in control. Trust His Word, pray with calm, and do not live dominated by fear.
exp.37:17:
This verse says that when Gog comes to attack the land of Israel, God will be filled with anger. The phrase about his anger rising up in his face is an old way of saying that his wrath will flare up with great force.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel. Gog is a leader who comes with many nations against the people of Israel. God says he allows this attack so that the nations will acknowledge him as holy. Interpreters differ: some see it as a historical event, others as something still to come, and others as a symbol of evil that rises up against God.

For today: we can trust that God is not indifferent to injustice or to those who harm his people. When evil seems strong, we can rest in the knowledge that God has the final word.
exp.37:18:
God says that he has spoken out of his zeal, that is, his steadfast love for his people and his holy name, and out of the fire of his wrath, his anger against evil. He announces that in that time there will be a great shaking, an earthquake or strong tremor, over the land of Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this prophecy, Gog, a leader from the north, attacks Israel, and God intervenes to defend his people. The verses that follow show that all of creation will tremble before him. Interpreters disagree about whether this will be fulfilled literally in the future or whether it is symbolic language.

For today: God is not indifferent to injustice, nor does he forget his own. We can rest in the knowledge that he cares for his people, and at the same time live with reverence, trusting in his justice rather than taking it into our own hands.
exp.37:19:
It says that when God intervenes against Gog, all of creation will feel his presence: fish, birds, animals, reptiles and people will tremble. There will also be a great earthquake: the mountains will be torn down, the steep places will fall, and every wall will come down to the ground. The phrase about the face of the earth means the surface of the land.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel. Gog comes to attack Israel, and God responds with zeal and anger to defend his people and to show who he is. Interpreters differ on whether this refers to a future event, something symbolic, or both, but all recognize that God is sovereign over the nations.

For today: no human force, no wall or power, can compare with God. We can live with reverence toward him and trust that he cares for his own, even when the world seems unstable.
exp.37:21:
God says that he himself will take up the case, that is, enter into judgment and fight, against Gog, the enemy leader. He will use disease, violent death, and a huge storm: heavy rain, hail, fire, and burning stones, as at Sodom. This will fall on his armies and on the allied peoples as well.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapters 38 and 39 he announces that a great alliance will attack his restored people, and that he will defend them. Interpreters disagree: some see it as a future historical event, others as a symbolic picture of God's final victory. The purpose, according to the next verse, is that everyone will know that he is the LORD.

For today: when evil seems strong, remember that final justice belongs to God. Trust him, pray, and do not repay evil with evil.
exp.38:3:
This verse says that the enemy army will fall dead on the mountains of Israel, together with its troops and allied peoples. Their bodies will be left as food for the birds and the wild beasts.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Chapters 38 and 39 announce a great invasion against Israel, led by a leader from the land of Magog. God promises to step in and defeat them, to show that he is the Lord. Christians interpret these chapters in different ways: as a future event, as a symbol of God's final victory, or as something partly already fulfilled.

For today: even when evil seems strong and well organized, God is still greater. You can rest in him and entrust your fears to him, while continuing to do good.
exp.38:5:
God says he will send fire on Magog, which is the land or people of the leader called Gog, and also on those who live at ease in the coastlands, or distant lands. The phrase about living at ease means that they live with confidence, without fear. The result will be that everyone will recognize that God is the Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he announces judgment on Gog and his allies, who attack Israel. Interpreters disagree: some see a historical event, others a future event, others a symbol of evil defeated by God. God wants to protect his people and show that he is holy.

For today: let us not trust in a false sense of security that ignores God. We can rest in the knowledge that he cares for his own and has the final word over all injustice.
exp.38:6:
God says he will make his holy name known in the midst of Israel, his people. He promises that he will never again let that name be polluted, and the nations will know that he is the Lord, the Holy One of Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, within the prophecy against Gog and Magog (chapters 38 and 39). Earlier, Israel had dishonored God's name through its idolatry and its exile. Now God promises to defeat a great enemy to show who he is. Interpreters differ: some see a future event, others see symbolic language of God's final triumph.

For today: let us take care how we live and speak, because our conduct can either honor or stain the name of God. Let us also trust that he guards his own honor and keeps his promises.
exp.38:8:
It says that, after the army of Gog is defeated, the people of Israel will go out to gather the enemy's weapons and use them as fuel for seven years. The shields in the verse, the large ones, and the clubs, the hand weapons, are the things it describes.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He tells the Israelites that he himself will defend them and show his holiness before the nations. Christians understand this scene in different ways: as a historical event, as something still to come, or as a symbolic picture. The number seven may indicate something complete, but there is no certainty about that detail.

For today: trust that God is greater than any threat. He can turn into peace what others used to harm, so hand him your fears and let him be your defender.
exp.38:9:
It says that Israel will not need to cut firewood or go into the forest, because it will have more than enough weapons to use as fuel. The weapons of the defeated enemy will be burned in the fire. "They shall spoil those that spoiled them, and rob those that robbed them" means that those who were once plundered will now gather what their attackers left behind. The large shields are the big shields carried in battle.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Ezekiel 38 and 39 announce the defeat of Gog, an enemy leader who attacks Israel. Some believe this is a prophecy about a future event, while others see it as symbolic language of God's final victory. What is clear is that God defends his people and changes history.

For today: trust that God can turn your struggles into provision. When you face injustice or fear, hand it over to him and wait for his justice, without taking revenge on your own.
exp.38:11:
This verse says that the people of Israel will spend seven months burying the dead of the defeated army, in order to cleanse the land. At that time it was believed that an unburied body defiled the place. "Cleanse" here means removing that uncleanness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. This part describes the defeat of Gog, an enemy leader who attacks Israel, and how God overcomes him. Interpreters differ: some see it as literal and future, others as a symbol of God's final triumph over evil. What is clear is that God protects his people and restores the land.

For today: God does not only defeat evil, he also wants to cleanse its consequences. We can ask him to help us patiently repair what sin has damaged in our lives and in our surroundings.
exp.38:12:
It says that all the people of the land, that is, the people of Israel, will be the ones to bury the dead of Gog's army. "Renown" means fame or something worth remembering. On that day, when God is honored, that is, when he shows his greatness and power, it will be a memorable day for them.

God himself speaks here through the prophet Ezekiel. Chapters 38 and 39 describe a great invasion against Israel led by Gog, and the defeat God brings upon him. The burials cleanse the land and show that God keeps what he promises. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future event, others a symbolic picture of God's final triumph over evil.

Today we can trust that God has the last word over evil. When the world seems chaotic, remember that his justice will come and that he deserves our honor.
exp.38:13:
After the great defeat of Gog's army, men will be hired on a permanent basis to travel across the whole land. Their task will be to search for and bury the bodies that remain, so that the land is made clean. The verse of the phrase about men hired for their work is that they are workers paid for their labor. The part about the land's surface means the face of the earth. After seven months, they will carry out a final inspection to make sure nothing is left behind.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapters 38 and 39 he announces that a great coalition will attack Israel and be defeated. The bodies would leave the land unclean, so a careful cleansing is required. Interpreters differ: some understand this as a literal future event, and others as a symbolic picture of God's judgment on evil.

For today: God takes cleansing seriously and does not settle for what is only partly seen. We can ask him to show us areas of our lives that need review and ongoing cleansing, and not leave them half-done.
exp.38:20:
He says that God will show his glory, that is, his greatness and his power, before all the peoples. The nations that were not Israel will see the judgment of God, that is, his justice in punishing evil, and the hand of God laid upon his enemies, which means his power at work.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapters 38 and 39 he announces the defeat of Gog, an enemy who attacks Israel. The images of the feast and the blood are very strong language, and scholars understand them in different ways: some take them literally and others as symbol. The purpose is seen in the verses that follow: that Israel and the nations may know that God is the Lord and that he is just.

For today: God is not indifferent to evil or to his people. We can trust that he will do justice, and in the meantime live with humility and acknowledge his holiness.
exp.38:23:
He says that God dealt with Israel according to their defilement and their rebellions. "Uncleanness" speaks of a life stained by sin, above all by idolatry. "Hid my face" means that God withdrew his favor and his protection, and left them to face the consequences of their own choices.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. God explains that the exile was not a defeat of his power, but the result of his people's sin. This verse comes just before a promise: God will bring the captives back and will have mercy on them.

For today: when you face the consequences of your mistakes, do not harden yourself or lose heart. Acknowledge your failure honestly and return to God. His discipline is not the final word; his desire is to restore you.
exp.38:28:
God promises that he will no longer turn his face away from his people, meaning he will no longer withdraw his nearness or his favor from them. The reason is that he will have poured out his Spirit upon Israel. The phrase "hide my face" is an old way of saying that God pulls away or stops helping. "Pour out" suggests something abundant and generous.

God himself speaks here through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel had been taken into exile because of its sin, and God had kept silent toward them. Here he promises to gather them, bring them back to their land, and renew them within. Some see this fulfilled in the return from exile, others in the future, and others in the Spirit given in Christ; Christians have understood it in different ways.

For today: even though we sometimes feel God is distant because of our failures, his desire is to draw near and give us his Spirit. We can return to him with confidence and ask him to renew us.
exp.39:0:
He describes Ezekiel receiving a new vision on a precise date: the twenty-fifth year of the exile, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month. Fourteen years had passed since the city was struck down. Then the hand of the Lord came upon him, that is, he felt the power of God guiding him, and he was brought to a place.

Ezekiel was a priest and prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. With this verse begins the last great vision of the book (chapters 40 to 48), in which God shows him a new temple. It was a message of hope for a discouraged people. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: literally, symbolically, or both.

For today: even when a loss has hurt for years, God has not forgotten you. He can speak hope to you at the exact time. Ask Him to help you look ahead with confidence.
exp.39:1:
He says that God, in visions, carried Ezekiel from Babylon to the land of Israel. He set him on a very high mountain, and from there he saw something that looked like the buildings of a city toward the south.

Ezekiel was a priest who lived in exile. He speaks in the first person and tells what God showed him, fourteen years after the fall of Jerusalem. His people were wounded and without hope. This vision of the temple and the city would give them encouragement. Scholars interpret it in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people.

For today: when everything seems lost, God can still show you hope. Ask him to let you see beyond your situation, and trust that he has not abandoned his promises.
exp.39:3:
A man whose appearance was bright, like bronze, speaks to Ezekiel. He asks him for three things: to look closely, to listen carefully, and to set his heart on what is shown to him. "Man" means a human being, and "son of man" is the way God usually addresses Ezekiel. At the end, he is told to tell everything to the house of Israel.

Ezekiel was in exile in Babylon. Around 573 BC, in a vision from God, he was taken to a high mountain in Israel. There this guide begins to measure a building, which many understand to be a temple. Scholars debate whether it is literal, symbolic, or about the future. The purpose is for Ezekiel to see and then report to a discouraged people.

When God teaches us something, a quick glance is not enough. Take time to read the Bible with attention, listen to it with humility, and keep what you have learned in your heart. Then share it with others simply.
exp.39:5:
