He says that the guide, a man whom Ezekiel sees in the vision, went to the gate facing east of the temple. He climbed its steps and measured with his rod the two posts of the gate, that is, the columns on each side of the entrance. Each post was one reed wide. The steps are stairs, and the reed was a measuring rod of six long cubits.

Ezekiel is in exile, and God gives him a detailed vision of a temple. The guide asks him to look, listen, and set his heart on what he sees, so that he can then tell it to Israel. Scholars interpret this vision in several ways: as a literal future temple, as something symbolic, or as a hope of restoration.

For today: God cares about details and asks for the attention of the heart. When we read the Bible, let us not rush; let us listen calmly and let his Word shape us.
exp.39:8:
It says the guide measured the porch, or inner entrance, of the gateway: it was eight cubits deep, and its posts or pillars measured two cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm (about 45 to 50 cm). The posts are the pillars on either side of the entrance. The final phrase indicates that the gate faced toward the side of the temple.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision of a temple. A man with a measuring reed guides him and shows him every detail. This takes place in a time of great discouragement for Israel. Scholars interpret the vision in several ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol of God's presence, or as a spiritual image.

For today: God is concerned with order and with details. We can approach Him with reverence and trust that, even in difficult times, He continues to build and has not forgotten us.
exp.39:9:
This verse describes the eastern gate of the temple that Ezekiel sees in a vision. On each side of its passage there were three small chambers, or little rooms, and all six were of the same size. The "posts" are the pillars or uprights that formed the entrance, and they too were the same on one side and on the other. The "measure" refers to the exact size they had.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision from God. A man with a measuring reed guides him through a new temple and shows him every detail. This happens in a time of grief, when the temple in Jerusalem had already been destroyed. Scholars interpret this vision in several ways.

God is a God of order, and He cares about the way we draw near to Him. We can ask Him to bring balance and steadiness into our daily lives, so that we live with integrity in the small things and in the great ones.
exp.39:10:
This verse continues the measurement of the east gate of the temple. The man measures the width of the entrance, which is ten cubits, and the length of the gateway, which is thirteen cubits. A cubit is an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about 45 to 50 centimeters. The gateway is the passage or building at the entrance.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, recounts a vision he received. A guide, who looks like a man, takes him to a new temple and measures each part in great detail. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol, or as a promise of restoration. For a discouraged people, it showed that God was still putting everything in order and wanted to dwell among them.

For today: God cares about order and care. We can draw near to Him with reverence and confidence, and trust that He has a plan, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.39:11:
This verse says that in front of the side rooms of the gate there was a small space, a border or barrier, one cubit on each side. And each room measured six cubits by six, that is, it was square. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about half a meter. The side rooms were small guard rooms beside the entrance.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he had during the exile, in which a man with a measuring reed showed him a new temple. This guide measures the east gate with care. Scholars disagree about whether this temple should be taken literally, symbolically, or as something yet to come.

For today: God cares about details and order. If He measures His house with such care, we can trust that nothing in our lives escapes His notice. Today, put a small area of your life in order with attention and faithfulness.
exp.39:13:
The verse says that the man who was guiding Ezekiel measured the posts, that is, the pillars or columns on the sides of the gateway, and gave them sixty cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, about half a meter.

Ezekiel tells of a vision he received while in exile, about twenty years after the temple was destroyed. A guide with a measuring reed shows him a new temple, and Ezekiel records each measurement carefully. Scholars disagree about whether this refers to a literal building, to something in the future, or to a symbol. Also, the Hebrew text of this verse is difficult, and translations vary in the figures.

For today: God attends to the details and wants his people to draw near with order and reverence. This week, take a quiet moment to pray without hurry, preparing your heart before you ask.
exp.39:14:
This verse gives a measurement: from the front of the entrance gate to the front of the porch of the inner gate, there are fifty cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, about 45 to 50 centimeters. So the gate passage measured about 25 meters, although scholars do not fully agree on the exact value of the cubit.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who lived in exile in Babylon, is the one speaking. In a vision, a guide takes him to a new temple and shows him each measurement in great detail. Many believe this encouraged a discouraged people, but there are different interpretations about whether that temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God cares about order and reverence when we draw near to Him. Before you pray or worship, take a moment to come in calmly and respectfully, without rushing.
exp.39:15:
It says that the temple gate Ezekiel sees had narrow windows in the small rooms, in the entrances, and in the passageways, all on the inside. Also, each post, or pillar, was decorated with palm trees. The small rooms are little chambers, and the entrances are the gateways with their structures.

Ezekiel was a priest and a prophet, and he lived in exile in Babylon. In a vision, a guide takes him through a new temple, measuring it with great detail. Scholars interpret this in different ways: some see a literal future temple, while others see a symbol of God's presence and holiness among his people. Palm trees are often associated with life and victory, but the text does not explain that here.

God cares even about the details of his house and of how we draw near to him. Today you can approach God with reverence and order, without rushing, trusting that he is concerned with both the great and the small things in your life.
exp.39:16:
He says that the man guiding Ezekiel brought him into the outer court of the temple he saw in the vision. There were thirty chambers there, that is, rooms or small halls, and a paved area around the court, that is, a stone floor. The chambers were arranged in a circle, next to that pavement.

Ezekiel was a priest and a prophet, and he was living in exile in Babylon. In 573 B.C. he received this vision, in which a guide with a measuring reed showed him a detailed temple. Scholars do not agree on its meaning: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence and of the hope of restoration for his people.

For today: God is a God of order and care, and he values having a prepared place where people can draw near to him. We can set aside a space and an orderly time each day to seek him with reverence.
exp.39:17:
It says that the pavement of the outer court, beside the gates, was the same length as the gateways, and that it was the "lower pavement." The word translated as "pavement" refers to a floor made of stone. This suggests that the court had a lower part near the gates and a higher part toward the temple, although the text gives no further detail.

Ezekiel describes a vision he received during the exile, about twenty years after the fall of Jerusalem. A man with a measuring reed guides him through the future temple and measures each part with care. At this point he walks through the outer court, with its chambers and its pavement. Interpreters disagree about whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God cares about details, even the floor we walk on to draw near to him. If he arranges his house with such care, we can approach him with reverence and also bring order to our daily lives, faithfully attending to the small things.
exp.39:19:
It says that the guide who accompanied Ezekiel measured the north gate of the outer court of the temple. He took its length and its breadth, just as he had done with the gate of the east. The outer court is the open yard that surrounds the main building, and the gate here is a large entrance with rooms and passageways.

Ezekiel tells of a vision he received in exile, years after the destruction of the first temple. A man with a measuring reed shows him a new temple in careful detail. Scholars debate whether it is a literal temple yet to come, a symbol, or both. What is certain is that the discouraged people receive the promise that God would dwell among them again, with order and holiness.

For today: God cares about order and care in drawing near to Him. Set aside a quiet, fixed time to pray and read His Word, preparing your heart with respect and gratitude.
exp.39:20:
It says the north gate of the outer court had three small rooms on each side, that is, small rooms for guards or for service. Its posts (the pillars of the entrance) and its arches (the porches or vestibules) had the same measurements as the east gate: fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide. A cubit measures about half a meter, although scholars vary on the exact figure.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, who in a vision is carried to Israel and sees a guide who measures a new temple. This takes place during the exile in Babylon, when the temple had been destroyed. The repeated measurements show order and holiness. Interpreters differ on whether this vision is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God is a God of order and care, and He wants us to draw near to Him with reverence. We can ask ourselves whether in our daily life there are well-kept gates for worshiping Him, such as set times of prayer and reading of His Word.
exp.39:21:
This verse describes the gate of the outer court of the temple that Ezekiel sees in his vision. Its windows, arches, and palm trees (decorations shaped like palm trees) had the same measurements as the east gate. One went up to it by seven steps, and the arches (probably a porch or entrance hall) stood in front of them.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, recounts what God showed him. A guide with a measuring reed teaches him about the temple with precision. Many see here a promise of restoration and of God's presence; others interpret it differently, and there is no single agreement on whether it describes a literal or a symbolic temple.

For today: God cares about order and detail, and He draws near to His people with purpose. We can approach Him with reverence, with calm, and with the desire to grow step by step, like someone climbing stairs.
exp.39:22:
It says that, on the north side of the temple that Ezekiel sees in the vision, the gate of the inner court stood directly opposite the gate of the outer court. The same was true on the east side. Between one gate and the other there were a hundred cubits. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so the distance would be about fifty meters.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest and prophet who was exiled in Babylon. A guide who appears as a man shows him the temple in vision and measures it with a reed. Scholars disagree about its meaning: some see it as a literal temple in the future, others as a symbol of God's presence and order among his restored people.

For today: God is a God of order and of clear access. Just as those gates were lined up, we can draw near to him with purpose and reverence, without confusion, and put our lives in order to receive him.
exp.39:23:
This verse says that the angel leads Ezekiel toward the south, and there he finds another gate of the temple. The man measures it, and its posts and its arches have the same measurements as those of the east gate.

Ezekiel recounts this vision in the first person, years after Jerusalem fell, when the people were living in exile. God shows him a new temple, measured in detail by a man who guides him. Scholars interpret it in several ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol of God's presence with his people, or as a spiritual image. But all of them note the order and holiness it displays.

For today: God is a God of order and faithfulness. If he took care with every measure of his house, he also cares for your life. Seek him with confidence and order in your daily life.
exp.39:26:
It says the inner court of the temple had a gate on its south side. The one who guided the measuring measured the distance between that gate and the south gate of the outer court, and it came to one hundred cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers. A "court" is an open yard, and here "south" means the southern side.

Ezekiel recounts a vision that God gave him. A man who looked like bronze led him through a new temple and measured everything with a measuring reed. The Jewish people were exiles in Babylon and the temple had been destroyed. Scholars disagree about whether this vision describes a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people.

God is a God of order and of detail, and his presence deserves reverence. Today we can ask ourselves whether we prepare our hearts carefully to draw near to him, without haste or carelessness, with respect and gratitude.
exp.39:28:
This verse describes the south gate of the inner courtyard of the temple. It says that its small chambers (little rooms used for guards), its posts (the side columns), and its arches (porches or entryways) had the same measurements as the other gates. It had windows all around, and it measured fifty cubits long by twenty-five cubits wide. A cubit is about 45 to 50 centimeters.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision. A guide takes him through a new temple and measures each part for him. This happens during a time of exile and pain, when the temple had been destroyed. Interpreters differ: some see a literal temple in the future, while others see a symbolic picture of God's presence and his order.

For today: God is a God of order, and everything in his house has its place and its measure. We can bring order into our own lives so that we approach him with reverence, caring for the details of our faith and of our everyday life.
exp.39:31:
He brought me to the inner court on the east side, and there he measured the gate. He used the same measurements as the gates before it. The inner court is an open courtyard of the temple. The word for the measure used here is an old unit, roughly the length of the forearm.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received in exile, when the temple in Jerusalem had already been destroyed. A man with a measuring reed guides him through the temple and measures everything with care. Scholars disagree about the purpose: some see a literal future temple, others see a symbol of God's orderly presence and of the hope of restoration.

For today: God is not disorderly or careless; He cares about the details of His work. When you find yourself in a time of ruin or waiting, remember that He continues to build with patience and purpose. Draw near to Him with reverence and trust.
exp.39:32:
This verse describes the gate of the inner court, the one facing the east... actually, here it is the gate facing east. It had chambers (small rooms for guards), posts (the columns of the entrance), and arches (the porch or vestibule), all with the same measurements as the other gates. It also had windows all around. It was fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide; a cubit was about half a meter.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, who in a vision is guided by a man with a measuring reed. He is in exile, and this vision of the new temple shows him order, holiness, and the presence of God. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future temple, others a spiritual symbol.

For today: God is a God of order and of care for details. We can approach Him with reverence and, at the same time, trust that nothing in our lives escapes His notice.
exp.39:33:
It says that the arches (the porch or vestibule) of this gate of the inner court faced toward the outer court. The posts (the pillars of the entrance) were decorated with palm trees, one on each side. To go up, there were eight steps.

Ezekiel speaks, recounting his vision. A guide leads him and measures the temple with a measuring reed. This takes place about twenty-five years after he was taken captive to Babylon, when the temple had already been destroyed. Scholars disagree about whether this temple was meant to be built literally, whether it is symbolic, or whether it points to something in the future. All agree that it shows order, holiness, and the presence of God.

Even the details of a gate matter: the palm trees and the steps suggest that approaching God is something worthy of care and reverence. Today we can come near to Him without haste, with respect and gratitude, knowing that God receives us.
exp.39:35:
This verse describes the measurements of the north gate of the temple that Ezekiel sees in a vision. It mentions its little chambers (the side rooms), the posts of the entrance, the arches (the covered passageways), and the windows. The whole structure measured fifty cubits long and twenty-five wide. One cubit was roughly half a meter, though its exact length is debated.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives this vision from God. A guide with a measuring rod leads him through the temple, gate by gate. Many see in this a promise of hope and restoration for a broken people. Scholars disagree on whether the temple should be understood literally, symbolically, or both.

For today: God cares about details and does things with order. We can trust that He is also interested in the details of our lives, and draw near to Him with reverence and hope.
exp.39:36:
It says that the gate on the north side had its posts (the columns on each side of the entrance) facing the outer court. Palm trees were carved on the posts on both sides. To go up to the gate there was a staircase of eight steps. The word for steps is the stairs leading up to the gate, and the court is the open yard around the temple.

The one speaking is Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who was living in exile in Babylon. In a vision, a guide who looks like a man takes him through a new temple and measures every detail. Interpreters do not agree on its meaning: some think of a literal future temple, others of a symbol of God's presence and holiness among his people.

For today: drawing near to God is something that deserves care and reverence. Here even the entrance has steps and order. We can prepare our hearts before praying or meeting with other believers, without haste or carelessness, remembering that God is holy and at the same time invites us to draw near.
exp.39:37:
This verse describes a room next to the temple gate, with its own entrance. There the burnt offering was washed, that is, the parts of the animal that would later be offered whole on the altar.

Ezekiel recounts a vision that God gave him. A guide showed him a new temple with very exact measurements. The Israelites were in exile in Babylon, and this vision spoke to them of order, purity, and the presence of God among them. Scholars interpret it in different ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol, or as a hope of restoration.

For today: drawing near to God requires preparation and a clean heart. Before praying or serving, we can pause and ask him to cleanse us and teach us to give him our best with reverence.
exp.39:38:
It says that in the porch of the temple gate there were four tables, two on each side. On them the animals were slaughtered, that is, killed and prepared, for three kinds of offerings: the burnt offering (an offering that was burned up completely), the offering for atonement, and the sin offering, which sought forgiveness and cleansing.

This takes place within a vision that the prophet Ezekiel receives, years after the destruction of Jerusalem, while the people were in exile. A guide shows him in detail a future temple. Scholars interpret it in various ways: some see it as a literal temple yet to come, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence restored among his people.

For today: this careful order reminds us that drawing near to God requires taking sin seriously. Christians believe that Christ offered the final sacrifice, so we can come to God with humility, confessing our failures and trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.39:40:
There were eight tables in total beside the gate of the temple: four on one side and four on the other. On them the animals were slaughtered, that is, they were killed and prepared for the sacrifice. It was an orderly place, arranged with care for that work.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision of a new temple, and a guide with a measuring reed shows him every detail. Scholars disagree about its meaning: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence restored among his people. For a discouraged people, it was a promise that God would once again dwell with them.

For today: God cares about order and reverence when we draw near to Him. We can prepare our hearts before we pray or worship, without haste or carelessness, remembering that Christ has already made the perfect sacrifice for us.
exp.39:41:
This verse describes four more tables, made of hewn stone, which measured about half a meter long and half a meter wide, and about 50 centimeters high (a cubit is roughly half a meter). There they would place the instruments used to slaughter, that is, to kill, the animals of the burnt offering and the sacrifice.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received during the exile, in which a guide shows him a new temple with very precise measurements. Interpreters do not agree: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence among his restored people. What is certain is that the text stresses the order and holiness of worship.

For today: God cares about the details when we worship him. We can approach him with order, reverence, and preparation, not in a hurried or careless way.
exp.39:42:
Inside the entrance hall of the gate there were hooks, or ledges, a handbreadth long (about eight centimeters, more or less), set all around. On the tables the meat of the offering was placed. The word "hooks" is hard to translate; some think they were hooks for hanging up the animals, and others think they were edges or shelves.

The prophet Ezekiel receives a vision of a new temple, and a guide who looks like a man shows him and measures every detail. Here he describes where the sacrifices were prepared. Interpreters do not agree: some see a literal future temple, others a symbolic picture of God's presence.

For today: God cares even for the details of how He is worshiped, with order and reverence. We can draw near to Him with seriousness and gratitude, remembering that Christ offered the perfect sacrifice for us.
exp.39:43:
In the inner court, near the north gate, it says there were rooms for the singers. Those rooms faced south. Another room was beside the east gate and faced north. The "court" is an open yard around the temple. The "chambers" are rooms.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision of a new temple. A guide who looks like a man shows him and measures each part. Scholars disagree: some see a literal future temple, others a symbolic picture of God's presence restored. What is certain is that the text gives room for singing within the order of the temple.

For today: praise is not an ornament. God gave it a place of its own in his house. We can care for our worship with consistency, preparation and reverence, not only when we feel like it.
exp.39:46:
He says the man who was guiding Ezekiel measured the inner courtyard: a perfect square, one hundred cubits on each side, roughly fifty meters. A cubit was an ancient unit of length, measured from the elbow to the tip of the fingers. The altar was before the house, that is, in front of the temple, at the center of that space.

Ezekiel is in a vision he received from God, and a guide with a measuring reed shows him a new temple. The priests, the sons of Zadok, look after the altar and serve the Lord. Scholars disagree about whether this temple would be built literally, whether it is symbolic, or whether it points to something in the future. What is clear is that God wants an orderly place for people to draw near to Him.

For today: the altar stands at the center, before one enters the house. We can make drawing near to God with sincerity and humility the center of our lives, before any other activity. Today, begin the day in prayer.
exp.39:48:
It says that the porch, that is, the entrance of the temple, was twenty cubits long and eleven cubits wide. One went up to it by steps or stairs. On each side of the entrance there was a pillar beside the posts, which are the frames or supports of the door. A cubit was roughly half a meter.

Ezekiel records what he sees in a vision. A guide who looks like a man leads him and measures each part of a new temple. This takes place while the people are exiled in Babylon. Scholars understand this vision in several ways: some see it as a literal temple in the future, others as a symbol of God's presence with his restored people.

Coming into the place where God is involves going up, not just passing by. We can draw near to him with attention and reverence, setting aside time for prayer and for his Word, and not in a hurry or in a casual way.
exp.40:0:
He says that the guide of the vision brought Ezekiel to the temple, that is, to the part called the holy place or sanctuary. There he measured the posts, which are the columns on each side of the entrance. Each post measured six cubits in width. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about half a meter. The word for the tent is understood here as a reference to the width of the ancient sacred tent, though some scholars explain it in other ways.

Ezekiel speaks, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. In a vision, God shows him a new temple, and a guide measures it carefully. This takes place after Jerusalem was destroyed, to give the people hope. Scholars disagree about whether it is a literal future temple or a symbolic picture.

For today: God is a God of order and of promises. Even when everything seems to have fallen apart, you can trust that He has a plan and that He desires to dwell among His people.
exp.40:1:
Here a man with a measuring rod walks through the temple and records each size. The entrance of the temple is ten cubits wide (a cubit was roughly half a meter), and on each side there is a wall of five cubits. Then he measures the main hall, called the sanctuary or holy place: forty cubits long and twenty cubits wide.

It is Ezekiel, a priest who was exiled in Babylon. In a vision, a guide takes him through a new temple and shows him its measurements. Scholars do not agree on its meaning: some think of a literal future temple, while others see it as a symbol of God's presence among his people.

For today: God is a God of order and care, and he wants us to draw near to him with reverence. Today we can set aside a quiet moment to pray with respect and attention.
exp.40:2:
He says that the guide of the vision went into the innermost part of the temple, the most holy place, and measured the entrance. The side pieces of the doorway are the frames on each side of the door, and each one measured two cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, about 45 to 50 centimeters. The door was six cubits, and the opening seven.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, is in exile in Babylon. In a vision, a guide who looked like a man shows him a new temple and gives him its measurements. This encouraged a discouraged people, because God still intended to dwell among them. Interpreters disagree: some see a literal future temple, others a spiritual symbol.

For today: God is orderly and cares about the details of his presence. Draw near to him with respect and reverence, knowing that Christ opened the way to God.
exp.40:4:
Here the heavenly guide continues measuring the temple that Ezekiel sees in the vision. First he measures the thickness of the wall of the house, which is six cubits (a cubit was about half a meter, so roughly three meters). Then he measures the side chambers, small rooms that surrounded the whole building, each four cubits wide (about two meters).

Ezekiel was a priest and a prophet, and he lived in exile in Babylon. God shows him this detailed vision when the temple in Jerusalem had already been destroyed, to give him hope and to remind him that He wants to dwell among His people in holiness and order. Scholars disagree about whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God cares about order and details. We can give our daily lives the same careful attention, understanding that every part of them can be a place where God dwells.
exp.40:5:
It says that around the temple there were three stories of side rooms, and that on each story there were thirty-three chambers, according to some interpretations. Beams or projecting supports were used to hold them up. Those supports went into the wall of the temple, but the rooms rested on them and were not attached directly to the holy wall.

Ezekiel describes a vision he received during the exile. A guide, described as a man with a measuring reed, shows him a new temple with very exact measurements. Scholars disagree about whether it is a literal future temple, a symbol, or both. Here the emphasis is on order and on reverence for the most holy place.

For today: God values order and reverence for what is holy. We can rest our daily life on good supports, such as prayer, the Word, and community, without trying to carry everything on just one thing.
exp.40:6:
It says that the side chambers of the temple grew wider as they went up. A spiral staircase, that is, one winding round in a spiral, went around the building on the inside and rose very high. That is why the house was wider at the top. One passed from the lowest chamber to the highest through the middle one.

The speaker is the prophet Ezekiel, who in a vision is led by a man holding a measuring reed. He is in exile, and the earlier temple had been destroyed. The vision describes a new temple with very exact measurements. Interpreters differ: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbol of God's presence with his restored people.

For today: this passage shows a space that opens up more as one climbs. We can ask God to make our spiritual life grow, step by step, and to give us more room for his presence, prayer, and service.
exp.40:8:
It says that the outer wall of the side chambers of the temple was five cubits thick (roughly two and a half meters). It also mentions an open space left over, that is, a free area between those chambers and other parts of the temple. A cubit was an ancient measure, the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers.

The speaker is the prophet Ezekiel, who recounts what he saw in a vision. A guide showed him a new temple, measuring it carefully. Ezekiel was among the exiles in Babylon, and this vision gave them hope that God would once again dwell with his people. Interpreters differ on whether it describes a literal future temple or a symbolic picture.

For today: God cares about details and values order and boundaries. Just as the temple had well-defined spaces, we can leave room in our lives for his presence.
exp.40:9:
It says that, between the side rooms of the temple and the other buildings around them, there was an open space twenty cubits wide, all the way around the house on every side. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers (about 45 to 50 centimeters). The rooms were small chambers built against the main building.

Here Ezekiel speaks, recounting a vision God gave him during the exile in Babylon. A guide showed him and measured a new temple in great detail. Scholars interpret it in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic message of hope and of the holiness of God.

For today: just as the temple had spaces that separated and protected what was sacred, we too need to leave room for silence and prayer in our routine, so that God does not get squeezed in among so many occupations.
exp.40:12:
It says that the angel measured the temple's length and gave it a hundred cubits. He also measured the separate area behind the temple, the building on the west side, and its walls, and the total came to a hundred cubits in length. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so we are talking about around fifty meters.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, is in exile in Babylon. In a vision, a guide with a measuring reed shows him a new temple, orderly and perfect. The measurements remind the people that God still has plans for them and that his presence is holy. Scholars disagree about whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God cares about details and seeks order and reverence. We can ask ourselves what place God has in our routine. Setting aside a fixed time each day to pray and read the Bible is a simple way to give his presence a place.
exp.40:14:
Here the prophet continues recording the measurements of the temple he sees in the vision. The building was a structure at the side and behind the temple, and the separate area around it was the open space set apart. The side rooms were chambers, and the courtyard was the open court. The whole complex was one hundred cubits (a cubit was roughly half a meter). The inner sanctuary and the porches facing the court are also mentioned.

Ezekiel speaks from exile in Babylon, and a figure with the appearance of a man shows him the temple and measures it. For a people without a temple, this vision was a hope of restoration and of God's presence. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future temple, others a spiritual symbol.

For today: God is a God of order and care, and what He does with His people is not improvised. You can trust that He also cares for the details of your life, and live with the same seriousness and reverence toward what is holy.
exp.40:17:
This verse describes the decoration of the temple walls that Ezekiel saw in a vision. Figures of cherubim and palm trees were carved into them, arranged in alternation: a palm tree, then a cherub, then another palm tree. Each cherub had two faces.

Ezekiel speaks here as a priest who was exiled in Babylon. A guide shows him and measures a new temple for him. The verses that follow say that the two faces were those of a man and a lion. Scholars do not agree on whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or future. The cherubim recall God's presence, and the palm trees may evoke life and beauty.

For today: God cares about the beauty and order of his presence. We can draw near to him with reverence, remembering that his house is a place of life and hope, even when we feel far away or in exile.
exp.40:18:
It says that on the temple walls there were carved figures: cherubim with two faces, one of a man and the other of a lion. The face of the man looked toward a palm tree on one side, and the face of the lion toward another palm tree on the other side. This was repeated all around the whole temple. The palm tree is a common decorative figure.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, describes a vision he received during the exile in Babylon. A guide showed him, with measurements, a new and orderly temple. The Israelites had lost the temple, and this vision gave them hope that God would once again dwell among them. Scholars disagree about whether this temple was meant to be built literally or is a symbolic image.

For today: God is a God of order and beauty, and he wants to dwell with his people. We can prepare our hearts to worship him with reverence, remembering that his presence is the greatest treasure.
exp.40:19:
This verse says that the walls of the temple were decorated, from the floor up to above the door, with carved figures of cherubim (angelic beings) and palm trees. This decoration covered the whole wall of the temple.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, describing a vision God gave him, while a guide who looked like a man measured the temple. This takes place when the people were in exile in Babylon. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future temple, others a symbol of God's presence and restoration. The cherubim and the palm trees recall the tabernacle and Eden.

For today: God cares about details and wants his presence to be honored with beauty and reverence. We can draw near to him with respect and joy, and also bring into our daily lives a sincere care for what we offer him.
exp.40:21:
Ezekiel describes a wooden altar, three cubits high (about a meter and a half) and two cubits long. All of it, its corners, its top surface and its sides, is made of wood. A guide says to him: "This is the table that is before the Lord." Here "table" and "altar" are used as one and the same thing. Some think it recalls the table of the bread of the presence or an altar of incense; this is not entirely certain.

Context: Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision of a new temple. A man shows him and measures each part. The people were wounded by the destruction of the temple, and this vision gave them hope that God would once again be near them. Interpreters disagree about whether it is a literal or a symbolic temple.

For today: God wants to be close to his people and to have fellowship with them. Set aside a moment each day to come before his table: pray, read his Word, and thank him calmly.
exp.40:22:
This verse says that the temple (the large hall, also called the holy place) and the sanctuary (the most holy place, the innermost part) each had a doorway, that is, an entrance with its frame and its doors. So there was one entrance for going into the temple and another for going into the sanctuary.

Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon, receives a vision of a new temple. A guide shows him and measures each part. Shortly before, he was shown the wooden table that stands before the LORD. Scholars interpret this vision in several ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol of the restoration of Israel, or as a spiritual picture of God's presence.

For today: drawing near to God is both serious and beautiful. The doors remind us that we should come to Him with reverence, and today, in Christ, we have open access to His presence.
exp.41:1:
This verse gives the measurements of the chamber building that stood on the north side of the temple. Along the side of the north door, it measured one hundred cubits in length and fifty in width. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, about 45 to 50 centimeters. So the building was large.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest who was exiled in Babylon. In a vision, a man sent by God guides him and measures the temple in detail. These chambers were for the priests (Ezekiel 42:13). Scholars debate whether this vision describes a literal future temple or teaches, in symbolic form, the holiness and order of God.

For today: God cares about details, and he wants his presence to be approached with reverence. We can ask ourselves what order and respect we give to our time of prayer and worship.
exp.41:2:
The chambers of the temple rose in three stories, one facing the other. On one side they stood opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court, and on the other side opposite the pavement (the stone-paved floor) of the outer court. A cubit measures about 45 to 50 centimeters. The outer court is an open yard around the temple.

Ezekiel recounts a vision that God gave him. A guide takes him through the temple and shows him very precise measurements. These chambers, according to the chapter, were located next to the area of the sanctuary. Scholars debate whether this vision describes a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people. The people were then in exile.

For today: God cares about order, space, and detail when it comes to worshiping him. We can give God an orderly place in our week, with set time for prayer and Bible reading.
exp.41:3:
It says that in front of the chambers of the priests there was a walk ten cubits wide (about five meters) going inward. The doors of the chambers faced north.

Through a vision, God shows Ezekiel a new temple with very exact measurements. Ezekiel writes in exile, and the people had lost the temple. These chambers served for the priests to eat the holy offerings and to dress for service. How this vision should be understood, whether literally or symbolically, is debated among interpreters.

God cares even for the details of how he is worshiped, with order and respect. Today we can ask ourselves what order and reverence we give to our time with God. Perhaps setting aside a fixed moment each day to pray and read his Word.
exp.41:4:
It says that the rooms on the upper floor were narrower than those below and in the middle. The reason is that the galleries, that is, the open walkways or terraces that surrounded the building, took up more space on the upper floors. So the upper chambers had less room left.

The prophet Ezekiel is seeing a vision of the temple, and a guide shows him and measures each part. These chambers were next to the outer court and were for the priests. The exact details of the construction are not easy to understand, and scholars interpret them in different ways. What is clear is that God wants an orderly and holy place for his service.

For today: God cares about details and order. We can ask ourselves whether we are leaving enough room in our daily lives to pray, read his Word, and serve him, or whether other things are filling up all the space.
exp.41:7:
This verse gives measurements. It says that the chambers on the side of the outer court were fifty cubits long, and that the chambers on the side facing the temple added up to one hundred cubits. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, about 45 to 50 centimeters.

Ezekiel recounts a vision that God gave him during the exile in Babylon. A guide shows him a new temple with very precise measurements. These chambers were sacred spaces for the priests. Scholars disagree about whether it is a literal future temple or a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people.

For today: God cares about order and reverence. We can set apart careful times and spaces to draw near to him, without haste or carelessness, because his presence deserves our attention.
exp.41:8:
This verse describes an entrance located below the chambers, on the east side. Through it one passed from the outer court into those rooms. The "chambers" are rooms or halls of the temple, and the "court" is the open yard that surrounded the buildings.

In a vision, God shows Ezekiel a temple with very exact measurements. A guide measures everything for him. According to the chapter, these chambers were for the priests, where they ate the holy offerings and kept their garments. Scholars disagree about whether this temple would be built literally or whether it is symbolic.

For today: God cares even about the details of how we draw near to Him. There is a way and an order for entering His presence. Today we can approach Him with reverence and gratitude, trusting that Christ has opened the door for us.
exp.41:9:
This verse says there were more chambers or rooms on the east side of the court, along the wall. They were across from the separate place, which is the open space or set-apart area beside the temple, and across from the main building. They are rooms set apart for use by the temple.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here, recounting a vision God gave him during the exile in Babylon. A guide shows him the temple and its measurements in great detail. These chambers, according to the context, were for the priests (Ezekiel 42:13). Interpreters disagree about whether the vision describes a literal future temple or has a symbolic meaning of God's presence and holiness.

For today: God cares about the details of his house, and he cares that there be order and set-apart spaces for worshiping him. We can set aside a time and a place each day, even a simple one, to be alone with him.
exp.41:10:
This verse describes the chambers on the south side of the temple. It says that the open passage in front of them was the same as that of the chambers on the north: the same length, the same width, with the same exits, doors, and entrances. A space that was open and clear beside the building is called the courtyard area, and the exits are the ways out.

The one speaking is the angel who guides Ezekiel through a vision of the temple, during the exile in Babylon. The verses that follow explain the purpose: these chambers were holy, and there the priests ate the offerings and stored them. Scholars disagree about whether this temple was meant to be built literally or whether it is a symbolic picture of God's presence.

For today: God cares about the details and desires order and holiness in worship. We can ask ourselves whether we set aside time and space to draw near to Him with reverence and with simplicity of heart.
exp.41:12:
It says that the north chambers and the south chambers, which stand beside the temple courtyard, are holy chambers. There the priests who draw near to the Lord will eat the most holy offerings, and they will keep the grain offerings, the sin offerings, and the guilt offerings. Everything is done there because the place is holy.

Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon, receives a vision of the temple. A guide shows him and measures each part. These chambers are for the priests. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic message about the holiness of God and his presence with his people.

God takes care that what is sacred is treated with reverence. Today we can approach him with respect and gratitude, setting aside time to pray and read his Word, not doing it in a hurry or out of mere habit.
exp.41:13:
They say that when the priests entered the holy place, they were not to go straight out into the outer court wearing the garments they used for ministering. First they had to leave those garments there, because they were holy, and put on other clothes. Only then could they approach the people.

This is part of the vision of the temple that the prophet Ezekiel received, while a guide showed him the building and measured it. The priests' chambers were holy, because there they ate the sacred offerings. The rule protected the difference between what was set apart for God and the ordinary life of the people. Interpreters disagree about whether this vision refers to a literal future temple or has a symbolic meaning.

For today: serving God deserves respect and reverence. At the same time, whoever serves should draw near to others with simplicity and humility. We can cultivate a life of sincere prayer and then go out to treat people with warmth.
exp.41:19:
This verse says that the man guiding Ezekiel measured the four sides of the temple area. The wall that surrounded it formed a square, five hundred reeds on each side. A reed was a measuring rod; many scholars calculate it was about three meters, though the exact figure is debated. The wall served to separate the holy from the common, that is, from what was ordinary and not meant for worship.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received during the exile in Babylon. In it, a guide with a measuring rod shows him a new temple. This vision gave hope to a discouraged people: God would remain present among them. Interpreters differ on whether it speaks of a literal temple in the future or of a symbolic picture.

For today: God values what is holy. We can set healthy boundaries, such as a daily time of prayer, so that what is ordinary does not crowd out what is sacred.
exp.42:0:
He tells us that a guide brought Ezekiel to the gate of the temple area that faces east. It is a short step, but it prepares what comes next.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks and recounts a vision he received. Earlier, in chapter 10 and following, he saw the glory of God leave the temple because of judgment on the people. Now, in a vision of the new temple, he is brought to the east gate, the gate through which that glory returns, as the verses that follow show. Interpreters disagree about whether this temple points to a literal future temple or to a spiritual picture of God's presence.

For today: God knows how to lead us step by step, even when we feel that He has withdrawn. We can pray and look with hope toward where He may yet work in our lives.
exp.42:1:
Ezekiel says he saw the glory of God coming from the east. Its sound was like the sound of many waters, something strong and awe-inspiring, and the earth shone with that glory. The word "glory" speaks of God's bright and majestic presence.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, speaks during the exile in Babylon. Earlier, in another vision, he had seen the glory of God leave the temple because of the people's sin. Now, in a vision of a restored temple, he sees the glory returning through the eastern gate. It is a message of hope: God did not abandon his people forever. Interpreters debate whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or future.

For today: God wants to dwell among his people. If you feel you have drifted away from Him, you can return with humility, trusting that He draws near with forgiveness and new life.
exp.42:2:
Ezekiel says that this vision of God's glory looked like the two he had already seen: the one of Jerusalem's destruction and the one by the river Chebar. When he saw it, he fell facedown on the ground.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here as a priest exiled in Babylon. Earlier he saw God's glory leave the temple because of the people's sin. Now, in a vision, he sees that glory returning through the east gate. It is a message of hope: God does not abandon his people forever. Some believe it refers to a restoration that was near, others to something still in the future.

For today: when God draws near, the natural response is humility. You can begin your prayer today with reverence, remembering who God is, before asking him for anything.
exp.42:4:
It says that the Spirit lifted up Ezekiel and brought him into the inner court of the temple. There he saw that the glory of the Lord filled the house. The verse's wording refers to the inner court of the temple, which is the courtyard surrounding the main building.

Ezekiel, a prophet and priest, describes a vision he received during the exile in Babylon. Earlier he had seen the glory of God leave the temple because of the people's sin. Now he sees it return through the east gate. God promises to dwell again among Israel and asks His people to give up idolatry. Interpreters differ on whether this temple is literal, future, or symbolic.

For today: God desires to dwell among His people, but He looks for clean and faithful hearts. We can ask Him to remove whatever draws us away from Him and to fill our lives with His presence.
exp.42:6:
God tells Ezekiel that the temple is the place of his throne and of the soles of his feet, that is, where he reigns and makes his presence known. He promises to live there with Israel forever. He also says that the people and their kings will no longer defile his holy name with their whoredom, which here means idolatry and unfaithfulness to God, nor with the carcasses of their kings, probably their tombs or idols near the temple (this is understood in several ways).

God speaks in a vision that Ezekiel receives after the exile in Babylon. His glory fills the house. Before, the people had placed their impure things right next to the temple, and that is why judgment came. Now God promises a new beginning with pure worship.

For today: God wants to live close to you, but he wants a clean heart with no rivals. Ask him today what you have placed beside him, and ask for help to remove it and give him first place.
exp.42:7:
God says that the Israelites set their threshold and their doorpost, that is, the entrance and frame of their own buildings, right up against those of his temple, with only a wall between them and God. In this way they defiled his holy name with their detestable practices, a word that refers to idolatrous practices God hates. Therefore, he says, he consumed them in his fury, meaning he judged them severely.

God speaks in a vision the prophet Ezekiel receives after the glory of the Lord returns to the new temple. He is referring to the earlier kings, who built next to the temple and mixed false worship with what was holy. Many scholars think this alludes to nearby royal palaces and tombs, although the details are interpreted in different ways.

For today: God wants to be the only Lord of our lives, not just one more loyalty alongside others. We can ask ourselves what we have set up close beside God, and hand it over to him.
exp.42:9:
God tells Ezekiel, called "son of man," to show the people of Israel the plan of the new temple that he has seen in a vision. He wants them to be ashamed of their sins and to measure the pattern, that is, to study the design and the measurements of the building. The plan is the blueprint or design.

He speaks himself, during the exile in Babylon. Before this, the kings and the people had placed their idols and their tombs next to the temple, and so they had defiled it. Now God promises to dwell with them forever. Interpreters differ on whether this temple would be built literally, whether it is an image of hope, or whether it points to the future.

For today: sincere shame over sin is not meant to crush us, but to turn us back to God. We can ask him to show us what things we have placed close to him and to help us let them go, so that we may live near him with a clean heart.
exp.42:16:
This verse continues describing the measurements of the altar. The upper part, the platform where the offerings were burned, was a square fourteen cubits on each side. It had a border of half a cubit, and a base of one cubit all around. The stairs, or steps, faced east.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of a new temple, while the people are living in exile. He gives exact measurements and rules for worship. Scholars debate whether this vision will be fulfilled literally, whether it is symbolic, or whether it points to something spiritual. Here there is no certainty.

For today: God cares about the details of how we draw near to Him. We can approach Him with respect, preparing our hearts with reverence, and remember that today we trust in Christ as our way to God.
exp.42:18:
God tells Ezekiel to give a young bull from the herd to the Levitical priests of the family of Zadok. They are the ones who draw near to God to serve him. The bull would be a sin offering, that is, an offering to cleanse sin.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of the future temple. God gives instructions for consecrating the altar on the day it is made. Before it was used, it had to be purified with blood. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a spiritual image.

For today: drawing near to God calls for reverence and a clean heart. Before serving him, we need to acknowledge our sin and trust in the forgiveness that Christ offered for us.
exp.42:19:
This verse says that the priest was to take blood from the young bull and put it on the four horns of the altar, on the four corners of the upper ledge (the hearth) and on the whole border. In this way the altar was made clean and pure. The horns were the points that stood out at the corners of the altar.

God speaks to Ezekiel in a vision of the new temple. After the exile, the people needed to understand that God was to be worshiped with reverence. Before the altar was used, it was to be consecrated with the blood of atonement. How this relates to the future is something Christians interpret in different ways.

For today: God does not come near lightly, and neither should we. Christians believe that Christ cleanses us by his blood. Before praying or serving, we can draw near with humility, thankful for his forgiveness.
exp.42:24:
For seven days, the priests are to offer a male goat every day as a sin offering (atonement). In addition, they are to offer a young bull from the herd and a ram from the flock.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a vision of a new temple. Before the altar could be used, it had to be purified and dedicated for seven days. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of restoration and of God's presence with his people.

For today: God draws near to us in holiness, and he deserves the best, not what is left over. We can prepare ourselves to worship him with a sincere heart, confessing our failings and giving thanks that Christ offered the perfect sacrifice for us.
exp.43:0:
Ezekiel tells us that a guide led him back toward the outer gate of the sanctuary, the one facing east. That gate was shut.

Ezekiel, a prophet and priest, is in the middle of a long vision of a new temple, given to the exiles of Israel. The following verse explains that God himself says the gate will remain shut because he entered through it. It likely recalls the glory of God returning from the east (chapter 43). Interpreters differ on whether this vision should be read literally, symbolically, or as a prophecy about Christ.

For today: the holiness of God deserves respect. We can approach him with reverence, remembering that he opens the way, and we respond with humility and gratitude.
exp.43:3:
In this verse, an angel leads Ezekiel to the north gate, in front of the temple. There the prophet looks and sees that the glory of the Lord, his bright and powerful presence, filled the house. Before that vision, Ezekiel falls on his face in a sign of reverence and humility.

Ezekiel writes this in exile, within a vision of the temple. Earlier, the glory had entered through the east gate, and for that reason that gate was shut. Shortly after, God commands him to pay attention to the rules of the temple and to confront Israel for its abominations. First he sees God's holiness; then comes the call to correct.

For today: before asking something of God, or correcting others, take a moment to acknowledge who He is. Standing in His presence with humility prepares us to listen and to obey.
exp.43:4:
God speaks to Ezekiel and asks him to pay close attention: to set his heart, look with his eyes, and listen with his ears. What the Lord is going to tell him concerns the rules (the instructions) and the laws of the house of the Lord. He must also notice carefully who may enter the temple and who must leave the sanctuary.

The Lord speaks, and Ezekiel has just seen the glory of God filling the temple in a vision, and he fell face down on the ground. Right away comes a message of correction to Israel, which had allowed foreigners who were uncircumcised in heart to serve in the sanctuary. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways, but all of them see the theme of holiness.

For today: when you read the Bible or pray at church, do not do it distracted. God asks for complete attention: heart, eyes, and ears. Before you read, offer a brief prayer asking him to speak to you and to help you obey.
exp.43:8:
He says that God will not allow any foreigner who is uncircumcised in heart and in flesh to enter his sanctuary. Being uncircumcised in heart means having a stubborn heart that neither obeys nor loves God. The sanctuary is the holy place of the temple.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the temple. God rebukes Israel because it had let foreigners serve in his house without respecting his rules, and so the place was defiled. Some understand that the emphasis is on the attitude of the heart, not only on the person's background. Unfaithful Levites would also be corrected.

For today: God seeks sincere devotion, not merely religious appearances. Let us examine whether our hearts are truly surrendered to him when we come to worship him.
exp.43:10:
This verse says that the Levites who turned away from God will not serve as priests, but they will still have service duties in the temple: guarding the gates, slaughtering the animals for the people's sacrifices, and helping the people. The gatekeepers are the ones who watch over the entrances. The burnt offering was the offering that was burned whole, and the sacrifice is the animal that was offered.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of the new temple. The Levites had served before idols and caused Israel to stumble, so God takes away their priesthood, but he does not abandon them altogether. He gives them humble service. Some scholars see discipline combined with mercy here; others debate how this vision of the temple is fulfilled.

For today: our failures have consequences, but God can still use us in humble service. Serve with gratitude wherever he places you, without demanding a place of honor.
exp.43:12:
God says that certain Levites will no longer be able to come near to him as priests. They will not touch the holy things or the most holy offerings. Those who "come near" are those who draw close, so they will bear their shame and the detestable practices they committed.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of the new temple. Those Levites had served before idols and caused Israel to stumble. For this reason they lose the office of priest, but they continue serving in humbler tasks: guarding the gates and helping in the house. The sons of Zadok, who were faithful, will indeed draw near. Interpreters explain the final meaning of this vision in several ways.

For today: serving God is not only a position but faithfulness. Let us examine whether anything holds in our heart the place that belongs to God, and return to him with humility.
exp.43:17:
God says that the priests will wear linen turbans on their heads and linen undergarments around their waists and thighs. The first word refers to turbans or caps, and the second refers to linen garments that cover from the waist down. The phrase about not girding themselves to sweat means they will not wear clothing that makes them perspire, nor belts that weigh them down.

God speaks through Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple. He is referring to the priests descended from Zadok, who would serve closely before Him. Linen, unlike wool, was light and clean. Many understand that sweat suggests human effort or impurity, but interpreters explain it in several ways, and they also debate how this vision is fulfilled.

For today: serve God with reverence, but without anxiety or strain. Your service rests on His grace, not on your exhausting effort.
exp.43:18:
Ezekiel 44:19 says that when the priests went out from the inner court to the outer court, where the people were, they had to take off the garments they had ministered in. They would leave them stored in the holy chambers of the sanctuary and put on other clothes. The phrase about them not sanctifying the people with their garments means that, by touching what was holy in those vestments, the people would be set apart or affected in a way that did not fit them.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the future temple, and gives him rules for the priests. Interpreters disagree about whether that vision will be fulfilled literally or whether it has a symbolic meaning. Either way, the message is that what is holy must be treated with reverence and order.

For today: serving God is a serious matter, but it should not become a spectacle. We can serve with reverence and humility, without presumption or displaying the spiritual to impress others.
exp.43:20:
It says that no priest was allowed to drink wine when he was about to enter the inner court of the temple, which was the place where they served directly before God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who describes in a vision a future temple. There he gives rules for the priests, so that they would guard the holiness of their service and not confuse what is sacred with what is ordinary. Christians interpret this vision in different ways: some see it in a literal way, others in a symbolic way. A similar rule appears in Leviticus 10:8-11.

For today: when you serve God, whether by praying, teaching, or helping others, do it with a clear mind and an attentive heart. Ask Him to help you avoid anything that clouds your judgment or distracts you from Him.
exp.43:22:
It says the priests will have the task of teaching the people to distinguish between the holy, that which belongs to God, and the profane, the common or what is not fit for his service. They are also to teach people to recognize the clean and the unclean, according to the law of Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Chapters 40 to 48 describe a vision of a temple and its service. Here God gives instructions to the Levitical priests of the family of Zadok, so that they will live with reverence and be guides for the people. Interpreters differ on whether this vision will be fulfilled literally or is symbolic.

Today, as God's people, we can ask him for wisdom to discern from the Bible what draws us closer to him and what pulls us away. And those who teach or advise others should do so with humility and by their own example.
exp.43:24:
It says the priest was not to go near a dead body, because that made him unclean according to the law. There was only one exception: if a very close relative died, such as his father, mother, son, daughter, brother, or an unmarried sister. In those cases he could become defiled, that is, ceremonially unclean, in order to attend to the mourning and the burial.

God speaks through Ezekiel, in the vision of the new temple. He is giving rules to the priests, so that they may teach the people to distinguish between what is holy and what is common. Death was regarded as an uncleanness that set a person apart from service in the sanctuary. This rule is similar to the one in Leviticus 21.

For today: God cares about holiness, but he also allows us to love and to grieve for our family. We can serve him with reverence without neglecting our own in their times of sorrow.
exp.43:26:
He says that when a priest, after having been unclean from touching a dead body, returns to serve in the sanctuary, in the inner court, he must offer a sacrifice for sin, that is, for the sin or for cleansing. The word "minister" means to serve. The Lord GOD says so.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the future temple. He gives rules for the priests descended from Zadok, so that they guard the holiness of the place. Interpreters differ on whether this vision describes something literal, symbolic, or yet to be fulfilled.

For today: God values that whoever serves others does so with a clean heart. Before serving in your church or family, take a moment to confess your faults and receive the forgiveness of Christ.
exp.43:27:
This verse says that the priests will not have a piece of land of their own in Israel, as the other families do. God himself will be their inheritance, that is, what they receive as their heritage, and their possession, what belongs to them.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the vision of the new temple. He is giving rules for the Levite priests who serve in the sanctuary. Because their work was the service of God, they lived from the offerings and sacrifices that the people brought, as the following verses describe.

For today: we can ask ourselves what it is that most assures us of life. Even if we have work, a home, or money, our greatest wealth is God himself. Trusting in him frees us from anxiety and helps us to be generous.
exp.43:29:
This verse says that the best and first of everything the people produce belongs to the priests. The "firstfruits" are the first produce of the harvest. The "dough" refers to the first batch of flour kneaded into bread dough. If the people give this to the priest, God promises that his blessing will rest on every household.

God speaks through Ezekiel in the vision of the new temple. The Levite priests received no land as an inheritance, so they lived from the offerings. God himself was their inheritance. Interpreters understand in different ways how this vision is fulfilled.

For today: offer God the first, not what is left over. When you receive your wages or income, set aside a portion first for God and for supporting those who serve, trusting that he cares for your home.
exp.44:0:
It says that when the land was divided among the tribes by lot, a special portion first had to be set apart for God. It would be a rectangle twenty-five thousand reeds long and ten thousand wide. "Inheritance" is what is received as a heritage, and "holy" means set apart for God. The reed was a measuring rod; its exact length is debated, but it was about three meters.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of the future of the people, after the exile in Babylon. He shows a new order for the land, with the sanctuary at the center. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as something literal, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people.

For today: before dividing what we have, whether time, money, or energy, we can first set a part aside for God. In this way we put him at the center of our life.
exp.44:2:
This verse says that, within the portion of land set apart for God, a plot would be measured twenty-five thousand reeds long and ten thousand wide. In it would stand the sanctuary, called the most holy place. A reed was a measuring rod, about three meters according to some scholars; the exact figures are debated.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during Israel's exile. In his vision, the people return to the land and divide it, but first a portion is set apart for the LORD. The priests and the Levites would live near the sanctuary. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future temple, others a spiritual picture of God's presence.

For today: before we divide up what is ours, let us put God first. We can set aside time, money and attention for him, and let his presence be the center of our lives.
exp.44:3:
This verse says that a portion of the land set apart for God will belong to the priests who serve in the sanctuary, those who draw near to minister to the Lord. There they will have room for their houses, and also a holy place where the temple will stand.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the future temple and of the land divided among his people. The Israelites were in exile, and this vision gave them hope of restoration and order in worship. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some see it literally, others as a spiritual symbol of God's presence with his people.

For today: God cares for those who serve him, and he also wants what is holy to hold a central place. Let us set apart time and space in our lives for him, and support with gratitude those who serve in the church.
exp.44:4:
This verse says that the Levites, those who serve in God's house, were given a portion of land measuring twenty-five thousand in length by ten thousand in breadth. It was a possession for them, and it had twenty chambers. Some older translations read differently here, which is why the detail of the twenty chambers is understood in several ways.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the land being divided again. First comes the holy district of the sanctuary, then the portion of the Levites, after that the city and the prince's share. Scholars debate whether this is literal, symbolic, or future.

For today: God cares for those who serve others in his name. We can support, with gratitude and generosity, the pastors, teachers, and servants of our church, so that they can devote themselves to their work with peace of mind.
exp.44:8:
Thus says the Lord God to the princes of Israel: enough is enough. He tells them to stop using violence and taking by force what belongs to others. Instead, they are to practice justice and right judgment, and remove the unfair charges and burdens they had placed on the people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, within his vision of a future temple and a divided land. Before this, God had said that the princes would no longer oppress the people, and that they would have their own portion of land. This way they would have no excuse to abuse others. What follows is about honest weights and measures. Interpreters differ on how to understand this vision, but the call to justice is clear.

For today: if you have authority, whether at work, in the family, or in the church, use it to serve and not to gain advantage. Be fair in money matters and in how you treat others.
exp.44:9:
God commands that there be just balances, and that the ephah and the bath, which were measures for dry goods and liquids, be accurate and honest. The balance is the scale; the ephah measured grain, and the bath measured liquids such as oil or wine. Both had the same volume, according to the following verse.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision about the restoration of Israel. He speaks to the princes, who had abused their power, and asks them to give up violence and unjust demands. Fixed measures protected people from deception in daily trade.

For today: be honest in small things, such as a fair price, work done well, a promise kept, and clean dealings with employees and customers. God cares about justice in everyday life, not only in religious matters.
exp.44:10:
This verse says that the ephah and the bath, which are measures, must be of the same size. The ephah was used to measure dry things, such as grain, and the bath to measure liquids, such as oil or wine. Both were to equal the tenth part of a homer, which was the large reference measure. In this way everyone would use the same fixed standard.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel. He rebukes the princes of Israel because they oppressed the people with violence, robbery, and unjust taxes. He asks them to practice justice, and exact measures were part of that, since they were used for buying, selling, and offering to the Lord. Scholars do not agree on the exact value of these measures in liters.

For today: be honest in small things, such as prices, work, and accounts. God cares about how we treat others in everyday life.
exp.44:11:
God establishes that the shekel, the basic unit of weight, will equal twenty gerahs (a gerah was a very small weight). He then adds 20, 25 and 15 shekels, which make 60, and says that this will be a maneh. This verse is difficult, and some older translations understand it differently, so there is no single certain explanation.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of a restored people and a new temple. Shortly before, he had rebuked the princes of Israel for their violence and abuse. For this reason he requires fair weights and measures, so that no one cheats when buying, selling or giving offerings.

For today: God cares about honesty in everyday life. Be just in your work, in your accounts and in your dealings, without deceiving or taking advantage of anyone. That too is a way of worshiping him.
exp.44:12:
It says the people were to give a grain offering: one-sixth of an ephah for every homer of wheat, and likewise one-sixth of an ephah for every homer of barley. An ephah was a measure for dry goods, and a homer was a large measure, equal to ten ephahs. So a small, well-defined portion was required, close to 1.7 percent.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the vision of a temple and a renewed life for Israel. Before this verse, God calls for honest weights and measures. The offering was part of an arrangement in which the people supported the prince and the worship. The exact details of how this vision would be fulfilled are interpreted in various ways.

For today: God joins worship with honesty. We can give with order and generosity, and be fair in our work, in our prices, and in our agreements, because what we offer to God matters, and so does how we treat others.
exp.44:13:
God sets how much oil is to be given as an offering: a bath, which is the tenth part of a cor. Ten baths equal a homer. The bath, the cor, and the homer were ancient measures; their exact amount in liters today is not known for certain, and scholars give different figures.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of a restored temple. There he gives clear rules for worship and also tells the rulers to stop oppressing people and to use honest measures. Some see something literal here, others something symbolic.

For today: God cares about order and honesty. Offer to God what is yours with sincerity, and be fair in your everyday dealings, without tricks or crooked measures.
exp.44:14:
God commands the people to give one lamb out of every two hundred from the flock, choosing the best and healthiest animals of Israel. These offerings would be used for the sacrifices: the burnt offerings (offerings completely burned) and the peace offerings (offerings of fellowship), to make atonement, that is, to cover the sin of the people.

The Lord speaks through Ezekiel in his vision of a renewed temple and worship. The people bring the offerings, and the prince presents them at the festivals. Scholars understand this vision in several ways: some see it as something literal and future, others as symbolic, and others as fulfilled in Christ.

Today we can learn to give God our best with gratitude, and not what is left over. And we remember that only God can forgive; Christians trust in the sacrifice of Jesus.
exp.44:17:
Thus says the Lord God. In the first month, on the first day of the month, God commanded that a young bull without defect be taken from the herd to cleanse the sanctuary. To cleanse means to take away guilt or cover it through a sacrifice.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of a restored temple and worship (chapters 40–48). After the exile, the people needed to see that the presence of God requires purity. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture. There is no complete agreement on this.
