For today: God cares for the holiness of his house and of his people. We can begin each year or each new stage with humility, asking for forgiveness. Christians believe that Christ is the perfect sacrifice who cleanses us completely.
exp.44:21:
It says that on the day of the Passover (the fourteenth day of the first month), the prince will offer a young bull as a sin offering, both for himself and for all the people of the land.

Ezekiel's words about the sin offering are drawn from the verse above, so the verse of what the offering does is given in plain terms: it is a way of covering over guilt and cleansing it, and it is meant for those who sinned without meaning to.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of a restored temple and worship. The prince is a leader of the people, distinct from the priests. It is striking that he must also make an offering for himself: no leader stands above the need for forgiveness. Interpreters differ on whether this vision is fulfilled literally, symbolically, or in Christ.

For today: if you lead in your home, church, or workplace, acknowledge your own failings with humility. Before guiding others, draw near to God to ask for forgiveness and help.
exp.44:22:
It says that during the seven days of the Passover feast, the prince was to offer a burnt offering to God each day: seven bullocks and seven rams without blemish. In addition, each day he offered a male goat as a sin offering. A burnt offering was one that was burned whole on the altar. "Without blemish" means without any physical flaw.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of a renewed temple and worship (chapters 40 to 48). These instructions differ in several details from the law of Moses, and interpreters understand them in different ways: some see them as something literal in the future, others as a symbolic picture of restored worship. What is clear is that the people were to approach God with reverence.

For today: God deserves our best, not our leftovers. We can offer Him each day our time, attention, and obedience with sincerity, trusting that Christ has already covered our sin.
exp.44:23:
It says that, along with each bull and each ram the prince offers, he must present a grain offering of one ephah, and for each ephah, a hin of oil. The "ephah" was a measure of capacity for dry goods, and the "hin" a measure for liquids. Its exact equivalent in liters is debated, but the ephah was considerably larger than the hin.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the vision of a renewed temple and worship. These rules regulate the prince's offerings during the Passover feast. Interpreters differ on whether this vision describes something literal, something symbolic, or something future. What is clear is that God wants orderly worship.

For today: come near to God with order and generosity, not with what is left over. Sincere worship includes preparation and concrete giving.
exp.44:24:
It says that in the seventh month, on the fifteenth day, when the feast arrives, the prince must offer the same things as during the seven days before it (those of the Passover). That includes the sin offering, the burnt offering (what was burned up entirely), the grain offering, and the oil. Measures of quantity are the ephah and the hin, which are not mentioned here.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of a new temple and an ordered worship (chapters 40 to 48). This feast of the seventh month seems to be the Feast of Tabernacles, or Booths. Scholars understand this vision in several ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of restoration and of Christ. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: God values consistency and order in worship. We can seek Him faithfully, not only in special moments, but in a regular and sincere way.
exp.45:0:
God says that the east gate of the inner court of the temple will be shut during the six working days. It will be opened only on the Sabbath and on the day of the new moon, when the month begins. The inner court is the courtyard closest to the temple, and the new moon was a monthly festival.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. In chapters 40 to 48 he receives a vision of a restored temple and worship. Interpreters differ about its meaning: some think of a literal future temple, while others see it as a symbolic picture of restoration and God's presence. What is clear is that worship was to be carried out with order and reverence.

For today: work has its place, but God deserves set-apart time. Keep a regular moment, such as on Sunday or each morning, to draw near to Him with calm and gratitude.
exp.45:1:
This verse says that the prince will enter through the porch of the outer gate and stand beside the post of the gate. While the priests prepare his burnt offering and his peace offerings, he will worship at the threshold of the gate. Then he will go out the same way he came in. The gate will not be shut until evening, so that others may also draw near.

God Himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of a new temple. It describes how worship should be carried out there. Scholars disagree about whether this vision will be fulfilled literally, or whether it is a symbolic picture of worship to God. What is clear is the order and the reverence with which a person should come near to Him.

For today: even someone who has authority approaches God with humility. Find a moment today to worship Him without rushing, recognizing that He is greater than you.
exp.45:2:
This verse says that the people of the land, that is, the ordinary people of Israel, will worship God at the entrance of the gate of the inner court, on the sabbaths and on the new moons. The new moons were the first days of each month. To worship means to bow down and acknowledge God as Lord.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of a restored temple and worship. The east gate was opened on special days, and the prince and the people worshiped there, while the priests offered the sacrifices. Interpreters disagree about whether this vision describes something literal, symbolic, or future.

For today: God values constant and orderly worship, offered together with his people. Set aside a fixed time each week to worship him, whether you are a leader or an ordinary person.
exp.45:3:
It says that the prince must present to God, on the sabbath day, a complete burnt offering: six lambs and a ram, all without blemish. A burnt offering is an offering that was entirely burned on the altar. Without blemish means without any harm or flaw.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the restored temple (chapters 40 to 48). There it is described how the people would worship with order and reverence. Interpreters do not agree on whether this will be fulfilled literally or whether it is a spiritual picture of future worship. What is clear is that even the prince draws near to God as one worshiper among others.

For today: God deserves the best of us, not the leftovers. We can give him first place with our time, our attention and our heart, especially on the day of rest, regardless of our position.
exp.45:6:
He says that the prince, at the festival of the new moon, was to offer a grain offering: an ephah (a measure of about 22 liters, though the exact calculation is debated) with the bull, and an ephah with each ram. For the lambs he would give whatever he was able. In addition, a hin of oil (about 3 or 4 liters) for each ephah.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the temple and its worship (chapters 40 to 48). God gives orderly instructions for worshiping him with reverence. Christians interpret this vision in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture.

For today: God values orderly worship, and also giving according to what we are able to give. With whatever you have, whether time, talents, or resources, offer God your best with a sincere heart.
exp.45:7:
When the prince comes in to worship at the temple, he will enter through the porch of the east gate and leave by the same way.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who describes in a vision a temple and an order of worship. This follows the offerings for the new moon. The text does not explain every detail, and interpreters understand it in different ways: some see it as a literal description of the future, others as a symbolic picture. What is clear is that even the prince submits to the order God set.

For today: no one stands above the reverent way of drawing near to God. Come to Him with humility, without haste or pride, and let Him shape the way you worship.
exp.45:10:
This verse states how much grain offering was to be given at the feasts and solemn assemblies: one ephah of flour for each bullock, and one ephah for each ram. For the lambs, each person gave what they were able to give. In addition, one hin of oil for each ephah. The ephah was a measure of capacity for dry goods, and the hin a measure for liquids. Its exact equivalence is debated.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile, in his vision of a renewed temple and worship. These instructions set out how the people, together with the prince, were to worship. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways, and not all of them agree.

For today: God cares about orderly worship, but also about generous and sincere worship. Today we can give God our best, according to our means, with a grateful heart.
exp.45:11:
If the prince wishes to offer to God, of his own free will and not out of obligation, a burnt offering (a complete offering that is burned) or peace offerings (offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving), the eastern gate of the inner court will be opened for him. There he will present his offering just as he does on the Sabbath. Then he will go out, and the gate will be shut after he leaves.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who describes a future temple and worship. Interpreters disagree about whether this is a literal vision, a symbolic one, or one tied to the Messiah. Here the emphasis is that even the prince must worship with order and reverence, under God's rules.

For today: God values an offering given freely and with joy. We can serve him and give him our time, prayer, or help to others, not under pressure, but with a willing and reverent heart.
exp.45:13:
Ezekiel 46:14 says that every morning, along with the lamb for the burnt offering, a grain offering was to be presented: one sixth of an ephah of fine flour (about a liter and a half or two, depending on how it is calculated), mixed with one third of a hin of oil (roughly a liter and a half). The verse calls this a meat offering, meaning an offering of grain. It is also a perpetual ordinance, a rule that was to be kept at all times.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple and its worship. The regulations aim at a worship that is orderly for Israel, and the daily offering shows that communion with God was not occasional. Interpreters differ on whether this vision is to be fulfilled literally, symbolically, or in Christ.

For today: we can give God the first fruits of each day. Before rushing into our tasks, a moment of prayer and simple gratitude can set the tone for the rest of the day.
exp.45:14:
Every morning, the text says, a lamb was to be offered to God, along with a grain offering of flour and oil.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple and the restored worship (chapters 40 to 48). There it is described how the people would once again worship in good order. Interpreters differ: some see a literal temple in the future, while others see a symbolic picture of worship and of Christ, the Lamb of God.

For today: God values a daily offering, not only an occasional one. We can begin each morning by offering Him our time, our strength, and our heart, with a simple prayer of thanksgiving and dedication.
exp.45:18:
It says that the angelic guide brought Ezekiel, in the vision, through an entry beside the gate into the holy rooms of the priests. Those rooms faced north, and behind them, toward the west, there was a separate space. The guide "brought me through" is the meaning of the verse, and the rooms are chambers, or halls.

Ezekiel receives a vision of a new temple, and a guide shows him each place in turn. What follows explains that this place was used for cooking the sacred offerings, so the priests did not have to carry them out into the outer court where the people were. Interpreters differ on whether this vision describes a literal future temple or is a spiritual picture of God's presence.

For today: God cares about order and reverence in what is holy. We can set apart a time and a quiet place to be with Him, taking care that what is sacred is not mixed up with the hurry of each day.
exp.45:19:
It says that in the vision there is a special place inside the temple where the priests boil or cook the meat of the sin offerings and the trespass offerings, and also prepare the meat offering. They do it there, inside, so as not to carry those holy things out into the outer court, where the people are. The phrase about the people being sanctified here means that what is holy should not improperly affect the people.

The one speaking is a guide who shows Ezekiel, in a vision, the future temple. He walks through its parts and its rules. The purpose is to teach that God is holy and that his service must be carried out with order and reverence. Interpreters disagree about whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

Today we can learn to treat what belongs to God with reverence and care. Before we speak, serve, or teach, it is good to approach with humility, remembering that God is holy and merciful.
exp.45:20:
Here the guide, who in Ezekiel's vision is a man with an appearance like bronze, leads the prophet into the outer court of the temple. He makes him walk to the four corners, and in each one he sees a small court. The outer court is an open space that surrounds the temple, and the corners are the places where the courts stand.

Ezekiel receives this vision of a new temple, with very exact measurements. Just before, the guide showed where the priests would cook the offerings, so that the holy things would not be carried out into the court where the people were. These courts, according to the text that follows, are places prepared for cooking the people's offerings. How this vision is fulfilled, interpreters understand in several ways.

For today: God cares about the details of worship, with order and respect. We can draw near to Him with reverence, also in everyday life, knowing that even simple things, like preparing a meal, can be done for Him.
exp.45:23:
He says the guide shows Ezekiel the kitchens of the temple, the places where the ones who serve the house cooked the meat of the sacrifices the people brought. The guide tells Ezekiel these are the places of them that boil, where the ministers of the house shall boil the sacrifice of the people.

The one speaking is the man who, in the vision, guides Ezekiel through the future temple and explains each part to him. This vision is found in chapters 40 to 48. The verses before describe four courts in the corners, with places for cooking. How this temple should be understood is something scholars interpret in different ways: literally, symbolically, or both.

For today: God cares even about simple services, such as cooking and feeding others. What you do in everyday life, such as preparing a meal for your family or for someone in need, can be a worthy service done with love for God.
exp.46:0:
Ezekiel sees that a guide brings him back to the entrance of the temple. There he discovers water flowing out from beneath the threshold, that is, the base of the doorway. It runs toward the east, because the temple faced the east. The water flows down from the right side of the building, on the south side of the altar.

Ezekiel was a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. This vision of the temple comes to encourage a people who had lost everything. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some see a promise for Israel, others an image of God's work that reaches to Christ and his Spirit. What is certain is that the water springs from the presence of God.

For today: true life does not begin in our own strength, but in God. Seek his presence every day and let it renew your heart.
exp.46:1:
It says that the guide brought Ezekiel out of the temple through the north gate and led him around the outside to the east gate. There he saw water coming out on the right side (the south). The phrases "brought me out" and "led me around" are the ones to note here, since they are the words in this verse that carry the movement.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received while in exile in Babylon. A man guides him and measures the temple. The east gate was shut, so they had to go around outside. The water comes from the temple, that is, from the presence of God, and then it grows. Interpreters understand it in several ways: as a future restoration of Israel, as a spiritual picture of the life God gives, or as both.

For today: the life God gives begins in his presence. Seek to spend time with him every day, and let that life flow out to others as well.
exp.46:2:
The man who was guiding Ezekiel went out toward the east with a measuring line in his hand. He measured a thousand cubits (about 500 meters, since a cubit is roughly half a meter) and led him through the water, which reached only to the ankles.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received during the exile, about a restored temple. From the temple flows a river that grows deeper with every thousand cubits measured. Many understand it as an image of the life and blessing that come from God's presence. Some see it as a promise for Israel, and others relate it to Christ and the Spirit. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: life with God can begin with little, like water up to the ankles. Take one more step, pray, read, obey, and let Him lead you deeper.
exp.46:3:
This verse says that the man guiding Ezekiel continued measuring another thousand cubits along the river that flowed from the temple. In the first stretch, the water reached the knees. In the next, it reached the loins, that is, up to the waist. With each measurement, the water grew deeper.

Ezekiel is the one speaking, recounting a vision that God gave him. A guide, holding a measuring cord, leads him step by step through the water flowing from the temple. Many understand this water to represent God's life and blessing, which keeps growing without end. Some see it as a promise for Israel's future, others as an image of the Spirit. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: God invites us to move forward in faith little by little, not staying only at the water's edge. Each step of trust brings us into a deeper life with Him.
exp.46:9:
When the river's water reaches the sea, there will be fishers along its shore. From En-gedi to En-eglaim the nets will be spread out to dry, and there will be fish of many kinds, as many as in the great sea. The phrase about the net-drying place refers to a spot where the nets are laid out to dry.

An angel guides Ezekiel through a vision of the new temple. From it flows a river that runs eastward toward the Dead Sea, whose waters are salty and lifeless. En-gedi lies on its western shore; the location of En-eglaim is not certain. Many see in this an image of the restoration and life that God gives; others also expect a literal fulfillment in the future.

For today: where God acts, He can bring life to what seemed dead. Bring Him that dry area of your life, your family or your work, and trust that He can renew it with patience and hope.
exp.46:10:
It says that the swampy places and the marshes along the sea, where the river reaches, will not be made healthy. They will remain salty and will serve as salt flats, that is, places where salt is harvested. Here the words for these low, wet areas refer to waters that stand still, without current.

Ezekiel recounts a vision God gave him while the people were in exile. A guide shows him a river flowing out from the temple that brings life to everything it touches. This verse is an exception within that healing. Some think the salt was useful and valuable. Others see a warning: what lies outside the river does not receive its life. The text does not explain this, so it is wise to be cautious.

For today: do not remain like stagnant water. Stay close to God through prayer, the Bible, and community, so that his life can flow through you.
exp.46:12:
This verse says that God himself gives an instruction: the people must divide the promised land among the twelve tribes of Israel. An inheritance is property that is received as a family's heritage. The boundary is the limit or border of the land. Joseph receives two portions, because his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, counted as separate tribes.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. After the vision of the river that flows from the temple and brings life, God shows how the land will be divided when his people return. It is a promise of restoration. Scholars understand this vision in different ways: some see it as something literal, others as a picture of God's future.

For today: God cares that there is a place for each of his own. You can trust that he has an inheritance prepared for you, and live with generosity, without envy for what others receive.
exp.46:15:
This verse lists places that mark the northern border of the land God promises to Israel: Hamath, Berothah and Sibraim, between the territory of Damascus and the territory of Hamath, and also Hazar-hatticon, next to the region of Hauran.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision about the restoration of Israel. He tells them to divide the land among all the tribes, and recalls that he swore to give it to their fathers. Today it is not known exactly where some of these places were, and there are different interpretations about whether this vision speaks of something literal or symbolic.

For today: God keeps what he promises and cares even for the details. We can trust that his faithfulness does not stay at the level of general ideas, but also reaches the concrete details of our lives.
exp.47:1:
It says that the tribe of Asher receives a strip of land, right beside the one belonging to Dan. That strip runs from east to west, from the east side all the way to the sea, which is the Mediterranean Sea. The word "border" means a limit or boundary line.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes from exile. In chapters 40 to 48 he describes a vision of Israel's restoration: a temple, a land, and a people set in order. Here the land is divided into strips of equal size, one for each tribe. Interpreters differ on whether this should be fulfilled literally or whether it is a symbolic picture of future hope.

For today: God does not forget anyone. Even a tribe that is seldom mentioned has its assigned place. You can trust that God has a place and a purpose for you too, and be encouraged to value others in your church.
exp.47:4:
It says that the portion of land belonging to the tribe of Ephraim lies right beside that of Manasseh. Each strip runs from east to west, from the east side to the west side. The sea mentioned at the far end is the Mediterranean Sea.

Ezekiel's text is the same verse as the English reading above; "border" is the word used for the boundary or limit between the strips.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. In this final vision, God shows how the land would be divided among the twelve tribes, in orderly strips. Interpreters do not agree: some see it as something literal for the future, others as a symbol of restoration and of God's presence with his people.

For today: God takes care that each person has a place and a portion. You can rest in the assurance that He does not forget you, and also make room for others with generosity, without envy.
exp.47:6:
It says that the tribe of Judah receives a strip of land next to that of Reuben. That strip runs from east to west, from the east side to the Mediterranean Sea. The sea is the Mediterranean, and the border is the boundary line.

God shows Ezekiel a vision of the future division of the land, after the exile in Babylon. The tribes appear in parallel strips. Judah lies right beside the holy portion, where the sanctuary will be. Interpreters understand this in different ways: some see it as a literal promise, others as a symbolic picture of restoration and of God's presence.

For today: God cares that each one has their place. We can live with confidence, knowing we have a place among his people, and seek to have God at the center of our lives.
exp.47:7:
It says that, right next to the territory of Judah, running from east to west, there will be a special portion set apart. It measures twenty-five thousand reeds wide, and long like the other parts, from east to west. In the middle of that portion will be the sanctuary.

Ezekiel, a prophet and priest, records a vision God gave him near the end of the book. The people were in exile, and the vision showed a restoration with the land divided in good order. Scholars interpret this in different ways: some read it literally, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people. The central point is that the sanctuary holds the center.

For today: ask yourself what occupies the center of your life. We can arrange our time, our work, and our family around God, so that his presence becomes the reference point for everything else.
exp.47:8:
This verse says that the portion of land that the people were to set apart for the Lord would measure twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth. The unit of measure is not specified in this translation, and its exact size in meters is debated, but it was a measure used in that time.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the final vision of the book. There it describes how the land would be divided among the tribes and a holy area set aside, with the sanctuary in the middle. Scholars interpret this vision in several ways: some see it literally, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people.

For today: God deserves the center and the first place. We can ask ourselves what real space, of time, attention and resources, we are setting aside for Him in our daily life.
exp.47:9:
1) What it says: God marks out a portion of holy land for the priests. It measures twenty-five thousand in length (north to south) and ten thousand in breadth (east to west). The portion is the share allotted to someone in the division of the land, and the measure is a unit of length. In the middle of that portion will be the sanctuary of the Lord.

2) Context: This is part of the vision God gave the prophet Ezekiel about the land divided again and a future temple. The people were in exile and needed hope. Interpreters differ: some see it as a literal future event, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people. The Bible does not fully explain it.

3) For today: God wants to be at the center, not at the edge. We can ask what place He holds in our decisions, our time, and our home, and set aside room for Him each day.
exp.47:12:
This verse says that the Levites will receive a portion of land next to that of the priests. It measures twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth. A measuring rod was the unit used for measuring; in this vision it comes to about three meters, though scholars do not fully agree on its exact measure. The border is the limit or boundary line.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a vision about the land being divided again. Earlier it was said that the priests, the sons of Zadok, were faithful, while the Levites went astray with Israel. Even so, the Levites are given a place and a service. There are different ways to understand this vision: some see it as something literal and future, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people.

For today: God cares for the place of each servant, even for one who has failed and turns back to him. Serve where he places you, with faithfulness and humility.
exp.47:17:
It says that the land left over beside the holy portion, on the east and west sides, ten thousand on each side, will be used for farming. Its crops will be for those who work in service to the city.

Ezekiel, speaking for God in his final vision of a restored and well-ordered land, says these servants will come from all the tribes of Israel. Some believe this describes a literal temple and city, while others see it as a picture of God's kingdom. Christians interpret it in several ways.

For today: God cares for those who serve others and provides what they need. We can generously support those who work for the good of the community, both in the church and beyond it.
exp.47:20:
It says the land that is left over on each side of the holy portion and of the city belongs to the prince. That land stretches toward the east and toward the west, alongside the twenty-five thousand (reeds, a unit of length). Even so, the sanctuary stands in the center of the holy portion.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, and in the final vision of the book he divides the land for the exiled people. The sanctuary is placed at the center, and the prince has his own share set apart. Scholars interpret this vision in several ways: some see it as literal, others as symbolic or related to the future.

For today: although the prince had his own land, God remained at the center. Put God at the center of your plans and your possessions, and let him order everything else.
exp.47:22:
This verse says that, after the holy portion, the one for the Levites, the city, and the prince, the rest of the land would be divided among the other tribes. Benjamin would receive a strip that runs from east to west. The sea mentioned in the original is the Mediterranean Sea, and the word for "portion" means share or inheritance.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a final vision about the restored people. By showing an orderly division of the land, God gave hope to an exiled people. Interpreters differ on the meaning: some read it literally, others as a symbol of God's future kingdom. Benjamin is placed beside the holy territory, near Judah.

For today: God makes sure that each person has their place and their share. You can rest in the knowledge that he does not forget you, and serve with gratitude where he has placed you.
exp.47:23:
This verse says that, next to the territory of Benjamin, the tribe of Simeon is given a strip of land. That strip runs from east to west, from the east all the way to the sea, which is the Mediterranean Sea.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the final vision of the book. There a land is described, divided into equal strips, with the temple and the city in the center. The exiled Jews needed the promise that God would restore them. Interpreters differ on whether this vision is literal, symbolic, or fulfilled in Christ and his people.

For today: God does not forget anyone. Simeon has his assigned place, and so do you. Trust that God cares for you and gives you a place among his people.
exp.47:24:
This verse says that, next to the territory of Simeon, lies the portion of the tribe of Issachar. Each tribe receives a strip of land running from east to west, reaching all the way to the sea, that is, to the Mediterranean Sea. A boundary or border is the line that marks where one area ends and another begins.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who describes a vision of the land being divided again among the twelve tribes, at the end of the book. The people were in exile, and this vision gave them hope of restoration. Interpreters differ: some understand it literally, others as a symbol of the restored people of God.

For today: God cares for each one and gives each a place. No one is forgotten. We can trust that he has a place for us, and live in peace with those who are beside us.
exp.47:30:
This verse says that the city will have twelve gates, and each one will bear the name of a tribe of Israel. Here the three gates on the north side are described: Reuben, Judah, and Levi. A measure of length was a reed, and an inheritance is the land received as a family's portion.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, at the end of his book. It is a vision given to a people in exile, to encourage them with the promise that God dwells in the midst of his people. Interpreters differ: some see it as a promise for Israel, others as a picture of God's people in general.

For today: in that city everyone has access, from the tribe of Judah to the tribe of Levi. God counts on every person. Today we can welcome with warmth those who seem different in our church.
exp.47:32:
This verse describes the south side of the city that Ezekiel sees in his vision. It measures four thousand five hundred reeds (a reed was a measuring rod, about three meters according to some calculations) and has three gates, named for the tribes of Simeon, Issachar, and Zebulun. The south side is the one that faces toward noon, the direction the sun is highest.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting what God showed him during the exile in Babylon. This is the close of the book: a vision of restoration, with a city whose twelve gates carry the names of the twelve tribes. Scholars understand it in different ways: as a literal temple and city yet to come, or as a symbol of God's presence with his people. The following verse calls the city by a name that means the LORD is there.

For today: God leaves no one outside his plan. Each tribe has its gate, and each person has a place. You can rest in the knowledge that God knows you by name and welcomes you.
exp.47:34:
It says the city that Ezekiel sees in his vision measures eighteen thousand measures all around (a measure was a rod of about three meters, though the exact calculation is debated). And from that day the city shall be called "The Lord is there."

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, for he received this vision during the exile in Babylon. The people were far from their land, and the Temple had been destroyed. At the end of the book, God promises restoration and, above all, his presence. Some believe the vision speaks of a literal future, others that it is symbolic of the church or of heaven; Christians understand it in different ways.

The most valuable thing about a place is not its walls or its size, but that God is present. Today we can ask him to be the center of our home, our work, and our daily life.
exp.29:2:
It says that God's judgment is very near. "The Day of the LORD" is a time when God acts to judge. "A day of clouds" speaks of darkness and distress, like a sky covered with clouds. "A time of doom for the nations" means a time of judgment for the nations, that is, the peoples who were not Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. The message announces judgment against Egypt and its allies, such as Ethiopia and Libya, who trusted in their power and their military strength. The text presents the sword as a sign of that judgment, and scholars often connect it with Babylon.

For today: let us not put our security in money, power, or human alliances. All of that can fall. Let us live with humility, trusting in God, and listen to his call to turn back to him while there is still time.
exp.47:31:
This verse describes the east side of the city that Ezekiel sees in his vision. It is 4,500 cubits long, and it has three gates: the gate of Joseph, the gate of Benjamin, and the gate of Dan. The cubit was a unit of measure based on the length of a forearm. Here "Joseph" stands for the tribes of his sons, Ephraim and Manasseh.

God shows Ezekiel this vision at the end of the book. The people were in exile, and God promises them restoration and his presence among them. The city ends up being called "The LORD is there." Scholars interpret it in several ways: some see it as literal, others as symbolic.

For today: in this city there is room for all the tribes, each with its own gate. God does not leave anyone outside of his people. We can welcome other believers with love, even when they are different from us.
exp.11:3:
It says that Ezekiel must bring out his baggage, his belongings packed for a journey. First he brings them out by day, where everyone can see them. Then, in the evening, he himself goes out in plain view of the people, like someone being taken away into exile.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who was living among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. The people did not want to listen or believe, so God asks him for a message that can be seen, like a sign. Many understand that it announced that Jerusalem would also go into exile. How exactly he did it, the text does not detail further.

For today: sometimes God speaks to us and we pretend not to hear, because his message makes us uncomfortable. Today you might pray: "Señor, dame oídos dispuestos," and obey that simple word you already know.
exp.7:12:
He tells us that God speaks to Ezekiel after showing him a terrible vision. God says, "You will see them committing even greater abominations." He is warning that there are still worse things to come, acts that God detests, and that the leaders and people of Jerusalem were doing them.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision. Before this, Ezekiel saw seventy elders of Israel burning incense in secret before images, thinking, "The LORD does not see us." God shows him that nothing is hidden and that his people had turned away from Him. This explains the judgment that comes afterward.

For today: God sees what we do in secret, and He does so with the intention of healing, not humiliating. Today we can ask Him to show us honestly what is in our heart, confess it, and return to Him without fear.
exp.32:25:
God asks those who remained in Judah after the fall of Jerusalem: how can they expect to possess the land if they live by violence? "You have relied on your swords" means that they trusted in their own strength and in weapons rather than in God. "Detestable acts" refers to practices that God hates, such as idolatry. "Each of you has defiled his neighbor's wife" means that they dishonored their neighbors' marriages through adultery.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. Those who stayed among the ruins of the land claimed it belonged to them, since Abraham was one man and received it, so they, being many, had even more reason to think so. But God shows them that their conduct contradicted that confidence, and announces judgment.

For today: it is not enough to claim God's blessings; He expects a faithful life. Examine whether your confidence rests on inherited promises or on sincere and humble obedience.
exp.19:7:
They say that the people of Israel, while still in Egypt, rebelled against God. They refused to listen to him, and they would not turn away from the detestable things they saw before them, the images and idols they worshiped. They did not give up the idols of Egypt either. Because of this, God said he would pour out his wrath on them and let his anger run its full course against them in the land of Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was in exile in Babylon. The elders of Israel came to consult him, and God reminds them that their disobedience goes back a long way. This account does not appear in the same way in Exodus, and some scholars think Ezekiel summarizes the history with his own emphasis. The verse that follows shows that God acted for the sake of his name.

For today: the heart easily grows accustomed to what it sees. Ask God to show you which thing around you has taken his place, and dare to let it go with confidence in his mercy.
exp.30:4:
It says that this great tree grew taller than all the other trees of the field. Its branches multiplied, and its boughs grew long as it spread them out, because it had abundant water. The phrase "towered higher" means that it rose up high above the rest. The branches and boughs are the limbs of the tree. "Spread them out" describes how the tree reached outward as it grew.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and tells him to speak to the pharaoh of Egypt. He compares him with Assyria, pictured as a majestic cedar that was powerful and then fell. Many understand the comparison as a warning: if Assyria fell, Egypt too can fall. Some scholars debate certain details of the image, but the general message is clear.

For today: everything we have, such as talents, success, or influence, comes from the hand of God. If we forget this and fill ourselves with pride, we fall easily. Let us thank God and use what he gives us to bless others.
exp.16:12:
This verse says that the king of Babylon took a member of the royal family of Judah, made a covenant with him, and put him under an oath of loyalty. He also carried away the leading men of the land. "A member of the royal family" means a descendant of the king's house, and "putting him under oath" means that he required him to swear an oath.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon, whom he calls "a rebellious house." He explains to them the parable of the eagles. The king of Babylon is Nebuchadnezzar, and the royal descendant appears to be Zedekiah. God reminds them that Zedekiah swore loyalty, but then broke that covenant by seeking help from Egypt.

For today: God takes a given word seriously. Keeping our promises, even the difficult ones, is a way of honoring him, and trusting in him is safer than looking for easy escapes.
exp.31:22:
It says that the graves of Assyria lie in the deepest parts of the Pit, and that its people are laid in graves all around its tomb. All of them were killed by the sword, though they once spread terror among the living. The Pit is the place of the dead, and "fallen by the sword" describes those who died in battle, without any covenant with God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who laments over Egypt. He shows Egypt in the realm of the dead, alongside mighty nations such as Assyria and Elam, which have already fallen. The message is that no empire, however fearsome, escapes God's judgment. The details of that world of the dead are poetic images, and scholars interpret them in various ways.

Today: do not let yourself be intimidated by human power or envy it. What is built on fear and pride does not last; trust in God, who rules over all.
exp.23:11:
It says that Jerusalem, compared to a rusty pot, has frustrated every effort to clean herself. Her thick rust is the dirt and wickedness stuck to her, and it has not been removed, not even by the fire. For that reason she will be burned in the fire. The image is of effort that goes nowhere, because the filth is so deeply fixed that it stays even under heat.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is among the exiles in Babylon. When the siege of Jerusalem begins, God uses the image of a pot to show that the city, full of violence and sin, will be judged. Before this, he had already called her to return, but she did not want to be cleansed.

For today: let us not hide sin or try to cleanse it with appearances or our own efforts. Let us ask God to truly cleanse us, and let us respond quickly when he calls us to change.
exp.17:15:
This verse describes a righteous man: he does not oppress anyone, he does not keep a pledge that someone gave him as security for a loan, he does not rob, he gives bread to the hungry and clothes the naked with clothing. To oppress means to mistreat or abuse another person, and keeping a pledge refers to holding on to an item that was given as security when it should have been returned.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel. They were saying that they suffered for the sins of their fathers. God answers that each person is accountable for his or her own choices. The son who sees the wrongdoing of his father and decides not to imitate it will live. This verse is part of a list of behaviors that show a life faithful to God.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we can help with something concrete: food, clothing, or fair treatment. And if we come from a family with bad examples, God invites us to choose a different path.
exp.40:23:
Each entrance of the temple had two doors, and these doors swung on their hinges. Each doorway, both the one to the temple and the one to the inner sanctuary, had two swinging panels.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, recounts a vision that God gave him. A guide who looked like a man shows him and measures a new temple, with many details. Scholars disagree about its meaning: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbol of God's presence with his restored people.

For today: God cares even about the details of how we approach him. The doors speak of orderly and respectful access. We can draw near to God with reverence, but without fear, remembering that in Christ we have open access to his presence.
exp.23:10:
It says that, after the meat has been cooked, God will set the empty pot on the coals. It gets so hot that its copper glows, and the impurity inside melts and the rust is consumed.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. Jerusalem is compared to a pot, full of violence and injustice (the "city of bloods"). With this image, God announces that the city will be purified by the fire of judgment, because it did not want to cleanse itself beforehand.

For today: we should not ignore God's calls to change. If he shows us something dirty in our hearts, such as resentment or deceit, let us respond quickly with repentance, trusting in his forgiveness and his grace.
exp.39:4:
He says that Ezekiel saw a wall surrounding the temple area. The man who was guiding him held a measuring rod six long cubits in length, each cubit being a cubit and a handbreadth: an ordinary cubit plus a handbreadth (about 52 to 53 cm, although experts are not completely sure). With that rod he measured the wall: one rod thick and one rod high.

Ezekiel was in exile in Babylon. In a vision, God took him to Israel, and a guide who appeared to be a man showed him a new temple. He was told to look closely, listen carefully, and take to heart what he saw, so that he could tell it to the people later. Scholars interpret this vision in several ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol, or as a promise that God would dwell again with his people.

For today: God attends to the details and invites us to give attention to his Word calmly, not in a hurry. Today, read a passage slowly and ask him to speak to you.
exp.13:2:
God tells Ezekiel that these men have set up idols in their hearts. On top of that, they keep before their faces the wicked stumbling blocks that lead them into sin. A stumbling block is a stone over which a person trips and falls. Then God asks whether He should let Himself be consulted by them at all. The question sounds like a refusal: one cannot seek God with a divided heart.

God speaks to Ezekiel, addressing him as "son of man." Some elders of Israel came to hear him, perhaps looking for a word from the Lord. But God sees that their hearts are still attached to their idols. His answer seeks to call them back to Him.

For today: before asking God for direction, we can ask ourselves what holds first place in our hearts. If there is something we love more than Him, let us sincerely give it to God, and He receives us.
exp.35:20:
God says that he was concerned for his holy name, that is, for his reputation and his honor. That name had been dishonored by Israel among the nations to which they had gone. "Nations" means non-Jewish peoples, and "dishonor" means treating what is sacred as common or worthless.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile. Israel had been scattered because of its sin. But the nations, seeing the exiles, thought that the God of Israel was weak or unable to care for his people. For this reason God announces that he will act, not because of any merit on their part, but to show who he truly is.

For today: the way we live speaks of God before others. We can ask him to help us live in such a way that his name is honored and not shamed, trusting that his mercy remains greater than our failures.
exp.22:17:
Oholah and Oholibah, the two sisters who stand for Samaria and Jerusalem, did not hide their unfaithfulness; they practiced it openly. "Openly prostituted herself" points to a faithlessness that was on full display, and "exposed her nakedness" refers to their shame and sin laid bare. "I turned away from her in disgust" means that God felt revulsion at her and withdrew from her, just as he had earlier turned away from her sister.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses a very harsh image: two sisters who were bound to Him. Through Oholibah, he shows how Jerusalem abandoned God to trust in Babylon, Egypt, and other nations, and in their idols. Many understand this as a warning before judgment.

For today: do not play with whatever draws you away from God, thinking nothing will happen. If you have placed your trust in anything more than in Him, return to Him with sincerity; God still calls people to repentance.
exp.33:11:
This verse says that God compares himself to a shepherd who looks for his scattered sheep while he is among the flock. In this way God promises to look for his people and to rescue them from all the places where they have been scattered on a day of clouds and darkness. The phrase "a day of clouds and darkness" refers to a time of misfortune and confusion, probably the time of judgment and exile.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The leaders of Israel, called shepherds, had taken advantage of the people instead of caring for them. Because of this, God says he will take the sheep away from them and will himself look for them. It is a promise of comfort for a people exiled and scattered.

For today: if you feel lost, forgotten, or far from home, remember that God knows you and looks for you. You can approach him with confidence, knowing that you are not invisible to him.
exp.6:22:
God tells Ezekiel to forge a chain. That chain is a picture of the captivity that is coming upon the people. The reason is that the land is full of crimes of bloodshed, and the city is full of violence.

God speaks in the middle of the announcement of Jerusalem's end, shortly before its fall to Babylon. The people had filled the city with injustice and idolatry. That is why God allows outsiders to plunder and defile it. Some understand the chain as a sign of captivity; the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: God takes injustice and violence seriously. We can ask ourselves where we mistreat others, and ask Him to make us just and peaceful people who defend the weak.
exp.12:4:
This verse says that the false prophets did not do what was needed to protect Israel. The "gaps" are the breaches or openings in a broken wall. To "restore the wall" means repairing and raising a defense. "The Day of the LORD" is the time of judgment, when the battle against the people would come.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who prophesied among the exiles in Babylon. God rebukes the prophets who made up messages of peace from their own ideas. Instead of calling the people to repentance, which would have been like repairing the wall, they left them unprotected before the judgment that was coming.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we speak God's truth even when it is uncomfortable, or only what comforts. Truly loving others includes speaking to them with honesty, with tenderness, and on the basis of the Bible, not on the basis of our own wishes.
exp.29:8:
God says that on that day he will send messengers out from himself in ships to frighten Cush out of its complacency, a nation that lived at ease and felt secure. Anguish will come upon them on the day of Egypt's doom, as Egypt's fall is felt across the region. The word "frighten" here means to cause great fear, and "complacency" refers to a settled sense of being safe and free from worry. What he announces is coming, and he says so plainly.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Egypt trusted in its power and its allies, among them Cush, which would be shaken by Egypt's fall. According to the context, God would use Nebuchadnezzar as an instrument of judgment. The details of these "messengers in ships" are understood in different ways.

For today: check where you rest your confidence too firmly, such as money, work, or influence. All of these can fail; only God is a firm trust. Bring it to him in prayer today.
exp.23:15:
God tells Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man," that he is about to take away the desire of his eyes with a fatal blow. That is, the person he loved most and whose presence gave him joy. Here it refers to his wife. God also tells him that he must not mourn or weep, and must not let his tears flow.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in the middle of the exile in Babylon. Earlier he has announced judgment on Jerusalem. The death of his wife would be a sign for the people: in the same way they would lose the temple, which they valued so highly. God speaks with firmness, but the text also shows Ezekiel's pain.

For today: when we go through losses we do not understand, we can bring our pain honestly to God, trusting that he is with us and that our suffering does not go unnoticed by him.
exp.26:34:
All who live in the islands and along the coasts are appalled at the fall of Tyre. Even their kings shudder with fear, and their faces are contorted, showing a look of horror at the shock.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a very rich seafaring city, compared to a great ship full of merchandise. Tyre had enriched many nations through its trade, but it became filled with pride. The text announces that its ruin will leave everyone stunned. Scholars agree that it is a judgment against its arrogance, although they debate how and when it was fulfilled in history.

For today: wealth and success are not a secure foundation for life. We can thank God for what He gives us, but it is wise to ask Him for humility and to trust in Him, not in what we have or achieve.
exp.19:30:
It says that Israel kept bringing its offerings and even sacrificed its sons in the fire to its idols. By doing this they defiled themselves, and they were still doing it up to this very day. For this reason God asks: "So should I be consulted by you?" He swears by his own life that he will not answer them, meaning that he will not listen when they come to seek him.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some elders of Israel had come to consult him, but God reminds them of their history of idolatry going back for generations. He does not want them to seek him while they continue serving other gods.

For today: we cannot mix the worship of God with whatever takes his place in the heart. Ask God to show you what competes with him, and surrender it to him sincerely.
exp.12:16:
God tells Ezekiel to turn his full attention toward the women of his people who prophesy out of their own imagination, and to speak out firmly against them. These were people presenting their own made-up messages as if they came from God, not from him. "Set your face against" means to confront someone with determination. "Son of man" is how God addresses Ezekiel, a reminder that he is an ordinary human being.

God speaks during the exile and in the middle of Israel's crisis. He had already condemned the male prophets who promised false peace. Now the message is aimed at women who were also misleading the people. The verses that follow show that they did this for gain, in exchange for barley and bread. The exact details of their practices are not entirely clear.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I listen to what God says in his Word, or only to what comforts me? Comparing everything with the Bible protects us from messages that sound pleasant but are false.
exp.10:12:
It says that while Ezekiel was prophesying, a man named Pelatiah, son of Benaiah, suddenly died. Ezekiel fell face down to the ground and cried out loudly. His question is: "Will You bring the remnant of Israel to a complete end?" The word "consumption" here means total destruction, and "the remnant" refers to those who were still surviving.

Ezekiel was among the exiles in Babylon, and in a vision he saw the leaders of Jerusalem giving deceitful counsel. Pelatiah was one of them (Ezek 11:1). His death seemed to be a sign of God's judgment. Ezekiel feared that the punishment would leave no one behind. We do not know for certain how he died; the text presents it only as part of the vision.

For today: when you see sin and its consequences, do not remain cold. Pray with humility and intercede for others, trusting that God is just and also merciful.
exp.31:25:
Meshech and Tubal are there, with all their multitudes, and their graves are all around them. All of them are uncircumcised, meaning they were outside Israel's covenant, and they were slain by the sword. The reason given is that they spread their terror in the land of the living.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a lament over Egypt and its fall. He pictures Egypt going down into the grave, where other violent nations already lie, such as Assyria, Elam, Meshech, and Tubal. Scholars debate how exactly to understand this scene of the place of the dead, but the message is clear: the power that terrifies others does not escape God's judgment.

For today: do not envy or imitate those who impose themselves through fear and violence. Their strength may seem great, but it comes to an end. Instead, seek to use your influence to protect, serve, and give life to others.
exp.39:47:
Here Ezekiel is still accompanied by a guide who leads him to the entrance of the temple, called the "portico." With a measuring rod, the guide records the width of the side pillars of the portico: five cubits on each side. A cubit was roughly half a meter. He also measures the gateway, which is fourteen cubits wide, with sidewalls three cubits on either side.

Ezekiel recounts this vision while he is exiled in Babylon. A man with the appearance of bronze measures the whole temple for him. Scholars interpret it in various ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbol of God's presence, or as a promise of restoration. No one knows for certain.

For today: God is a God of order, and he attends to the details of his house. We can draw near to him with respect and reverence, and trust that, even in times of discouragement, he has a plan to restore his people.
exp.40:20:
The verse says the outer sanctuary had a rectangular doorframe, and the doorframe of the sanctuary was similar. The doorframe is the frame around the entrance. The sanctuary is the holy place within the temple, and the outer sanctuary is the main room in front of it. So the entrance to the holy place matched the shape of the entrance to the main room, with the same measurements and the same arrangement.

Here Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, describes a vision he received during the exile in Babylon. A guide shows him a new temple in detail. The Jewish people were discouraged because the first temple had been destroyed. This vision gave them hope that God would once again dwell with his people. Interpreters disagree about whether it is a literal temple or a symbolic one.

For today: God cares about order and harmony, and he wants our lives to be steady and consistent, the same inside and out. Let us strive to be the same in private and in public.
exp.24:4:
God says that Rabbah, the capital of Ammon, will become a pasture for camels, and that Ammon will become a resting place for sheep. The verse uses plain words for the animals and their rest, and it ends by saying that through this judgment they will know that he is the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile of Judah in Babylon. The Ammonites, neighbors of Israel, rejoiced when the temple was defiled and the land lay in ruins. God judges them for mocking the suffering of his people. Rabbah was their main city, and the image of camels and sheep speaks of ruin and abandonment.

For today: God takes mockery in the face of another's suffering seriously. We can examine our hearts and ask ourselves whether we rejoice over the falls of others. It is better to pray, to help, and to show compassion, trusting that God is just.
exp.0:4:
It says that within that cloud of fire, Ezekiel saw four living creatures. Here "living creatures" is the sense of the word, not common beasts. They had a human form, though, as the text goes on, with very different features: four faces and four wings.

Ezekiel was a priest and writes from exile in the land of the Chaldeans, beside the river Chebar. There, far from the temple, God reveals Himself to him in an impressive vision. The one speaking is Ezekiel, telling what he saw. Many understand that this vision shows the glory and throne of God, and that He was not limited to Jerusalem. The details of these beings are interpreted in various ways.

For today: even when you feel far from everything familiar, God is not far away. He can meet you in your own "Babylon," in a difficult season, and show you that He still reigns. Seek Him in prayer, even where you feel like an exile.
exp.6:2:
This verse says the final moment has now arrived for Israel. God says he will unleash his anger against the people and will judge them according to the way they have lived. "Anger" here is an intense, burning wrath, and "abominations" are the detestable practices, especially idolatry and injustice, that the people had committed.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man." The message is for the land of Israel, shortly before Jerusalem fell to Babylon. After much patience, the people had again and again rejected God's call to turn back to him.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and God takes them seriously. Today you can ask him to show you what you should leave behind and return to him with sincerity, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.35:13:
It says that the land of Israel will no longer "devour" its people or take away their children. "You will no longer devour men" and "deprive your nation of its children" are strong words: they speak of a land that seemed to swallow up its inhabitants. The phrase "your nation" refers to your people or your inhabitants. God promises this firmly: "declares the Lord GOD."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the mountains and the land of Israel, which had been left in ruins by judgment and exile. Other nations mocked, saying that the land consumed its people. God promises to restore the land and return his people to it, removing that shame. Interpreters differ on how this is fulfilled: in the return from exile, in the future, or in both.

For today: when you feel that your story is marked by loss or shame, remember that God knows how to restore. Bring that pain to him in prayer and trust that his word has the final say over your life.
exp.37:7:
It says that after a long time God will summon Gog to account. The phrase "you will be summoned" here means that God will act against him. This will happen "in the latter years," when Israel is living in a land that has recovered from war and whose people were gathered from many nations. Its mountains had been desolate for a long time. Now its inhabitants dwell securely.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces a future attack against Israel, after its restoration, led by Gog with many allies. Christians interpret this in several ways: as something still to come, as a symbol of the evil that attacks God's people, or as something partly fulfilled already. There is no single view that is universally accepted.

For today: the firmest security does not depend on the peace we see, but on the faithfulness of God. We can rest in Him, while still remaining watchful.
exp.44:20:
It says that on the fourteenth day of the first month, the people are to observe the Passover, a feast of seven days during which unleavened bread is eaten. Unleavened bread is bread made without yeast.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of a renewed temple and worship (chapters 40 to 48). Earlier, there is talk of cleansing the house from sin, and afterward the sacrifices of the prince are mentioned. The Passover remembers when God brought Israel out of Egypt. How this vision will be fulfilled, whether literally or symbolically, is interpreted in different ways.

For today: God wants his people to remember their deliverance with gratitude. We can set aside a regular moment to remember what God has done for us and to remove from our lives whatever draws us away from him.
exp.17:29:
God says that he will judge each person according to their way of life. Then he issues an invitation: "Repent and turn from all your transgressions." That means change direction and leave sin behind. "Transgressions" are the wrongs people commit. The promise is that if they turn away from them, their wrongdoing will not become their downfall.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Israel, who were living in exile. The people were saying that God was unfair and blaming their ancestors for their situation. God answers that each person is responsible for their own choices, and he offers a way out: to turn back to him and live.

Today, we do not have to stay tied to past mistakes or blame others. Think of one habit or attitude that pulls you away from God, and today ask him for forgiveness and for help to change. He welcomes the one who returns.
exp.17:10:
This verse continues to describe the son of a righteous man who does not follow his father's example. Though his father has done none of these wrongs, the son goes on to eat at the mountain, which refers to taking part in idol worship at high places, and he defiles his neighbor's wife, which means committing adultery with another man's wife.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their ancestors. God answers that each person is accountable for their own choices, and that a father's faith does not automatically save his son.

For today: let us not live on inherited faith or excuse ourselves with the mistakes of our family. Today you can choose to be faithful to God in your home, your work, and your relationships, with humility and sincerity.
exp.27:6:
God says he will bring against the ruler of Tyre foreigners, that is, people from other nations, and the most ruthless of the nations, meaning the most brutal peoples. They will draw their swords against what he prized so much: his wisdom and his splendor. Their coming will bring ruin to his reputation and his glory.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The message is addressed to the prince of Tyre, a city made rich by trade. He became so proud of his success that he regarded himself as a god. Many believe it refers to an actual king of Tyre; some also see a hint of something greater, but the text does not make this fully clear.

Everything we have, whether intelligence, talents, or money, is a gift. If we use these to feel superior, we drift away from God. Today we can respond with thanks and serve others with humility.
exp.29:7:
The verse says that when God sets a fire in Egypt and all its helpers are shattered, people will know that he is the LORD. The image of setting fire points to God bringing judgment on the land. The word for "shattered" carries the sense of being broken or defeated. The "helpers" are the nations that stood alongside Egypt and supported it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel at a time when Babylon held power over the region. Egypt was a proud nation, and many people had placed their trust in its strength. God declares that this power will fall, and the verses that follow name Babylon as the force that carries out the judgment. The fire is generally read as a picture of judgment and ruin.

For today: let us not place our ultimate security in power, money, or human alliances, since all of these can fall. Let us rest in God, who remains faithful and is still the LORD over history.
exp.15:50:
God tells Jerusalem that Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, did not commit even half of the sins she did. Jerusalem committed more abominations than Samaria, and by doing so she made her sisters, Samaria and Sodom, appear righteous by comparison.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was writing to the exiles in Babylon. In this chapter he compares Jerusalem to an unfaithful woman who forgot God. He mentions Sodom and Samaria, cities already judged, to show that Jerusalem, which had received so much light and so much of God's care, failed more gravely.

For today: it is easy to compare ourselves with others and feel better. But God looks at the heart and at what we have received from Him. Instead of pointing out other people's errors, let us ask Him to examine our own, and remember that He also promises restoration.
exp.1:7:
God speaks to Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man," meaning simply a human being. He tells him to listen to what he says and not to be rebellious like that rebellious people. Then he tells him to open his mouth and eat what God gives him.

God speaks, calling Ezekiel as a prophet among the exiles of Israel, a stubborn people who may not listen to him. Before Ezekiel speaks, God wants him first to receive the message. What follows is a scroll written with laments and woes, and in the next verse it becomes clear that this scroll is what Ezekiel must "eat," an image of receiving the message completely.

For today: before speaking about God to others, let his Word fill you first. Read the Bible with a heart willing to obey, not just to offer opinions.
exp.21:16:
This verse is an introductory phrase. It says that the word of the LORD came to Ezekiel, meaning that God spoke to him again. The important part is not in this verse but in what God says right after it.

The one speaking is God, and he does so through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier, God had announced that he would scatter his people because of their sin and that in this way he would cleanse them of their impurity. Now a new message begins: God compares Israel to dross, the worthless residue left behind when metals are melted down.

For today: God continues to speak through his Word. Before reading it, ask him for a heart willing to listen, even when he corrects you, because his correction seeks to cleanse and restore you.
exp.33:21:
He says that God himself will rescue his people, who are compared to sheep. In addition, God will bring order among them, judging between one sheep and another, that is, doing justice between those who harm and those who suffer.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, while the people were in exile. Israel's leaders, called shepherds, had cared for themselves and not for the flock. Some strong sheep also pushed and scattered the weak ones. God promises to intervene and, later, to send a shepherd called "David." Many Christians see this as a sign pointing to Jesus, although the original text speaks of a future ruler from David's line.

Today, we can trust that God sees injustice. And if we have any kind of influence, we should use it to protect and care for the weakest, not to take advantage of them.
exp.41:6:
The verse describes an outer wall running alongside the rooms and the outer court. That wall was fifty cubits long. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm, about half a meter, although scholars do not fully agree on the exact figure. The rooms were chambers or living spaces within the temple complex, and the outer court was an open yard.

Ezekiel is speaking, recounting what he saw in a vision while a guide measured the temple. He was among the exiles in Babylon. These very detailed measurements showed that God cared about order, about the separation between the common and the holy, and that his presence would once again dwell among his people. Interpreters differ on whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God is concerned with order and with the boundaries that protect what is sacred. We can ask ourselves what healthy "walls" we need in order to guard our time with God.
exp.25:14:
God asks Tyre whether the coastlands will not quake at the sound of its downfall. He speaks of the groans of the wounded and of a great slaughter inside the city. "Coastlands" refers to the shores and distant peoples who traded with Tyre.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich city, proud of its sea trade, and it had rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking of its own gain. The text announces its judgment, and the kings of the sea will be astonished when they see it. There are different opinions about how it was fulfilled, since Babylon is mentioned and then other conquerors.

For today: power and wealth do not give us true security. It is wise to live with humility, without rejoicing in the misfortune of others, and to trust in God rather than in what we have.
exp.21:9:
Serious sexual abuses were committed in Jerusalem within families. "Uncovering the nakedness" is a biblical expression that refers to forbidden sexual relations with a father's wife or with someone in his close family. Violating women during their menstrual impurity, which the law of Moses forbade, is one form of this sin. The verse describes violence and abuse.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He is accusing Jerusalem, called the city of blood, for its sins: despising what is holy, violence, idolatry, and abuse. These wrongs show that the people had forgotten God, and for that reason judgment would come.

For today: God cares about protecting the weak, especially within the home. If you know of abuse, do not hide it; seek help and protect the person who has been harmed. A life that honors God cares for and respects others.
exp.20:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel. The phrase "The word of the LORD came to me" is the way Ezekiel often introduces a new message. Here it does not yet say what the message is; it only announces that God is going to speak.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon with other Jews. God gives him a message about Jerusalem and the land of Israel, and in the verses that follow it speaks of judgment, using the image of a sword. The verse serves as an opening: what comes next is not the prophet's own ideas, but the word of God.

For today: before we speak or decide something important, it is good to stop and listen to God in his Word and in prayer. God still speaks, above all through the Bible, and he asks for our sincere attention and obedience, even when the message is not easy to hear.
exp.45:21:
This verse describes four small courts, one in each corner of the outer court of the temple. Each one measured forty cubits long by thirty cubits wide, and a cubit was roughly half a meter. The corners are the places where the sides of the outer court meet, and the verse says that each of the four corner areas had the same dimensions.

A guide speaks here, showing Ezekiel a vision of the future temple. These courts were kitchens, where the people's sacrifices and the priests' offerings were prepared, so that holy things were not carried out into the outer court. How this vision is fulfilled, whether literally or symbolically, is understood in several ways.

For today: God cares about order and respect in the way we approach Him. We can take care of what is sacred, such as prayer, the Bible, and meeting with other believers, by giving them a clear and set-apart place in our week.
exp.18:2:
It says the lioness raised one of her cubs until it became a strong young lion. After it learned to tear its prey, it devoured men, that is, it attacked and destroyed people. "Tear its prey" means it seized and killed its victims. "She brought up" means she raised it.

God speaks through Ezekiel and tells him to chant a dirge, a song of mourning, over the princes of Israel. The lioness is usually understood as the mother of the kingdom of Judah, and the cub as one of its kings, probably Jehoahaz, who was taken to Egypt. Scholars debate exactly which figure represents whom. The point is that the rulers used their power to oppress, and in the end they fell.

For today: power without justice harms others and also the one who wields it. Whether at home, at work, or in the church, let us ask God to teach us to use our influence to serve and care, not to take advantage.
exp.31:18:
Egypt, which thought itself so splendid and better than the other nations, will fall just like all of them. The question "Whom do you surpass in beauty?" is ironic: it mocks Egypt's pride, since no one is more beautiful than the nation that is about to be brought down. "Go down and be placed with the uncircumcised" means that Egypt will be placed among the dead of the pagan nations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, around 585 B.C., as the text indicates in its dating. It is a lament, that is, a funeral song, over Pharaoh and his multitude. God announces judgment on them for their arrogance. For an Egyptian, being counted among the uncircumcised and among those slain by the sword was a great humiliation. The details about the grave, the realm of the dead, are understood in several ways, and many see them as poetic language.

For today: beauty, power, or success do not protect us from God's judgment. Ask him to give you humility, and trust in his grace, not in your achievements.
exp.17:19:
This verse says that each person is responsible for their own actions. The "soul" means the person themselves. "Bear" means to carry the guilt or the punishment. "Wickedness" means living without reverence for God. A son does not pay for the father's sins, and a father does not pay for the son's.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people kept repeating a saying: "The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge" (v. 2). By this they meant that they were suffering because of their ancestors. God corrects that excuse and calls them to answer for themselves, and He shows them that they can always turn back to Him.

For today: do not use your family's past as an excuse, and do not stay trapped in guilt for other people's mistakes. Today you can choose to obey God and start over with Him.
exp.34:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. The phrase that you see here, "Moreover, the word of the LORD came to me, saying," is the way the book marks the start of a new message. The name God is given in the text is the LORD, the name of God.

The one speaking is God, and the one receiving the message is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles from Judah in Babylon. The verses that follow show that the message is about Mount Seir, that is, the region of Edom. The Edomites lived there, neighbors of Israel, who according to the book acted with hostility against God's people. God announces that he is going to judge them.

For today: God speaks, and we can hear him in his Word. Before we give our opinion or react to injustice, let us begin by opening the Bible with attention and humility, trusting that God sees everything and acts with justice.
exp.15:30:
