Ezekiel 16:31 says that Jerusalem built her mounds at the head of every street and made her lofty shrines in every public square. Here "mounds" and "lofty shrines" refer to places of false worship. The verse then compares her to a prostitute, but in a worse way: an ordinary prostitute takes payment, while she scorned payment, because she paid her lovers instead of receiving anything in return. The point of the comparison is that she was not seeking gain, only following her own desire.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He uses the image of an unfaithful wife to show that Israel abandoned God and gave herself to other nations and their gods. It is strong language, meant to awaken repentance in a people who had become accustomed to their sin.

Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts: money, fame, pleasure, or approval. If we are honest and return to Him, God remains faithful and forgives those who come to Him sincerely.
exp.20:25:
God tells the king of Israel to take off his turban, the royal headdress, and remove his crown. Things will not stay as they are: God will lift up the humble and bring down the one who thinks himself high. "Bring down" means to pull down or humble.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The message is directed to the ruler of Israel, whom many understand to be King Zedekiah. Because of the sins of the people and their leaders, God allows judgment to come upon Jerusalem. The verse that follows speaks of one who holds the rightful claim, and many Christians see in it a sign of the Messiah, though others interpret it in other ways.

For today: let us not cling to power, position, or pride, because everything is in God's hands. Let us ask him for a humble heart and trust that he is the true King.
exp.12:7:
God says that the prophets of Israel uttered vain words and saw false visions. Vain words are empty, hollow things, without true worth or truth. Because these prophets claimed their messages came from God when He had not sent them, God declares: I am against you. It is a firm and direct warning.

The Lord GOD speaks through Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. There were false prophets who made up visions and promised peace when there was no peace. In this way they gave false hope, and the people did not turn back. God defends the truth of His word and protects His people from deception.

Today we can examine carefully what we hear in God's name and compare it with the Bible. Also, if we speak of God to others, let us do so with humility and honesty, without saying "God told me" just to give weight to our own ideas.
exp.45:22:
It says that around the inside of each of the four courtyards there was a row of stone wall, and that along the base of the walls, on all sides, there were ovens. The word for the cooking places in this version probably refers to hearths or ovens; the original is uncertain.

Ezekiel recounts a vision of the new temple. A guide takes him through the outer court and shows him the kitchens, where the temple servants cooked the meat of the people's sacrifices. Interpreters differ: some see a literal future temple, others a symbolic picture of God's presence restored.

For today: God cares about the details of everyday life, such as shared meals. We can make our table, our kitchen, and our simple service a place where others are fed and welcomed with gratitude.
exp.27:16:
Your heart grew proud because of your beauty. You corrupted your wisdom because of your splendor. That is why God says he will cast you down to the earth and make you a spectacle before kings, so that they may see your fall. Here "grew proud" is clearly the pride in view, and "splendor" refers to his glory and fame.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament against the king of Tyre. Many believers see in the images of Eden and the guardian cherub also an allusion to Satan; others understand it only as poetic language about the king. This is debated, so it is good to read it with humility. In either case, the theme is the fall that comes from pride.

For today: what God gives us, such as talents, success, or good looks, is a gift. Be thankful for it and use it to serve, not to boast, because pride pulls us away from God.
exp.32:15:
This verse says that when a wicked person turns away from his sins and changes the way he lives, God no longer holds those sins against him. "Judgment and justice" means acting with uprightness and doing what is right toward others. "He will surely live" means he will have real life, without any doubt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, whom He appointed as a watchman for His people, who were in exile in Babylon. Some were saying that God's way was not fair. God answers that He offers forgiveness to whoever turns back to Him, and that the change must be seen in actions, such as giving back what was stolen.

For today: if there is something you need to correct or give back, do it with humility. God invites you to start again, and His forgiveness is real.
exp.29:5:
God himself declares the fall of Egypt. It will not only be Egypt that falls, but also its allies, those who support it. Its proud strength will collapse. The words "by the sword" mean in war, that is, through battle.

The place names "from Migdol to Syene" are usually understood as from one end of Egypt to the other, from north to south, although some locate Syene differently.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. Egypt was a power in which Judah trusted for its defense. God warns that this security was false and that he is the one who governs the nations. Many understand that Babylon would be the instrument of this judgment.

For today: examine where you place your ultimate security, whether money, reputation, or people. All of these can fail. Trust first in God, who does not change, and live with humility.
exp.42:5:
He says that while a man was standing beside him, Ezekiel heard someone speaking to him from inside the temple. The wording is simple: the man is just a man, and "beside me" means at Ezekiel's side.

Ezekiel is seeing a vision in which the glory of God fills the new temple. The one speaking from inside the temple is the Lord himself, as the following words show ("the place of my throne"). The man standing beside Ezekiel is a guide who shows him the temple; the text does not say who he is, and some think he is an angel. God speaks to promise that he will dwell among his people and to ask them to give up idolatry.

Today we can learn that God wants to be close to us and to speak to us. If we make room for him, through prayer and attention to his Word, we will be able to hear his voice and live with reverence.
exp.37:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. "And the word of the LORD came to me" is the way the message is introduced. It is not an idea that came from the prophet himself, but a message he receives from God before passing it on.

The one speaking is the LORD, the God of Israel, and the one listening is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. This phrase opens a new message, directed against Gog, of the land of Magog. Scholars disagree about who or what Gog represents: some see a historical enemy, others a future or symbolic one.

For today: before speaking on God's behalf, we must first listen to him. We can set aside time to read the Bible calmly, asking God to speak to us, before we give our opinion or make decisions.
exp.31:5:
It says that God will drench the land with the flow of the pharaoh of Egypt's blood, all the way to the mountains, and that the ravines will be filled with him. "Drench" means to soak or pour out completely. The pharaoh is pictured as a creature of the river, so the image of him "swimming" fits the setting of the Nile.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. It is a lament against the pharaoh, who believed himself as powerful as a crocodile or dragon of the Nile. God uses this strong image to announce that his pride will end and that Egypt will fall. It is poetic and symbolic language, not a literal description.

For today: no one is so great that they stand above God. If today we trust in our power, money, or fame, this text invites us to humility and to place our trust in the Lord, who is just and has the final word.
exp.33:27:
God promises that his people will no longer be prey for the nations, and the wild animals of the land will not harm them. "Prey" is what a hunting animal seizes in order to consume. The promise that "they will dwell securely" means they will live in peace and confidence, and "no one will frighten them" means no one will terrify them or drive them from their homes.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the time of Israel's exile. Earlier, he had rebuked the shepherds who mistreated the flock, and now he promises that he himself will care for it. This peace is part of a covenant of blessing: rain in season, fruit, and freedom from oppression. Some see here a future fulfillment, and others see a foretaste in Christ, the good Shepherd.

For today: if your fears weigh you down, remember that God cares for his own. Bring to him in prayer what frightens you, and trust in his protection.
exp.16:7:
It had been planted in good soil beside abundant water, so that it could put out branches, bear fruit, and grow into a splendid vine. The verse stresses that nothing was lacking for it to prosper.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and tells a parable about two eagles and a vine. Many understand the vine to represent Judah and its king Zedekiah, placed there by Babylon. Instead of remaining faithful, he sought help from another "eagle," which would be Egypt. God shows that this alliance would fail and that the vine would wither.

For today: having good conditions does not guarantee a firm life if we stop trusting God. When we face pressure or fear, it is wise to ask ourselves whether we are seeking security in something human instead of remaining faithful to Him.
exp.28:19:
God declares that he will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as the reward for his hard work against Tyre. The Lord affirms that, even though the king did not know it, that effort was done for God. The phrase declares the Lord GOD stresses that the one speaking and deciding is God himself.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. According to the passage, Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre with great exhaustion, but did not receive the spoil he expected. God compensates that effort with Egypt, which was already under judgment. Historians debate how exactly this was fulfilled, but the text shows God directing the nations.

For today: even when the world seems to move by human interests, God continues to govern history. We can trust that he sees every effort and that his plans advance, even when we do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.30:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel and tells him to deliver a message to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, and to his multitude. The question is: "Who can be compared to your greatness?" In other words, with whom do you think you can be compared?

The message comes in the eleventh year of the exile, as it is understood, when Egypt felt powerful. God speaks through Ezekiel. Next he compares Assyria, once so great, to a very tall cedar that fell. In this way God warns Pharaoh that his pride will end in the same way.

Some scholars debate details of the image, but the message about pride is clear.

For today: when we feel strong because of our success, money, or position, it is good to remember that everything comes from God. We can ask him for a humble and grateful heart.
exp.30:13:
God let the great tree fall so that no other tree beside the waters would grow proud of its height and lift its top up among the clouds. None of the well-watered trees would be able to match its towering size. Every one of them is given over to death, sent down to the depths of the earth, to live among mortal people who go down to the Pit.

God speaks through Ezekiel and addresses the pharaoh of Egypt. He is compared to a huge tree, and Assyria is also described as a great tree that fell. Many scholars see here a warning: if an empire so mighty was brought down, Egypt will not escape either. Some details of the poetic language are understood in several ways.

For today: success, a position, or talent does not make us superior or lasting. We can be thankful for what God has given us and practice humility, remembering that everything we have comes from Him.
exp.5:8:
God says that some who survive the judgment will be taken captive to other nations. There, they will remember Him. They will understand that God was grieved because of their adulterous hearts, which turned away from Him, and because of their eyes that lusted after idols. Their unfaithfulness was like betrayal in a marriage. Then they will loathe themselves for the evil they have done and for all their abominations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Israel had abandoned God for idolatry. Even in punishment, God preserves a remnant, and His goal is that the people recognize Him and return to Him.

Today we can remember that our sin does not only break rules; it also grieves the heart of God. If anything has taken His place in our lives, let us thank Him for correcting us, and return to Him with humility and sincerity.
exp.6:24:
This verse says that anguish is coming. People will look for peace, but they will find none. The word "anguish" here can also be understood as "distress" or "calamity," depending on how the Hebrew is translated.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Judah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. The city was full of violence, injustice, and pride. God announces judgment as the consequence of those ways. The verses that follow show that neither the prophet, nor the priest, nor the elders would be able to offer a way out. The ultimate purpose was that they would know that the LORD is God.

For today: true peace is not achieved in a hurry once the crisis has already arrived. It is wise to seek God now, with humility, correcting injustice and pride in our lives, before distress comes.
exp.31:21:
Assyria is there, along with its whole army and its people. Its graves lie all around it, and every one of them is a soldier who was killed by the sword. The word "sword" here refers to weapons of war, and "people" refers to its soldiers and its nation.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a funeral song against Egypt. Assyria was an empire feared for its violence, and here it appears as an example of a great power that fell. The message is that Egypt, with all its pride, will meet the same end. The language is poetic and describes the grave as a place of shadows, without teaching details about the afterlife.

For today: the power, success, or fear that we cause in others does not protect us before God. It is better to live with humility and justice, knowing that only He endures.
exp.30:8:
God himself made this great tree beautiful and gave it many branches. It was so impressive that even the trees of Eden, the garden of God, were envious of it. The verse says God made it beautiful, and that the other trees envied it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and addresses the pharaoh of Egypt. He compares him to an enormous tree, as he does with Assyria, to show his greatness. Many scholars understand that the tree represents a powerful nation. But the passage warns that pride would lead him to his fall, as seen in the verses that follow.

For today: everything good we have, whether talents, success, or influence, comes from God. Remembering this helps us give thanks instead of boasting, and not to trust in our own greatness.
exp.32:12:
God says that if he promises life to a righteous person, and that person then trusts in their own goodness and does evil, none of their good deeds from the past will be remembered. Here "righteous" means living in an upright way, and "iniquity" means evil. Because of the evil he has done, he will die.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, whom He set as a watchman over Israel. The exiled people were saying that God was unfair, and God answers them that He takes no pleasure in anyone's death. He warns them that neither a reputation for goodness nor a record of past faithfulness protects someone who turns to evil, and that the one who turns back always has a way open to him.

For today: do not live off your past good deeds, nor settle into thinking you are already good enough. Walk each day with humility, depending on God, and if you fail, return to Him soon, because He wants you to live.
exp.44:16:
This verse says that the prince will be responsible for providing the animals and offerings for Israel's festivals: the burnt offerings (offerings burned completely), the grain offerings, the drink offerings (wine poured out), the sin offerings, and the peace offerings (offerings of fellowship). The "festivals" are the appointed feasts, and the "New Moons" are the beginning of each month. "To make atonement" means to cover sin in order to restore the relationship with God.

The Lord GOD speaks through Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple and the order of worship. The people contribute the offerings, and the prince presents them on behalf of everyone. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: some see it as literal and future, others as symbolic, and others connect it with Christ.

For today: those in leadership should serve responsibly, helping the people worship God with order and sincerity. And all of us can give with joy.
exp.11:6:
Ezekiel tells us that he obeyed God exactly as he was told. He brought out his bags for exile, the things he would carry as someone going into captivity. He did this by day, so that people would see. In the evening he dug through the wall by hand, making an opening with his own hands. He took his belongings out at dusk and carried them on his shoulder, in full view of everyone watching.

Ezekiel is a prophet who lives among the exiles in Babylon. God commanded this action as a sign, an acted-out prophecy, for the rebellious people. It represented what would happen to Jerusalem and its people: they would go into exile secretly and in haste. Many did not want to believe that the punishment would come.

For today: Ezekiel obeyed even though it seemed strange and exposed his reputation. Let us ask God for the courage to do what He shows us, without waiting for everyone to understand or approve.
exp.4:16:
God says he will send famine and wild beasts against Jerusalem, and they will leave the people childless. He also speaks of plague, meaning sicknesses that spread quickly, and of bloodshed, meaning violent deaths, and of the sword, meaning the sword of war. He ends with the words "I, the LORD, have spoken," which shows that this word is serious and will be fulfilled.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. The message is for Jerusalem, whose people had turned away from God and followed other religious practices. These punishments had already been warned about earlier in the law of Moses. The tone is harsh, but it aims to help the people recognize their sin.

For today: God is in earnest, but his warnings are an opportunity to return to him. Today we can ask ourselves with humility whether there is something in our lives we need to correct, and draw near to God before the consequences arrive.
exp.35:27:
God promises that his people will live again in the land he gave to their ancestors. He also renews the relationship that has always existed. The phrase "you will be my people" and "I will be your God" expresses that bond: God claims his people, and he commits himself to them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who wrote while the people of Israel were in exile, far from their land, because of their disobedience. Before this promise, God announces a new heart and his Spirit within them. First he changes the inside; then the restoration comes. Some see here a fulfillment in the return from exile, and others also see it in the work of the Spirit in the church or in a future complete fulfillment.

Today, God does not only want us to change our behavior; he wants to change our heart and to live in fellowship with us. Today you can pray to him, "Lord, give me a heart that is tender toward you."
exp.47:19:
The whole portion set apart for God is a square measuring 25,000 cubits by 25,000 cubits. This section of land is marked off for three purposes together: the sanctuary, the priests, and the city. The cubit was a unit of length, and scholars estimate it at roughly 45 centimeters, though estimates vary.

The prophet Ezekiel receives this vision during the exile in Babylon. God shows him how the land will be divided when his people return. The tribes receive equal strips, and the center is reserved for what is holy. Christians read this vision in different ways: as a literal restoration, as a symbol of the Church, or as an image of the coming kingdom.

For today: just as this land places what is holy at the center, we can order our week and our finances by giving God the principal place, setting aside time and resources for Him first.
exp.36:12:
God says that when he opens your graves and brings you up from them, his people will know that he is the LORD. "Graves" are burial places. Here God calls Israel "my people," even in its worst moment.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in the vision of the valley of dry bones. The bones represent Israel in exile, which said, "Our hope is lost." God answers by promising restoration and bringing them back to their land. Some see here only the restoration of Israel; others also see a hope of future resurrection.

For today: if you feel without strength or without hope, remember that God can give life where it seems everything has ended. Bring him your weariness honestly, and trust that he still calls you his own.
exp.3:16:
It says that in Jerusalem the people will lack food and water. Going without, they will look at one another in horror and dread, watching each other waste away because of their sin. The phrases "appalled" and "wasting away" in the verse are explained as follows: to be appalled means to be stunned and filled with dread, and to waste away means to slowly grow weaker and decline. The cause the text gives is their iniquity, that is, their sin.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. He commands him to act out a warning: to ration his own food as a sign of the siege that would come upon Jerusalem. The people had been unfaithful to God for a long time. The consequences He announces are harsh, but He had already given warning before, giving them the chance to turn back to Him.

For today: let us not take God's warnings lightly. If something in my life pulls me away from Him, it is wise to recognize it and return to Him soon, for His correction seeks to restore us.
exp.20:12:
God says that the sword of judgment has already been tested, meaning it is ready and proven. He asks what will happen if that sword despises even the scepter, which is the symbol of the king and his authority. The answer is that the scepter will not continue: not even royal power will be spared.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem and its princes because of their sin. This verse is difficult in the original, and scholars translate and interpret it in various ways. Even so, the general message is clear: neither power nor titles deliver anyone from God's judgment.

For today: do not rely on your position, your success, or your merits to feel secure before God. In humility, ask him to correct your heart before sin grows.
exp.2:18:
This verse says that if the prophet warns a wicked person, and that person does not turn from his wickedness or his wicked way, the wicked person will die because of his own sin. But the prophet will have saved himself. To "warn" means to give a clear caution. A "wicked" person is someone who lives without respect for God. To "save yourself" means to be free of responsibility for what happens.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. God calls him a watchman, that is, a lookout who sounds the alarm when danger comes. His task was not to make people change, but to faithfully announce what God said. The decision to respond belonged to each person.

For today: if God puts it on your heart to warn someone you love, do it with love, truth, and humility. You cannot control how they will respond, but you can be faithful in speaking and leave the result in God's hands.
exp.15:0:
This verse says that God's word came to Ezekiel. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to me" means that a message from the LORD reached him. It is the formula the prophet uses to show that what follows does not come from his own opinion, but from God.

Ezekiel was a priest and a prophet, living among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. Here God gives him a message for Jerusalem, and in the verses that follow he prepares him to confront the city for its sins. God speaks with clarity, but he does so as one who knows the history of his people from the beginning.

For today: before correcting or judging others, it is wise to first listen to what God says in his Word. Reading the Bible with humility helps us distinguish between our opinions and the truth of God, and to speak with love and honesty.
exp.33:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. The phrase "Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying" is a way of saying that a message from God came to him. It is how the book introduces a new message from God.

Here God is the one speaking, and Ezekiel is the one who receives the message. The prophet lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. The verses that follow show that God is going to speak against the people's leaders, called shepherds, because they looked after themselves and not the flock.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before wanting to lead or teach others, it is good to stop and listen to what he says, and to let it first examine us.
exp.45:17:
This verse says that the prince may not take anything from the people's inheritance, so that they are not left without their property. Whatever he wants to give to his sons must come from what is his own. In the verse you are reading, the words "evicting" and "property" carry this same meaning.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple and the restored land. The chapters before this one show a just order for worship and for government. God protects each family in its land and sets limits on those who hold power. Some understand this literally, and others as a picture of God's just rule.

For today: if you have authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, do not use it to benefit yourself at the expense of others. Use what is yours with generosity, and respect what belongs to other people.
exp.26:19:
Ezekiel 27:20 says that Dedan traded with Tyre, supplying it with "saddlecloths for riding." The phrase seems to refer to fine cloths or blankets placed on horses for riding. Some scholars think these were saddle blankets. The word "merchant" refers to the people or city that does the trading.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, the great trading city of the sea. A list of peoples is given who brought goods from many places. The purpose is to show Tyre's enormous wealth and pride, a city that would soon be judged. Dedan was a region of Arabia, although its exact location is debated.

For today: wealth and success can make us feel secure apart from God. Ask yourself what you truly trust in. Use what you have with gratitude and humility, remembering that everything comes from God and that our security is in him.
exp.25:3:
God announces that the enemies of Tyre will destroy its walls and demolish its towers. He says that he will scrape the soil from her and make her a bare rock, leaving nothing built and nothing covering the stone.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre, a trading city by the sea, rejoiced when Jerusalem fell, thinking that now it would grow rich. God answers that he will judge that attitude of mockery and greed. Historians recall that Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre and that centuries later Alexander the Great attacked it; not all of them agree on how each event relates to this prophecy.

Today, this verse invites us not to rejoice in the misfortune of others, and not to trust in our wealth or security. We can ask ourselves: do I feel glad when someone else is doing badly? Better to pray for those who suffer and to place our trust in God.
exp.32:4:
It says that if someone hears the sound of the horn, a signal that gave warning of danger, and pays it no attention, he himself is responsible for whatever happens to him. "His blood will be on his own head" means that the guilt for his death rests on him. But whoever heeds the warning, that is, becomes alert and acts on it, will save his life.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls a watchman for Israel. A watchman warned the city when the enemy was coming. God uses that image to explain that Ezekiel must warn the people, and that each person is accountable for how he responds to the warning.

Today, when the Bible, wise counsel, or your conscience warns you of a spiritual danger, do not ignore it. Listen with humility and change in time, because God warns us out of love.
exp.47:18:
This verse says that the people who work in the city will come from all the tribes of Israel. "Cultivate" means they will be dedicated to tending to and sustaining the city. "Common land" is the shared ground around it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision near the end of the book. There he divides the land among the tribes and describes a city with its sanctuary. That the workers come from every tribe shows that the city does not belong to just one group, but to the whole people. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: as literal, as symbolic, or as referring to the future.

For today: In the church and in the community, all of us have a place to serve. We can ask ourselves what part of the shared work falls to us and do it gladly, no matter where we come from.
exp.16:6:
It says that another eagle appeared, a great one, with large wings and many feathers. The vine bent its roots toward this eagle and stretched its branches out to it from its planting bed, so that it would water the vine.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a parable or riddle addressed to Israel. Many understand that the first eagle represents Babylon, the vine represents the kingdom of Judah and its king, and the second eagle represents Egypt. Judah broke its covenant with Babylon to look for help in Egypt. God shows that this trust was a mistake.

Many times we look for security in the wrong places, when we already have everything we need where God has planted us. Before running to a "second eagle," whether it is money, influence, or human promises, ask God and trust in Him.
exp.19:13:
He says that God, for the sake of his name, decided not to destroy Israel in the desert. In this way he kept his name from being profaned in the eyes of the nations that had seen him bring them out of Egypt. The phrase "I acted for the sake of My name, so that it would not be profaned" means that he acted so that his name would not be stained or treated with contempt. The nations are the non-Israelite peoples.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel during the exile. He reminds them of their history: although the people rebelled in the desert, rejected his laws, and profaned the Sabbaths, God held back his anger. His reason was to protect the honor of his name before the other peoples, not because of Israel's merits.

For today: our lives represent God before others. We can ask him for help to live with integrity, and trust that his mercy is greater than our failures, but without taking it lightly.
exp.46:21:
It says that, when the land was divided, the people were to draw lots to give inheritance to the Israelites and also to the foreigners who lived among them and had children there. Those foreigners would be treated as native-born, that is, as if they had been born in Israel. The phrase "as native-born" means they are treated as Israelites by birth, and "who have children" means they have built their family there.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision about the restoration of Israel and the division of the land among the tribes. The preceding verses set the boundaries, and the following one clarifies that the foreigner would receive his share in the tribe where he lived. Interpreters debate whether this is fulfilled literally or whether it announces, in symbolic terms, the inclusion of all peoples in the people of God.

Today it reminds us that God opens the door to those who seem to be outsiders. We can welcome the immigrant or the newcomer into the church and the community, and treat them as one of the family.
exp.27:25:
This verse promises that Israel will live in its land in peace. They will build houses, plant vineyards, and live without fear. The phrase "dwell securely" means living safely and without anxiety. The verse also speaks of those who treat them with contempt, meaning the neighbors who looked down on them and harmed them. God says he will judge those neighbors. The result will be that Israel comes to know that the LORD is their God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier he had announced judgment on Sidon, a neighboring city that had been hostile to Israel. Then he promises to gather his scattered people and bring them back to the land given to Jacob. Some see here the return from exile; others also see a future fulfillment. Christians have understood it in different ways.

Today we can trust that God cares for his people and does justice in his time. When you suffer or feel threatened, do not carry revenge or fear: hand them over to God and keep working with hope, like someone who plants a vineyard.
exp.41:14:
This verse says that, when the man had finished measuring the inside of the temple, he led Ezekiel out through the gate that faces east and measured the area all around. The phrase "the interior of the temple area" refers to the temple building and its inner courts.

Ezekiel describes what he sees in a vision. A guide with a measuring reed shows him the temple in full detail. He has just spoken of the holy chambers of the priests, where the separation between the holy and the common is stressed. The measurements that follow, five hundred reeds on each side, show an orderly enclosure. Interpreters differ on whether it is a literal future temple or a symbolic picture of God's presence.

For today: God is a God of order and holiness, and he cares about details. We can approach him with reverence and put our lives in order, so that there is room for his presence.
exp.43:21:
It says that the priests were not to marry a widow or a divorced woman. They were to marry a virgin from the descendants of the house of Israel, or a widow who had been married to a priest. The word "divorced" in this verse means a woman whose husband had sent her away.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple. He gives special rules for the priests, who were to live in a very set-apart way because they served near what is holy. This rule is similar to the one in Leviticus 21, though here it is stricter, since it allows a widow only if she had been married to a priest. Interpreters differ on how to understand this vision: some read it literally, others symbolically.

For today: God values a life of service that is whole and careful. Although we are not under these rules today, we can ask ourselves whether we are guarding our witness and our commitments, especially if we serve others in the church.
exp.22:27:
For this is what the Lord GOD says: God announces that he will hand Oholibah, the woman in the story, over into the hands of those she hated, that is, the very people she turned away from in disgust and grew weary of.

Ezekiel tells a parable about two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, who represent Israel and Judah. Oholibah is Jerusalem, who sought political and religious alliances with Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt instead of trusting in God. God declares that these same nations will become the instrument of her judgment, and this will end her habit of depending on Egypt.

For today: whatever we put in place of God, whether money, approval, or power, usually ends up failing us. Today you can identify what you are seeking security in and hand it back to God in prayer.
exp.28:9:
God says to Egypt that he is against it and against its rivers, meaning the Nile, the source of its wealth. He promises to turn the land into a ruin, a desolate wasteland. Where the verse names the places, it runs from Migdol to Syene, and as far as the border of Cush. Migdol is in the north and Syene in the south, so the picture is of the whole country laid waste from one end to the other. Syene is identified with Aswan, though not everyone agrees. Cush refers to the region to the south of Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. Egypt and its pharaoh believed they owned the river and its power, and they had been a deceptive support for Israel. God judges that pride so that they will acknowledge that he is the Lord.

For today: everything we have comes from God, not only from our own effort. Ask him to free you from pride and thank him every day for what he has given you.
exp.15:44:
God tells Jerusalem that she is like her mother and her sisters. They "despised" their husbands and their children, meaning they turned against them and abandoned them. The words "Hittite" and "Amorite" name peoples who were pagan inhabitants of Canaan. By this it is said that Jerusalem was acting like the nations that did not know God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He is accusing Jerusalem of unfaithfulness, and he uses the image of a wife who betrays her husband. The part about the mother and the father speaks of the Canaanite origin of the city, not of a literal genealogy. Interpreters understand it as a way of showing that her sin was an inheritance from her surroundings.

For today: let us not copy without thought the customs that surround us. Let us ask God to show us where we have drifted away from him, and return with humility.
exp.21:2:
This verse is a message from God against a city, which from the context is Jerusalem. It accuses the city of two serious sins: shedding innocent blood and making idols. The reader's wording says the city brings her own doom, and that is what the verse means when it says judgment is already drawing close. The sin of making idols is described as defiling herself, meaning becoming unclean in God's sight.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man," and charges him to declare publicly the sins of the city. This takes place during the time of exile, when the people still remained in rebellion. God does not act on whim: first he makes the guilt clear, and then he announces the consequences.

For today: one cannot worship God and at the same time harm others. Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken the place of God in our hearts and whether our treatment of others reflects justice and compassion. God invites us to repent before the harm grows.
exp.15:16:
It says that Jerusalem took the fine jewelry of gold and silver that God himself had given her, and with it she made male idols to worship.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16 he presents Jerusalem as an abandoned girl whom he rescued, cared for, and enriched. Then she used those gifts to give herself over to idolatry. God wants the people to see their ingratitude and recognize their sin. Scholars debate exactly what those male idols were, but they are clearly idols.

For today: everything we have, such as talents, money, or health, comes from God. Ask yourself whether you use it to honor him or to feed things that take his place in your heart.
exp.10:3:
God commands Ezekiel to speak on his behalf against certain men. The repetition, "prophesy; prophesy," stresses that the command is serious and urgent. "Son of man" is the title by which God addresses Ezekiel throughout the book, and it reminds him that he is an ordinary human being carrying a divine message.

God speaks in a vision. Ezekiel sees leaders of Jerusalem who plan evil and give bad advice. They say, "It is not near; let us build houses," meaning that judgment is not close at hand. They feel safe, like the meat inside the pot. God confronts them because he knows what they think and what they have done.

Today, God sees beyond our words and knows our thoughts. It is wise to examine whether we live with false security, putting off repentance for later, and to listen humbly when God corrects us.
exp.46:18:
This verse describes the southern boundary of the land that God promises to divide among the tribes of Israel. The line runs from Tamar to the waters of Meribath-kadesh, follows the Brook of Egypt, and reaches the Great Sea, the Mediterranean. The phrase "this will be the southern boundary" simply marks the south.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who is among the exiles in Babylon. In his vision, He shows them a restored land, with clear borders and a division among all the tribes. It was a message of hope for a people without a home. Scholars understand these boundaries in different ways: literally, symbolically, or as tied to the future.

For today: God cares about the details and keeps His promises, even when everything seems lost. Today you can entrust your dreams and your waiting to Him, asking Him to guide you step by step.
exp.33:6:
God calls the shepherds to attention and asks them to listen to what He is about to say. The word "Therefore" shows that what follows is a result of what came before. The word "hear" means "listen." "LORD" is the name of God.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel. In these chapters, the "shepherds" are the leaders of Israel, above all the kings and rulers. The "sheep" are the people. God accuses them of having neglected the people, who were scattered, unprotected, and without anyone to seek them out, while they took care of themselves.

Today, anyone who has some responsibility over others, in the church, the family, or the workplace, can ask: am I serving those I care for, or am I only seeking my own benefit? Before acting, it is wise to first listen to the word of God.
exp.26:24:
This verse says the ships of Tarshish carried your merchandise across the sea, much like the trading ships of your own commerce. The phrase "in the heart of the sea" is understood to mean far out on the open water. Thanks to this trade, Tyre was filled with heavy cargo and grew wealthy and great, standing in the middle of the sea. Tarshish was probably a distant port, though it is not known for certain where it was.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament over Tyre, a very rich and proud port city. The passage describes its great trade with many peoples. But the verses that follow announce that this greatness will sink like a ship destroyed by a storm.

Today we can ask ourselves what our security rests on. Having work, possessions, or success is not wrong, but trusting only in these is fragile. Let us first place our trust in God and use what we have with humility and generosity.
exp.24:15:
It says that God himself will act against the Philistines. The phrase "stretch out my hand" means he will intervene with power to punish them. To "cut off" means to wipe out or cut down completely. The Cherethites were a people linked to the Philistines, and "the coast" is the shore of the Mediterranean, where they lived.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a series of messages against the nations that bordered Israel. The Philistines had acted with spite and revenge, driven by an old enmity. God promises to answer that wickedness. Some scholars also see here God's defense of his people.

For today: let us not hold on to old grudges or seek revenge. We can leave our wounds in the hands of God, who is just, and ask him for the strength to forgive.
exp.0:26:
He describes Ezekiel seeing someone seated on the throne. From the waist up, this figure looks like glowing amber, like metal at red heat. From the waist up he seems surrounded by fire, and from the waist down it also looks like fire, with brilliant light all around him.

The phrase "from what seemed to be His waist" refers to the middle part of the body. The word "amber" here probably refers to a bright metal, though some understand it another way.

Ezekiel was a priest living in exile in Babylon, by the river Chebar. He tells what he saw himself. God appears to him in an overwhelming vision, and Ezekiel makes clear that what he saw was only a appearance of the glory of the LORD, not God himself as he truly is. This prepares him to be a prophet among a people in exile.

For today: God is still glorious, even when we live through difficult times. Before we ask him for things, we can pause to worship him with reverence and humility, as Ezekiel fell on his face.
exp.35:24:
God promises to cleanse his people completely. "I will sprinkle clean water on you" is an image of purification, like the washing done in the rituals of the temple. "Impurities" refers to the things that keep people away from God, and "idols" are the false gods the people had worshiped.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. They had dishonored God's name with their idolatry and their injustice. Even so, God promises to restore them, not because they deserve it, but for the sake of the holiness of his name. This cleansing prepares the way for the "new heart" and the Spirit that come right after.

For today: we cannot cleanse ourselves alone of what harms us inside. We can come before God with sincerity, acknowledge whatever has taken his place in our lives, and ask him to purify and renew us. Many Christians see in this text a foreshadowing of forgiveness and of the work of the Spirit in Christ.
exp.28:17:
It says that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, made his army labor strenuously against the city of Tyre. The soldiers ended up with their heads rubbed bald from carrying helmets and their shoulders rubbed raw from bearing loads. And despite all that effort, neither the king nor his troops received any pay or plunder from Tyre. "Wages" means reward or gain.

God speaks, addressing the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man." We are in the twenty-seventh year of the exile, and God explains that Babylon, though it did not know it, was carrying out a purpose of his. Scholars believe that the long siege of Tyre left Babylon with little gain, and that is why God promises to give it Egypt as compensation.

For today: God sees the labor of every person, and nothing that is done lies outside his care. We can trust that he governs history and that he is just.
exp.46:20:
The land promised to Israel is to be divided among the twelve tribes. After describing the southern and western borders, God commands that everyone receive a portion. The word "divide" here means "to share out" or "to split up," and "you" refers to the people as a whole.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He gives them a vision of restoration: the land will once again be their inheritance, with clearly defined boundaries. The verses that follow add that foreigners living among them will also receive an inheritance. Some interpret this vision literally, others as a spiritual picture of God's kingdom; opinions vary.

For today: God cares that there be justice and a place for everyone. We can ask ourselves whether we share what we have generously and whether we welcome the stranger who arrives, as God does.
exp.19:35:
He says that God will enter into judgment with his people, that is, bring them into a legal case and confront them face to face. He will do it in the same way he dealt with their ancestors in the wilderness of Egypt. "Your fathers" refers to the ancestors of Israel, and "the Lord GOD" is the name of the covenant God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The leaders of the people wanted to consult him, but they remained devoted to their idols. God reminds them that their rebellion is not new. The wilderness here can be understood as a place of testing and purification. The verses that follow speak of separating out the rebels, and interpreters see this in different ways.

For today: God's correction is not rejection, but a care that seeks to cleanse and restore us. When he confronts us, it is wise to listen with humility and return to him with sincerity.
exp.21:27:
These verses say that the prophets of Jerusalem covered over the people's sins with false comfort, like someone painting over a weak wall so that it looks solid. They announced false visions and lying divinations, and they said, "This is what the Lord GOD says," even though the LORD had not spoken to them.

God speaks through Ezekiel shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. God accuses all the leaders: priests, princes, and prophets. The prophets reassured the people with lies, and so no one turned back from their sins. That is why God looked for someone to stand in the gap and did not find anyone.

Today we can examine what we hear and what we say in God's name. Let us compare everything with the Bible, and if we speak to others, let us do so with truth and love, without dressing up sin to please people.
exp.25:17:
The verse says that when Tyre falls, the islands and coastal lands will tremble in fear. "Shall tremble" means they will shake with fright. The word "departure" here refers to her leaving or ending. What frightens them is seeing how the end of a city that seemed so powerful unfolds.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich seaport that lived by trade and felt secure. God announces her judgment, and the rulers of the coasts mourn her fall with a funeral song. Scholars debate how it was fulfilled, but the central message is clear: no human power stands without God.

For today: do not place your security in money, success, or prestige, because all of that can disappear. Trust instead in God, who remains firm.
exp.6:20:
God says he will hand these things over as plunder to foreigners, and as loot to the wicked of the earth, who will defile them. The "wicked of the earth" are pagan peoples, and they will defile the city, that is, they will profane it. "Plunder" and "loot" refer to goods taken in war. The "foreigners" are people from another nation.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. The people had filled the temple with idols and trusted in their wealth. That is why God announces judgment. Many understand "my secret place" to refer to the temple or its holiest part, though there are different opinions.

For today: silver and gold cannot save us when we fail before God. Today we can ask ourselves what we are placing in the place of God, and return to trusting him with humility.
exp.40:15:
This verse continues the description of the temple in Ezekiel's vision. It mentions the thresholds, the beveled windows, and the galleries that run all around on three levels, facing the threshold. Everything was covered with wood on all sides, from the floor up to the windows, and the windows were covered over. The phrase "all around" means on every side, and "opposite the threshold" means facing the entrance.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, recounts what he sees while a guide with a measuring reed shows him the temple. This takes place during the exile in Babylon. God shows him an orderly, measured temple, perhaps to bring hope to a discouraged people. Scholars interpret it in several ways: as a literal future temple, as a symbolic image, or as a sign of God's presence.

For today: God cares about order and detail. Pay careful attention to your prayer life and your community, so that they may be places where God dwells.
exp.31:15:
This is the lament they will chant for her, and the daughters of the nations will chant it. They will chant it over Egypt and all her multitudes, declares the Lord GOD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Egypt was a proud power, and God announces its fall as judgment. The verses before this one describe the land laid waste, so that everyone will know that He is the Lord. Afterward, Ezekiel is commanded to chant the lament. This is a prophetic poem, using figurative language.

For today: power, wealth and fame are not secure forever. You can trust in God, who is above every nation, and live with humility, without resting your life on things that pass away.
exp.10:0:
The Spirit of God lifted Ezekiel up and brought him to the gate of the Lord's house that faces east, the gate toward the place where the sun rises. There, at the entrance of the gate, he saw twenty-five men. Among them he recognized two: Jaazaniah, son of Azzur, and Pelatiah, son of Benaiah. The text describes them as leaders of the people.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet and priest who was living in exile in Babylon. This scene is a vision: his body did not move, but God showed him what was happening in Jerusalem. In the verses that follow, God says that these leaders were giving bad advice and making wicked plans. They felt secure, even though God was warning them of judgment. The twenty-five men may be the same as those in Ezekiel 8:16 or a different group; the text does not make this clear.

For today: those who have influence should ask themselves whether their advice comes from God or from their own comfort. Let us ask for wisdom before we guide others.
exp.31:10:
This verse says that the Lord GOD himself announces that the sword of the king of Babylon will come against Egypt. "You" refers to the pharaoh, the one to whom the prophecy is addressed. The "sword" stands for the army and for war.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is among the exiles in Babylon. This chapter is a lament over the pharaoh, who was thought to be powerful and proud. God tells him that his fall will be seen by many nations. Here Babylon is presented as an instrument of judgment, not as a power acting on its own. This is understood as part of God's rule over the nations.

For today: let us not place our security in power, wealth, or prestige, because all of these can fall. Better to trust in God and live with humility, knowing that He governs history.
exp.12:19:
God says he is against the magic charms with which certain women ensnare people, the way a hunter traps birds. Those charms were the objects they used in their rituals. God promises to tear them from their hands and to free the souls they had trapped.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some women claimed to prophesy and practiced spells to gain bread and barley. With lies they discouraged the righteous and encouraged the wicked to keep to their evil way. The exact nature of the charms is uncertain, but the deception is clear.

For today: do not follow anyone who manipulates your faith with lies for their own gain. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and trust that God defends his people and sets them free.
exp.38:10:
It says that, when that day comes, God himself will give Gog a burial place in Israel. It will be the Valley of the Travelers, east of the Sea (probably the Dead Sea or the Mediterranean; this is not known for certain). There will be so many bodies that they will block the way of those who travel through. There they will bury Gog and all his hordes, and the place will be called the Valley of Hamon-gog, which means "multitude of Gog."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Gog leads a great alliance that attacks Israel, and God defeats it. Interpreters disagree: some see a future event, others a symbolic picture of God's final victory over evil. Chapters 38 and 39 show that God protects his people and is glorified.

For today: trust that God has the last word over all evil. You can rest in the knowledge that He cares for his own and will do justice in his time.
exp.47:14:
This verse describes a narrower strip of land, 5,000 cubits wide, that remains after the holy portion has been set apart. That part is not sacred but is set aside for ordinary use. It will serve the city: a place for houses, with pasture land around it. The city will stand in the center.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. In his final vision, God shows how the land would be divided: first what is dedicated to Him, then what is for common use. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as literal, others as symbolic or spiritual.

For today: even when daily life is ordinary, like home and work, God wants it in order and at the center, with what is holy close by. Put God in the middle of your routines.
exp.15:5:
He says that God passed by a newborn girl, left in the open field and wallowing in her own blood. No one cared for her, but God saw her and told her, "Live!" and then repeated it. The blood mentioned here is the blood of childbirth.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem. He uses the image of an abandoned girl to remind her of her humble beginnings: everything she became, she received from God's compassion. Afterward God cares for her, covers her, and makes a covenant with her. This prepares the later charge of her unfaithfulness. Scholars agree that this is a symbolic image, not a literal historical account.

For today: when you feel worthless or carry a shameful past, remember that God looks on you with compassion and calls you to live. Respond to him with gratitude and faithfulness.
exp.29:1:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," that is, an ordinary human being. He is told to deliver a message: the people must wail, meaning cry out loudly, because a terrible day is coming. "Alas for that day!" expresses pain and dread at what is approaching.

The Lord is speaking, and the message is directed against Egypt, as the following verses make clear. Ezekiel prophesied during the exile, and this judgment speaks of the sword, fear, and the fall of a powerful nation. Scholars disagree about the exact date of its fulfillment, but the theme is clear: God rules over all nations.

For today: let us not trust in power, money, or fame, for none of these protects us before God. Let us be humble, live with justice, and trust in Him, who offers us mercy while there is still time.
exp.26:5:
This verse says that the oars of Tyre's ship were made of oak wood from Bashan, a region known for its strong trees. The deck is described as made of wood from the coasts of Cyprus and inlaid with ivory. The phrase about the people who made the ship's work is difficult to translate, and scholars understand it in several different ways.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre, a trading city, is presented as a beautiful and luxurious ship, proud of its wealth. This poetic lament prepares the announcement of its fall.

Today: we may have things that are very valuable and beautiful, but they must not be the center of our security. Ask yourself what you truly trust in, and thank God for everything you have, using it with humility and generosity.
exp.0:11:
Each of these living creatures moved straight ahead, in the direction its face pointed. They went wherever the Spirit wanted them to go, and as they moved they did not turn or change direction. Saying they went straight ahead simply means they moved forward without swerving. "Spirit" can be understood as the Spirit of God or as the will that moved them; scholars interpret it both ways.

The one speaking is the prophet Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon beside the river Chebar. He recounts a vision God gave him: living beings with four faces beside a throne of glory. This vision showed him that God was still governing, even far from the temple in Jerusalem.

For today: we can learn to follow God's guidance with determination, without looking back or being led off course. Before deciding, pray and seek his direction in the Bible. Then move forward with firmness and confidence in what he shows you.
exp.20:24:
God addresses the king of Israel and calls him "profane," meaning one who does not respect what is holy, and "wicked," meaning one who lives without fearing God. He tells him that the day has come for his final punishment: the moment when his wickedness has reached its limit and judgment will fall. The word "final" points to the end of his time in power.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Many understand this to refer to Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, who broke his oath to Babylon. The text does not give the name, so this is a common identification, not a completely certain one. God announces that he will take away the crown until the one "whose right it is" comes, which many Christians see as a promise of the Messiah.

For today: those who hold authority answer to God. Let us be honest and humble in what has been entrusted to us, and remember that Christ is the righteous King.
exp.29:24:
God says he will strengthen the arms of Babylon's king, while Pharaoh's arms will fall limp. "Arms" stands for power and the ability to fight. The "sword" is God's judgment, which he places in the hand of Babylon's king so that he wields it against the land of Egypt. The final purpose is that they will know he is the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during Israel's exile in Babylon. Egypt was a power in which Judah sometimes trusted for protection, and God announces its fall. Babylon appears as an instrument of judgment, not as someone God approves of in every way.

For today: No human power, whether money, position, or influence, is as firm as it seems. Today you can examine what you trust most and place your security again in God, who rules over everything.
exp.34:12:
Ezekiel 35:13 says that Edom, also called Mount Seir, spoke proudly and poured out many words against God. The phrase "You boasted against Me with your mouth" means they bragged and grew arrogant. The phrase "multiplied your words against Me" means they spoke without restraint. Then God declares, "I heard it Myself!" None of that went unnoticed.

God himself is speaking here, through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom had held an old hostility toward Israel, and it rejoiced when Israel was laid waste, even claiming that their lands were theirs to take. By speaking this way about the land and the people of God, they spoke against God. That is why the judgment announced in the following verses comes.

For today: our words matter, and God hears them, including those we speak in private or in mockery. Before we speak with pride or rejoice in another's misfortune, let us ask him to guard our mouths.
exp.27:12:
This verse describes someone who was in Eden, the garden of God, adorned with precious stones and gold. It speaks of beauty and of a splendor made ready from the day of his creation. "Your mountings and settings were crafted in gold" refers to the gold settings in which the stones were set, and the stones named include ruby, topaz, diamond, beryl, onyx, jasper, sapphire, turquoise, and emerald.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and commands him to raise a lament over the king of Tyre. Many believe the language goes beyond a human king and alludes to Satan; others understand it as a poetic image of that king's pride. Christians interpret it in both ways. The central theme is the fall of one who grew proud of his beauty and wisdom.

For today: everything good we have, whether talents, beauty, or success, is a gift from God. Let us thank him with humility and not allow it to lead us into pride.
exp.22:43:
This verse says that the men sought out Oholah and Oholibah the way one seeks a prostitute. A prostitute is a woman who sells her body, and "lewd" means corrupt and without shame. "Slept with her" describes sexual relations, here used as an image of the men pursuing these two women for their own use.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Oholah and Oholibah represent Samaria and Jerusalem, two kingdoms of God's people. With this harsh image, God accuses them of having abandoned him to seek foreign alliances and gods. For that reason he announces judgment, as seen in the verses that follow.

For today: faithfulness to God is lost little by little when we look for security, pleasure, or approval in other things. Today you can ask yourself what has taken God's place in your heart, and return to him sincerely before that thing enslaves you.
exp.28:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel on an exact date: the tenth year, on the twelfth day of the tenth month. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to me" marks the start of a new message.

The one speaking is God, and Ezekiel is the prophet who receives it. He was among the exiles in Babylon. Many scholars place this date around 587 B.C., when Jerusalem was under siege. Here God begins a series of messages against Egypt, a nation in which Judah had put its trust instead of trusting in Him.

For today: God speaks at concrete moments in history, and He remains Lord over the nations and over our circumstances. We can learn to place our trust in Him and not in human powers, whether money, governments, or influence. Let us listen to His Word carefully and respond with faith.
exp.20:4:
Then all people will know that God himself has drawn his sword from its sheath, meaning that he has brought judgment. "All people" means every human being. The sheath is the case that holds the sword. The Berean Standard Bible says God will not return the sword to its sheath again, so this time the judgment will not stop until it has accomplished its purpose.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God announces judgment against Jerusalem and the land of Israel for their persistent sin. The sword is usually understood as the invasion by Babylon. The text says that "the righteous and the wicked" would fall, and scholars explain this in several ways: as the scale of the disaster, or as the shared experience of a nation under judgment.

For today: God is serious, but he also warns before he acts. If we sense he is calling us to change, let us not postpone it. Today we can pray sincerely and correct something concrete.
exp.15:32:
Ezekiel 16:33 says that prostitutes are normally the ones who receive payment, but Jerusalem did the opposite: she gave gifts to her lovers. She paid them so that they would come to her from every side. The word "lovers" in this verse is what the passage calls the men who came to her, and the act described is unfaithfulness to her husband.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an unfaithful wife to accuse Jerusalem of abandoning God and seeking alliances and gods of other nations. Many understand that the "gifts" include riches and political dealings, although the details are interpreted in various ways.

For today: examine what you are paying for with your time, money and heart in order to feel secure or loved. God does not want us to buy affection somewhere else, since He already offers us His faithful love. Return to Him with sincerity.
exp.36:19:
The verse describes two sticks on which Ezekiel wrote, one for Judah and one for Joseph (Ephraim). He was to hold them in his hand, in full view of the people. Sticks here are pieces of wood, like rods. In this way the people would see the symbolic act for themselves.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile. For centuries the people had been divided into two kingdoms, and now they were scattered. God asks him to join the two sticks together in his hand as a sign that one day he will gather Israel into one nation, under one king. The people would ask what it meant, and so Ezekiel could explain the promise to them.

For today: God can heal divisions that seem impossible. We can pray and seek reconciliation in the family or in the church, trusting that He is the one who unites.
exp.45:12:
Every day, in the morning, a lamb one year old and without fault was to be offered to God as a burnt offering. A burnt offering was a gift burned whole on the altar. "Without fault" means the animal had to be healthy, with no spots and no defects.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of a new temple and an orderly worship (chapters 40 to 48). Before this, he speaks of the prince and of the offerings at feasts and on the Sabbath. This verse establishes the daily offering. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a spiritual picture of worship to God.

For today: God deserves the best of our day, and the beginning is a good time for it. Today we do not offer lambs, but we can dedicate the morning to him with prayer and devotion. Many Christians see in the unblemished lamb a sign that points to Christ.
exp.2:2:
God tells Ezekiel to eat the scroll he hands him, to fill his stomach with it. Ezekiel does so, and it tastes as sweet as honey. "Son of man" is a way of addressing him as a simple human being. "Eat and fill your stomach" means taking in the message fully, so that it becomes part of him.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who will be a prophet to the exiles of Israel. Before speaking, he must receive the message completely. The scroll contains God's words, though according to the passage it also includes laments and mourning (2:10). The sweetness shows that God's word is good, even when the message is hard.

For today: before sharing the Bible with others, let it first enter your own heart. Read it calmly, meditate on it, and obey it, trusting that it is sweet and good even when it corrects.
exp.20:10:
The verse says the sword is already appointed to be polished, so that it can be grasped in the hand. It is sharpened and polished, ready to be placed in the hand of the one who will strike. Polishing makes a weapon bright and ready for use. God had the sword made sharp and polished so that it would be at hand, prepared, and placed in the hand of the one who will carry out the punishment.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces judgment on Jerusalem and its people for their disobedience. The sword is often understood as the army of Babylon, though the text presents it as an instrument of God. The verses that follow show that the blow would reach even the princes of Israel.

For today: God speaks in earnest, but he warns so that there may be repentance. Today I can examine my life honestly, correct what I know is wrong, and return to God before the consequences arrive.
exp.24:8:
He says God will "expose the flank" of Moab, meaning its side would be left without protection. The frontier cities, which were its pride and "the glory of the land," would be left exposed: Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim. "Frontier" here means the border or edge of the territory.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Moab said that Judah was just like the other nations, as if their God had nothing special with them. By this, it looked down on Judah and on the Lord himself. So God announces judgment. The passages that follow speak of peoples from the east who would take the region, though the text gives no further details about who they would be.

For today: God takes seriously the contempt shown toward his people and his name. We can avoid mocking the faith of others or rejoicing when someone falls, and trust that God is just and cares for his own.
exp.20:11:
God tells Ezekiel to cry out and wail, because the sword is coming against the people and against their leaders. "Wail" means to cry out loudly in grief. The sword brings terror to the people, and the prophet is told to strike his thigh as a sign of pain and deep distress.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man." The people of Judah had ignored his warnings again and again. The "sword" is commonly understood to be the army of Babylon, which God uses to bring judgment. God does not want Ezekiel to announce this coldly, but with genuine sorrow.

For today: when we speak about sin and its consequences, let us do so with humility and tears, not with pride. And if God corrects us, let us take his voice seriously and return to him in time.
exp.15:39:
This verse says that God will bring a mob against Jerusalem. They will stone her and cut her to pieces with their swords. The word "mob" in the verse refers to a crowd of people gathered together. These were punishments that the law of Moses applied to adulterers and murderers.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout the chapter he describes Jerusalem as an unfaithful wife who abandoned God for idols and alliances with other nations. These words announce judgment upon her. It is often linked to the invasion of Babylon, although interpreters explain it in different ways. At the end, the text speaks of God's anger coming to rest.

Today it reminds us that God takes faithfulness seriously. We can ask ourselves what things occupy the place that belongs to Him, and turn back to Him sincerely, trusting in His mercy.
exp.47:29:
This verse says that the city will have gates on its north side, and that this side is 4,500 cubits long. The cubit was a common unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the fingertips, though its exact value is debated.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who received this vision during the exile in Babylon. The people were far from their land and discouraged. God shows them a well-ordered city, with a place for each tribe. Scholars interpret it in several ways: as a literal temple and city in the future, or as a symbol of God's presence and order among his people.

For today: God attends to every detail and has a place for each of his own. If you feel far away or without direction, trust that he continues to work with order and faithfulness. Pray today, giving thanks for the place you have among his people.
exp.31:26:
The verse says that these powerful warriors will not receive an honorable burial alongside the fallen heroes of other peoples. They went down to the grave with their weapons, and their swords were placed under their heads, as a sign of military glory. Their shields rested on their bones. But their violence goes with them into death, and the terror they once caused in the land of the living is remembered against them. The phrase "the fallen warriors of old" refers to the peoples outside Israel who had fallen in battle.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he announces judgment against Egypt and describes it going down to the place of the dead, where other nations that spread terror are already present, such as Assyria, Meshech, and Tubal. The passage is prophetic poetry, with strong images. Not all scholars agree on the details of how that scene should be understood.

For today: power that is used to oppress and cause fear does not leave a good record before God. It is better to use whatever strength we have to serve and protect others.
exp.39:7:
The verse says that the man guiding Ezekiel measured the portico of the gateway inside, the covered area that opens toward the temple courtyard, and that it was one reed in width or depth. A "reed" was a measuring rod, about three meters long, though its exact length is debated. The phrase "inside" means toward the inner side of the gate.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives a vision from God. A guide with a measuring reed shows him a new temple, beginning with the east gate. Such precise measurements gave a defeated people hope that God would restore his presence among them. How that temple should be understood is a debated question.

For today: God cares about details and works with order. We can trust that nothing in our lives escapes his notice, and we can draw near to him with reverence and hope.
exp.47:2:
This verse says that the tribe of Naphtali receives a strip of land beside that of Asher, running from east to west, from the eastern side to the sea (the Mediterranean). "Border" means boundary or edge, and "one portion" means a single share of the land that was divided out.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. In his final vision a restored land is described, divided into horizontal strips for the twelve tribes, running from north to south. Naphtali is third from the north. Interpreters differ: some see it as a promise for the restored Israel, others as a spiritual or future picture.

God does not forget anyone; each tribe has its assigned place. Today we can trust that God also has a place and a purpose for you. Rest in his care and serve with joy where he has placed you.
exp.39:12:
He measured the gateway from the roof of one gate chamber to the roof of the opposite one. The distance from doorway to doorway was twenty-five cubits, about twelve meters, since a cubit is roughly half a meter. The gate chambers were small rooms set inside the entrance.

Ezekiel describes a vision that God gave him during the exile, about fourteen years after the fall of Jerusalem. A man with a measuring reed shows him a new temple, and Ezekiel records each measurement. Scholars disagree on whether it is a literal future building or a spiritual picture of God's presence. The measurements show order and care.

For today: God pays attention to details, and he cares that his people approach him with order and reverence. Ask yourself what "gate" you need to tend in order to draw near to God each day.
exp.41:0:
He led me out northward into the outer court, and brought me to a group of chambers opposite the temple courtyard, facing the outer wall on the north side.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received from God, in which a guide shows him a new temple and measures it with great detail. This takes place while the people are living in exile in Babylon. Interpreters differ on what this temple represents: some think of a literal temple in the future, others of a spiritual picture of God's presence. What is clear is that God desires to dwell among his people, with order and holiness.

God cares even about the details of how we worship him. Today we can draw near to him with reverence, and also with the confidence that God does not forget us, even in difficult times.
exp.25:10:
The verse says the invading army will enter the city with such force that the hooves of its horses will trample all the streets. The people will be slaughtered with the sword, and your mighty pillars will fall to the ground. The "mighty pillars" were probably columns or monuments of the city, and their fall to the ground shows how completely its strength will be broken. "Trample" means to stomp down under the feet.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing Tyre, a city rich and proud because of its trade. It rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking of its own gain. King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon is the instrument of judgment. Scholars debate how all of this was fulfilled, since Tyre resisted for a long time and the prophecy has several stages.
