For today: wealth, power and pride do not protect us from God. We can examine whether we trust in what we have more than in Him, and rejoice with humility, never at another's misfortune.
exp.26:16:
Ezekiel 27:17 says that Judah and the land of Israel traded with Tyre. They exchanged wheat from Minnith, cakes and honey, oil and balm for Tyre's merchandise. Tyre's goods were brought to market there, and Judah and Israel offered their own products in return. The meaning of "cakes" is not certain, though some think of a kind of sweet or pastry, and others of a different product entirely.

God speaks through Ezekiel and composes a lament over Tyre, a city made rich by sea trade. The list of nations shows its great fame and wealth. Shortly afterward, the message announces that this greatness would not save it from judgment.

Today: We can work and trade honestly, but without placing our security in money or success. What we have is a gift to manage well and share, because only God is a firm foundation.
exp.29:19:
This verse marks the date of a new prophecy. It says that in the eleventh year, on the seventh day of the first month, the word of the LORD came to Ezekiel. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to me" means that a message from the Lord reached him.

Here the speaker is Ezekiel, the prophet, who was living in exile in Babylon. He introduces a message against Egypt and its king, the pharaoh. Many understand that the eleventh year is counted from the exile of King Jehoiachin, that is, around 587 B.C., although the text does not state this in full. Egypt seemed a secure source of help for Judah, but God announces that this power will be broken.

For today: God speaks at specific moments in history and is not caught off guard by anything. We can rest in Him and place our ultimate trust not in governments, money, or people, but in the LORD, who keeps His word.
exp.19:6:
God reminds Israel of what he asked of them in Egypt: that each one throw away the abominations before his eyes, that is, the images and detestable things they worshiped. He warns them not to defile themselves, meaning not to make themselves spiritually unclean, with the idols of Egypt. And he closes by saying: "I am the LORD your God."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes during the exile. He tells them the story of Israel to show that their rebellion goes back a long way. From Egypt, God chose them and promised them a good land, but they did not let go of their idols. Even so, God acted for the sake of his name.

For today: ask yourself what thing captures your gaze and competes with God in your heart. With his help, let it go, remembering that he is your God and remains faithful to you.
exp.46:19:
This verse marks the boundary of the west side of the land. The "great sea" is the Mediterranean Sea. The border would follow that coast up to a point opposite Lebo-hamath, in the north. "Boundary" means the limit or dividing line, and "opposite" means directly across from that place.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile. In a vision, he describes to him how the land would be divided among the tribes of Israel. This gave hope to a people who had lost everything. The boundaries on all four sides show that God cares even about the details. Afterward, the land is also shared with the foreigners who live among them, and they are treated as children of the people. Some understand this literally, others symbolically.

For today: God is a God of order and of promises kept. Trust that he has a place for you, and open your heart and your table to those who come from outside.
exp.26:18:
This verse says that traders from Izal and from Dan and Javan brought goods to the markets of Tyre. Their wares included casks of wine, wrought iron, cassia, and sweet cane, a plant used in perfumes and in worship. Markets like these were large and busy centers of trade. The place name Izal is hard to identify with certainty, and scholars differ on who or where Javan and Dan refer to in this passage, so the exact details remain uncertain.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. This is a lament over Tyre, a city very rich from its sea trade. The long list of merchants shows its fame and its pride. Then God announces that this wealth will not save it from its fall.

For today: enjoying work and possessions is not wrong, but we should not place our trust in them. Ask yourself today: "Where do I place my security?" God invites us to trust Him first.
exp.15:17:
Jerusalem took her embroidered garments and used them to cover the images she had made for herself. She also set before those images the oil and incense that God had given her. The comment about covering them refers to this same act. The word "fornicate" is not used in the verse you are reading, so it is left out here.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16 he describes Jerusalem as a young woman whom he rescued, cared for, and adorned. Instead of being grateful, she used those gifts to worship idols. In this way God shows how serious her ingratitude and betrayal were.

For today: everything we have, such as time, money, and talents, comes from God. We can ask ourselves whether we are using these things to honor him or to serve other things that have taken first place in our hearts.
exp.32:18:
This verse says that if a wicked person turns away from his wickedness and does what is just and right, he will live because of it. "Wicked" describes someone who lives without respect for God. "Turns" means to leave or turn away from something. "Does what is just and right" means acting in line with what is fair and good.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was with the exiles in Babylon. Some of the people were saying, "The way of the Lord is not fair," that is, they were accusing God of being unjust. God answers that He judges each person according to their own way, and that the door of repentance is open. Soon after, news arrives that Jerusalem has fallen.

For today: no one is condemned by their past if they return to God. Instead of making excuses or blaming others, take one concrete step of change today, such as asking for forgiveness or letting go of a bad habit, trusting in God's mercy.
exp.4:2:
God tells Ezekiel that from the hair he has cut and divided, he is to take a few strands, counting them, and secure them in the folds of his garment. "A few strands" means a small number, carefully counted out. "The folds of your garment" refers to the fabric of his clothing where the hair can be kept safe.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. With this symbolic act he announces judgment on Jerusalem: some would be burned, others would fall by the sword, and others would be scattered. These few strands kept aside show that some would survive. However, the next verse indicates that even among them some would be thrown into the fire, so God's care does not lessen the seriousness of the judgment.

For today: God sees and cares for his people one by one, even in difficult times. This invites us to take his correction seriously and to trust that his faithfulness sustains us.
exp.47:16:
It describes an open space around the city, called the "pastureland," meaning free and shared ground with no buildings. This space would extend 250 cubits in each direction: north, south, east, and west. A cubit was a unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the fingertips; in Ezekiel it is usually understood to be about 45 to 50 centimeters, although scholars do not fully agree.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during Israel's exile in Babylon. In this final vision, a land is described as divided in an orderly way, with a holy place and a city at the center. Some believe it is a symbolic picture of God's restoration; others think of something literal and future. The Bible does not fully make this clear.

For today: God values order and shared space. We can leave "open spaces" in our lives: time to rest, pray, and care for others, without filling every corner with activities.
exp.16:20:
God says that all who flee from the king, together with his choice troops, will fall by the sword, and that the survivors will be scattered to every wind. The phrase "choice troops" is the wording of the verse itself, and "to every wind" means in every direction. In the end, everyone will recognize that God has kept his word.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. King Zedekiah of Judah had made an oath of loyalty to Babylon in God's name and then broke it, seeking help from Egypt. God regards that oath as his own. Later in the same chapter, God promises to plant a tender shoot that will become a great cedar. Many Christians see this pointing to the Messiah, although it is interpreted in different ways.

Today: God takes our promises seriously. Keeping the word we have given, even when it costs us, is a way of honoring him, and trusting in him is safer than seeking ways out on our own.
exp.25:5:
This verse says that the villages on Tyre's mainland, which depended on the city, would be destroyed by the sword. The result would be that the people would know that God is the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a trading city, proud of its wealth, and it rejoiced when Jerusalem fell (26:2). God announces judgment against her, and the following text names Nebuchadnezzar as the instrument. Scholars discuss how all this was fulfilled in detail, but the central message is clear: no human power stands above God.

For today: let us not place our security in money, success, or our own strength. All of that can disappear. Let us instead trust in God, and let us rejoice with humility, never with pride, when others suffer.
exp.32:11:
This verse says that the good someone did in the past will not save them if they now turn away from God in rebellion. Nor does the past wickedness of a wicked person condemn them forever if they turn away from it. "Wickedness" means living against what is right, and "stumble" means failing or falling into ruin; "turns" means that a person repents and changes direction.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to a discouraged people. The Israelites, already in exile, were saying that their sins were crushing them and that there was no hope left. God answers that he does not desire the death of anyone, but that all should turn back to him and live.

For today: do not live either on your past mistakes or on your past merits. If you have failed, God invites you to return today. If you are walking well, keep trusting and obeying each day, without boasting of what you have already done.
exp.39:6:
It says that in the east gate of the temple there were small rooms for guards, each one square, one rod long and one rod wide. Between one room and the next there were five cubits of wall or space. The threshold of the gate, on the inner side by the portico, was also one rod deep. A "rod" here equals six long cubits (about three meters, although the exact measure is debated). The rooms are the gate chambers, and the threshold is the base of the gate's entrance.

Ezekiel speaks, recounting his vision. A man with a measuring rod guides him through a new temple and measures it carefully. This takes place while Israel is in exile, and God shows him that his presence and his order have not been lost. Scholars disagree about whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or future.

For today: God cares about details and values order and holiness. Ask yourself which small area of your life you can put in order and offer to him with care.
exp.0:1:
This verse gives the date of the vision: the fifth day of the month, in the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's exile. The key word here is "exile," which refers to the forced removal of the people from their land. Jehoiachin was taken away to Babylon along with many Jews, and among them was Ezekiel.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest who had been carried into exile, living beside the river Chebar in Babylon. He records the date carefully because his message comes from a real and painful moment: the people are far from their land and from the temple. Scholars differ on what the "thirty years" in verse 1 refers to; some think it is his age, and others think it is a different way of counting the years.

For today: God does not stay far from us when we go through a time of loss or exile. He can find us and speak to us even in places we did not choose. Today you can open your heart to him, no matter where you are.
exp.17:18:
This verse records a question people were asking: "Why shouldn't the son bear the iniquity of his father?" God answers that the son who has done what is just and right, carefully keeping all His statutes, will surely live. To "bear" means to carry the guilt and its consequences.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. They were repeating a saying: that children paid for their parents' sins. By this they implied that God was unjust. God makes clear that each person answers for his or her own choices. Interpreters debate how far this touches the social consequences of sin, but the emphasis here is personal responsibility before God.

Today, do not use your family past as an excuse or as a sentence of condemnation. With God's help, you can choose to walk in justice and mercy, and He receives you just as you are.
exp.30:9:
God says that, because this great tree grew very tall, it set its top among the clouds, and it grew proud because of its height. The phrase "it became great in height" means that the tree rose to a great size and thought itself superior. The "top" is the highest part, the crown of the tree.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He directs this message to the pharaoh of Egypt, who is compared to a huge cedar, just as Assyria was before. Many understand the tree to represent the power and glory of a nation that believed itself invincible. God reminds him that his greatness was a gift from God, and for that reason He announces that his pride will bring his fall.

Everything good we have, such as talents, success, or position, comes from God. When we begin to feel superior, it is wise to pause, give thanks, and serve with humility.
exp.31:27:
God tells Pharaoh of Egypt that he will be broken and will lie down among the uncircumcised, that is, among pagan peoples who did not belong to the covenant with Israel. "Lie down" means you will be lying there, dead. "With those slain by the sword" means those who died by the sword.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and pronounces a lament over Egypt. That kingdom was powerful and proud, and it had caused terror to other peoples. The prophet describes it in the place of the dead, alongside other nations that also fell. In this way he teaches that no empire escapes God's judgment.

For today: power, fame, and strength do not protect us before God. It is wiser to live with humility, to treat others well, and to trust in Him, not in our own resources.
exp.14:3:
It says that a vine branch which has already been thrown into the fire, burned at both of its ends and also in the middle, is no longer good for anything. The "ends" are the two extremes of the branch, and "devours" means that the fire destroyed it. The final question calls for a clear answer: no, it can no longer be useful for anything.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He compares Jerusalem to the wood of the vine, which is useful for bearing fruit but not for building. Because Jerusalem was not faithful to him, God announces that he will give her over to the fire, that is, to judgment through her enemies.

For today: our worth does not lie in how we appear, but in remaining joined to God and bearing fruit for him. Let us ask him to keep us faithful and humble, and to lead us back to him in time.
exp.0:19:
This verse says that the living creatures and the wheels moved together, as one thing. Wherever the spirit would go, they went, and the wheels rose alongside them. The reason given is that the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels.

Ezekiel speaks here, a priest and prophet who was exiled in Babylon. He recounts the vision he had of the glory of God beside the river Chebar. The wheels full of eyes speak of movement and of complete sight. Many believe they show that God is not bound to one place and rules over everything. Some think "the spirit" is the Spirit of God; others, a force that guided them. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: even when your life seems far from home or out of control, God keeps guiding. Ask Him to direct you and move in step with what He shows you.
exp.17:22:
God asks a question that already contains its answer: does he take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? Clearly not. What he wants is for the wicked person to turn away from his evil ways and live. "Wicked" describes someone who lives with his back turned to God, and "turn" means to change direction and come back.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some of the people were saying that God's way was not fair, and they felt punished for the sins of others. God answers that each person is accountable for his own actions, and that the way back to him is always open.

For today: if you feel that your past condemns you, remember that God takes no delight in your ruin, but in your return. Today you can come back to him sincerely and begin to live in a different way.
exp.29:4:
God announces that the fall of Egypt will drag down its allies as well: Cush, Put, Lud, all the various peoples, Libya, and the men of the covenant land. The phrase "will fall with Egypt by the sword" gives the sense of the verse's ending. Some of these places cannot be located with certainty, and "the men of the covenant land" is understood in several ways.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, at the time of the fall of Jerusalem. Egypt seemed a secure power, and Judah trusted in its help. God warns that this support would fail, because He governs all nations and their alliances.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether money, connections, or power. All of that can fail. Trust first in God, who sustains your life when everything else collapses.
exp.8:6:
He says that God orders the executioners of judgment to "defile the temple," that is, to make it unclean by filling the courts with the slain. The word translated "fill" means to fill up, and the courts are the open yards of the temple. Then they go out and begin killing throughout the city.

God speaks in a vision that the prophet Ezekiel receives. The people had filled Jerusalem with violence, injustice, and idolatry, even inside the temple, and they said that God did not see. Judgment begins at the sanctuary, and those who bore the mark were protected. Ezekiel responds with grief and intercedes.

For today: God is not indifferent to sin, and his judgment begins with his own house. Today we can examine our hearts with humility, seek his forgiveness, and, like Ezekiel, pray with compassion for others.
exp.15:1:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," a way of saying "human being." He tells him to confront Jerusalem with her abominations, that is, to make her face the detestable things she has done.

The LORD, the God of Israel, is speaking. Ezekiel was a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God wants Jerusalem to see her sin, and in the verses that follow he reminds her of her humble origins and how he cared for her. Many understand this to be a harsh message, but it is given in the hope that the people will recognize their error.

For today: God tells us the truth because he loves us. We can ask him to show us our faults, accept his correction with humility, and return to him, remembering that everything good we have comes from his grace.
exp.33:15:
God promises to care for each sheep according to its need: he will seek the lost, bring back the strays, bind up the broken, and strengthen the weak. The verse shows that God's care is shaped by what each one needs. The sheep that is sleek and strong, meaning the one that takes advantage of its power, he will destroy. He will shepherd them with justice.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel's leaders, called shepherds, took advantage of the people and neglected the weak. That is why God says that he himself will be the shepherd.

For today: if you are wounded, lost, or weary, God seeks you. And if you have any power or influence, use it to care for the weak, not to take advantage of them.
exp.35:17:
God says that he poured out his wrath on Israel for two sins: the bloodshed they committed on the land, and the idols with which they defiled it. To "defile" means to make dirty what was holy. "Poured out" describes his wrath as something that fell on them with force.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He explains to the exiles why they lost their land: it was not chance or God's abandonment, but the consequence of their violence and their idols. Then the chapter announces that God will restore them for the sake of his holy name.

For today: God cares about how we treat people and whom we worship. We can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our hearts and how that affects those around us. He corrects, but he also offers forgiveness and a new beginning.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that the word of the LORD came directly to Ezekiel, who was a priest and the son of Buzi. This happened in the land of the Chaldeans, which is Babylon, beside the River Kebar. The phrase "the LORD's hand was upon him" speaks of God's power resting on him and preparing him to receive the message.

Ezekiel writes this as an exile. He had been carried away captive along with King Jehoiachin, far from the temple in Jerusalem where he would have served as a priest. God reveals himself to him right there, in a foreign land. This is how his calling as a prophet begins. Scholars debate exactly what "the thirty years" in verse 1 refers to, and it is best to acknowledge that uncertainty.

For today: God is not limited by the places where we feel far away or out of place. Even in times of loss or exile, he can speak to you and give you purpose. Stay attentive to his voice.
exp.43:30:
The priests were not allowed to eat the meat of any bird or animal that had been found dead or that had been torn apart by wild beasts. They could eat only the meat of animals that had been slaughtered in the proper way.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple and the rules for the priests. Earlier, rules had already been given about their purity and their food. This law is similar to Leviticus 22:8, where priests are also forbidden to eat such animals. Their service was to show care and holiness, and their food was part of that.

For today: let us take care with what we allow into our lives, not only at the table but also in our minds and hearts. Whoever serves God seeks to live with integrity, even in everyday matters.
exp.21:18:
God says that all his people have become "dross," meaning the worthless waste that is left behind when metal is melted down. For that reason, he will gather them into Jerusalem, the way someone gathers metal into a furnace to melt it down. The phrase "have become" in this verse means that they have turned into this.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. The people had fallen into injustice, violence, and idolatry. Jerusalem would be like a furnace where God would gather them to face his judgment before the city fell. The verses that follow speak of anger, but the image of melting also suggests a purpose of purification.

For today: God sees the truth of our hearts, not just appearances. If you notice areas of your life that have filled up with "dross," such as lying or selfishness, do not wait for trials to arrive. Bring them to God today with humility and ask him to cleanse you.
exp.33:29:
It says that the people of Israel will come to know clearly that God is with them and that they belong to him. The sentence about knowing it "by experience" is rewritten for the verse's own words: "Then they will know" means they will come to know it through what they experience.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel was scattered and wounded because its leaders, called shepherds, had neglected it. God promises to be the Shepherd who cares for, protects, and gives security to his people. This promise of peace and food is one that he would fulfill, and that trust would be born from seeing his faithfulness.

For today: when you feel alone or insecure, remember that God promises to care for his own. You can set aside a few minutes today to pray, thank him for his care, and hand over the worry that weighs on you most.
exp.15:37:
It says that God himself will be the judge of Jerusalem. He will sentence her to the punishment given to women who commit adultery and to those who shed blood. "So I will bring upon you the wrath of your bloodshed and jealousy" means that God will bring a violent punishment, born of his anger and his jealousy, that is, of his love wounded by the unfaithfulness of his people. "Lovers" are the nations and the idols to whom she gave herself.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile. Throughout this chapter, God compares Jerusalem to a wife he cared for who then betrayed him with other gods and alliances, even sacrificing their children. God announces judgment for that unfaithfulness.

For today: God takes our loyalty seriously. Examine where you place your trust and your heart, and return to God with sincerity, because his judgment seeks to awaken us and his mercy always waits for us.
exp.27:13:
The verse calls this figure an anointed guardian cherub, meaning a being set apart by God to watch over and protect. God himself says he ordained him for that role. He was placed on the holy mountain of God and walked among the fiery stones, an image of brilliance and of God's holy presence.

God speaks through Ezekiel to the king of Tyre, a ruler known for his wealth and pride. The language is poetic and very elevated. Some believe it is only a picture of the human king. Others think Satan is also reflected behind that pride. Christians have read it both ways, so it is wise to speak with humility.

For today: everything we are and have was given to us by God. When we remember that, pride loses its place, and we can live thankful and simple.
exp.11:26:
This verse says that the people of Israel were mocking Ezekiel. They said his vision was for many years from now, meaning something that would happen far in the future, and that he prophesied about the distant future, so remote that it did not concern them. "Son of man" is the way God addresses Ezekiel.

God speaks to Ezekiel while the people are in exile in Babylon. The people used sayings to make light of the warnings of judgment and to stay comfortable in their rebellion. God answers that his words will not be delayed any longer: what was announced would be fulfilled in their own days.

For today: do not use "it is still a long way off" as an excuse to postpone your obedience. If God is speaking to you through his Word, respond today with humility, because his patience is an opportunity to return to him.
exp.9:14:
The cherubim rose upward. Ezekiel recognizes them as the same living creatures he had seen earlier by the River Kebar.

The word "creatures" here means "living beings," not ordinary animals. "Rose upward" means they lifted off the ground.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. In his vision, the glory of God leaves the temple in Jerusalem, a sign of judgment for the sin of the people. When he says "these were the living creatures I had seen," Ezekiel connects this scene with his first vision in chapter 1: it is the same God who called him.

For today: God is not bound to a place or to our circumstances. Even if you feel far from home or from what you once knew, the Lord remains present and in control. Seek him where you are, with reverence and confidence.
exp.32:14:
What it says: God promises that if a wicked person truly turns back, he will live. Restoring a pledge means returning what was held as security for a debt. Making restitution means paying back what was taken. Walking in the statutes of life means living by God's commands, which lead to a good life. Doing these things without practicing wrongdoing means he will not die.

Context: God speaks to Ezekiel, whom he appointed as a watchman to warn Israel. The people were in exile and said that God was unjust. God answers that his door is open to repentance and that each person answers for his own way. The exact meaning of "life" and "death" here is debated: they may refer to physical life, to the survival of the people, or to life with God.

For today: Repentance includes actions. If you have hurt or harmed someone, ask for forgiveness and, if you can, repair the damage. God offers a new beginning.
exp.43:16:
The priests, when they went into the inner court of the temple to serve, were to wear linen garments and not anything made of wool. The verse says they must not wear wool when they serve at the gates of the inner court or inside the temple, and it describes those duties as the sacred work of worship.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of a future temple. Earlier He praises the priests descended from Zadok, who remained faithful when Israel turned away from Him. Now He gives them rules for serving with order and reverence. Interpreters differ on whether this vision will be fulfilled literally or is symbolic. The following text explains that linen avoided sweat, meaning the service was to be done with calm and purity.

For today: serving God deserves care and respect. Whether you help in your church or at home, do it with a clean heart, without anxiety or pride, and with gratitude for the privilege of drawing near to Him.
exp.47:15:
The verse says the city will be a perfect square: each side measures four thousand five hundred cubits, so the north, south, east and west sides are all the same length. A cubit was an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the fingertips, and in plain modern terms it comes to about three meters, though scholars do not fully agree on its exact value. The sides are named simply as north, south, east and west.

God shows the prophet Ezekiel a vision of the land divided again, with a sacred area at the center. The city lies in the common, non-consecrated part. This vision comforts the exiled people, for God promises to be with them. Christians interpret it in several ways: literally, symbolically, or as a foretaste of the new creation.

For today: the equal measure on all four sides reminds us that God loves order and justice. We can ask ourselves whether, in our lives, we give God the central place and put everything in order around Him.
exp.31:4:
It says that God will leave the dead body of the pharaoh lying on the mountains, and that his remains will fill the valleys. The word "flesh" refers to his body, to what is left of it. "Fill" describes what will happen to the valleys. The phrase about the valleys being filled is clear in your reading, so there is no need to puzzle over it: his remains will lie where they fall, across the land.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament against the pharaoh of Egypt. The pharaoh thought of himself as a mighty monster of the Nile, and God announces that he will trap him like an animal in a net. It is a poetic image of judgment on a proud nation that oppressed others.

For today: power, fame, or success do not make us untouchable before God. We can examine whether there is pride in our hearts and ask Him for humility, remembering that all our strength comes from Him.
exp.23:12:
God tells Jerusalem that she will suffer for her filthiness, that is, her wickedness and her idolatry. He wanted to cleanse her, but she would not be purified. Therefore she will not be pure again until his wrath against her has subsided, that is, until the judgment is fully carried out and his anger is satisfied. The phrase "you will not be pure again" means that she will remain unclean and cannot be made clean on her own.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Jerusalem is compared to a dirty, rusted pot set on the fire. God had given her warnings and opportunities, but the people rejected them. The verses that follow show that the judgment is firm and just.

For today: when God corrects us or points something out to us, let us not harden our hearts. His call to change is an offer of cleansing. We can respond to him today with sincerity and repentance.
exp.3:4:
God tells Ezekiel that each day he lies on his side stands for one year of Israel's sin. He will lie there for 390 days, and in this way he will carry the guilt of the people. "Guilt" here means blame or sin, and "bear" means to carry its consequences, in a symbolic way.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet and priest who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Before the final attack against Jerusalem, God commands him to act out this message as a visible drama, together with the drawing of the siege. Many think the 390 days stand for years of sin of the northern kingdom or of the whole people, but scholars do not agree on the exact calculation.

Today we can learn that God does not hide the reality of sin or its consequences, and He speaks to us with clarity to lead us to repentance. If anything in our life pulls us away from Him, it is wise to acknowledge it honestly and return to God while there is still time.
exp.12:8:
God says he will act against the prophets who see false visions and speak lying divinations. They will not belong to the council of his people, their names will not be recorded in the register of Israel, and they will not enter the land of Israel. In the end, everyone will know that he is the Lord GOD. The words "false visions" and "lying divinations" describe prophets who claim to receive messages and present them as God's word, when those messages are empty and without truth.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Some false prophets claimed to speak for the Lord when God had not spoken to them, and they promised peace when judgment was coming. In this way they gave the people a false sense of security. Scholars understand in different ways exactly what the register was, but it seems to refer to the record of God's people.

Today we can examine what we hear in the light of the Bible, and if we teach, we should speak with honesty. A truth that makes us uncomfortable is better than a sweet promise that God has not made.
exp.24:11:
This verse says that God holds Edom accountable for acting vengefully against Judah. Edom acted out of spite and hostility, and in doing so incurred grievous guilt. The phrase about incurring grievous guilt means that they committed a very serious wrong. The description of Edom acting vengefully shows that Edom sought to get even with God's people.

The one speaking is God himself, through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom was a neighbor of Israel and, according to the Bible, had a long-standing enmity with that people. Here God announces that he will judge the nations that rejoiced in or took advantage of Judah's fall. The verses that follow explain the punishment that would come upon Edom.

For today: let us not take vengeance into our own hands. If someone has wounded us, we can hand the matter over to God, who judges with justice, and ask him for a heart free of resentment.
exp.19:3:
God asks Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man," whether he will judge the people. It is a rhetorical question, and it invites Ezekiel to say yes and to act as God's spokesman. To confront them with the abominations of their ancestors means to lay before them the wrongs their forefathers committed. Above all, these were acts of idolatry, and God wants the people to see them clearly.

God speaks to Ezekiel when some elders of Israel come to seek his counsel, probably during the exile in Babylon. God refuses to answer them because their hearts remain far from him. Before giving them any answer, he wants them to remember their history of rebellion and his own mercy from Egypt.

For today: before asking God for direction, it is wise to look honestly at our lives and turn away from what we know displeases him. God listens to a sincere heart.
exp.36:20:
God promises that he will take the people of Israel out from the nations where they have gone and gather them from all around. He will bring them back into their own land. The nations here are the foreign places where they had been scattered.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people were discouraged and divided: the northern kingdom (Ephraim) and the southern kingdom (Judah). With the sign of two sticks that become one, God announces that there will be restoration and unity. Some see a partial fulfillment in the return from exile; others see a future or spiritual fulfillment in Christ.

For today: even if you feel far away, scattered, or broken inside, God is still the one who gathers and restores. Trust that he can heal your relationships and give you hope again.
exp.8:4:
God speaks to six other men, and Ezekiel hears it with his own ears. He tells them to follow the man who marks the faithful through Jerusalem and start killing, showing no pity or sparing anyone.

The LORD speaks in a vision that Ezekiel receives while in exile. Jerusalem had filled up with idolatry and violence, and God decides to judge it. But first he commands that those who grieved over those evils be marked, to protect them. The judgment begins at the sanctuary, where the guilt was greater. Scholars understand this as a real judgment, though not all of them interpret its details the same way.

For today: God sees both the wickedness and the pain of those who suffer because of it. We can ask him for a sensitive heart, one that does not grow used to sin, and trust that he cares for his own.
exp.43:19:
It says that the priests must not shave their heads completely, nor let their hair grow long, but must carefully trim their hair to keep it short and neat. "Carefully trim" means cutting the hair so that it stays even and tidy, which is what the verse calls for.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the vision of the new temple (chapters 40 to 48). There he gives rules for the priests descended from Zadok, who would serve with reverence. These rules aimed to make their appearance show order and respect for what is holy. Some understand that both the mourning customs of the pagans and carelessness were being avoided. About how this vision will be fulfilled, there are several interpretations.

For today: serving God with order and reverence, without excess or carelessness. We can ask ourselves whether our way of living and of presenting ourselves shows respect for God and cares for our witness before others.
exp.35:1:
This verse begins a message from God. He says that the enemy mocked Israel and cried out, "Aha!", an expression of scorn and triumph. The enemy declared that the ancient heights had become their possession. Because means "because" in the sense of "for the reason that," so the sentence simply gives the cause of what follows.

Ezekiel speaks to the mountains of Israel on God's behalf. The people were in exile and the land had been left in ruins. The neighboring peoples, and the text names Edom in particular, took advantage and boasted. God answers because the land and his people matter to him.

For today: when others mock your situation or write off your life, remember that God sees and hears. You can bring him your pain with confidence, because the last word belongs to him, not to the one who mocks.
exp.43:14:
God says that the Levitical priests, who are descended from Zadok, will be able to come close to Him to serve Him. They faithfully kept charge of the sanctuary when the people turned away from God. They will be able to stand before Him and offer the fat and the blood of the sacrifices. "Approach" means come close; "minister before Me" means serve Me in His presence.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the temple. Earlier, other Levites had gone after idols and were restricted to lesser tasks. The descendants of Zadok, on the other hand, were faithful, and God gives them the privilege of serving Him up close. How this vision is to be fulfilled is interpreted in several ways.

For today: God values faithfulness when everyone around us is turning aside. Be steadfast in what He has entrusted to you, even when no one notices; God does see it, and He honors those who are faithful to Him.
exp.10:22:
This verse says that the visible presence of God, his "glory," rose up from within the city of Jerusalem. It came to a stop over the mountain east of the city, which is usually identified with the Mount of Olives. The phrase "stood over" means it came to rest there.

Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon, sees this scene in a vision. Earlier he saw that Jerusalem had idolatry and wickedness, even in the temple. That is why God withdraws gradually. It is a very serious judgment, but also a sign that God is not bound to a building and would remain with the exiles.

For today: God desires a faithful heart, not merely outward religion. Today we can ask ourselves whether there is something we are putting in God's place, and return to him sincerely, trusting that he remains near those who repent.
exp.12:5:
This verse says that certain prophets saw false visions and spoke deceptive messages. Their visions were empty and worthless, and what they presented as a word from God was false. They claimed, "Thus declares the LORD," but God had not sent them. Even so, the people waited for their words to come true.

God speaks through Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He is rebuking the false prophets of Israel. They did not stand up for the people or call them back to God; instead they soothed them with false words. That is why God says He is against them.

Today we can learn to test what we hear against the Bible, even when it comes with phrases like "God told me." We should also take care that our own words do not claim God's authority for what He has not said.
exp.47:25:
Zebulun will have one portion bordering the territory of Issachar, running from east to west. The east is one end and the west is the other, and the boundary lines of the land run across the strip in the same direction. The strips lie side by side, one after another.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. In the final vision of the book, God shows how the land will be divided among the twelve tribes, with a clear order and with his presence at the center. Interpreters understand this in different ways: some as a promise of literal restoration, others as a symbolic picture of God's people restored.

For today: God does not forget anyone. Even a small tribe, mentioned in just one verse, has its assigned place. If you feel overlooked, remember that God knows you and has given you a place among his people.
exp.18:12:
It says that the vine, which once was strong and full of branches, is now planted in a wilderness, in a dry land without water. The phrase "a dry and thirsty land" describes hard soil with no moisture, where nothing grows well. It is a picture of loss and weakness.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who is among the exiles in Babylon. This chapter is a lament, a song of mourning over the kings of Judah. The vine is usually understood as Jerusalem or its royal line, uprooted and carried into exile. Scholars disagree about exactly which kings are meant, but the general sense is clear: pride and injustice brought their consequences.

For today: when you go through a dry season, do not ignore it. Humbly ask what God wants to teach you, and seek again the fountain of living water, which is Christ.
exp.0:25:
Ezekiel saw something like a throne above the expanse spread over the living beings. Its appearance was like sapphire, a bright blue stone. Seated on the throne, high above, was a figure with the appearance of a man. The word "firmament" means a solid expanse, like a sky or a vault. Notice that Ezekiel keeps using words like "appearance" and "likeness." He is trying to describe something that goes beyond words.

Ezekiel speaks in the first person. He was a priest who was among the exiles in Babylon. There, far from the temple, God revealed himself to him. Verse 28 calls this vision "the likeness of the glory of the LORD." God was not limited to Jerusalem; he also reigned in exile.

For today: when you feel that your life is disordered or far from what is familiar, remember that God is still on his throne. Before asking him to fix everything, you can pause, worship him, and trust that he governs.
exp.43:6:
This verse says that the people brought strangers into the sanctuary who were uncircumcised in both heart and flesh, and that they let them occupy God's sanctuary. The verse's word "defiled" means made unclean or profaned what was holy. The phrase "my food, the fat and the blood" refers to the offerings: the food of the sacrifice, the animal's fat, and the blood that was presented. "Broke my covenant" means they violated the agreement God had made with his people.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet in exile, to rebuke Israel. The priests had neglected the care of the temple and allowed people without commitment to God to serve in holy things. Interpreters explain the temple details in these chapters in different ways, but the rebuke is clear: a faithful heart was lacking.

For today: God looks for a surrendered heart, not merely religious appearances. We can ask ourselves whether our worship and our service come from sincere faith, and take care that what is holy is treated with reverence.
exp.42:8:
God says that Israel must remove far from him their prostitution, which here means idolatry and spiritual unfaithfulness, and also the funeral offerings for their kings. If they do this, he promises to dwell among them forever.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of the new temple. Earlier, the people and their kings had defiled his name with idols, and it seems they also had tombs or funeral monuments near the temple, separated by only a wall. Some understand the funeral offerings as lifeless idols; others understand them as royal tombs. It is uncertain which meaning predominates.

For today: God desires to be near us, but he asks for a heart with no rivals. We can ask ourselves what thing has taken God's place in our lives, and with his help remove it so that he may be the center.
exp.42:15:
This verse says that the top of the altar, where the offerings were burned, is square in shape. It measures twelve cubits long and twelve cubits wide, so all four corners are equal. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, about 45 to 50 centimeters. Because the verse describes a square with twelve cubits on each side, the altar's hearth had matching sides all the way around.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, receives in vision a new temple. God himself shows him the measurements and gives him the instructions for the altar. The people were in exile, and this vision gave them hope that God would once again dwell with them. Scholars disagree about whether it is a literal future temple or a symbolic image.

For today: God cares about order and reverence when we draw near to him. We can set aside fixed, attentive times for prayer and for his Word, without doing it in a hurried or careless way.
exp.24:12:
God says that he himself will punish Edom. "I will stretch out my hand" means that God will act with power to judge. The verse says he will cut off man and beast from the land and make it a wasteland, and that people from Teman to Dedan will fall by the sword. Teman and Dedan were known places, one within Edom and one nearby, and they are named to show that the judgment would reach the whole region, from one end to the other.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, at a time when Jerusalem had already been struck by Babylon. Edom, Israel's neighbor and distant relative, took advantage of Judah's fall and took revenge with cruelty. God responds to that attitude of resentment and lack of compassion.

Today, this text reminds us that we should not rejoice in the suffering of others or take advantage of someone who falls. If someone has wronged us, we can leave justice to God and ask him for a compassionate heart, instead of seeking revenge.
exp.38:26:
This verse says that God will bring his people back from the nations where they were scattered. He will gather them out of the lands of their enemies. The phrase "bring them back" is the core idea here, and "show My holiness" means that God will make clear that he is holy, that is, unique and worthy of respect. This will happen in the sight of many nations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel had been taken into exile because of its rebellion, and the nations could think that God was weak. By restoring his people, God shows that he is faithful and that he cares for the honor of his name. The context says that Israel would acknowledge its shame and that God would pour out his Spirit. Some believers see the fulfillment in the return from exile, others in the future, and others in both.

For today: even if you have failed or feel far from God, he can restore you. Trust in his mercy and let your life show his goodness.
exp.17:5:
This verse describes a righteous man by what he avoids. He does not eat at the mountain, that is, he does not take part in pagan worship meals held on the high places. He does not look to the idols of Israel, meaning he does not give them his trust or his worship. He does not defile his neighbor's wife, and he does not approach a woman during her period, something the law of Moses forbade.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their fathers. God answers that each person answers for himself, and he shows what a righteous life looks like: faithful to God and respectful toward others.

For today: examine where you place your trust and your worship. Ask God to be first in your life, and guard your faithfulness in your relationships.
exp.2:4:
God tells Ezekiel that he is not being sent to a people whose speech is unfamiliar or whose language is difficult, but to the house of Israel, his own people. The phrase "unfamiliar speech or difficult language" refers to a foreign tongue, with sounds that are hard for the listener to understand.

God is speaking to Ezekiel, who has just been given a scroll to eat, a sign of receiving God's word deep within himself. Ezekiel was a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. God warns him that the difficulty will not be the language, but the stubbornness of Israel's heart. Foreigners, he says, would have listened better.

For today: sometimes we think the obstacle to sharing our faith is not knowing what to say. But often the real challenge is the attitude of the heart. Speak clearly and with love to your own people, and leave the results in God's hands.
exp.17:27:
This verse says that the person who recognizes his wrongdoing, turns away from all the transgressions he has committed and changes his course will not be condemned, but will live. Now, "considered" means that he thought it over and came to see clearly what he had done. "Transgressions" are rebellions or serious offenses against God. "Turned from" means that he deliberately stepped away from them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. They were saying that God was unfair, since they were suffering for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person is responsible for himself and that He always offers a way back to Him. Some understand "live" to refer to life on earth, others also to life with God.

For today: no matter what you have done, God invites you to stop, recognize your error and return to Him. Today you can speak with God sincerely and take a concrete step of change.
exp.16:4:
It says that the eagle also took some of the seed of the land and planted it in fertile soil. It placed it beside abundant waters and set it out like a willow. The verse's phrase "some of the seed of the land," meaning a seed from that place, and the words "planted it," both refer to the same act described in the verse above.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is in exile in Babylon. This is a parable or allegory. Later in the same chapter it explains that the first eagle represents the king of Babylon, and that the top of the cedar is the king of Judah, taken captive. The seed that was planted would be a descendant of the royal family, placed under Babylonian control. God wants to show that Judah rebelled and sought help from Egypt.

For today: even when a situation seems good and secure, we should not trust human powers more than God. Seek your security in Him and keep your promises faithfully.
exp.19:27:
God says that he brought them into the land he had promised them with an oath, "lifting up his hand." But as soon as they arrived, they looked for any high hill or leafy tree to worship there. The sacrifices they offered were animals killed on the altar, the drink offerings were liquids poured out as an offering, and the fragrant offering was the incense or smell of their sacrifices. They offered all of it to other gods.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the leaders of Israel during the exile in Babylon. He reviews their history to show that the rebellion was not new: their ancestors were already doing the same thing. With this he asks them whether they are going to follow the same path.

For today: God gives us good gifts, and it is easy to use them to worship other things. Today, ask the Lord which thing is occupying the place that belongs only to him, and surrender it to him.
exp.35:33:
This verse says that the land that was laid waste and abandoned will be worked again and planted. "Desolate" describes land left in ruins, emptied and destroyed. "Cultivated" means prepared and worked so it can grow crops. What once was looked upon with pity by everyone who passed through will now be seen full of life and fruit.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites, who had suffered exile and the ruin of their land because of their sin. God makes clear that he will restore his people not because they deserve it, but for the sake of his holy name. First he promises to cleanse them from their wickedness, and then to rebuild cities and fields.

For today: if there are areas of your life that look like ruins, they are not lost to God. Come to him with sincerity, ask for his forgiveness, and get to work with hope, trusting that he can make life grow where there was destruction.
exp.26:2:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to Tyre, a city on the coast that sits at the gateway to the sea and trades with the peoples of many distant coasts. The verse calls her a merchant, which means a trader. The word translated here as "lament" refers to songs of mourning. Tyre had described herself as "perfect in beauty," meaning she thought of herself as completely beautiful and without flaw.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was in exile in Babylon with Israel. Tyre was a rich and proud port. God announces a lament over her, for her confidence in her beauty and wealth would lead her to fall. The passage that follows compares her to a great ship that was very well built.

For today: the good things we have, such as talent, success, or money, can make us believe we do not need God. We can be thankful for what we have, but place our security in Him and not in our achievements.
exp.10:9:
You will fall by the sword. God will judge you even to the borders of Israel. "The sword" means the blade itself, or war. "Then you will know that I am the LORD" means that through the punishment they will recognize that God is real and that he means what he says.

God speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. He addresses the leaders of Jerusalem who gave unjust counsel and felt secure, like meat inside a protected pot. God reminds them that they feared war, yet they lived far from his laws and copied the customs of the neighboring peoples. Some scholars see a fulfillment here in what happened near Riblah, although this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: do not settle into false security. Examine whether your life follows the Word of God or only what most people do.
exp.26:31:
This verse says that those who watch the fall of Tyre will compose sad songs, the kind of lament sung over someone who has died. As they weep, they will ask, "Who was ever like Tyre, silenced in the middle of the sea?" In other words, no other city could be compared with her. They speak of her as silenced in the middle of the sea, because part of the city of Tyre stood on an island.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a very wealthy trading power, and the chapter presents her as a great ship that sinks. The sailors and merchants, who had grown rich through her, mourn her ruin. God judges her for her pride, although the lament shows how much others depended on her wealth.

For today: riches and success are not a secure foundation. It is wise to trust in God and not in what can be lost in a single day.
exp.39:45:
This verse says that the room facing north was set aside for the priests who keep charge of the altar. They were descendants of Zadok, and they were the only Levites who could approach the Lord to serve before him. A "chamber" is simply a room, and those who "keep charge" are the ones entrusted with caring for and watching over the altar.

This is part of the vision given to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile when he was taken in a vision to a new temple. A guide walks him through it and measures each part. Here the order and holiness of the place are shown: each group had its own space and its own task. Scholars disagree about whether this temple would be built literally or whether it is symbolic.

For today: God values service done with order, reverence, and faithfulness. Whatever your task in your church or family, do it with care, as one who serves the Lord.
exp.20:23:
It says that God, the Lord, speaks to Jerusalem. The people have drawn attention to their guilt, and their transgressions have been exposed, so that their sins show up in everything they do. Because of this, they will be taken in hand, meaning they will be seized by force.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The king of Babylon uses divination to decide whether to attack Jerusalem, and the people do not believe it, because they trust in their alliances. But God uses that attack to judge the people's wickedness. The verses that follow announce that the king of Israel will lose his crown.

For today: we cannot hide sin as if God did not see it. It is better to acknowledge it sincerely and ask Him for forgiveness before it brings harsher consequences. God is just, but He also forgives those who turn back to Him.
exp.15:10:
It says that God adorned the woman of the story with jewelry: he put bracelets on her wrists and a chain around her neck.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an abandoned girl, whom he took in, cared for, and enriched. She represents Jerusalem and the people of Israel. God reminds them of how much he gave them, because later they forgot his kindness and were unfaithful to him. This image is a comparison, not a literal story.

For today: Everything good we have comes from God's grace, not from our own merit. Today you can pause and thank him for three concrete blessings, so that the heart does not become proud or forgetful.
exp.19:26:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to speak to the people of Israel. The message is that their ancestors blasphemed him, that is, they were unfaithful to him and rebelled against him. The phrase "in this way also" points to one more way of failing God, beyond what has already been said: they did not stay faithful to him.

Here God himself speaks, through Ezekiel, to the exiles in Babylon. He reviews their history to show them that their unfaithfulness goes back a long way. The verses just before this one are difficult: they speak of statutes that were not good and of sacrificing children. They are interpreted in several ways; many understand that God gave them over to the consequences of their own idolatry.

For today: let us not minimize our faults or excuse them by pointing to what others did. Let us humbly acknowledge where we have turned away from God and return to him, who is always ready to forgive.
exp.6:26:
This verse says that sorrow will reach everyone: the king will mourn, the prince will be wrapped in despair, and the people of the land will tremble with fear, their hands left without strength. It says the people will be shaken, filled with terror. God will deal with them according to their conduct, and will judge them by their own standards. In the end, they will know that he is the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem for its idolatry and injustice. The verses before this one show that no one will find help: neither prophet, nor priest, nor elders. Here the blow falls on the leaders and on the common people alike.

For today: do not wait for a crisis to seek God. Listen to his Word now, correct your course, and live with honesty, because God takes seriously what we do.
exp.17:13:
Ezekiel 18:14 describes a man who is violent and sinful and has a son. That son sees all the sins his father has committed. The verse notes that the verse's phrase "does not do likewise" means that although he sees his father's sins and considers them, he does not copy them. This begins a third case: the son who decides to live differently.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel in Babylon. They were saying, "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge," as if they were suffering only for the sins of their ancestors. God answers that each person is responsible for his or her own life. The son is not condemned for the wickedness of his father if he does not follow it.

For today: your family past does not decide your future. If you grew up seeing bad examples, with God's help you can break that cycle and choose a different path, one of justice and mercy.
exp.36:1:
He says that God led Ezekiel all around among the bones, walking him through the valley. There were a great many of them, lying on the ground across the valley floor. And they were very dry: they had been there so long that no trace of life remained.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting a vision God gave him. Later in this same chapter, God explains that the bones represent Israel, which lived in exile and felt that its hope had run out. God first shows him the worst of the situation before he acts.

For today: God is not alarmed by situations that seem hopeless to us. You can honestly bring to him whatever you feel is dry or beyond repair, and trust that he knows what he is able to do, as Ezekiel answered: "you know."
exp.38:18:
God invites the birds and the wild animals to a great feast. He says they will eat fat until they are gorged and drink blood until they are drunk. This feast is called "the sacrifice I am preparing," but what is offered is the bodies of the fallen enemies. "Fat" refers to the richest part of the animal.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. This follows the defeat of Gog, a powerful enemy who attacks Israel on the mountains of Israel (chapters 38 and 39). The image is very strong and symbolic: it shows that God judges evil and protects his people. Interpreters disagree about whether it will be fulfilled literally or symbolically. Revelation 19:17-18 uses a similar image.

For today: we can rest in the fact that God is just and has the final word over evil. When we see violence or injustice, let us trust in him, pray, and seek peace, without taking revenge.
exp.45:16:
This verse says that if the prince gives part of his land to one of his servants, that gift belongs to that servant only until the "year of freedom," and then it returns to the prince. But what the prince gives to his sons remains theirs as an inheritance.

God speaks through Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple and of the life of the restored people. Many understand the "year of freedom" to refer to the Jubilee year, according to the law in Leviticus 25, although some interpret it in other ways. The rule aims to protect the people's lands from being taken away by the prince.

For today: God cares about justice and does not want those who have power to abuse what belongs to others. If you have any authority, in your home, work, or church, use it with honesty and respect what belongs to other people.
exp.35:9:
God promises that the people of Israel will grow in number again, and that it will be the whole house of Israel, not just a part of it. The empty cities will once again have people living in them, and the ruins will be rebuilt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He speaks to the mountains of Israel, which had been left desolate and mocked by the neighboring nations. God announces that he will restore the land and his people. Some see here a fulfillment in the return from exile, and others also see it pointing to a future and more complete restoration.

For today: if there are areas of your life that seem to be in ruins, remember that God knows how to rebuild. Trust in him and take small steps of obedience while he works.
exp.15:15:
It says that Jerusalem took some of the fine clothing God had given her and used it to decorate shrines on high places, where she gave herself to other gods. "Prostituted yourself" here speaks of spiritual unfaithfulness. "High places" were sites of pagan worship. The final sentence says that such things should not have happened and never should have occurred: it describes an extreme case of betrayal.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He describes Jerusalem as a wife whom he rescued, clothed, and honored, but who used those gifts to give herself to other gods. It is a powerful image, deliberately harsh, to show God's grief over the unfaithfulness of his people.

For today: everything good we have, talents, possessions, and opportunities, comes from God. Let us ask ourselves whether we use them to honor him or to serve other things that take his place.
exp.14:5:
God says that Jerusalem will be like a branch of a vine that has already been thrown into the fire. The people who live there are the inhabitants, and their unfaithfulness is their betrayal of God. Just as that wood burns, God will hand the people of Jerusalem over to judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. In the Bible, the vine often represents Israel. But here the wood of the vine is not useful for building anything; it has value only for its fruit. Because the people were not faithful, they became worthless for God's purpose. Scholars understand in different ways how this connects with the fall of Jerusalem, but the general meaning is clear.

For today: our life bears fruit only when we remain united with God. Jesus said, "Apart from me you can do nothing." Let us ask him for faithfulness and a sincere heart.
exp.41:15:
He says that the man who was guiding Ezekiel measured the east side of the temple grounds with a measuring rod. It came to five hundred cubits, and the same is repeated for the other sides. A "cubit" is an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the fingertips.

Ezekiel recounts a vision God gave him, in which a guide carefully measures the temple and its grounds. It was a message for the people in exile. The space formed a large square, and the wall separated the holy from the common. Scholars disagree about whether it describes a literal future temple or a spiritual picture of God's presence.

For today: God is a God of order and holiness, and He cares how we draw near to Him. Set aside a defined time today to pray and read His Word, and take care that what is holy does not get mixed up with the rush of everyday life.
exp.12:20:
God says he will tear away your veils, the coverings those women used in their divination practices. He promises to rescue his people from their hands, so that they will no longer be prey to them, like animals caught in a hunt. In the end, everyone will know that he is the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He was speaking against false prophetesses who deceived the people with lies and magic in exchange for barley and bread. Scholars are not sure exactly what those objects were like, but the meaning is clear: they used deception to dominate people.

For today: God cares for those who are manipulated by false voices. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and if someone has deceived you, remember that God can set you free and give you the truth.
exp.13:13:
God says that even if three very righteous men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in a sinful land, their righteousness could save only themselves. Saying their righteousness could deliver only themselves means that they alone would be saved. Their faithfulness to God would protect them, but it would not protect anyone else.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Judah. Some believed that Jerusalem would be saved because of the good people within it. God answers that the people's sin was so grave that neither the prayers nor the righteousness of others would rescue them. The three men were well-known examples of faith. About Daniel, some scholars think of the Daniel of the exile and others of an ancient figure; this is not entirely certain.

For today: faith is not inherited or lent. We can pray for others, but each person must respond to God. Seek out a sincere relationship with Him yourself.
exp.12:11:
It says that when the wall falls, people will mock those who covered it with whitewash and ask them: "Where is the whitewash with which you covered it?" The whitewash is the thin layer put over the wall to make it look sound, and covering it means applying that layer. It was a show of appearance, with no strength.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The false prophets said "peace" when there was no peace, and they encouraged the people with pleasant messages. They were like someone who builds a weak wall and only covers it with paint. God announces that his judgment, like a storm, would expose the falsehood.

For today: let us not build our lives, our families, or our faith on appearances or on words that only sound good. Let us seek God's truth, even when it corrects us, because only it can stand the storms.
exp.35:36:
God, the Lord, says that he will allow Israel to seek him so that he can do one more thing: make his people grow in number, like a flock. "Hear the plea" means God will listen when they come to him and ask. "I will multiply their people" says the same thing in plain terms. "People like a flock" is an image: very many people gathered together, like sheep.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The people were living in exile, and their land lay in ruins. God had just promised to restore cities and fields. Here he adds that he will also restore the people, and he will do it in response to his people coming to him in prayer.

For today: God promises, but he also invites us to ask him. Even when something in your life, your family, or your church seems ruined, you can pray with confidence and wait for God to restore it. Today, take a few minutes to ask him for something that needs to be lifted up.
exp.22:41:
It says that in Jerusalem (Aholibah) there was the sound of a carefree crowd. Drunkards were brought in from the desert along with men from the rabble, who put bracelets on her wrists and beautiful crowns on her head.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of two sisters, Aholah (Samaria) and Aholibah (Jerusalem), to show how his people allied themselves with foreign nations and their gods, leaving behind faithfulness to him.

For today: what adorns us on the outside does not replace loyalty to God. Ask yourself what things you seek to feel valuable or secure, and put God first again.
exp.13:20:
God says he will send four severe judgments against Jerusalem: the sword (war), famine, wild beasts, and plague. "Cut off" means to destroy, and "judgments" are punishments. Earlier, God spoke of judgment on a land, but now the question is how much worse it will be when he sends all four against Jerusalem together.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. The people believed Jerusalem would not fall, and some thought the righteousness of a few would save it. God answers that the wickedness was great and the punishment was not without cause. Even so, he shows that a remnant would remain.

For today: we cannot rely on the faith of others or on our religious activity. Each person needs to turn to God sincerely and trust in his mercy, which is also shown in the remnant.
exp.10:7:
God says to the leaders of Jerusalem: "You fear the sword, so I will bring the sword against you." The word for the weapon here means the sword, that is, war.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The city's leaders believed they were safe, like meat inside a pot, but they had filled the streets with the dead because of their injustice and violence. God answers that he will not protect them in their sin, but will judge them. Some scholars see here the siege of Jerusalem by Babylon; the text gives no further details.

Today we can learn that there is no true security in our own plans or in our own power. If we live with injustice, our fears can become reality. It is better to turn back to God with humility, seek his justice, and trust in his care.
exp.15:23:
It says that Jerusalem, pictured as an unfaithful woman, built herself a mound and made a lofty shrine in every public square. A "mound" refers to a raised place for worship, and here it speaks of shrines of idolatry. The verse uses the image of building for herself, and "public square" means the open places of the city where people gathered.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of a girl rescued and cared for by Him, who then gives herself to other lovers. With this He shows that Judah abandoned God and sought idols and alliances with other nations. The tone is one of grief and judgment, not only of anger.

For today: we can ask ourselves what things we have placed in the place of God, such as money, fame, or approval. Remembering how He has cared for us helps us return to Him with humility and gratitude.
exp.11:9:
God tells Ezekiel to deliver a message: what he has just acted out is a "burden," meaning a heavy word of judgment. That burden concerns the prince in Jerusalem (the king, Zedekiah, as is commonly understood) and all the house of Israel who are there with him.

The Lord speaks through Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. The prophet had shown with actions, such as carrying his baggage, that Jerusalem would be taken into captivity. The people, called a rebellious house, asked with curiosity or mockery, "What are you doing?" God answers by explaining that the sign was a real warning.

For today: God does not leave his people without warning. When one of his words makes us uncomfortable, instead of mocking it or ignoring it, we can stop, sincerely ask what he wants to teach us, and correct our course in time.
exp.3:6:
Here God tells Ezekiel to turn his face toward Jerusalem, which is pictured as a city under siege, and to bare his arm, ready to act. In this way he is to prophesy against the city. The phrase "turn your face" means keeping a steady and determined gaze.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a priest and prophet who was living in exile in Babylon. He commands him to act out, lying down and bound with cords, the siege of Jerusalem and the weight of its sin. It was a way of teaching that judgment was coming because of the people's rebellion. Some understand that the days stand for years of punishment, but scholars interpret this in several ways.

For today: God asks us to be faithful and steadfast when we speak the truth, even when it costs us. Let us speak with love and humility, without cowardice, and with our eyes fixed on Him.
exp.36:26:
He says that God will set his dwelling place in the midst of his people. The "dwelling place" is the tent or home where God lives among the Israelites. The phrase "I will be their God" appears here, and "they will be My people" expresses the same promise from the other side. It is a promise of closeness and mutual belonging.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. They had just lost their land and their temple, and they felt hopeless. Shortly before, God showed him the valley of dry bones that came back to life. Here he promises restoration, peace, and his lasting presence. Some understand this as the future of Israel; many Christians see it fulfilled also in Christ and in the church.

For today: even when you feel far away or defeated, God desires to be with you. Seek him every day in prayer, knowing that you belong to him.
exp.19:38:
God tells the people of Israel: "Go and serve your idols, every one of you." Yet God makes clear that this is not his final word, since afterward they will listen to him. He asks them not to dishonor his holy name any longer by mixing their gifts with that idolatry. The words "go" and "serve" in the verse mean exactly what they say, and "defile" means to dishonor or treat as something common.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the leaders of the people, who were in exile. Many wanted to worship God and at the same time keep other gods. Many read these words as a severe irony: God rejects divided faith. Then he promises to purify the people and restore them, so that they may truly serve him on his holy mountain.

For today: God is not satisfied with a half-hearted faith. Examine whether something in your life occupies the place that belongs to him, and give it up to him with sincerity.
exp.39:2:
He took me there, and I saw a man whose appearance was like bronze. He was standing in the gateway with a linen cord and a measuring rod in his hand. "Man" means a male person, "appearance" is how he looked, and the "measuring rod" was a tool used for taking measurements.

Ezekiel wrote this in the twenty-fifth year of his captivity, while already in exile, about fourteen years after the fall of Jerusalem. God carries him in vision to the land of Israel and to a very high mountain. This guide will show him a temple and ask him to tell everything to Israel. Scholars disagree about whether that temple is literal, symbolic, or future.

For today: even when everything seems destroyed, God still has a plan and ordered measurements for restoration. We can trust Him and pay attention to what He shows us in His Word.
exp.47:11:
It says that the priests descended from Zadok would receive as their inheritance a special portion of land, set apart from the rest of the territory.
