It calls this portion a most holy portion, meaning the most sacred, and it would lie next to the territory of the Levites. The word "portion" means a share or inheritance, and "territory" means the land or area assigned to a group.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision about the restoration of Israel. He divides the land and places the sanctuary at the center. The priests of Zadok are rewarded because they remained faithful when others turned aside. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: some see it as literal and future, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people.

For today: God notices and honors faithfulness, even when many around us turn aside. We can ask him for help to stay firm in the small things of each day, trusting that he sees and cares for his own.
exp.26:12:
This verse says that Greece (in Hebrew, Javan), Tubal, and Meshech were merchants who traded with Tyre. They exchanged enslaved people and bronze utensils for the goods Tyre offered in its markets. The "utensils" were containers, not only cups.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a city very rich because of its sea trade. The chapter lists its trading partners to show its fame and its pride. Then comes the announcement of its fall. Here the trade in people is also mentioned, something the Bible does not approve as an ideal, but presents as part of an arrogant economy.

For today: check where your earnings and your purchases come from. Prospering is not wrong, but God calls us to work with justice, without taking advantage of others or trusting in money more than in Him.
exp.42:12:
These are the measurements of the altar in long cubits, meaning a cubit and a handbreadth, which is a little more than the ordinary measure. Its gutter is to be a cubit deep and a cubit wide, with a rim of one span around its edge. The gutter is the channel at the base, and the rim is the raised edge around the top of it. This base and rim together form the altar's lower part, and the verse ends by saying this is the height of the altar.

God speaks to Ezekiel while the people are in exile in Babylon. He shows him a new temple with exact measurements so that the people will feel shame for their sin and learn to live with order and reverence. Interpreters differ: some see a literal temple still to come, while others read it as a symbolic picture of God's presence.

For today: God cares about the details of how he is worshiped. Come near to him with respect and sincerity, and never lightly.
exp.31:8:
This verse says that God will trouble the hearts of many peoples when news of Egypt's fall spreads. "Destruction" means ruin or collapse. The nations are the peoples of the earth, and the countries you do not know are lands far from Egypt. Even those distant places would hear of its downfall.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over the Pharaoh of Egypt. Egypt considered itself powerful and secure, but God announces that Babylon would come against it. The images of darkened skies show how serious the judgment is. Scholars understand this language as poetic, not necessarily literal.

For today: no human strength, wealth, or fame is so secure that it can set God aside. Today we can examine what we truly trust in, and draw near with humility to the One who sustains all things.
exp.12:1:
God says to Ezekiel, "Son of man," a way of addressing him as an ordinary human being, and tells him to speak against the prophets of Israel who are now prophesying. These prophets spoke out of their own imagination, that is, from their own ideas rather than from what God was saying. Even so, God commands them: "Hear the word of the LORD!" They too were to listen. The word "Hear" means "listen."

The LORD is speaking, and his messenger is Ezekiel, who prophesied during the exile in Babylon. God confronts those who announced comfortable and false messages, claiming they came from him. The verses that follow call them "foolish" because they followed their own spirit and "saw nothing."

For today: before we repeat or teach something as "the word of God," let us compare it with the Bible. And when we speak of God, let us do so with humility, without confusing our opinions with his voice.
exp.8:9:
God says that he will show no pity and will not spare them. "I will not look on them with pity" means that he will not regard them with leniency. "I will bring their deeds down upon their own heads" means that he will repay them with the consequences of their own actions.

God speaks in a vision received by the prophet Ezekiel. Jerusalem was full of violence and injustice, and the people thought that God saw nothing. Ezekiel intercedes and asks whether God will destroy all the remnant of Israel. God answers that the wickedness is very great. Then the man clothed in linen reports that he has carried out the command, which in this chapter includes marking those who grieved over the sin.

Today we can remember that God does see, even though at times he may seem silent. This invites us to live with honesty, to reject injustice, and to seek his forgiveness with humility, without taking his patience for granted.
exp.46:7:
This verse says that the water flowing from the temple runs toward the east, goes down into the Arabah, the low plain of the Jordan Valley, and empties into the Dead Sea. When it enters there, the water that was salty and lifeless becomes fresh. Here "fresh" means the water becomes clean and able to support life.

The one speaking is a heavenly guide who shows Ezekiel this vision. The prophet was living in exile, and his people were discouraged. The vision promises that God will dwell with them again and that his presence will bring life. Some understand it symbolically, others as something yet to come; the text does not fully settle the question.

For today: where God acts, he can bring life even to what seems dead. We can bring Him our dry places, such as a broken relationship or deep weariness, and trust that his grace keeps renewing us little by little.
exp.46:8:
It says that wherever the river flows, there will be swarms of living creatures and a great number of fish, because the river flows there and makes the waters fresh. Wherever it flows, everything will flourish.

Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon, receives a vision of the restored temple. An angel guides him and shows him a river flowing out from the temple and down toward the Dead Sea, whose salty waters are made healthy. Scholars understand this in several ways: as a promise of restoration for Israel, as a spiritual picture of the life God gives, or as a foretaste of a future renewal.

Today we can remember that where God acts, there is new life. Ask him to heal the dry places of your heart and of your surroundings.
exp.36:27:
This verse says that the nations will recognize that the Lord is the one who sets Israel apart as his own people, because his sanctuary, the place where God dwells among them, will be among them forever. The word "sanctify" in the verse means setting apart as holy, belonging to God. The nations are the other peoples around Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier, in the vision of the dry bones, God promised to restore his people and unite them under one king. Here he promises a lasting covenant of peace and his permanent presence. Christians often see this fulfilled in Christ and in the Church, though others understand it as a promise still future for Israel. There are different interpretations.

For today: God not only forgives us, he also wants to live close to us. We can set aside a few minutes each day to pray, remembering that his presence goes with us and that the way we live can show others who he is.
exp.31:24:
Among the slain they prepare a resting place for Elam with all her hordes, with her graves all around her. Their graves surround them, and all of them lie uncircumcised, slain by the sword. Their terror once spread through the land of the living, but now they bear their disgrace with those who go down to the Pit. They are placed among the slain.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Egypt, which runs through the chapter. Many understand the "bed" to be for the pharaoh and his multitude. He announces to them that, like other violent nations, they will end up defeated. The language is poetic, not a literal description of the afterlife.

For today: power used to intimidate others does not last. It is worth more to live with humility and justice, because God sees how we treat people.
exp.13:4:
It says that God will answer those who come to him with idols in their hearts, so that he may reach the hearts of the people of Israel. Reaching them in their hearts means getting to the very core of who they are. God says that all of them have turned away from him because of their idols, and he wants to wake them up.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Some leaders of the people came to seek him out, but they kept idols within themselves. God does not answer them with a comfortable piece of advice, but with a call to return to him. Scholars agree that this is about inward idolatry, though not everyone agrees on how much outward idolatry was also involved.

For today: before asking God for direction, ask yourself what thing is occupying the place that belongs only to him, and surrender it to him sincerely.
exp.42:11:
This verse says that the "law of the temple," meaning the main rule for the temple, is that the whole area on top of the mountain, all around its edge, is to be "most holy," that is, completely set apart for God. "Surrounding territory" here means the land and boundary that lie around the temple. The verse repeats the phrase "the law of the temple" to give more weight to what it says.

God speaks to Ezekiel during Israel's exile in Babylon. He tells him to show the people the vision of the temple so that they will be ashamed of their sins and understand what a life close to God should look like. How this vision will be fulfilled is interpreted in different ways: some see it as a future temple, others as a spiritual picture.

For today: God wants holiness to cover everything, not just certain moments. Today we can ask ourselves which areas of our lives we still keep far from Him, and hand them over to Him with humility.
exp.20:26:
God says he will bring the kingdom of Judah to ruin. "A ruin, a ruin, I will make it a ruin!" repeats the word three times to stress that everything will be torn down. "It" refers to the crown or the kingdom. That power will not be restored until the one to whom it truly belongs arrives, the one who holds the right of judgment. God says he will give it to him.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and addresses King Zedekiah, whom he calls the wicked prince. Babylon was about to conquer Jerusalem. Many Christians see in "the one to whom it belongs" a promise of the Messiah, Jesus, a descendant of David. Others explain it more broadly, but the underlying idea is the same.

For today: no human power lasts forever. We can entrust our future to Christ, the rightful King, and live with humility.
exp.15:27:
It says that Jerusalem, compared to an unfaithful wife, went after the Assyrians, and she did so because she was still not satisfied. Here "prostituted yourself" means being unfaithful, above all turning to other gods or allies in place of God. To be "not yet satisfied" means still wanting more and not being content. Even after doing this, she still was not satisfied.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Judah, who were living in exile or near it. He uses a strong image to show how Jerusalem turned away from Him and trusted in alliances with powerful nations and in its idols. God wants the people to see how serious their unfaithfulness is, and in the same book He also promises restoration.

For today: when we look for money, success, or the approval of others to fill the emptiness of the heart, they never satisfy. We can return to God and ask Him to be our true satisfaction.
exp.45:5:
On the new moon, the first day of each month, the prince was to offer to God a young bull from the herd, six lambs, and a ram. The Berean wording says he was to bring a young, unblemished bull, six lambs, and a ram without blemish. Every animal had to be healthy and free of any flaw.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who describes a vision of a temple and of a renewed worship. In it, rules are given for the prince, who would lead the people in worship. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: some read it as literal, others as symbolic, and there is no complete agreement.

For today: God deserves our best, not what is left over. We can give Him the first of our time, affection, and resources, with a sincere heart.
exp.3:9:
God tells Ezekiel that his daily food will be small and measured: twenty shekels by weight, which comes to roughly 230 grams, and he is to eat it at set times.

God speaks to Ezekiel, his prophet, so that he will represent the siege of Jerusalem with his own body. This rationing showed the scarcity that would come upon the people because of their rebellion. Scholars debate some details of this symbolic action, but the central message is clear: there would be hunger and distress.

For today: learn to receive what God gives you with humility and to live with moderation. If you go through scarcity today, remember that God sees you and that obeying him is always better than ignoring his voice.
exp.7:13:
In the vision, the Lord brought Ezekiel to the entrance of the north gate of the temple in Jerusalem. There he saw women sitting and weeping for Tammuz. The word "north" simply names the direction of that gate. Tammuz was a god worshiped in the religions of Mesopotamia, and many scholars connect him with rites of mourning over his death, though the details remain debated.

God speaks to Ezekiel while the people are living in sin, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. The leaders were saying that God did not see them, but He shows them that He sees everything. This is the third of several abominations: worship of idols inside His own house.

For today: honestly examine what things occupy in your heart the place that belongs to God. God sees what is hidden, and His gaze is an invitation to return to Him with confidence.
exp.17:28:
The people of Israel kept saying, "The way of the Lord is not just." God answers with a question: are my ways unjust? He then turns the question back on them and concludes that the unjust ways are theirs. Here "just" means fair and upright.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their ancestors and that God was not being fair. God makes it clear to them that each person answers for himself, and that the one who turns away from evil will live. His desire is that they turn back to him.

When things go wrong, it is easy to blame God or others. This verse invites us to look honestly at our own way, to recognize what we need to change, and to return to God, who always offers forgiveness and a new heart.
exp.25:4:
It says that Tyre, the great trading city by the sea, will become a place where fishermen spread their nets to dry. A "place to spread nets" is a place where fishing nets are laid out. "In the sea" means the sea itself. God adds that the city will be plundered by many nations, and stresses that he has spoken it.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich and proud city, and this chapter announces its fall, partly for rejoicing at the ruin of Jerusalem. The following verses name Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon as the one who would come against it. As for how the detail about the nets was fulfilled, scholars understand it in several ways.

For today: riches and success are not a secure foundation. Trust God more than your achievements, and avoid rejoicing when others fall.
exp.30:15:
The passage says that the fall of this great tree made the nations quake when God brought it down to Sheol, the place of the dead, along with those who go down to the Pit. The Pit and the grave both refer to the tomb or the place of the dead, and "the earth below" is the world of the dead. The other trees of Eden, the choicest and best of Lebanon, and all the well-watered trees were consoled down there when they saw that the mighty one had fallen too.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He compares Pharaoh and Egypt to a huge, proud cedar, as a warning to Egypt, which believed itself invincible. The trees represent nations and rulers. Scholars understand the part about consolation in different ways, but the central idea is that no human power escapes God's judgment.

For today: pride and power do not protect us. We can live with humility, remembering that everything we have comes from God and that He is the one who exalts or humbles.
exp.13:14:
He says that God could send wild and dangerous animals through a sinful land. They would leave it so ruined and empty that no one would dare to cross it for fear of those beasts. The word for "ruined" means to lay waste or leave in ruins. The word for "desolate" means empty, without people. The phrase "for fear of the beasts" means that the beasts are the cause.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in exile, to a people who thought they were safe. God lists four judgments: famine, beasts, sword, and plague. With them he warns that a rebellious land is not saved by the merits of others, not even by righteous men such as Noah, Daniel, and Job. Each person answers before God.

For today: do not live on the faith of your parents or your church. Seek God yourself, with humility and repentance, because his mercy also invites you to return to him.
exp.34:7:
It says that God will fill the mountains of Seir, that is, of Edom, with the dead. The phrase "I will fill its mountains with the slain" pictures the whole land covered with the bodies of those who died. The people who are killed by the sword will fall on the hills, in the valleys, and in all the ravines. The picture is of total defeat across the whole territory.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom, a descendant of Esau, had long shown hatred toward Israel, and according to this chapter it rejoiced when Israel fell and wanted to take its land for itself. That is why God announces a judgment that matches that violence: "blood shall pursue you."

For today: resentment that is held onto can grow until it destroys us. Ask God to heal any bitterness you carry, and when someone falls, do not rejoice; help them. God sees injustice, and he is the one who judges with justice.
exp.10:14:
God tells Ezekiel that his brothers, the people exiled along with him, and the whole house of Israel are the ones of whom the people of Jerusalem have said, "They are far away from the LORD; this land has been given to us as a possession." "Your relatives" means his family and his people, and "the LORD" is the name of God.

Ezekiel is among the exiles in Babylon. He has just seen Pelatiah die while he was prophesying, and he cries out in distress, fearing that God will finish off the rest of Israel. God answers him. Those who remained in Jerusalem looked down on the exiles, thinking they were far from God and that the land now belonged only to them. God corrects that idea with a promise of care.

We may think that God is far from someone who suffers or has failed, but He promises to be present in the midst of pain. Today, instead of judging others by their trials, let us remember that God remains near to those who seek Him.
exp.11:7:
This verse says that the next morning, God spoke to Ezekiel again. "And in the morning the word of the LORD came to me" means that God's message came to him. The phrase "in the morning" marks that the night had already passed in which the prophet went out carrying his belongings on his shoulder.

God speaks, and He speaks to Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God had asked him to represent with his own body the flight from Jerusalem, as a sign before a rebellious people. Now God is going to explain the meaning of what he did, since the people were asking him what he was doing.

For today: God does not leave His actions unexplained. If we do not understand something He asks of us, we can come to His Word with patience and listen. Often the light comes "in the morning," after we have obeyed in the dark.
exp.1:2:
God says to Ezekiel: "Son of man," meaning simply a human being, and sends him to the Israelites. He calls them "a rebellious nation," because they had turned away from God. That rebellion has passed down from their ancestors and has continued to this very day.

God speaks, and Ezekiel listens after the Spirit has set him on his feet. Ezekiel was a priest and was among the exiles in Babylon. God calls him as a prophet and warns him from the start that the people may not pay attention to him. His task is to speak faithfully.

For today: God asks us to be faithful in speaking his truth with love, even when others do not receive it. Our calling does not depend on the results. We can also ask ourselves whether, in some area of our lives, we are resisting God, and return to him with humility.
exp.38:22:
This verse says that the nations will understand why Israel was taken away as prisoners: not because God was weak, but because of the people's sin. They were unfaithful to God, and so he hid his face from them, meaning he withdrew his protection and his closeness. He handed them over to their enemies, and they all fell by the sword.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Before promising Israel's restoration, he makes clear the reason for the punishment. In this way the nations will see that God is holy and just. The following verse announces that he will have mercy and bring his people back.

For today: God corrects with justice, but not in order to destroy us; he does it to bring us back to himself. If you recognize a sin, do not hide; return to God with sincerity, trusting in his mercy.
exp.45:9:
He says that the prince does not enter the temple separately or as someone above the others, but goes in together with the people when they come to worship, and goes out when they go out. The wording here is simply plain: when the people enter, the prince enters with them, and when they leave, he leaves. The picture is that the prince mixes with the people during the festivals.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the vision of a new temple (chapters 40 to 48). He gives instructions about the order of worship. It is not known with certainty who "the prince" is: some think of a future leader, others of a symbolic figure, and others connect him with the Messiah. What is clear is that he too worships and submits to God's order.

For today: no leader stands above worship. We can remember that, whatever our role or position, we come to God alongside others, with humility and unity.
exp.39:25:
This verse says that the gate on the south side of the temple had a staircase of seven steps. In front of those steps stood a porch, the open space before the entrance. On the side pillars of the entrance there were carved palm trees, one on each side. The "cubits" were an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of a forearm.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here, recounting a vision God gave him. A guide leads him through and carefully measures the temple. The people were exiled in Babylon, and this vision showed an orderly place where God would dwell. Scholars disagree about whether it describes a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture.

For today: drawing near to God is not something disorderly or rushed. The steps invite us to come with respect and reverence, and the palm trees remind us that before Him there is life and joy. Today, before you pray or read the Bible, pause to calm your heart.
exp.9:17:
This verse says that the visible presence of God, called "the glory of the LORD," moved away from the threshold of the temple and came to rest above the cherubim, which are heavenly beings with wings. The "threshold" is the entrance of the temple, and "moved away" means God's glory left that place.

The prophet Ezekiel, a priest who was exiled in Babylon, speaks here. He describes a vision in which he sees God gradually leaving the temple in Jerusalem. This happens because the people had fallen into idolatry and sin. Some scholars see here a judgment, and also a warning that God is not bound to a building.

For today: let us not take God's nearness for granted. Let us care for our lives with humility and obedience, and remember that he remains faithful and can be with us in any place.
exp.15:43:
This verse says that everyone who speaks in proverbs will quote a saying about Jerusalem: "Like mother, like daughter." People who repeat sayings and popular expressions are the ones who would pass along something like this. The idea is that the daughter behaves the way her mother does.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he describes Jerusalem as a woman whom He cared for and who later became unfaithful to Him, following idolatrous practices. The verses that follow explain the saying: her roots were Canaanite, and she resembled her neighbors Samaria and Sodom in their sin. God shows her her guilt in order to lead her to repentance.

For today: it is good to examine which habits and attitudes we inherit from our surroundings or family. What is good we thank God for, and what is harmful we hand over to God so that He may change us.
exp.28:3:
God says he will put hooks in the jaws of Pharaoh, as if he were a great monster of the river. The fish of the Nile will cling to his scales, and God will haul him up out of the water with all of them. "Cling" here means to hold on tightly, and the reed staff is a weak stick that breaks when leaned on.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Pharaoh, compared to a dragon or crocodile, boasted that the river was his and that he himself had made it. Egypt was a great power, but it proved a fragile support for Israel, and God judges it for its pride.

For today: everything we have, such as strength, work, or success, is a gift from God. When we believe we made it all ourselves, we become proud. Today you can give thanks to God and trust in Him, not in your own resources.
exp.41:16:
He measured the north side to be five hundred cubits long. This explanation says that the man guiding Ezekiel measured the north side of the temple area, and that it was five hundred cubits long. A cubit was a standard unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the fingertips. The measuring was done with a measuring rod, and the measurements cover the whole enclosure. With the other three sides, the enclosure forms a perfect square.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest who was exiled in Babylon. In a vision, a guide with the appearance of bronze shows him a new temple and measures it. Interpreters differ: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence and holiness. The equal measurements suggest order and separation between the holy and the common (v. 20).

For today: God is a God of order and holiness, and He cares how we approach Him. Take some quiet time to prepare your heart before prayer, setting aside distractions, as one who enters a sacred place.
exp.15:36:
God says he will gather all of Jerusalem's "lovers," both those she desired and those she despised, and set them against her. They will see her "shame" (her nakedness, her disgrace) and her "vileness" (her filthy and indecent conduct).

The LORD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of an unfaithful wife to describe Jerusalem, who left God and sought alliances with other nations and with idols. The "lovers" probably represent those nations. God announces that the same people she trusted will be the ones who expose and judge her.

For today: whatever we put in God's place, whether money, approval, or power, never protects us in the end. We can return to God sincerely today, trusting that his faithfulness is more secure than anything else.
exp.21:5:
This verse says that the leaders of Israel, the princes, used the power they had to shed blood, each one using his own authority and position to harm innocent people in Jerusalem. The verse points to the way each prince misused what he held.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He accuses Jerusalem, called a city that sheds blood, of its crimes, its idolatry, and its injustice. The verses that follow show that they mistreated the fathers, the foreigners, the orphans, and the widows. God especially condemns the leaders, who were supposed to protect the people.

For today: if you have any authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, use it to care for the weak and not to take advantage of them. Ask God to give you a just and humble heart.
exp.0:17:
Their rims were high and awesome, and the four rims were full of eyes all around. The verse describes the wheels of the vision as having rims or edges so tall that they inspired fear and wonder. The rims of all four wheels were covered with eyes on every side.

Ezekiel is speaking, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon with his people. He recounts a vision of the glory of God, with living beings and wheels that moved alongside them, guided by the Spirit. The eyes are usually understood as a sign that God sees everything, though not all interpreters explain it the same way. The message was that God was not bound to Jerusalem.

For today: even if you feel far from everything or in a difficult place, God sees you and continues to work. Trust that his watchful eye and his guidance accompany you wherever you are.
exp.35:25:
God promises to change his people from the inside out. A "stony heart" is a hard heart, one that does not listen or obey, while a "heart of flesh" is a tender one, one that responds to God. Here God says he will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you, and that he will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh. Beyond a new heart, he also promises a new spirit.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. They had been scattered because of their disobedience and idolatry. God promises to gather them, cleanse them, and bring them back to their land. The verses that follow explain that his Spirit will help them obey. Some Christians see here a foreshadowing of the new covenant.

For today: it is not enough simply to try harder to behave better. We can ask God each day to soften our hearts and help us listen to him with humility.
exp.33:25:
God promises to bless his people and the places around his hill, that is, the mountain where he makes his presence known, probably Zion or Jerusalem. He says he will send the rain at the right time. He calls these showers of blessing.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel's leaders had mistreated the people, who were like a flock left without a shepherd. So God promises to be the shepherd who cares for them. He offers them a covenant of peace, safety, and good harvests. Many Christians see in the promise about "my servant David" a sign of Jesus, the good shepherd, though some understand it in other ways.

For today: God cares for his people and gives what is needed in its time. We can trust him when waiting becomes long, and thank him for the simple blessings of each day.
exp.3:1:
It says Ezekiel should portray a siege against Jerusalem. The siege is the blockade of the city. A siege wall is built around it to cut it off, a ramp of earth is built up to reach the city walls, camps are set up for the attacking soldiers, and battering rams are placed around the city on every side to break down its gates and walls.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. He asks him to draw Jerusalem on a clay tablet, a brick of mud, and act out a siege. It was a sign for Israel, which thought the city was safe. God was warning that his judgment for the people's sin was real and would come.

For today: God speaks to us clearly before the consequences arrive. We can ask him to show us any sin we are ignoring, listen to him with humility, and return to him in time, trusting in his mercy.
exp.27:10:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel once again. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to me, saying" means that a message from the LORD came to him. It is the way the prophet marks the beginning of a new message.

The one speaking is God, and he speaks to Ezekiel. Before this, the message was against the prince of Tyre, who considered himself a god. Now God asks the prophet for a lament, a song of mourning for the king of Tyre. Some understand the words that follow only as referring to that human king; others also see an echo of Adam or of Satan. The Bible does not fully clarify this here.

For today: before you speak or act, be quiet and let the Word of God speak to you first. What he says matters more than what we think of ourselves.
exp.6:10:
Violence has grown until it has become a rod to punish their wickedness. That is, their violence has turned into the very thing that brings their punishment. The image is hard to pin down, and some readers take the rod to be the violent people themselves, while others take it to be the punishment that falls on them. The verse announces that none of them will remain, not their crowd, not their wealth, and nothing of value. It adds that no one will mourn for them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem and Judah, which were full of violence, injustice, and idolatry. God had already warned them many times, and now he says that the time has run out.

For today: God sees injustice and does not take it lightly. We can ask ourselves whether there is harshness or abuse in our words, our business dealings, or the way we treat others. While there is still time, we can repent, seek justice, and turn to God, who is merciful to those who come to Him.
exp.19:45:
God tells Ezekiel to turn his face toward the south and to speak a message against a forest in the Negev. "Son of man" is the way God addresses the prophet. The south is the direction Ezekiel is told to face, and the message is to be delivered with force, without holding anything back.

God himself speaks and sends Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. The verses that follow explain that the forest will be set on fire and that the fire will not go out. Many understand that the forest represents Judah and Jerusalem, and that the fire is God's judgment. Later on, Ezekiel himself tells that people were saying he only spoke in parables, so the message was not always understood.

Today we can learn to listen to God even when his message is uncomfortable. Before asking God to correct others, it is wise to ask him what he wants to correct in us.
exp.22:37:
God says that, on top of everything else, his people had done something else seriously wrong: "On that very same day, they defiled My sanctuary," meaning they made the holy place unclean, and "they profaned My Sabbaths," meaning they treated as ordinary the day of rest that God had set apart for himself.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses two sisters, Aholah and Aholibah, as an image of Samaria and Jerusalem, who turned away from God. The verse before this one explains the accusation: they offered their children to idols and then entered the temple that same day, as if nothing had happened. Their worship was a false mixture.

For today: we cannot serve God and other gods at the same time. It is worth examining whether our daily life agrees with what we say at church, and returning to God with a sincere heart, not only with rituals.
exp.32:19:
God quotes what the people were saying: "The way of the Lord is not just," meaning that God's way of acting is unfair. God answers that he will judge each person according to their own ways. The word for "way" means path or manner of living, and "judge" here means dealing with each person according to what they have done.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The Israelites accused God of being unjust, because it seemed to them that he was not treating them well. God shows them that he always offers the chance to turn back to him: the wicked can repent and live, and the righteous must persevere. Shortly afterward comes the news that Jerusalem had fallen.

For today: instead of blaming God for what happens to us, we can examine our own path. If we have failed, we can turn back to him with confidence, for his mercy awaits us.
exp.10:6:
This verse says that the people who lie dead in Jerusalem, killed by its leaders through violence and injustice, are like the meat inside a pot (a large cooking vessel). God tells them that they think they are safe in the city, but He will remove them from it. "The slain you have laid within this city" means the people you killed. "I will remove you from it" speaks of judgment, not rescue.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who is in exile in Babylon, and sees in vision the leaders of Jerusalem. They had said the city was a pot that would protect them (v. 3). God answers that what really fills the city is the fruit of their injustice. Interpreters see here a judgment upon them.

For today: let us not trust in our position or our security, but in living with justice and compassion, because God sees what we think and do.
exp.15:29:
God says that Jerusalem's heart is weak-willed. She has no firm resolve and cannot hold steady. He accuses her of acting like a shameless prostitute, doing all these things without shame or restraint.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16 he describes Jerusalem as a woman he cared for and made a covenant with, but who turned away from him. Her unfaithful dealings represent idolatry and alliances with Assyria, Canaan and Babylon, instead of trusting in God.

For today: our hearts can seek to be satisfied in things that do not fill them, such as success, money or the approval of others. Today we can stop, honestly acknowledge this, and return to God, who is faithful and forgives.
exp.12:21:
This verse says that God accuses certain false prophetesses of doing two kinds of harm: with lies they discouraged the righteous and made his heart heavy with sorrow, even though God had never caused him any grief, and they encouraged the wicked to keep going in their evil ways, promising them that this would save their lives. Their lies gave the wicked support and kept him from turning away from his sin.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was in exile in Babylon. Earlier in this chapter, God condemns prophets and prophetesses who invented messages and said they came from God. The details of the "pillows" and the "veils" are objects tied to their practices of divination; scholars are not entirely certain how they were used. God promises to rescue his people from their influence.

For today: before accepting or repeating a "spiritual" message, let us compare whether it is faithful to the Bible. A true word corrects the one who sins while speaking truth, and comforts the one who suffers without deceit.
exp.15:56:
Before your wickedness was uncovered, you did not see it for what it was. Now that it has been exposed, you are scorned by the daughters of Edom and by the other neighboring nations, and by the daughters of the Philistines, who look down on you on every side.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he compares Jerusalem to an unfaithful wife who forgot everything God had done for her. She came to think herself so superior that she did not even mention Sodom, and yet her sin ended up being worse. Some scholars understand that the shame came with the defeats at the hands of those neighboring peoples.

For today: do not compare yourself with others to make yourself feel better. Ask God to show you your heart honestly, and return to Him before sin grows in secret.
exp.6:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. The phrase "And the word of the LORD came to me, saying," means that a message from the LORD came to him. It is the way Ezekiel introduces a new message that he did not make up himself, but received from God. Here only the arrival of a word is announced; what God says begins in the following verse.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. He tells that God gave him a message for the people of Israel. What follows is a strong warning: God's judgment was drawing near because of the people's wickedness and crooked ways. God does not speak on a whim, but to call them back to Himself.

For today: God still speaks through His Word. Before reading the Bible, we can pray with humility and readiness, prepared to listen, even when what God says confronts us or invites us to change.
exp.36:14:
Again the word of the LORD came to Ezekiel, and God spoke to him once more. This opening line simply marks the start of a new message from God.

The one speaking is God, and He speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. Just before this, God had promised to bring His people back to life, like dry bones coming back to life. Now He continues with another lesson: that of the two sticks, which represents the joining of Judah and Israel into one people. Many understand this as a promise of unity and restoration.

For today: before you act or speak, take a moment to listen to God in His Word. He continues to guide and heal His people, even when there is division.
exp.2:13:
The verse tells how the Spirit of God lifted Ezekiel up and carried him away. The phrase "I went in bitterness" refers to going with a heavy heart, and "in the anger of my spirit" speaks of inner anger or turmoil. Even so, "the strong hand of the LORD upon me" means that God held him firmly and did not let him go.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here. He lived in exile in Babylon with other deported people. He had just seen the glory of God and received the call to bring a hard message to a rebellious people. That is why it is understood that he went with a heavy heart. The text does not explain in detail the cause of his bitterness, and it can be interpreted in several ways. He then spent seven days stunned and silent among the exiles.

We can obey God even when we feel sadness or anger. He does not pull away from us because of our emotions; his hand remains firm over us. Bring to him honestly what you feel.
exp.26:27:
It says that when the sailors of Tyre cry out in anguish, the people of the nearby lands and coasts will tremble with fear. The word "countryside" in the verse refers to the surrounding land and shores that depended on the city.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and composes a lament over Tyre, a city rich from its sea trade. The prophet compares it to a great ship that is sinking. Its pride and its wealth will not save it, and its fall will shake everyone who depended on it.

For today: nothing we build, whether money, success, or reputation, is a secure foundation on its own. It is wise to trust God and live with humility, using what we have with generosity and justice.
exp.47:21:
This verse says that the prince's land lies on both sides of the sacred zone, which includes the portion of the Levites and that of the city. That zone is in the center, and the prince has his share of land between the territory of Judah and that of Benjamin. Here "share" means a set-apart piece of land. "Border" means the edge or limit of a territory.

This is the final part of the vision that God gave to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. God shows him how the land would be divided, with the sanctuary at the center. It is understood in several ways: some see it as a promise for a restored Israel, others as a spiritual or future picture. What is clear is that God places his presence at the center of the people.

For today: ask yourself what sits at the center of your life. Just as in this vision everything is arranged around the holy place, we can organize our time, work and family around God.
exp.32:16:
Some of the people of Israel say that God is not just. They claim: "The way of the Lord is not just." The word "way" here means the path or manner of acting. But God answers that the wrong way is theirs, not his.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who had been appointed as a watchman to warn the people. Those exiled in Babylon thought God was being unfair because he said he would forgive the wicked person who repented and would judge the righteous person who turned away from good. God shows them that his dealings are just and that he always offers a way to return.

For today: before blaming God for what we do not understand, let us examine our own hearts. His invitation remains open: if we repent and walk in his truth, he receives us and forgives us.
exp.22:16:
This verse says that the Babylonians came to Aholibah, the woman in the story, to her bed of love, and in their lust they defiled her. After she had been defiled by them, she turned away from them in disgust. Here the image of unlawful sexual relations also points to spiritual unfaithfulness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of two sisters, Aholah (Samaria) and Aholibah (Jerusalem), to show how his people abandoned God and sought alliances with foreign nations. Aholibah was drawn to Babylon and pursued it, but that alliance ended in disappointment and judgment.

For today: what seduces us away from God promises much but leaves emptiness. Before you chase after something, ask yourself whether it draws you closer to Him or farther away, and return to God when you notice you are drifting.
exp.29:16:
This verse says that the young men of two Egyptian cities, On and Pi-beseth, will die in war, and that the cities themselves, referred to as "those cities," will be taken away into captivity. The phrase "will fall by the sword" means they will be killed in battle. On is usually identified with Heliopolis, and Pi-beseth with Bubastis, though this identification is made through historical study.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who announces judgment against Egypt. That country was powerful and proud, and Judah had put its trust in Egypt instead of trusting in God. The nearby text says that the Lord will break Egypt's strength so that they will know that He is the LORD.

For today: let us not place our ultimate security in power, money, or human allies, for all of these can fall. Let us rest in God, who is faithful and just.
exp.19:41:
This verse says that the people of Israel will truly come to know who God is when he brings them back to the land he promised to their ancestors. The land is the one he swore to give their fathers, so the return is presented as the keeping of a solemn promise.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier, God had recalled Israel's rebellion throughout its history. Now he promises restoration, not because the people deserve it, but because of the faithfulness of his name and his word. Some understand this as the return from Babylon, and others also see a future fulfillment.

For today: when God fulfills what he has promised, we learn what he is like. If you have failed, remember that his goodness does not depend on your merits. Trust his word and respond with gratitude and obedience.
exp.37:9:
This is what the Lord GOD says. He tells us that on that day, thoughts will arise in Gog's mind, meaning plans will take shape in his thinking. Those thoughts will be an evil plan: an idea of doing harm. The phrase "you will devise" means he will form it and let it grow inside himself.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel. He speaks of Gog, a leader who will come against Israel when that nation is living in peace, after being gathered from among the nations. Interpreters differ about when this happens and whether it is literal or symbolic. Here we see that God knows the hidden plans and directs them for his purposes.

For today: evil plans begin as thoughts. Ask God to examine your heart, and reject harmful ideas toward others before they take root. God sees everything.
exp.2:6:
God tells Ezekiel that the people of Israel will be unwilling to listen to him. The reason is that they are also unwilling to listen to God himself. The Berean Standard Bible describes them as hard-headed and hard-hearted, meaning stubborn in their thinking and unyielding in their hearts, refusing to change even when the truth is plainly spoken.

God speaks to Ezekiel when he calls him as a prophet, during the exile in Babylon. He explains that he is not sending him to foreigners whose language is hard to understand, who, God says, would have listened. He is sending him to his own people, who understand the message but reject it. Right away God promises to make him strong enough to endure that opposition.

For today: sometimes the problem is not understanding God's Word, but being unwilling to obey it. We can ask God for a soft and willing heart. And if we share his message and others do not respond, we remain faithful without losing heart.
exp.17:31:
God takes no pleasure when someone dies because of their sin. The phrase "turn around" means to change direction, to stop going the wrong way. The word "live" points to a real life, one that begins when a person comes back to God. The invitation is clear: repent and live.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people were saying that God was unfair and that they were suffering for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person is responsible for their own life, but that He offers a way out: repentance. His judgment is serious, and His desire is that people be saved.

Today we can come near to God without fear, even though we have failed. If there is something you need to leave behind, ask Him for help right now. He does not wait to condemn you, but to receive you and give you a new heart.
exp.1:6:
God tells Ezekiel that he must faithfully deliver his words to the people, whether they listen or refuse to listen. The reason is that they are rebellious, that is, stubborn and unwilling to submit.

God speaks, having just called Ezekiel as a prophet among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. He warns that the people will be hard, like briers, thorns, and scorpions. Even so, the prophet must not be afraid. His task is not to get them to listen, but to be faithful. Then God asks him not to be rebellious like them, and to receive his message.

For today: when you share God's truth with love, do not measure your faithfulness by other people's reaction. Be faithful and entrust the result to God. Before you speak, first listen to what He tells you.
exp.43:11:
God speaks with seriousness about certain Levites. They ministered before idols and became a stumbling block of iniquity to the house of Israel, meaning they were a cause through which others trip and fall into sin. Their conduct led others into wrongdoing. God declares that they will bear the consequences of their iniquity, the results of their guilt.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the vision of the new temple. Some Levites had turned away and had served before the idols. For this reason they lose the privilege of being priests, although God still allows them to serve in tasks of care and support. Both his justice and his mercy are shown. Interpreters explain this vision in different ways.

Those who serve God carry a greater responsibility, because their example influences others. We can ask him to help us live in such a way that our lives bring others closer to him, and not cause them to stumble.
exp.17:12:
If someone lends money and charges excessive interest, taking advantage of a brother in need and growing rich from it, he will not live. The "excess interest" in the verse is the extra amount taken above what was lent. The "abominations" are the things God detests, like those in the earlier verses: idolatry, theft, adultery, and oppressing the poor. The phrase "his blood will be on his own head" means that he himself is responsible for his punishment.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. They were saying that they were suffering because of their parents' sins. God answers that each person answers for his own actions. Here he describes a son who repeats the sins of a righteous father.

For today: examine whether your profits and your dealings with others, especially with the most needy, are just. Do not use other people's hardships to enrich yourself. God invites each one to live with integrity, without making excuses based on what others did.
exp.9:19:
Here Ezekiel says that the beings he now sees are the same ones he saw years earlier by the River Kebar. Earlier he called them "living creatures." Now he understands that they are cherubim, beings who serve God and surround his throne. The phrase about the God of Israel means that they were beneath him, carrying his glory.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest and prophet who was exiled in Babylon. In this vision he sees the glory of God leaving the temple in Jerusalem, a sign of judgment for the people's idolatry. Recognizing the cherubim confirms to him that it is the same God who called him at the beginning.

For today: even when we feel far from home or confused, God does not change. He is the same in every place, and we can trust that he is still present and in control.
exp.9:4:
This verse says that the sound of the cherubim's wings could be heard as far as the outer court of the temple. It is compared to the voice of God Almighty when He speaks. A "roar" means a very loud noise, like thunder.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, describes a vision. The glory of God, shown as a cloud and a great brightness, moves within the temple in Jerusalem. This happens as God prepares to judge the city for its idolatry. The man clothed in linen will carry fire over Jerusalem. Many interpreters see here a sign that God is withdrawing from his temple, although the text does not explain every detail.

God is not small or manageable. His presence deserves respect and awe. Today we can draw near to Him with confidence, but also with reverence, taking seriously his voice and his Word, without treating Him lightly.
exp.33:10:
God says that he himself will go out to look for his sheep and take care of them. Here the phrase "I will search" is rendered as "I will search for My flock," and "I will seek them out" means he will find them, examine them, and attend to each one. It is a personal promise, spoken with the word "I" emphasized.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people of Israel are scattered and in exile. Their leaders, called shepherds, had taken advantage of the people instead of caring for them. That is why God confronts them and promises that he himself will rescue and gather his flock. Many Christians see here a foreshadowing of Jesus, the good shepherd.

If you feel lost, tired, or neglected, remember that God has not forgotten you. He seeks you out and knows you. Open your heart to him today in prayer, and if you have responsibility over others, care for them with that same love.
exp.9:16:
This verse says that the wheels moved exactly like the cherubim: when the cherubim stood still, the wheels stood still too; when they ascended, the wheels ascended with them. The reason is that the spirit of the living creatures was in the wheels. Here "living creatures" means the same beings described in chapter 1. The word "ascended" means they rose up.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, is in exile in Babylon. He describes a vision in which the glory of God leaves the temple in Jerusalem because of the people's sin. The detail of the wheels shows that everything moves in perfect unity under God's direction. Scholars interpret the exact symbolism of the wheels in several different ways.

For today: God is not confined to one place, and his work moves with order and purpose. We can ask him that his Spirit guide us, to move forward or to stop when he indicates.
exp.35:15:
This verse says: "Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying." The word "again" shows that God is speaking once more. It is a phrase Ezekiel uses many times to signal that God is going to speak to him again.

Ezekiel speaks here as a prophet who lived in exile with the people in Babylon. Earlier, God had promised the land of Israel that it would no longer suffer shame or the loss of its children. Now a new message begins, in which God explains why Israel was punished: they defiled the land with their sins, their idols, and the blood they shed. This helps us better understand the need for restoration.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before asking him for comfort or change, it is good to open the Bible with humility and listen also to what he says about our lives, even when it is difficult. His truth corrects us so that we may be healed.
exp.12:6:
God asks the false prophets a sharp question: haven't they seen false visions and spoken lying predictions? They proclaim, "Thus declares the LORD," but God makes clear that He had not spoken. A "lying divination" is an invented message presented as if it came from God.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Some prophets offered false hopes of peace without calling the people back to God. Because of this, they did not help repair the cracks in the wall, that is, they did not protect the people like someone fixing breaches in a wall. God announces that He will stand against them.

Today, before accepting a message said to come from God, it is wise to check it against the Bible. And when we speak of God to others, let us do so with humility and truth, never putting into His mouth what He has not said.
exp.18:3:
The nations heard about what this young lion was doing. He was trapped in their pit, and with hooks they led him away to the land of Egypt. The hooks here are the tools used to lead a captured animal, and "trapped" means that he was caught.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who sings a lament for the princes of Israel. The mother lioness is usually understood as Judah or its kingdom, and the cub as King Jehoahaz, whom Pharaoh Necho took captive to Egypt. Some scholars connect it to that historical event, although the text does not give the name. His violence led him to ruin.

Whoever uses their power to harm others does not remain safe forever. Today we can ask God for a just and humble heart, so that whatever we have, little or much, we use to serve and not to take advantage of others.
exp.39:18:
He says the man who was guiding Ezekiel measured the distance from the front of the lower gateway to the outside of the inner court. The measurement was one hundred cubits, taken along the east side and also along the north side. A cubit was roughly half a meter, so we are talking about about fifty meters. The inner court is an open courtyard of the temple.

Ezekiel tells of a vision he received in exile, when the temple in Jerusalem had already been destroyed. A guide with a measuring reed shows him a new temple in full detail. Interpreters do not agree: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbol of God's presence and holiness among his people.

For today: God cares about details and desires order and reverence when we approach him. We can come near with calm and respect, knowing that he dwells with his people.
exp.15:51:
Ezekiel 16:52 is about Jerusalem, which looked down on Samaria and Sodom and now must bear its own shame. Its sins were worse, so much so that those sisters appear "more righteous" by comparison. The idea that she "justified" her sisters means that by sinning more, she made the others look less guilty. "Disgrace" means dishonor or shame.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. In this chapter He compares Jerusalem to an unfaithful woman who forgot God's love. Samaria and Sodom are the "sisters," well-known examples of judgment. God wants the people to see how serious their sin is, and the verses that follow announce restoration.

For today: before pointing out the faults of others, let us examine our own hearts. Humbly acknowledging our guilt brings us closer to God's mercy, which humbles in order to heal and restore.
exp.20:16:
God says that He too will strike His hands together, which means He will clap them. In that time, this gesture could express anger, grief, or the sense that something is settled. Then He says He will satisfy His wrath, meaning He will bring His anger to its full measure once the judgment has been carried out. It ends with the seal of His authority: "I, the LORD, have spoken."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces that the sword of the king of Babylon would come against Jerusalem because of the people's sin. The verses before describe that sword as sharpened and ready. Some scholars understand the clapping as anger, others as the seal of a judgment that has been decided.

For today: God is serious and does not mock sin, but His anger is neither eternal nor capricious. We can heed His correction in time, return to Him with humility, and trust that His justice has an end and a purpose.
exp.35:10:
God promises that the mountains of Israel will be filled with people and animals once again. He says they will multiply and be fruitful. He also promises that the land will be as inhabited as it once was, and that the people will prosper more than they did before. In the end, they will know that God is the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel had been taken into exile, its land lay in ruins, and its neighboring nations mocked it. Here God addresses the mountains of Israel and promises to restore the land and its people, not because of anything they deserved, but to show who He is.

For today: when your life feels like it lies in ruins, remember that God knows how to rebuild what has been destroyed. Trust that He can restore, and wait for His work with patience and faith.
exp.25:16:
Ezekiel 26:17 describes what will happen when Tyre falls. Others will raise a funeral song over her and ask in amazement, "How you have perished, O city of renown, inhabited by seafaring men!" A lament is a song of mourning for the dead, and the verse pictures the city's neighbors grieving her loss. They remember a city that was famous, powerful at sea, and feared by everyone around her.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a wealthy and proud trading city, and she had rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem (Ezek 26:2). God announces that she too will fall, and the rulers of the sea will be shaken when they see it.

For today: fame, wealth, and power are not a secure foundation. We can be thankful for what we have without placing our trust in it. Today is a good day to ask ourselves where we truly rest, and how we use what God has given us with humility.
exp.26:21:
The merchants of Sheba and Raamah came to Tyre with the best of their goods, trading their gold, the finest spices, and precious stones for the goods Tyre offered. "Spices" in this verse refers to aromatic spices, the kind used in fragrances and incense, and the city's markets were where this trading took place.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a seaport city very rich from its trade. The list of trading partners shows how great its fame and wealth were. The prophet describes the city as a beautiful ship that would soon sink because of its pride. Many scholars place Sheba and Raamah in southern Arabia, although their exact location is debated.

For today: wealth and success can make us feel secure without God. Examine where you place your trust, and thank God for what you have by using it with humility and generosity.
exp.40:7:
He said that Ezekiel looked at the temple's raised base all around it and saw that it formed the foundation of the side rooms. That base measured the full length of a rod, which here equals six long cubits (a cubit is roughly half a meter, so about three meters).

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received during the exile, in which a guide showed him a new temple and measured every part of it. The precise details stress order and holiness. Scholars disagree about whether it is a literal future temple or a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people.

For today: God cares about what seems small, like a foundation measured with care. Ask yourself what foundations hold up your daily life, such as prayer, the Word, and community, and strengthen one of them this week.
exp.37:20:
God says he will summon a sword against Gog, the invading leader, on all of his mountains in the land of Israel. The result will be confusion: the enemy soldiers will turn on one another, and each man's sword will be against his brother. "Summon a sword" means calling for destruction to be sent.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Gog and his allies come to attack Israel, and God acts to defend his people and to show his holiness. Interpreters differ on whether this prophecy speaks of a historical event, a future one, or a symbolic picture of the final judgment. All agree that God is in control.

For today: when the powers that oppose God seem unstoppable, remember that he still rules. Trust him instead of living in fear, and seek to be a peacemaker, not someone who raises the sword against his brother.
exp.20:28:
God says that the prophets and diviners of Ammon offer false visions and lying predictions to the people. Those false promises will not save them: the sword will fall upon them, along with other wicked people who are condemned to die. "Empty" means something without value. "Their final punishment" refers to the time when their wrongdoing reaches its end.

God speaks through Ezekiel, at the time of the fall of Jerusalem. This part is a message against Ammon, a neighboring people who mocked Israel. Ammon trusted in its diviners, but God announces that its judgment will come anyway.

Today, do not let yourself be comforted by pleasant messages that do not come from God. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and respond to God with humility before it is too late.
exp.31:9:
He says that God will cause many peoples to be appalled at what will happen to Egypt. Its kings will shudder in horror when God brandishes his sword before them. The word "appalled" here means deeply shocked, left speechless. "Will shudder in horror" means they will tremble with fear, every moment, on the day Egypt falls.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament over Pharaoh and Egypt. God announces judgment because of their pride. The verses that follow say that the sword of the king of Babylon would be the instrument. The language of darkness and dimmed stars is poetic and symbolic, and not everyone interprets it the same way.

For today: power and fame do not make us safe. We can ask ourselves where we place our trust, and ask God for a humble heart, one that depends on him and not on what it boasts of having.
exp.4:6:
God asks Jerusalem with both sorrow and firmness: how can it be that, being a numerous and blessed people, you have not obeyed his commands? The reader will see that the people are described as more insubordinate than the nations around them. They had not walked in God's statutes or kept his ordinances, and they had not even lived up to the standards that the pagan peoples around them kept.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Jerusalem was placed at the center of the nations to be a witness, yet it despised God's laws. That is why the judgment announced in the following verses is coming.

For today: blessings are no excuse for drifting away from God, but one more reason to obey him. Today we can ask ourselves whether what God has given us draws us closer to him or makes us forget him.
exp.5:12:
God says that when their slain lie among their idols, around their altars, on the hills, the mountaintops, and under the green trees and leafy oaks, then they will know that He is the Lord. The phrase "fragrant incense" refers to the smoke they offered to their idols. The "leafy oak" is a large, shady tree.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. The people of Israel had filled the land with false altars on the high places, and God announces a judgment by sword, famine, and plague. Most likely these words were meant to wake the people up and bring them back to God, even though it was late.

For today: everything we put in God's place, such as money, success, or prestige, ends up failing us. Today you can ask yourself what thing is receiving your best time and your trust, and give it back to the Lord.
exp.15:45:
Ezekiel 16:46 speaks of Jerusalem as having two "sisters": Samaria, the older, who lived to your north, and Sodom, the younger, who lived to your south. The "daughters" are the smaller towns and villages near each of them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In a long account, God presents Jerusalem as a woman he had cared for, but who was unfaithful to him with idols and alliances with other nations. By comparing her with Samaria and Sodom, cities known for their sin and their judgment, God shows that Jerusalem had become even worse.

For today: we should not compare ourselves with others in order to feel better. When we believe we are better than other people, we can forget our own need to return to God with humility and ask his forgiveness.
exp.30:3:
It says that a great cedar grew very tall thanks to the abundant waters. The deep springs beneath the earth fed it, and they made it tall. Their streams were directed all around its base, and their channels reached all the other trees of the field. In this way, the tree grew and also gave life to others.

God speaks to Ezekiel and tells him to speak to the pharaoh of Egypt. To warn him about his pride, He compares Egypt with Assyria, described as an enormous cedar that fell. Some scholars debate the details of this comparison, but the message is clear: no great nation is safe if it exalts itself.

For today: everything we have, our talents, success, or influence, comes from the hand of God. If we receive it with humility, we can bless others instead of becoming proud.
exp.41:18:
The verse describes the guide, a man whom Ezekiel sees in a vision, who came around and measured the west side of the temple grounds, five hundred cubits long. "Came around" means he walked around the enclosure. A cubit was a common unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the fingertips. Here the measurement of all four sides is completed, and all of them come out equal.

Ezekiel speaks of a vision he received in exile, when the temple in Jerusalem had already been destroyed. The guide measures the whole enclosure carefully. The next verse explains the purpose: to separate the holy from the common. Scholars disagree about whether it describes a literal future temple or a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people.

For today: God is a God of order and holiness. We can ask what healthy boundaries we need to care for our spiritual life, such as times of prayer and decisions that honor God.
exp.42:17:
Then God speaks to Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man," and tells him that he is going to give the rules for the altar of the new temple. He speaks of the time when the altar is built: there the burnt offering will be sacrificed, a sacrifice burned completely for God, and blood will be splattered on it. "Statutes" means instructions or rules.

God speaks in a vision that Ezekiel receives of the temple, after the people had been taken into exile. Before the altar is used, God asks that it be set apart and purified. Interpreters differ: some see a real temple that was expected to be rebuilt, others see a symbol of God's presence, and others see a future promise.

For today: before serving God, it is good for us to draw near with reverence and humility. We can begin the day by asking him for forgiveness and cleansing, remembering that Christ opens the way for us to God.
exp.11:13:
It says that God will scatter all who surround the prince to protect him: his attendants and all his troops. "Scatter to every wind" means that he will throw them out in every direction. "Chase after them with a sword" means that he will draw the sword to pursue them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. He announces the punishment that would come upon Jerusalem and its king, generally understood to be Zedekiah. The people had rebelled against God, and the message aimed to make them acknowledge that He is the LORD.

For today: there is no true security in power, money, or the people around us if we live with our backs turned to God. It is worth asking ourselves what we are truly trusting in, and returning with humility to rest in Him.
exp.23:9:
This verse describes someone who piles on more logs and keeps the fire burning to cook the meat thoroughly. "Cook the meat well and mix in the spices" refers to letting the broth become thick and rich, and in the end even the bones are burned. It is an image of judgment that grows more and more intense.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. He compares Jerusalem to a cooking pot and calls it a "city of bloodshed" because of its violence and injustice. With this image he announces that judgment will come upon her and that she will no longer be overlooked.

For today: God takes injustice and harm done to others seriously. We can humbly examine what things in our lives we need to recognize and leave behind, and turn to God in repentance, trusting in his mercy.
exp.30:16:
They too went down with it to Sheol, to those who had been killed by the sword. As its allies, they had lived in its shade among the nations.

God speaks through Ezekiel and compares Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to a towering cedar of Lebanon. Like Assyria before it, Egypt trusted in its greatness, but it falls because of its pride. The text is poetic and symbolic: it does not describe a literal place, but shows that no empire escapes God's judgment. Its allies fall with it.

For today: do not place your ultimate security in power, money, or influential people. All of that can fall. Rest in God, who endures, and be humble with what He has given you.
exp.10:16:
God promises his scattered people that he will gather them. "Gather" means to bring together those who had been dispersed among other nations, and God says he will bring them back home. He will also give them back the land of Israel.

Ezekiel speaks on God's behalf while many Israelites are exiled in Babylon. Those who remained in Jerusalem looked down on them and said that they were far from the LORD and that the land now belonged to those who had stayed behind. God answers that he has not forgotten them: even in exile he would be with them as a small sanctuary. The following verses show that the promise includes an inner change, a new heart.

For today: If you feel far away, rejected, or lost, remember that God does not abandon his own. He can sustain you wherever you are and make your heart new. Draw near to him with confidence.
exp.44:1:
Within the portion of land set apart for God, a square measuring 500 cubits on each side would be reserved for the sanctuary, with 50 cubits of open land running all the way around it. Ezekiel's verse does not say what unit of measure the 500 refers to. The cubit is an ancient measure of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger. The open strip around the sanctuary works like a buffer zone of protection, a space kept free and unbuilt.

God speaks through Ezekiel, a prophet who was living in exile in Babylon. This vision of the temple and of the land divided among the people gave hope to those who had been taken far from home. Scholars interpret it in different ways: some read it as a literal temple to be built in the future, while others read it symbolically, as a picture of God's presence among his people. What is clear is that the center of everything is the holy.

For today: just as there was a space of respect around the sanctuary, we can cherish spaces of silence, prayer, and rest that protect our relationship with God from the rush and distractions of daily life.
exp.35:18:
God says that he dispersed Israel among the nations, and they were scattered throughout the lands. God himself is the one doing the scattering. The word "scattered" describes them being spread out across the countries. "According to their ways" refers to how they lived. God judged them according to their ways and deeds, not unfairly or arbitrarily.

The passage is spoken by God through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Before this verse, God explains that the people had defiled the land with idolatry and violence. The exile was the consequence. But the passage continues and shows that God will act afterward for the sake of his holy name.

For today: our choices have consequences, and God invites us to acknowledge them with humility. Even so, his discipline is not the end; he seeks to restore us. We can draw near to him with sincerity, trusting in his mercy.
exp.0:13:
This verse says that the living creatures darted back and forth with a speed like that of lightning. Your verse says the creatures were "darting back and forth," so the image conveys speed, energy, and a light that flashes.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here, a priest who was exiled in Babylon beside the river Chebar. He describes a vision of God that he received there. The living creatures, the fire, and the wheels show the glory and power of God, who is not confined to the temple in Jerusalem but is with his people in exile. Scholars interpret the details in different ways.

For today: when you feel far from home or feel that everything has come to a standstill, remember that God moves and works with power even where you cannot see it. Pray today with confidence, knowing that he is present with you.
exp.23:21:
Here God tells the people that they will do just what Ezekiel did: they will not cover the lower part of their face with a cloak or veil, as mourners did, nor will they eat the bread of mourners, the food that friends would bring to those in grief. Ezekiel's own mourning customs are the sign. The phrase "bread of mourners" most likely refers to the meal that friends brought to people who were mourning.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who had just lost his wife and was not allowed to mourn in public. That was a sign for Israel: Jerusalem and the temple would be destroyed, and the grief would be so great that there would be no way to express it through the usual customs. Some understand it to mean a silent, deeply shocked weeping.

For today: when God corrects us, it is better to respond with humility and sincere repentance, rather than mourning only when it is already too late.
exp.31:17:
God tells Ezekiel, called "son of man," to raise a funeral song of mourning over the vast crowds of Egypt. To "consign" them means to hand them over to the depths. Egypt and the daughters of other mighty nations are sent down to the depths of the earth, a poetic picture of the place of the dead, together with those who go down to the Pit.
