God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the twelfth year of the exile, when Judah was already falling before Babylon. Egypt seemed strong and secure, but God announces its fall. Many understand this scene as symbolic and poetic language about God's judgment, not as a literal description of the afterlife.

Today, this text reminds us that no human power, wealth, or fame is eternal. We can trust God, not what seems strong, and live with humility today.
exp.10:13:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel once more. The phrase "Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying," means that a message from the LORD came to him. It is the way the prophet announces that God is going to answer him.

Ezekiel has just watched Pelatiah, one of the leaders, die while he was prophesying. Frightened, he fell face down to the ground and asked God whether He would destroy all the rest of Israel. Now God speaks, and He does not answer in anger, but with a word about the exiles, whom He has not abandoned.

When we are distressed and full of questions, we can bring our fear before God with honesty, as Ezekiel did. God listens, and in His time He answers us, often through His Word.
exp.32:6:
God tells Ezekiel that he has made him a watchman for the house of Israel, that is, a lookout who keeps guard and gives warning when danger approaches. Ezekiel must hear the word from God's own mouth and give the people the warning that comes from God.

God speaks to Ezekiel and addresses him as "son of man." The people of Israel were in exile in Babylon. God gives Ezekiel the responsibility of giving warning, but not of forcing anyone: each person answers for what they decide to do with the warning.

For today: if God places us near someone who is turning away from Him, we can speak to them with love, truth and humility. We do not have to force anyone or judge them, but we are called to be faithful in saying what God shows us, and to entrust the outcome to Him.
exp.34:5:
God swears by his own life that Mount Seir, that is, Edom, will be given over to bloodshed. "Give you over" means God will hand Edom over to violence. "Since you did not hate bloodshed" means Edom did not refuse or turn away from shedding blood. Because Edom did not reject violence, violence will pursue Edom itself. The punishment fits what Edom did.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom, a descendant of Esau, kept up an old hostility against Israel, and when Jerusalem fell, it handed many Israelites over to the sword. God responds by defending his wounded people and showing that he sees the injustice. The text does not say how each detail was fulfilled; that is interpreted in several ways.

Today we can examine whether we hold on to resentment or take pleasure in the misfortune of others. God calls us to reject violence and hatred, to leave justice in his hands, and to ask for mercy for others.
exp.4:14:
God tells Jerusalem that it will become a public disgrace, a source of mockery, a warning to others, and a cause of horror to the nations around it. This will happen when He carries out His judgments against the city in anger, wrath, and raging fury. He closes by declaring, "I, the LORD, have spoken," as a guarantee that what He has said is certain.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Jerusalem had rejected God's laws and practiced idolatry, so God announces a severe judgment. What made it serious was that the chosen people were meant to show the nations who God is, and instead they had failed in that.

For today: God takes seriously the faithfulness of those who bear His name. We can honestly examine whether our lives reflect what we say we believe, and turn back to Him without delay, trusting in His mercy.
exp.15:53:
You will bear your disgrace and be ashamed of everything you did. Your own sin will bring you to see yourself as you truly are, and in that way you become a comfort to Sodom and Samaria. Here "disgrace" means dishonor, and "to comfort them" means that your case brings them relief.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem, who is portrayed as an unfaithful woman. She had proudly judged her "sisters," Sodom and Samaria, yet her own sin was worse. God promises to restore all three. Some see the comfort in the fact that God treats everyone with the same justice; others see it in the fact that their restoration includes Jerusalem.

Today we can look honestly at our own failings before we judge others. When we admit our sin with humility, God opens the way to restoration and to showing compassion toward others.
exp.5:9:
They will come to know that I am the true God, the LORD. The verse also affirms that his warnings were not empty words: "I did not declare in vain" means his declaration had a purpose and was not made for nothing. The "calamity" here is the punishment that was announced, not any wrongdoing on God's part.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Israel had turned away from God and worshiped idols, which God describes as an unfaithful heart, meaning disloyal, like a broken marriage. Even so, he promises that some will escape and, in exile, will remember God and feel shame for their sin.

For today: when God corrects us, it is not to destroy us but to wake us up. If we notice that something has taken God's place in our heart, we can return to him with humility, without waiting for the consequences to teach us by force.
exp.19:28:
God asks with a note of irony: "What is this high place to which you go?" The Hebrew word "Bamah" means "high place," and here it sounds as if he were saying, "What is this so-called high place you go to?" He notes that the name has stayed in use "to this day," that is, until the days of Ezekiel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the leaders of Israel who are exiled in Babylon. He reminds them that their ancestors, as soon as they entered the promised land, worshiped on hills and under leafy trees. The high places were pagan sanctuaries. God shows them that their children are repeating the same sin, even offering their children to the fire.

For today: God invites us to examine where we go looking for help, peace, or meaning. If we have inherited customs that do not honor God, we can leave them behind and worship him his way, with sincerity and obedience.
exp.22:36:
Aholah and Aholibah, names that stand for Samaria and Jerusalem, were unfaithful to God. Here "committed adultery" is used as an image of idolatry, that is, turning away from God to serve other gods. "Blood is on their hands" speaks of violence and death. And "sacrificed their children... in the fire as food for their idols" describes burning their own children as offerings to the idols.

God speaks, and gives his message to the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. God compares his people to two unfaithful women to show how much pain their betrayal caused him. In accusing them, he notes that they mixed those sacrifices with visits to the temple, as if nothing were wrong.

For today: examine what things are taking the place of God in your life. Do not try to mix faith with what God rejects; give him your heart completely.
exp.6:21:
God says he will turn his face away from them. "Turning away the face" means withdrawing his favor and his care. Then violent men will enter his treasured place, which many understand to be the holiest sanctuary of the temple, and they will defile it, that is, treat it as common and unclean.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, before the fall of Jerusalem. The people had made images of idols, had filled the land with violence, and took pride even in the jewels of the temple. Because of this, God allows foreign nations to plunder it. Some debate whether the treasured place is the Most Holy Place or the treasury of the temple.

For today: let us not take God's favor for granted while we live in pride or with hidden idols. Let us examine humbly what things hold his place in our hearts, and return to him soon.
exp.19:25:
God says that he made them unclean through their own gifts, because they were offering the sacrifice of every firstborn in the fire. "So that I might devastate them" means that they would be left horrified and ruined. The purpose was that they would recognize that God is the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and recounts the rebellion of Israel. Because the people rejected his commands, God gave them over to the practices they preferred. The Law forbade sacrificing children, so many understand that God did not command this, but allowed that path as judgment. Some scholars interpret it in other ways, and the text is difficult.

For today: when we insist on living our own way, God may let us reap the consequences. Let us seek his word soon, before our paths hurt us and those we love.
exp.42:23:
This verse tells us that the bull and the ram were to be brought before the Lord. The priests would sprinkle salt on them and then sacrifice them as a burnt offering to the Lord. A burnt offering was an offering burned completely on the altar, nothing held back for the worshiper or the priests.

Here God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, giving him instructions for consecrating the altar in the temple he saw in a vision. This takes place after the glory of God returns to the temple. Interpreters differ on whether these visions refer to a literal future temple or have a symbolic meaning. Salt was used in offerings as a sign of purity and of covenant (Leviticus 2:13).

For today: God deserves our best and our whole selves. We can ask ourselves whether we give our lives to him sincerely and without holding back, not just parts of them.
exp.21:29:
God says that he searched for someone who would repair the wall and stand in the gap. It is the picture of a city wall with a break in it: God was looking for a person who would mend the wall and stand in that breach to defend the city. He would do this "before me," that is, to plead on behalf of the land, so that God would not have to destroy it. But he says: "But I found no one."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He has just accused the prophets, priests, leaders, and the people of lying, robbery, and oppressing the poor and the foreigners. No one rose up to intercede or to correct. Then comes the judgment.

Today we can be someone who "stands in the gap": praying for our family, church, or country, and speaking the truth and defending the weak, without waiting for someone else to do it first.
exp.2:10:
God tells Ezekiel to go to the exiles, the Jews taken as prisoners to Babylon, who are his own people. He must speak to them and tell them what the Lord God says, whether they listen or refuse to listen. The phrase "whether they listen or refuse to listen" in the Berean Standard Bible shows that the message is to be delivered regardless of how it is received.

God is speaking, having just called Ezekiel as a prophet among the exiles. He had already warned him that the people were rebellious, so he strengthened him with a forehead as hard as diamond. His task did not depend on the results, but on being faithful to the message.

For today: when you share God's truth with love, your responsibility is to be faithful and clear, not to control other people's response. Trust that God works in hearts.
exp.10:4:
This verse says that the Spirit of the Lord came upon Ezekiel and told him to declare a message from God. God tells the people that he knows what they are thinking and the thoughts that rise up in their minds.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles. The leaders of Jerusalem felt secure; they believed the punishment would not come soon, and they talked about building houses. They saw themselves as the meat protected inside the pot. God answers that he has heard everything they are saying and thinking, and that his judgment is real.

For today: God knows both my words and my hidden thoughts. I can be honest with him, ask him to correct my false sense of security, and live with humility, without assuming that my decisions have no consequences.
exp.20:14:
God says that he has set a sword of judgment at all the city's gates. The result is that their hearts will melt with fear, many will fall, and destruction will spread. The sword is shown as ready to flash like lightning and drawn for slaughter. "Melt" means that courage drains away. "Stumble" means to fall in defeat. "Slaughter" means to kill with the sword.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem because of its rebellion and idolatry. The sword is commonly associated with Babylon as the instrument of that judgment. God commands Ezekiel to act out the message with his hands to show how serious it is.

For today: let us take God's voice seriously before the consequences arrive. If He points out something in our lives, it is better to listen and repent today, trusting in His mercy.
exp.23:17:
Ezekiel says he spoke to the people in the morning, and in the evening his wife died. The next morning he did what he had been commanded: he did not weep openly or observe the usual mourning.

Ezekiel is a prophet and speaks in the first person. God took away his wife, "the delight of his eyes," and asked him not to show mourning. His silence was a sign for Israel: soon Jerusalem and the temple would be destroyed, and the grief would be so great that there would be no way to express it. The people asked him what all this meant.

For today: God sometimes asks us to obey in the midst of very deep sorrow, and we do not always understand why. We can be honest with Him about our pain and ask Him for strength to keep trusting Him, even when the path costs us a great deal.
exp.23:8:
Here God announces judgment on Jerusalem, which he calls "the city of bloodshed," meaning a city full of violence and the unjust killing of people. He says that he himself will pile the kindling high, building up a large fire like one used for cooking, and in this way he will show that he will not overlook so much wickedness.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Jerusalem was under siege, and God uses the image of a pot set over the fire. The blood on the smooth rock shows that the crime was in plain sight, not hidden. God sees what is done, even when no one punishes it.

For today: God cares about justice and about those who suffer harm. Let us not hide or excuse injustice. Let us ask him to cleanse us from all evil and help us to defend and care for the lives of others.
exp.35:32:
It says that when God cleanses the people from all their iniquities, He will also cause the cities to be resettled, and the ruins will be rebuilt. "Iniquities" refers to wrongdoing and evil acts, and "ruins" refers to places left broken and abandoned.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites who were in exile, far from their land, because they had turned away from Him. Before promising restoration, He tells them to remember their evil ways, but He makes clear that He acts for the sake of His own name and not because they deserve it. First comes the cleansing, and then the rebuilding.

For today: God does not only want to repair what looks broken in our lives, but He begins by cleansing us from wrongdoing. Today you can honestly acknowledge what you have done wrong, ask Him for forgiveness, and trust that He can rebuild what seems lost.
exp.27:4:
It says that the king of Tyre was very skilled in business. With his skill in trading he increased his wealth. But that wealth led him to pride: his heart had grown proud, that is, it was filled with arrogance.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and addresses the prince or king of Tyre, a city rich from sea trade. God reminds him of his reputation for skill, but shows him that his success made him believe himself almost divine. For this reason, in the following verses, he announces judgment. Some believe the passage also alludes to a spiritual power behind the king, although it is interpreted in several ways.

We can work with intelligence and prosper, but it is good to remember that every good thing comes from God. Give him thanks, be generous, and examine your heart: may success not make you proud.
exp.21:6:
It says that in Jerusalem the people treated their parents with contempt, exploited the foreign residents among them, and oppressed the fatherless and the widow. "Treated with contempt" means to regard someone with disdain and scorn; "exploited" here means taking unfair advantage of someone who is defenseless; "oppressed" means keeping someone down through cruel or unjust treatment.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He is accusing Jerusalem of its sins: violence, injustice, and idolatry. The leaders and the people had forgotten the law that commanded honoring one's parents and caring for the weakest (Exodus 22:21-22). For God, this was not a minor social matter but part of faithfulness to Him.

For today: God pays attention to how we treat those who cannot defend themselves. Think of a vulnerable person near you, such as an elderly person, an immigrant, a widow, or a child without support, and help them in a concrete way this week.
exp.42:3:
What it says: Ezekiel sees the bright presence of God, called "the glory of the LORD," enter the temple through the gate facing east. The gate faces toward the east, the direction where the sun rises.

Context: Ezekiel, a prophet living in exile in Babylon, speaks. Earlier, in another vision, he had seen the glory of God leave the temple because of the people's sin. Now, in this vision of hope, God returns through the same side from which he had left. Interpreters differ on whether this temple describes a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture of restoration.

For today: God desires to dwell again with his people when there is repentance. We can ask ourselves what we should open or correct in our lives to receive him, and pray with confidence, knowing that he is faithful to restore.
exp.14:2:
God asks whether the wood of the vine is good for anything useful. Can any piece of furniture or tool be made from it? Can one make from it a peg, a wooden nail or hook, on which to hang a container? The expected answer is no. The wood of the vine is weak and is not fit for building.

God speaks, giving His word to the prophet Ezekiel, whom He addresses as "son of man." In this chapter, the vine represents Jerusalem and its inhabitants. A vine is valued for its fruit, not for its wood. If it does not bear fruit, it has no worth. God uses this image to show that the people, unfaithful to Him, had nothing to boast about.

For today: our worth does not lie in how we appear, but in remaining joined to God and bearing fruit. Jesus said something similar in John 15. Let us ask Him to keep us close to Him.
exp.44:5:
Here it says that, next to the portion set apart for the sanctuary, an area of land is to be set aside for the city. It is 5,000 cubits wide and 25,000 cubits long. That land is not for the priests or for the princes but belongs to the whole house of Israel. "Property" here means land held as an inheritance.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in the vision of a restored temple and land. This vision comes to a people in exile. The territory is divided in an orderly way: first the holy district, then the city, and then the portion for the prince. Interpreters differ on whether this is meant to be fulfilled literally or is symbolic.

For today: put God at the center and make sure what is shared belongs to everyone. We can arrange our time and possessions so that God has first place, and so that no one is left outside the blessing.
exp.6:4:
God announces through Ezekiel that a disaster is coming upon his people. The phrase "Disaster! An unprecedented disaster—behold, it is coming!" uses the word "disaster" twice to stress that the calamity is certain and very near. Here "disaster" means a catastrophe or misfortune, not only something morally wrong.

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. His message is for Israel, which had practiced idolatry and violence. God says he will judge them according to their ways. Many understand this as the announcement of the fall of Jerusalem, which took place in 586 BC.

For today: God warns us clearly because he wants us to return to him. If you sense that something in your life does not please God, do not put it off. Confess it today, and ask him for forgiveness and for his help to change.
exp.0:14:
As Ezekiel kept looking at the living creatures, he saw a wheel on the ground beside each of them. Each wheel stood beside one of the four beings, and each of them had four faces.

Ezekiel was a priest who had been taken into exile in Babylon along with the people of Judah. He describes the vision he received near the river Chebar, when God revealed himself to him. The wheels appear as part of that chariot of glory. Scholars interpret their meaning in various ways, and the text does not fully explain it. Many see in them the presence of God in motion.

For today: even when you are far from home or going through a hard time, God is not bound to one place. He moves and is present with you. Pray today trusting that he sees you and walks with you.
exp.31:20:
From the realm of the dead, the mightiest warriors will greet Egypt's king as he arrives. With them are his allies, who have already gone down to lie among the uncircumcised, those slain by the sword, peoples who were outside Israel's covenant. The word translated here as "Sheol" is the grave or dwelling place of the dead, not necessarily a place of eternal punishment.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a lament over Egypt and its Pharaoh. The language is poetic: Egypt, proud and feared, will end the same way as other mighty nations that fell. God shows that no empire escapes his judgment.

For today: power, success, and fame do not make us invincible. It is wise to live with humility before God, because He is the one who upholds or brings down the great, and our true security is in Him.
exp.38:4:
It says that Gog, the enemy leader, will fall dead "in the open field," that is, out on the open ground. No one will bury him right away, since his body will be food for the birds and the wild animals. The phrase "for I have spoken" shows that God presents this as certain, a word that will come to pass.

God himself, "the Lord GOD," speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces that a powerful enemy, called Gog of the land of Magog, will attack Israel, but God will defeat him. The purpose is that the nations and his people will know that he is the Holy One. Scholars interpret in different ways who or what Gog represents: a historical event, a future event, or a symbol of evil.

For today: we can rest in the knowledge that no power, however great it may seem, stands above God. When you feel fear before threats or injustice, remember that his word is fulfilled and that he cares for his own.
exp.28:2:
God speaks through the prophet and declares that he is against Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. He calls him "the great monster who lies among his rivers", an image of a water creature, perhaps a crocodile, resting calmly in the Nile. Pharaoh boasted: "The Nile is mine; I made it myself."

The Lord speaks to Ezekiel around 587 B.C., when Egypt seemed a safe ally for Judah. God denounces the pride of a king who believed himself the owner of the source of his wealth and power. The verses that follow show his fall.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we boast of what we have, as if it were only our own merit. Everything we have comes from God. Recognizing this leads us to live with gratitude and humility.
exp.10:11:
It says that Israel will come to know who God is through judgment, because it did not live according to God's statutes and ordinances, but adopted the practices of the nations around it. "Statutes" are his commands, and "ordinances" are his righteous rules. "Nations" are the peoples around them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He had shown the leaders of Jerusalem that they were giving bad counsel and filling the city with violence. They said they were secure, like meat in a pot. God answers that it will not be so: they will be judged. Then Pelatiah dies, and Ezekiel cries out in concern for the rest of the people.

For today: examine whom you imitate. It is easy to copy what the majority does. Ask God that his Word, and not fashion or social pressure, guide your daily decisions.
exp.13:17:
It says that even if three very righteous men lived in a sinful land (in context, Noah, Daniel and Job), they could not save their own sons or daughters. They alone would be saved.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, swearing "as surely as I live." Some elders of Israel had idols in their hearts, and God warns that a people who turn away from him will face judgment. God shows that the righteousness of others does not cover the guilt of someone who persists in sin. Scholars disagree about how this relates to intercession, but the central point is personal responsibility.

Today: faith is not inherited or borrowed. Pray for your family, but seek God yourself with sincerity and return to him each day.
exp.19:33:
God promises to bring Israel out from the peoples among whom they are scattered and to gather them from the lands where they have been dispersed. He will do this "with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and outpoured wrath," images of power, like the rescue from Egypt. "Outpoured wrath" means that his discipline will be firm and real. Gathering them means bringing them back together.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the leaders of the people exiled in Babylon. They were considering becoming like the pagan nations and worshiping idols of wood and stone. God answers that he will not allow this: he will remain their King. The verses that follow show that there will be judgment, as there was in the wilderness with their ancestors, before the restoration.

For today: God does not let go of us even when we want to live like everyone else. His correction is not rejection, but love that seeks to bring us back. If you have wandered away, return to him with confidence and humility.
exp.13:7:
God says he will set himself against the person who keeps idols in the heart and yet comes to ask him for an answer. "Setting my face against" means confronting that person with judgment. "A sign and a proverb" means that he will become a public example, something people will talk about as a warning. "Cut off" means removing him from among God's people. The purpose is that they will know that I am the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile. Some of the people's leaders were coming to consult him, but they kept idols in their hearts. God calls them to turn back and does not accept a faith that is only outward appearance. Some understand "cut off" as exclusion from the covenant people; the text gives no further detail.

For today: before seeking God's guidance, ask yourself what thing is occupying the place that belongs to him alone. Confess it honestly, turn away from it, and draw near to God with a whole heart.
exp.32:3:
If someone hears the sound of danger, the alarm (the "horn" was a ram's horn or trumpet blown to give warning), but pays it no attention, and then the enemy's sword arrives and takes his life, the blame is his own. "His blood will be on his own head" means that he is responsible for his own ruin. "Fails to heed the warning" means that he does not get ready or take any precautions.

God speaks to Ezekiel, whom He appoints as a watchman, for the people of Israel who were living in exile. God uses the image of a city that chooses a lookout. If he gives warning and the people do not respond, the responsibility falls on them. If he does not warn them, the watchman answers for it.

For today: when God warns us through His Word, or through someone who speaks to us with love and truth, let us not ignore it. Listening in time and correcting our course is a sign of wisdom and humility.
exp.45:8:
In the appointed feasts, the people of the land who came in through the north gate were to leave through the south gate, and those who came in through the south gate were to leave through the north gate. No one was to go back out through the gate they entered by, but each was to leave through the opposite gate. The south is the direction of midday, and the appointed feasts were Israel's set times of sacred celebration.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of a new temple and of how worship was to be arranged. Scholars explain the reason for this rule in several ways: perhaps it was meant to keep order among the crowds, or to show that no one came before God and left the same way they arrived. The text does not make this clear.

For today: when you come before God, try to leave different from how you came in, with a more renewed heart, and do not repeat the same old path.
exp.29:18:
God says he will bring punishments on Egypt, and the result will be that they recognize who he is. The words "I will execute judgment" mean that God will pronounce sentence and carry it out. The phrase "they will know that I am the LORD" is one that Ezekiel repeats many times: God acts to make himself known.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. Egypt was a nation proud of its strength, and Judah had trusted in Egypt instead of trusting in God. Before this verse, the fall of its cities, the captivity of its people, and the end of its pride are announced. Scholars agree that this is a historical judgment against Egypt, although the details of how it was fulfilled are debated.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in money, work, or people. All of that can break. Rest in God, who is the only one who never fails.
exp.13:9:
They will bear their punishment, and the punishment of the one who inquires will be the same as that of the prophet. This means that each person will answer for their own guilt, and the guilt of both will be the same. Sin here means wrongdoing, and "the inquirer" is the person who goes to seek a word from God.

God speaks through Ezekiel to Israel during the exile in Babylon. Some elders had idols in their hearts and yet still wanted to consult the prophet. God warns that whoever seeks answers with a divided heart, and whoever tells them what they want to hear, will fall together under judgment. The passage is difficult, and scholars interpret it in various ways, but its aim is to bring the people back to God.

For today: before seeking spiritual counsel, examine your heart. Ask God for honesty, and seek voices that tell you the truth, not only what pleases you.
exp.36:0:
The verse says that God took hold of Ezekiel and brought him by His Spirit to a valley full of bones. "The hand of the LORD" is an expression meaning that God's power acted upon him. The words "brought me out" and "set me down in the middle of the valley" describe Ezekiel being led out and placed in the middle of that valley. The verse does not make clear whether this was a vision or a physical journey; the most common understanding is that it was a vision.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet and priest who was living in exile in Babylon. The people of Israel were discouraged and felt there was no hope of returning to their land. God shows him this scene to speak to that wounded people. The dry bones represent a nation that felt lifeless.

For today: when your situation seems dry and without a way out, do not ignore it or sink into it. Bring it honestly before God, and trust that He can give life where we no longer see anything.
exp.12:3:
The verse says that the prophets of Israel were like foxes among ruins. A fox roams among the wreckage, looking for what it can take for itself, and it takes no care of anything and protects no one.

God speaks through Ezekiel, during the years when Jerusalem was near its fall. He accuses the false prophets, who claimed to speak for the LORD when they were only speaking from their own hearts. With comforting words, they did not help the people see their sin or repair the breaches in the wall. So the people were left without defense.

Today, before accepting a message as coming from God, it is wise to compare it with the Bible. And when we speak of God, let us do so with humility and truth, even when that is not the most comfortable thing to hear.
exp.19:15:
It says that God did not allow Israel to enter the promised land, because that generation kept rejecting his ordinances, refused to walk in his statutes, and profaned his Sabbaths. The word "ordinances" can be understood as his decrees or rulings; "statutes" are his commands; "profaning" means treating as common what was holy. The root of the problem was that their hearts continually went after their idols.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes in exile in Babylon. God reviews the history of Israel from the desert, after leaving Egypt. He wants to show the elders of the people that their present situation comes from a very ancient rebellion, and that He, even so, acted with patience for the sake of his name.

For today: our actions grow out of what we love. Ask yourself what truly occupies your heart, and ask God to draw it back to himself, so that obeying him becomes a response of love and not merely an obligation.
exp.17:25:
The verse says that if a person who lived in righteousness turns away from it and practices iniquity, they will die for this, because of the wickedness they have committed. "Iniquity" means wickedness or injustice, and "die" here refers to death as the result of sin, probably both physical and spiritual.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Israel, who were in exile. Some were saying that the way of the Lord is not fair, blaming God or their ancestors for their situation. God answers that each person is accountable for their own choices, and that He always offers the opportunity to turn back to Him.

Today it reminds us that it is not enough to have walked well in the past; we need to keep trusting God each day. If we become careless, let us ask for forgiveness, for His desire is that we live.
exp.14:4:
It says that the wood of the vine is useless for making anything, even when it is whole and uncut. How much less, then, can it ever be useful once fire has consumed it and charred it. The verse's own wording gives the point plainly: the wood could not be made useful while whole, and it cannot become useful after the fire has charred it.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who was among the exiles in Babylon. He compares Jerusalem to a vine whose wood is useless. In the Bible, the vine represents God's people, and its value lies in bearing fruit. Jerusalem was not bearing the fruit of faithfulness, and for that reason judgment would come upon it.

For today: our worth does not lie in how we appear, but in remaining joined to God and bearing the fruit of obedience and love. We can ask ourselves with humility: in what area do I need to return to God before I harden myself further?
exp.40:10:
Each side room of the temple had a door that opened onto the open area that was left around the building. One entrance faced north and another faced south. That open area was five cubits wide all the way around. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers.

Here the prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting a vision he received while in exile. A guide with a measuring reed shows him a new temple in great detail. Interpreters do not agree: some see a literal temple in the future, while others see a symbol of God's presence with his people. The measurements speak of order and care.

For today: God cares even for the small details. Leave room in your life too, orderly and open spaces to draw near to him, such as a daily time of prayer.
exp.21:8:
The verse says that among the people there are slanderous men who are set on bloodshed. It also describes people who eat on the mountain shrines, which were places of worship to false gods, and who commit acts of indecency. The shameful sins it names are immoral and indecent conduct. The phrase "slanderous men" refers to those who spread lies about others.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. God accuses Jerusalem as the city that sheds blood. The list of sins includes injustice, idolatry, and contempt for what is holy. Many understand that this explains why judgment would come upon the city.

For today: let us take care with our tongues. Speaking badly of someone or spreading lies can seriously harm their life. Let us ask God to make us people of truth, who defend the innocent and do not let ourselves be carried away by gossip.
exp.17:21:
This verse says that God will not keep a record of the wrongs of the one who turns back to Him. "Transgressions" are the times a person rebelled against God, and "none of the transgressions he has committed will be held against him" means that God will not count them against him. "He will live" refers to having life before God, not to being punished with death.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel in Babylon. Some were saying that they suffered for the sins of their fathers and that there was no remedy. God answers that each person answers for himself, and that there is always an open door to return to Him. He then clarifies that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but in his turning from his evil way.

For today: if you feel trapped by your past or by your family's history, God invites you to return to Him. With sincere repentance, you can begin again, trusting in His mercy.
exp.25:9:
This verse says that the enemy army will be so large that its horses will stir up a cloud of dust that covers the city. The noise of the cavalry, the wagons and the chariots will make the walls shake. The invader will enter through the gates as an army enters a city whose walls have already been broken open. A "breach" is a gap or opening made in a wall, and "cavalry" means soldiers who fight on horseback.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel against Tyre, a very wealthy trading city. The text says that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, would come against it (v. 7). Tyre had rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking only of its own gain. God announces judgment and shows that no powerful city stands above Him.

For today: let us not place our security in money, status or success, because all of that can fall. Let us seek our refuge in God, and avoid rejoicing in the misfortune of others.
exp.35:37:
It says that, just as Jerusalem was filled with numerous flocks of animals for sacrifice during its appointed feasts, so the cities now in ruins will be filled with flocks of people. The appointed feasts are the set times of worship, and the flocks of people are the great crowds that will gather in them. Seeing this, they will know that God is the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites in exile. Their cities were destroyed and their neighbors mocked them. God promises to restore the land and the people. He makes clear that he will do it, but he also wants his people to ask him for it: "Yet I will be sought by them."

For today: God can restore what seems empty or ruined, such as a family, a church, or a hope. We can pray with confidence and wait for his work, remembering that he does it so that we may know him better.
exp.1:0:
God speaks to Ezekiel and calls him "son of man," a way of saying "human being" or "mortal." He tells him to stand up because he is going to speak with him. The phrase "stand up on your feet" is simply a call to rise and get ready to listen.

The one speaking is God. Ezekiel has just seen an impressive vision of the glory of the Lord and fell face down on the ground. God does not leave him lying there, but raises him up to give him his mission: to speak to a rebellious people. According to the text that follows, the Spirit enters him and sets him on his feet.

For today: God treats us with respect and equips us to hear and obey him. When you feel weak or overwhelmed, ask him to lift you up by his Spirit, and pay attention to his voice, because he speaks to give you strength and direction.
exp.12:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel. "Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying," is the way the book usually introduces each new message from God, and it simply means: a message from the LORD came to me.

The one speaking is the LORD, and he addresses Ezekiel, a priest who prophesied among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. This message opens a new section. God will give a warning against false prophets, who claimed to speak in his name but only presented their own ideas. That is why Ezekiel must listen first and speak afterward.

For today: before teaching, offering an opinion, or giving advice in God's name, it is wise to listen to him first in his Word. This keeps us from repeating what comes only from our own hearts and helps us give a true message.
exp.38:21:
The verse says that, after what God will do on that day, Israel will know clearly and lastingly that the LORD is their God. "From that day forward" means that this knowledge would not be passing, but would mark a before and an after.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Chapters 38 and 39 describe the defeat of Gog, an enemy who attacks Israel. God delivers his people and shows his glory before the nations. Interpreters disagree about whether this refers to historical events, to a future time, or to symbolic language. What is certain is that the purpose is for Israel and the nations to know God.

For today: do not wait only for difficult moments to recognize God. Today, remember how he has cared for you, and trust that he remains your God.
exp.26:7:
Ezekiel 27:8 says that Tyre, a great trading city, was like a very splendid ship. The men of Sidon and Arvad, other Phoenician cities, served as the oarsmen who rowed. And the skilled men of Tyre itself, that is, its capable experts, served as the captains who steered the ship. The "oarsmen" are those who work the oars; the "captains" are those who command and guide the course.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and composes a lament over Tyre. He describes her as a beautiful ship, built with the best of many nations. With this image he shows her wealth and her pride. Later on, the same ship sinks, and so he announces her fall.

For today: having good resources and capable people does not guarantee a secure future. We can be thankful for and make good use of what God gives us, but without trusting in those things as if they were our salvation. Let us place our trust in Him.
exp.38:27:
God says that the people of Israel will know He is the LORD their God when He regathers them to their own land after their exile among the nations. Not one of them will be left behind. "The LORD" is God's personal name, and "regather" means bringing them back together.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel had been exiled because of its rebellion, and this message promises restoration. The nearby verses speak of shame for sin, of living in safety, and of God pouring out His Spirit. Some believers see here the return from Babylon; others see a future fulfillment. It is interpreted in several ways.

For today: even when we have failed or feel far away, God knows how to restore and gather His own. We can acknowledge our faults honestly and trust that He is faithful to lift us up again.
exp.10:5:
God tells the leaders of Jerusalem that they have caused a great many deaths in the city. The verse says they filled its streets with the dead, so the picture is one of bodies lying everywhere because of what these men had done.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision where he sees the leaders of the people giving bad counsel in Jerusalem. Many understand that these dead were victims of the violence and injustice of the rulers, although the text does not give all the details. God confronts them because he knows what they think and say, and announces that judgment will come.

For today: God sees how we use the authority or influence we have. Let us ask him to help us care for people, not to take advantage of them, and to defend justice.
exp.23:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel on an exact date: the ninth year, the tenth month, the tenth day. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to me" means that Ezekiel received a message from the LORD.

The one speaking is God, and the message comes to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. The following verses explain that on that same day the king of Babylon began to besiege Jerusalem. Many understand the date to correspond to January 588 B.C., though the exact calculation may vary. God wanted his people to understand that what was happening was not chance.

God acts in real history, on specific days and in specific places. Even when everything seems to be falling apart, he continues to speak and remains in control. Today we can approach his Word with humility, especially in difficult times, trusting that God is not absent.
exp.37:5:
This verse continues the list of nations that God says will join Gog. It names Gomer and Beth-togarmah, "from the far north," with all their troops, and adds "the many nations" with Gog. The word for "troops" here refers to armies or groups of allies. Today people debate where these peoples lived; many place them in the region of Anatolia, north of Israel, but there is no complete certainty.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces that, in a future time, a great coalition will come against Israel, now restored. God says that He Himself leads it, to show that He is above all human power. Christians interpret this prophecy in different ways: literally, symbolically, or both.

For today: even when you see great threats and powerful alliances, remember that none of them escapes God's control. Trust in Him, pray, and live with calm, without letting fear rule you.
exp.6:19:
God says that the people took their beautiful jewelry, the gold and silver that He had given them, and used it to feed their pride. With that material they made their vile images and detestable idols. Therefore God will turn those riches into something unclean for them. The verse here points to something unclean that one turns away from. Some think that "his beautiful ornaments" also refers to the temple, but the text does not make that entirely clear.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem for its idolatry. Its riches could not save it, because they had become its stumbling block.

For today: examine which of God's blessings might be feeding your pride or taking His place in your heart. Use your possessions with gratitude and generosity, and not as a source of security or of self-glory.
exp.6:15:
Some will survive the disaster and get away to the mountains. There they will live like doves of the valley, moaning with a sorrowful sound. Each one will grieve over their own wickedness. The verse says "survivors," meaning those who are left alive after the destruction, and the word about sin refers to wickedness or sin.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem and Judah for their idolatry and their injustice. Even the few who are spared will not remain indifferent: they will recognize their guilt. Some scholars see in the doves an image of sorrow rather than of peace.

For today: it is not enough to escape the consequences; God seeks a heart that acknowledges its sin. Today you can confess to Him, sincerely, what you have done wrong, trusting that He forgives those who repent (1 John 1:9).
exp.20:19:
God tells Ezekiel to mark out on the ground a road for the sword of Babylon to travel: one path leading toward Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, and another leading toward Judah, to attack Jerusalem, the city with strong walls. The command to mark out the road is the key action here, since Ezekiel is to draw the route clearly.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. With this action, like a drawn map, he announces that the Babylonian king would advance and that Jerusalem would not escape judgment for its sin. The king seeks guidance through divination, but the Bible shows that God directs events.

For today: although we may sometimes feel secure in what seems strong, only God is our true refuge. We can examine what we trust in and return to him with humility.
exp.26:20:
Ezekiel 27:21 says that Arabia and all the princes of Kedar were Tyre's customers, trading lambs, rams, and goats with the city. These were small livestock, and the verse describes Tyre buying and selling directly with these peoples.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a very wealthy port city. He describes her trading relationships with many peoples to show her greatness and her pride. Later in the same chapter, he announces that this glory will sink like a ship in the sea.

For today: wealth and success may seem like a firm foundation, but they are not. Today we can thank God for what we have, work with honesty, and place our trust not in money but in Him.
exp.15:18:
God reminds Jerusalem that He gave her the finest food: the best flour, oil and honey. But she took what He had provided and set it before idols as a pleasing aroma, that is, as an offering that delighted them. The words "That is what happened" mean: this really took place.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout the chapter He describes Jerusalem as a woman whom He cared for and clothed, but who turned away from Him. The unfaithfulness described here is a picture of idolatry: breaking faith with the covenant with God.

For today: everything good we have comes from God. We may ask ourselves whether we are using His gifts to honor Him, or whether we are putting them to the service of things that take His place, such as money, success or comfort.
exp.39:27:
He led me into the inner court through the south gate, and he measured the south gate. It had the same measurements as the others. The guide brought Ezekiel into the inner court by entering through the south gate, and he measured that gate. Its size matched the other gates. A "cubit" was an ancient unit of length, roughly the length of the forearm.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet who was in exile in Babylon. In a vision, a man with a measuring reed guides him through a new temple and shows him every detail. Scholars understand this vision in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbol of God's presence and holiness among his restored people. For a discouraged people, it was a promise of hope.

For today: God cares about details and order. We can draw near to him with reverence and trust that he has a plan to restore what seems lost.
exp.22:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. The phrase "Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying," tells us that a message from the Lord came to him once more. It is how Ezekiel usually introduces what follows, showing that it does not come from his own ideas but from God.

The one speaking is God, and Ezekiel is the messenger. He lived among the exiles of Judah in Babylon. In this chapter, God uses the story of two sisters to speak about Samaria and Jerusalem, and about their unfaithfulness to Him. It is strong language, meant to awaken the conscience of the people.

For today: before we speak or give our opinion, it is worth pausing to listen to God. We can read the Bible with humility, willing to receive even uncomfortable messages, because God speaks to correct us and also to heal us.
exp.26:3:
Ezekiel 27:4 says that the borders of Tyre were in the heart of the seas, and that its builders perfected its beauty. Tyre was a great city of trade, and its location in the middle of the sea helped make it wealthy. "Borders" means its limits or edges. Those who built the city brought it to a state of complete beauty, like a lovely and well-equipped ship.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and tells him to sing a lament for Tyre. This city was rich and proud, and it boasted of its perfect beauty. The passage describes Tyre as a great ship, but that praise sets up the announcement of its fall. Its beauty was real, but its pride would lead it to ruin.

Everything good we have, such as talent, success, or possessions, comes with help from others and from God. Let us give thanks with humility, without trusting in what we accomplish or boasting about it.
exp.10:8:
It says that God will bring the leaders of Jerusalem out of the city, deliver them into the hands of foreigners, and punish them. "Foreigners" means people from other nations. "I will execute judgments against you" means that God will apply his justice to them.

It speaks God through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. The leaders of Jerusalem felt secure, like the meat inside a pot that protected them, but they had filled the city with injustice and violence. God tells them that this false security will not save them. The exact historical details of how this was fulfilled are explained in several ways, but the central message is clear.

Today we can learn that neither power, nor position, nor walls protect us from God. It is wise to examine our hearts, correct what is wrong, and trust in God's mercy, not in our own security.
exp.13:0:
It says that some leaders of the people of Israel, called "elders," came to Ezekiel and sat down in front of him. This was the posture of someone who comes to listen or to ask for a word from God.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. These elders were probably seeking an answer from the Lord. But right away God shows Ezekiel that these men had idols in their hearts. They appeared to be seeking God, but their loyalty was divided.

For today: we can draw near to God with religious attitudes, such as praying, attending church, or asking for advice, and still hold on to something that takes his place. Today it is good to ask him to show us what we love more than him, and to surrender it to him sincerely.
exp.24:3:
God tells the Ammonites that he will hand them over to "the people of the east," meaning nomadic tribes from the desert to the east. These people will take his land as their own, set up their camps and pitch their tents there, eat the fruit of his fields, and drink his milk. It is a picture of complete loss.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The Ammonites, neighbors of Israel, celebrated when the temple was defiled, the land was left in ruins, and Judah was taken into exile. God answers that mockery by announcing judgment. The text does not say exactly which peoples "the people of the east" would be; it describes them in general terms.

Today: let us not rejoice in the pain of others, not even when someone seems to deserve it. God sees the heart and cares for those who suffer. Let us instead pray, help, and show compassion.
exp.28:8:
God says that Egypt will be left desolate and empty. The word for "desolate" here means destroyed, left in ruins. In this way Egypt will know that the LORD is God, because its king used to say, "The Nile is mine; I made it," as if all his power and wealth came from himself alone.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was writing while the people of Judah were exiles in Babylon. Egypt had been to Israel like a fragile reed: when they leaned on it, it broke and wounded them. God judges Egypt for its pride and for the false security it offered. The Nile River was the source of its strength.

Today we can ask ourselves what we lean on. Everything good we have, such as our work, our health, and our accomplishments, comes from God. Living grateful and humble, trusting him and not our own strength, frees us from pride and from leaning on reeds that break.
exp.0:22:
Under the expanse, above the heads of the living creatures, their wings stretched out toward one another, meeting and lined up side by side. Each creature had four wings: two it used for flying, and two it used to cover its body.

The prophet Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, describes a vision of God's glory beside the river Chebar. God revealed himself to him in the middle of the exile, when the people felt that he was far away. Some see in the covered wings a sign of reverence, though the text does not explain it.

For today: God deserves our respect and awe. Before we ask or act, we can pause to worship him with humility, remembering that he is present even in difficult times.
exp.22:13:
Ezekiel 23:14 tells us that Oholah, one of the two sisters in this story, did not stop at her first sin but carried it even further. When she saw men portrayed on the wall, images of the Chaldeans (Babylonians) engraved in vermilion, she was drawn to them. Here "prostitution" refers to unfaithfulness in general, not only sexual sin.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Using the image of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem), he shows how his people were unfaithful to him by seeking foreign alliances and gods. This part describes Jerusalem, which copies the error of Samaria and goes even further, drawn to what she sees.

For today: what we look at can awaken desires that pull us away from God. Be careful about what you let into your eyes and your heart, and return to him quickly when you notice you are going astray.
exp.15:7:
God says that he passed by Jerusalem, whom he describes as a young girl, and saw her when she was old enough for love, that is, of an age for marriage. He spread his cloak over her and covered her nakedness, a gesture of protection and of a commitment to marry her. He pledged himself to her and entered into a covenant with her. In the end he says, "you became Mine."

The LORD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile. He uses a parable: Jerusalem is an abandoned girl whom God rescues and with whom he joins himself in a covenant. He does this to remind her of his grace before rebuking her unfaithfulness, which comes later in the chapter.

For today: God loved us and cared for us when we had nothing to offer. Remembering that grace helps us live with gratitude and faithfulness, not out of obligation, but because we are loved.
exp.19:37:
God says that he will separate the rebels from the rest of his people. "I will purge you of those who rebel" means he will remove them from among the others. He will bring them out of the land where they now live, but they will not enter the land of Israel. In the end, the people will recognize that he is the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel. He reminds them how he corrected their ancestors in the wilderness after they left Egypt. He will do the same now: he will bring them under his authority, like a shepherd who counts and examines his sheep, to tell the faithful apart from the rebels. His goal is a people who truly serve him.

For today: God is not satisfied with a faith that only looks good on the outside. Examine your heart honestly and ask him to help you obey him, knowing that his correction seeks to restore you.
exp.16:2:
God tells Ezekiel to say a parable. A great eagle, strong, with large wings and feathers of many colors, comes to Lebanon and takes away the top of a cedar tree. The top of a tree is its highest, most tender shoot. The phrase about long pinions refers to the eagle's long wings and feathers.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. This picture is aimed at Israel. Later in the same chapter, God explains that the eagle stands for the king of Babylon and the cedar for the royal house of Judah, whose king was taken captive. God wants his people to understand what happened and why.

For today: God sees history and the powers of this world with clarity. When life feels out of control, we can trust that he still rules and listen to his word with humility.
exp.47:28:
This verse says that the land described will be divided by lot, meaning by casting lots, like a drawing, to give each tribe of Israel its inheritance. The portion each tribe receives is its share of the inheritance. The verse ends with God's own declaration: "declares the Lord GOD."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, toward the end of his book. It is a vision of restoration for Israel, who was in exile. God shows that his people will have a place and that each tribe will have its portion. Scholars understand this vision in different ways: some see it as literal, others as symbolic.

For today: God cares for each of his own and forgets no one. You can trust that He has a place and a purpose for your life, and receive with gratitude what He gives you, without comparing yourself with others.
exp.45:15:
It says that if the prince gives a portion of his property to one of his sons, that gift will belong to his descendants as an inheritance. It will become their property by inheritance. The words "gift," "inheritance," and "property" each name something: a gift is something freely given, an inheritance is the land or property passed down within a family, and property is what someone holds as their own.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, in his vision of the future temple and the life of the people. These rules protect each family's land. What the prince gives to his sons stays within the family, but what he gives to a servant returns to him in the year of liberty. Interpreters differ on whether this vision is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God cares about justice and does not want those who hold power to abuse others. If you have authority, whether at home, at work, or in the church, use it with honesty and take care of what belongs to others.
exp.46:6:
This verse says that Ezekiel, as he came back along the edge of the river, saw a great number of trees along both banks. "Came back" means he returned to where he had been, "banks" are the edges of the water, and the "river" here is the one flowing from the temple. "A great number" means a large quantity.

The one speaking is Ezekiel, who describes a vision God gave him. A guide led him to measure a river that flowed out from the temple and grew deeper and deeper. After he had watched it grow, he returned to the water's edge and saw the trees. Many see in this an image of the life and healing that come from the presence of God, although it is understood in several ways. Some take it literally, others symbolically.

For today: just as trees grow beside water, we can seek God every day in prayer and in his Word. If we stay close to him, our lives can bear fruit and be a blessing to others.
exp.28:16:
This verse gives a date and announces that God spoke again to Ezekiel. It says it came in the twenty-seventh year, on the first day of the first month. "The word of the LORD came to me" means that God's word came to Ezekiel, that is, God spoke to him.

Ezekiel was a prophet among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. This is one of the latest dated messages in the book. It is generally understood that the twenty-seventh year is counted from the exile of King Jehoiachin, which brings us to roughly 571 BC. After this introduction, God speaks about the army of Nebuchadnezzar, which worked hard against Tyre and received almost no pay, and announces that Egypt will be his compensation.

For today: God speaks in his own time and does not forget his promises or his plans. We can approach his Word with patience and confidence, knowing that he is at work even when we do not understand everything right away.
exp.4:5:
God says that Jerusalem turned his ordinances and statutes into wickedness, and that she did so more wickedly than the nations around her. "Rebelled" means openly defied; "ungodly" means living without reverence for God; "rejected" means refused. In other words, they not only drifted away from God, but set aside what he had taught them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier, God had placed Jerusalem at the center of the nations, probably so that his people would be an example of a faithful life. Because they rejected his Word, God announces judgment on the city.

For today: the more we have received from God, the greater our responsibility to obey him. It is worth asking ourselves whether we only hear the Word or whether we truly put it into practice in our daily lives.
exp.19:16:
Ezekiel 20:17 says that, although the people deserved a harsh punishment, God had compassion. "Yet I looked on them with pity" means that God looked on them with mercy. "did not destroy them or bring them to an end in the wilderness" means that he did not completely destroy them, even though they rebelled.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel who are in exile. He reminds them of their history: from Egypt and the wilderness, their ancestors rejected God's laws, broke the Sabbaths, and followed idols. Even so, God did not wipe them out and kept speaking to his children, inviting them to obey him.

For today: God is patient and does not treat us according to what we deserve. His mercy is not an excuse to keep doing the same things, but an invitation to return to him. Today you can respond with gratitude and let go of something that pulls you away from God.
exp.26:26:
This verse says that everything that made Tyre great would go down with her: her wealth, her goods for sale, her sailors, her captains and her shipbuilders, her merchants and even her soldiers. "Wares" means goods offered for sale. The "shipwrights" were the workers who built and repaired the ship's hull. The "merchants" were the people who handled the buying and selling. "Sink into the heart of the sea" means to be swallowed up in the deep ocean.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a rich seafaring city. Ezekiel describes her as a great, beautiful ship sinking in a storm. It is prophetic poetry: it announces that her pride and commercial power would not save her from judgment.

For today: money, success and strength can disappear suddenly. It is worth asking where we have placed our security, and trusting first in God, who does not sink.
exp.5:4:
He says that God will leave the corpses of the people of Israel lying in front of the idols they worshiped, and that their bones will be scattered around their altars. The word "around" in this sentence is the word "round" from the verse, meaning "all around." It is a harsh image: the idols they trusted could not save them, and the places of their false worship will be filled with death.

The passage is spoken by God through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God addresses the mountains of Israel, where the people had set up altars to other gods. He announces judgment by the sword, and the final purpose is that they will know that he is the Lord.

For today: let us ask ourselves what things we place our trust in instead of God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. None of these can save us. Let us return to God with humility, for he wants us to know him and live.
exp.42:21:
On the second day, the priests were to offer a male goat without defect as a sin offering. With this offering the altar would be cleansed, just as it had been cleansed the day before with the bull. "Atonement" means covering over or taking away guilt; "cleanse" means making something clean for the service of God.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of a new temple. After the exile, God gives him instructions for dedicating the altar, over seven days in a row. Interpreters differ on whether this temple would be built literally, whether it is symbolic, or whether it points to something in the future. What is clear is that God desires a holy and clean place where people can draw near to Him.

For today: let us not take lightly sin or the holiness of God. We can come to Him sincerely, confessing what is wrong, and trust that Christ, according to the New Testament, offered the perfect sacrifice that cleanses us.
exp.15:33:
She behaved the opposite of other women who give themselves to prostitution. Normally a prostitute is paid, but she paid her lovers, and no one came looking for her. The lovers she gave herself to are the nations and idols she sought alliances with, and her prostitution stands for her unfaithfulness. In her case, everything was turned around; she was the very opposite of what is expected.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Jerusalem, who were living in exile or on the verge of falling. He uses the image of an unfaithful wife to show how Israel left God, trusted other peoples, and worshiped idols. It is harsh language, meant to awaken their conscience.

For today: examine what you pursue with so much effort, money, or time to feel secure or valued. Return to God, who does not ask you to pay for his love.
exp.44:18:
The verse says that the priest will take some of the blood from the sin offering and put it in three places: on the doorposts of the temple, on the four corners of the ledge of the altar, and on the gateposts of the inner court. "Atonement" means covering or cleansing sin. A doorpost is the upright frame on either side of a door.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of a restored temple. There a cleansing of the sanctuary is described at the beginning of the year. The blood showed that sin is serious and needs to be cleansed. Interpreters differ on whether this vision refers to a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture of the renewal of worship.

For today: Christians believe that Christ offered his blood once for all. We can draw near to God with sincerity, confess our faults and receive his forgiveness, without hiding anything or treating sin lightly.
exp.10:2:
Some leaders of Jerusalem spoke with false confidence. Their words, "Is not the time near to build houses?", suggest that the punishment was not close at hand, so people should keep building and carry on as usual. They said the city was the cooking pot and they were the meat, meaning that inside the city they felt protected.

God himself shows Ezekiel, in a vision, twenty-five men at the east gate of the temple. They were leaders of the people who gave bad counsel. God commands the prophet to speak against them, because He knows what they say and what they think. Scholars debate the exact meaning of the phrase, but the idea of false confidence is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security. If we think that nothing will happen to us, or that God will not call us to account, we deceive ourselves. It is better to listen to his voice with humility and seek his correction in time.
exp.42:13:
This verse gives the measurements of the altar that Ezekiel saw in his vision. It describes the base, which was one cubit high and one cubit wide. From the gutter on the ground up to the lower ledge there are two cubits, and the ledge is one cubit wide. From the smaller ledge up to the larger ledge there are four cubits, and that ledge is also one cubit wide. Ezekiel's readers would have known the cubit as roughly half a meter, so these measurements describe a structure of modest but carefully planned proportions.

God himself shows Ezekiel the new temple and its altar through a guide. The people were exiled in Babylon, and this vision gave them hope: God would once again dwell among them. The precise measurements show that God is orderly, and that worship of him should be carried out with reverence and holiness. How this vision is fulfilled, interpreters debate.

For today: God cares even about the details of how we draw near to him. Come with reverence and sincerity, and remember that Christ has already opened the way for you.
exp.11:23:
He says that God will put an end to false prophecies in Israel. A "false vision" is a vision with no truth behind it, and a "flattering divination" refers to false predictions that only pleased the people, telling them what they wanted to hear even though they did not come from God.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who prophesied among the exiles in Babylon. The people repeated a saying: "the days go on and no vision is fulfilled." In this way they mocked the warnings of judgment. In addition, false prophets gave them comfort with pleasant messages. God answers that his words will be fulfilled soon and that there will no longer be room for those lies.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we seek God's truth or only words that make us feel comfortable. Reading the Bible with humility helps us distinguish what is true, even when it sometimes corrects us.
exp.27:11:
God tells Ezekiel, who is called "son of man," to sing a lament over the king of Tyre. A lament is a song of grief for someone who has died. The phrase "you were the seal of perfection" is difficult, and readers understand it in different ways: as a king who thought of himself as a model of perfection, or as one who appeared complete and without fault. The king is described as full of wisdom and perfect in beauty.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel around 587 B.C., in a message against Tyre, a rich and proud city. The king saw himself as almost a god. Many believers read the verses that follow as describing only a human king in poetic language, while others also see a reflection of the fall of Satan. Interpreters do not agree.

For today: wisdom, talent, and beauty are gifts from God. If they fill us with pride, they will bring us down. Let us receive everything with gratitude and humility.
exp.13:21:
Although the judgment on Jerusalem will be severe, a group of survivors will be left behind, sons and daughters, who will be brought out of the city. Their presence is a sign that God has not wiped out everyone. They will come to the exiles in Babylon, and when the exiles see how these survivors live and act, they will be comforted, understanding that the disaster that fell on Jerusalem had a reason.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was himself among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier in this same chapter, God said that even Noah, Daniel, and Job could not save others by their own righteousness. The exiles believed Jerusalem was suffering without cause. Many readers understand that the conduct of the survivors would make clear that the city had been guilty, though the text gives no further details about this.

For today: when you do not understand pain or correction, do not stay only with your questions. Ask God for humility to see his justice and his mercy, which always leaves open a door of hope.
exp.32:17:
If a person who has been living uprightly turns away from that path and begins to do wrong, that person will face the consequences of that wrongdoing. "Righteous" describes someone who lives according to God's will; "iniquity" means wickedness or injustice; and the phrase "turns from his righteousness" means that he turns away from the path he was on and abandons it.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who serves as a watchman over Israel. The people, living in exile, said that the way of the Lord was not fair, meaning that it was not just. God answers that He judges each person according to how they are living now, and that both forgiveness and consequence depend on where the heart turns. Christians read this alongside other passages about perseverance.

For today: let us not live confident in the good we did yesterday. Each day it is wise to return to God, keep a humble heart, and ask Him for help to keep walking in what is right, without blaming Him when we face the consequences of our decisions.
exp.8:10:
This verse says the man clothed in linen, with the writing kit at his side, went back to report. His reply is brief: "I have done as You commanded." The "writing kit" held the ink and pen that scribes used, and the "linen clothing" is the linen he wore.

In Ezekiel's vision, God ordered this man to mark the foreheads of those who grieved over the wickedness of Jerusalem, so they would be spared from judgment. Afterward, others carried out the punishment. Now the man reports that he has completed his task. God had said the city was full of violence and that the people thought He did not see. The scene shows that He did see, and that He knew who belonged to Him.

For today: God sees both injustice and those who suffer because of it. We can live with sensitivity toward evil, pray with sincerity, and trust that He takes care of His own.
exp.15:48:
This verse tells us what the sin of Sodom was: arrogance, being overfed, and complacency. Sodom and her daughters, the nearby towns, did not help the poor or the needy. "Overfed" means having more than enough to eat. "Complacent" means being comfortable and content with life, without concern for others.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem. She believed herself better than others, but God shows her that her sin was even greater than Sodom's. The passage goes on to say that Sodom also committed abomination, so this verse is not the full list of her sins, but one aspect that God emphasizes here.

For today: when I have more than I need, pride and comfort can harden my heart. Today I can ask myself whom I can help with my time or my resources.
exp.22:48:
God says that the consequences of their wrongdoing will fall back on Oholah and Oholibah. Here "indecency" refers to their shameful and immoral behavior, especially their unfaithfulness. "You will bear the consequences of your sins of idolatry" means they will carry the punishment for worshiping other gods. The final result is that they will know that the Lord is God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Oholah and Oholibah are two symbolic women who represent Samaria and Jerusalem. With this harsh image, God accuses his people of being unfaithful to him by seeking foreign alliances and gods. The chapter shows the judgment on that betrayal. Scholars agree that this is symbolic language, though they debate some details.

Today we can ask ourselves what things are taking God's place in our hearts. Recognizing them with humility and returning to him in time is better than learning through the consequences.
exp.9:21:
This verse says that the living beings Ezekiel now sees in the temple look just like the ones he saw beside the River Kebar at the start of his calling. "Their faces looked like the faces I had seen" means their outward appearance matched exactly what he had seen before. "Each creature went straight ahead" means every one of them moved directly forward, without turning aside.

Ezekiel speaks as a prophet and priest who was exiled in Babylon. In this vision, the glory of God is about to leave the temple in Jerusalem because of the people's idolatry. Ezekiel recognizes that these are cherubim, and that it is the same God who spoke to him in exile. God's presence was not tied to one place.

For today: God remains the same in every place and circumstance. If you feel far from home or are going through a hard time, remember that he is with you, and move forward with purpose, without turning aside. Walk with confidence and with a clear direction.
exp.2:1:
It says that Ezekiel opened his mouth and God fed him a scroll, that is, a rolled-up scroll with messages written on it.
