The sentence that explains the wording "He fed me" in the verse above shows that God was the one who gave the scroll. Ezekiel did not swallow it by force; he opened his mouth in obedience.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. God calls him to be a prophet to a rebellious people. Before speaking, he must receive the message within himself. Eating the scroll is an image: just as food enters the body, God's words must enter the heart. Scholars agree that it is symbolic.

For today: before sharing the Bible with others, let it first nourish you. Read it calmly, obey it, and let it transform your life.
exp.38:19:
God invites the birds and the wild beasts to a great feast. Eating until one is satisfied is what the phrase "to be filled" means here. God's table is the battlefield, and what is eaten are horses, riders, mighty men, and warriors of every kind from the defeated armies.

The Lord GOD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Chapters 38 and 39 describe Gog, an enemy leader who attacks Israel and is defeated by God. The image of the feast is vivid and forceful, and it shows a complete defeat. Interpreters differ: some understand it as something that will literally happen in the future, while others read it as symbolic language of God's final triumph.

For today: God has the last word over all human power, however great it may seem. We can rest in the knowledge that he does justice, leave vengeance in his hands, and trust him when evil seems strong.
exp.19:47:
It says that all people will see that the LORD himself kindled this fire, and that no one will be able to put it out. The phrase "all people" means every human being. "LORD" is the name of the God of Israel.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and tells him to prophesy against "the south forest." Many understand this as a picture of the judgment that would come upon Judah and Jerusalem because of their disobedience. The fire consumes green trees as well as dry ones, meaning no one escapes. Afterward Ezekiel complains that the people do not take him seriously and see him as someone who speaks in riddles. Some believe the fire represents the invasion of Babylon, but the text uses symbolic language.

Today we can remember that God speaks in earnest and that his word is not a mere story. Instead of hardening our hearts or mocking his warnings, we can stop, examine our lives, and turn back to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.38:25:
This verse says that when the people of Israel live peacefully in their land again, they will remember their disgrace and their betrayal of God with shame. The phrase "treachery against Me" in the verse means that they were unfaithful to God. Living "securely" means living without danger. The verse says there will be "no one to frighten them," so they will be at peace, with no one threatening them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel had been taken into captivity because of its idolatry and disobedience, and God explains that this punishment was just. But now he promises to restore them out of mercy and out of concern for his holy name. Some see here the return from Babylon; others, a fulfillment still in the future.

For today: when God forgives and restores us, it is good to remember our failings with humility, not to sink into guilt, but to give thanks for his grace and to live with greater faithfulness.
exp.46:5:
Here the guide asks Ezekiel, "Son of man, do you see this?" That is, "Did you really take in what you have just experienced?" Then he leads Ezekiel back to the bank of the river.

Ezekiel is in a vision of the future temple. A guide, who looks like a man with a measuring reed, leads him along a river that flows out from the temple. At every thousand cubits the waters are deeper, until it can no longer be crossed on foot. The question invites him to reflect before he sees the trees and the healing that come afterward. Some see here a symbol of God's blessing; others expect a literal fulfillment.

For today: do not rush past what God shows you. Stop and meditate, and ask yourself what he is teaching you. His work in us often grows slowly, and he invites us to trust him more deeply.
exp.0:0:
This verse tells us that in the thirtieth year, on the fifth day of the fourth month, Ezekiel was among the exiles by the River Kebar. There the heavens opened, and he saw visions of God. The phrase "among the exiles" describes people taken far from their homeland. The phrase "in the thirtieth year" is not fully explained in the text; some think it refers to Ezekiel's own age, while others think it refers to a different way of counting time.

The one speaking is Ezekiel, a priest who lived in Babylon with the Jewish people who had been carried away from their land. The following verse places him in the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin. God calls him to be a prophet in the middle of a wounded people, far from the temple and from their land.

For today: God is not limited to a beautiful or comfortable place. Even in exile, in sorrow or uncertainty, he can reveal himself and speak to you. Today you can pray with confidence, even when you feel far from home or without direction.
exp.25:13:
God says that Tyre will become a bare, smooth rock, a place where fishermen spread their nets to dry. A "bare rock" is a rock with nothing built on it, and "a place to spread the fishing nets" is a spot where fishing nets are laid out to dry. God adds that the city will never be rebuilt, and he states this with his own authority.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a trading city, rich and proud, which rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking it could profit from it (Ezekiel 26:2). God announces judgment for that pride. Scholars debate how it was fulfilled: some think of Nebuchadnezzar and later Alexander the Great, and others understand it in a broader way.

For today: do not place your security in your riches, and do not rejoice in the misfortune of others. What God affirms remains, and what we build with pride can fall.
exp.33:5:
God says that his sheep wandered and were scattered across the mountains and every high hill, and over the whole surface of the earth. No one went looking for them or asked after them. The phrase "over the face of all the earth" means the surface of the earth. The verse says there was no one to search for them or seek them out, meaning no one looked for them with real concern.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He accuses the leaders of Israel, called shepherds, of caring for themselves and neglecting the people. The sheep are God's people, who were left scattered and exposed to harm because of the lack of good leadership.

For today: God pays attention to those who wander or are hurt. We can ask ourselves who we know that has drifted away or is alone, and seek them out with a phone call, a visit, or a prayer, without waiting for someone else to do it.
exp.43:15:
This verse says that the faithful priests, the sons of Zadok, will be the only ones who may enter God's sanctuary. They will draw near to his table, that is, to the altar where the offerings are presented, in order to minister before him. The phrase about drawing near is explained by the word "approach," and the phrase about keeping God's charge is explained as the duties God gave them to guard.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple. Earlier he had rebuked the Levites who went astray after idols. By contrast, he rewards the descendants of Zadok, who remained faithful when Israel turned away. Interpreters disagree about whether this vision will be fulfilled literally or symbolically.

For today: God values faithfulness when almost no one practices it. We can ask ourselves what God asks of our lives and obey him steadily, even when others drift away. Drawing near to him is both a privilege and a responsibility.
exp.17:23:
This verse says that if a person who has been living uprightly turns away from their good path and commits wrongdoing, doing the same detestable things the wicked do, they cannot count on their past goodness. The word "unfaithfulness" in the verse points to betraying or failing in one's duty. "He will die" speaks of the consequence of turning away from God; many understand it as physical death or separation from God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel in Babylon. They were saying that God was unjust and blaming their ancestors for their suffering. God answers that each person is accountable for their own way, and that He takes no pleasure in anyone's death, but desires that all turn back to Him.

For today: do not live on yesterday's faith. Keep your heart close to God every day, and if you have strayed, return to Him, because His mercy remains open.
exp.23:5:
God declares a "woe" against Jerusalem, called "the city of bloodshed," meaning a city full of violence and death. He compares it to a pot whose rust was never scrubbed off, and that rust will not come off. God commands that the meat be emptied out "piece by piece," with no casting of lots, that is, without picking out who is spared and who is not: judgment will reach everyone.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel, while Jerusalem is under siege by Babylon, around 588 BC. The pot is a parable: the city and its inhabitants will be put into the fire. Their sin was not hidden; the blood spilled was in plain sight, like blood on bare rock.

For today: let us not minimize or hide our faults. Let us ask God to cleanse us, and seek justice and compassion toward others.
exp.15:62:
This verse says that Jerusalem will remember her wrongdoing and feel ashamed. Because of this, she will no longer have anything to say in her own defense or to boast about. This will happen when God makes atonement for all she has done. The phrase "make atonement" means that God makes things right and covers her guilt. Having no way to boast or make excuses is what it means to be unable to speak up for oneself.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem, who was unfaithful to him like a wife who betrays her husband. After announcing judgment, God promises to restore her and confirm his covenant. The forgiveness is not based on what she deserves, but on God's faithfulness.

For today: when God forgives you, remember your failures without being crushed by them, and let his grace make you humble. In this way you stop making excuses or boasting, and you can treat with mercy those who also fail.
exp.19:48:
Here Ezekiel speaks with God and complains. He says "Ah, Lord GOD!" like someone sighing in worry. He tells that the people are saying of him, "Is he not just telling parables?" That is, they think he is only telling stories with figurative language that no one needs to understand or take seriously.

God has just given him a message about a fire that would burn a forest, an image that probably refers to the judgment on Judah and the land of the south. Ezekiel, a prophet in exile, fears that the people will not take him seriously and will dismiss him as a storyteller. In the Hebrew text this verse is 21:5, and that is where the clarification in the next chapter comes from.

For today: when people reject or ridicule the truth you share, bring it to God honestly, as Ezekiel did, and stay faithful without depending on their approval.
exp.43:2:
It says that only the prince may sit inside the gateway, the eastern gate that is kept shut, to eat in the presence of the Lord. He must come in through the portico of the gateway from the outer court and leave the same way. "Bread" here means a meal eaten before God, probably a holy meal or a sacrificial meal.

The Lord speaks, and Ezekiel hears it in a vision of the new temple (chapters 40 to 48). The gate stays shut because the glory of God entered through it. Interpreters differ on who the prince is and on whether the temple is literal, symbolic, or prophetic. What is clear is that God is holy and sets the way we draw near to Him.

For today: draw near to God with reverence and gratitude. Even those who hold authority live under God's order, and eating in the presence of the Lord reminds us that we can live each day aware of His presence.
exp.28:10:
It says that Egypt will be so empty and ruined that no one will pass through its land, neither person nor animal, and that it will be uninhabited for forty years. "No foot of man or beast will pass through" means that no person or animal will travel through it. "Uninhabited" means that no one will live there. "Ruined" means left in ruins or destroyed.

The passage records God speaking through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Egypt had considered itself very powerful, and the pharaoh claimed that the Nile River was his. God answers that he is the true Lord. Scholars debate whether these forty years were literal or symbolic, since history does not clearly confirm it. The text goes on to say that God would later gather Egypt back together.

For today: let us not place our security in what we have, such as money, success, or strength. All of that can fall. Let us place our trust in God, who sustains all things and also knows how to restore.
exp.30:2:
The verse describes Assyria as a cedar in Lebanon: beautiful, with lovely branches that shaded the forest, very tall, with its top reaching up among the clouds.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He tells him to warn the king of Egypt, who was proud of his greatness. God asks him what he is to be compared with, and he holds up Assyria as an example, a powerful empire that had already fallen. Some scholars doubt whether the original text says "Assyrian" or refers to a different tree, but the message is the same: if Assyria fell, Egypt will fall too.

For today: everything we have, whether strength, success or influence, comes from God, so there is no reason for pride. Whoever thinks himself invincible can fall; whoever lives in humility before God remains firm.
exp.40:3:
Here the guide measures the room next to the innermost sanctuary of the temple. He measures it as twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, a perfect square. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers. Then the guide says to Ezekiel, "This is the Most Holy Place," the most sacred room, where the presence of God was symbolized.

Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon, receives a vision of a new temple, and a man shows him each measurement. It is Ezekiel who tells what he sees. Interpreters do not agree on its meaning: some think of a literal future temple, others of a spiritual picture of God's hope to be with his people. For the exiles, it was a promise that God had not forgotten them.

Today we can remember that God is holy, but he also wants to be close to his people. Set aside a quiet moment each day to pray, with reverence and trust.
exp.11:20:
This verse is a transition phrase. "Again the word of the LORD came to me" means: "God spoke to me again." It is the way Ezekiel signals that a new message is beginning.

Ezekiel speaks here as a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God has just announced that Jerusalem will suffer for its wickedness. Now a response begins to a popular saying, by which people claimed that the prophet's visions would never come true or would take far too long.

For today: God does not stay silent, and his word deserves attention, not mockery or delay. We can ask ourselves whether we are putting off what God has already told us. Today is a good day to listen and to obey with humility.
exp.29:11:
God says he will dry up the streams of Egypt, that is, take away the source of its wealth and its life. He will hand the land over to the wicked (violent and cruel people), and by the hands of foreigners he will bring desolation upon it and everything in it. The phrase "everything in it" refers to all that the land holds. Finally, God declares, "I, the LORD, have spoken."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The message announces judgment on Egypt, which was proud and trusted in the Nile and in its idols. The text says that God would use Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, as the instrument of that judgment.

For today: what seems most secure, such as money, power, or prestige, cannot replace God. Today we can ask ourselves where we are placing our trust, and return to rest in him.
exp.20:7:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel again. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to me" is used many times by the prophet to announce that he is about to receive new instructions from God.

Here Ezekiel is speaking, and the one addressing him is God. He has just been told to groan with grief before the people, as a sign of the tragedy approaching Jerusalem. Now God continues with another message: the image of the sharp sword is introduced, which represents judgment. Some understand that sword to refer to the army of Babylon, and the Bible itself makes this clear later in the chapter.

For today: God continues to speak through his Word. Before acting or offering opinions, it is good to pause and listen humbly to what he says, even when the message is not easy to hear.
exp.15:21:
Ezekiel 16:22 describes Jerusalem, with all her idolatry and acts of prostitution, forgetting what she was at the beginning. "The days of your youth" means the time when she was young. She was "naked and bare" and "wallowing in your own blood": weak, without help, and with no worth of her own, like a newborn baby left abandoned in a field.

God speaks here through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16 he uses the image of an abandoned girl whom he finds, cares for, and makes his wife. Then she is unfaithful to him with other gods, and even sacrifices her children. God reminds her of her origin to show her the seriousness of her ingratitude.

For today: remembering where God rescued us from keeps us humble and thankful. When we forget his grace, it is easy to feel self-sufficient and to look for security in other things. Today you can give thanks for one specific way God has helped you.
exp.43:9:
The verse says that the Levites who wandered away from God when Israel went astray, following after their idols, will bear the consequences of their wrongdoing. "Bear their iniquity" means they will answer for their guilt.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a vision about the new temple. He rebukes Israel for having brought foreigners with no commitment to him to serve in his sanctuary. The Levites who failed are not destroyed, but they lose their closest service: they remain as gatekeepers and assistants. Some interpreters see here discipline mixed with mercy, since they continue to serve.

Today: whoever leads or serves others carries greater responsibility. If we have gone astray, God invites us to acknowledge it and return, even though at times the consequences remain while we continue serving with humility.
exp.40:11:
It says that, on the west side of the temple, there was another separate building that measured seventy cubits wide. Its walls were five cubits thick all around, and its length was ninety cubits. The phrase "temple courtyard" refers to the open ground set apart around the temple. A cubit was an ancient measure, about 45 to 50 centimeters.

Ezekiel recounts what he saw in a vision, while a guide who looked like a man measured the temple for him. He was among the exiles in Babylon. Scholars debate whether this vision speaks of a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture of God's presence and his order among his people. The details of this verse are difficult to interpret with certainty.

God cares about order, holiness, and his presence among his people. Today we can ask ourselves whether there is a cared-for and set-apart place for him in our lives. Setting aside a fixed time each day to pray and read his Word is a simple step.
exp.29:3:
A sword will come against Egypt, and the land will be filled with fear and anguish, reaching even to Cush to the south. When the slain fall in Egypt, its wealth will be carried away and its foundations torn down. The Hebrew name Cush refers to the region south of Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. It is a message of judgment against Egypt, described as "the day of the LORD." The next chapter indicates that Babylon would be the instrument of this judgment (30:10). Egypt had been an unreliable support for Judah, and its pride would fall.

For today: no human strength, no money, no power, no alliances make a secure foundation. Ask yourself what you are leaning your life on, and trust first in God, who stands firm when everything else falls.
exp.14:7:
God says that he will leave the land turned into ruins and desolation. "Desolation" means total destruction, an empty and devastated place. "Acted unfaithfully" means breaking faith with someone to whom you owe loyalty, like failing to keep a sacred promise. The phrase "I will make" simply means "I will turn" or "I will bring about."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the people's exile in Babylon. Earlier, he compared Jerusalem to the wood of a vine, which is useless for building anything and is used only as firewood. Jerusalem was not producing the fruit of faithfulness that God expected, and so judgment would come. God makes it clear that the cause was the people's unfaithfulness toward him.

For today: God expects our lives to bear the fruit of faithfulness, not just outward appearance. Today you can ask yourself, in prayer, where you have been unfaithful to God, and return to him with sincerity, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.6:16:
This verse says that fear and weakness will overcome everyone. "Every hand will go limp" means the hands will lose their strength and grip, as if they had been knocked out of place. And "every knee will turn to water" describes knees that tremble and give way, like water that spills and cannot hold its shape.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Judah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. He announces judgment for their idolatry and their wickedness. Before that judgment, neither strength nor wealth will be able to save them, as the verses that follow show.

For today: let us not place our security in money or in our own strength, because they fail. It is better to turn back to God now with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.21:26:
This verse says that the officials of Jerusalem were like wolves tearing their prey. By shedding blood and destroying lives, they were seeking only to enrich themselves. The word "prey" in the verse is what their greed fed on. "Lives" here refers to people, to human beings.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God denounces the sins of Jerusalem: prophets, priests, officials, and people had failed. Those who were meant to care for and guide others were taking advantage of them. For that reason, judgment was coming upon the city.

For today: if you have some authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, ask yourself whether you are using it to serve or to profit. God expects those who lead to care for people, not to use them. Ask Him for a just and generous heart.
exp.22:19:
Here the prophet describes Aholibah, who represents Jerusalem, lusting after her "lovers," the foreign nations who had used her. The comparison to donkeys and stallions is deliberately blunt. It speaks of a desire that is unrestrained and almost animal in nature, and it points to the strength and power of the nations that attracted her.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of two unfaithful sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, to show how his people abandoned God and sought security in Egypt and other powers. The language is harsh so that the people would feel the seriousness of their betrayal. Scholars agree that this is a symbolic image, though they differ on the details.

For today: examine the things in which you place your trust apart from God, such as money, prestige, or powerful people. Return to Him sincerely, because only He truly sustains you.
exp.17:24:
They said that some in Israel were complaining that God was not just. The word "unjust" means that their ways are not fair or right. God answers with a question: is it really his way that is unjust, or are the ways of the people the ones that are unjust? The word "hear" is an invitation to listen carefully.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The people said they were suffering for the sins of their fathers and that God was not just. God makes clear to them that each person answers for himself, and that He wants the sinner to turn back and live, not to die.

When something goes wrong, it is easy to blame God or others. This verse invites us to examine our own hearts honestly. God always leaves the door open to repentance, and we can return to Him today.
exp.23:3:
God tells Ezekiel to put the pieces of meat into the pot, every good piece, the thigh and the shoulder, and to fill it with the choice bones. The pieces are chunks of meat, and everything that goes into the pot is the best.

God speaks through Ezekiel to a rebellious people, on the day Babylon began to besiege Jerusalem. The pot is a parable of the city: the people of Jerusalem believed they were safe, but the fire of judgment was already lit. The best cuts may represent its important inhabitants, though scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: let us not trust in our position, our strength, or our good appearances to feel secure. When God calls us to turn back to Him, it is best to respond quickly, with humility and repentance.
exp.33:28:
He says God will raise up for his people "a garden of renown," meaning something famous and fruitful that flourishes and bears good things. Because of it, the people will no longer suffer famine in their land, nor bear the scorn of the nations. To "raise up" here means to bring forth or set up. The "nations" are the foreign peoples.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during Israel's exile in Babylon. Earlier he has criticized the bad shepherds who neglected the sheep, and he promises to be their Shepherd himself. Many Christians see in this "garden" a sign of the Messiah, such as Jesus; others understand it as the prosperity God would give his people. Both ideas can coexist, but the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: when you feel empty or ashamed, remember that God cares for his own. You can bring that burden to him in prayer and trust that he knows how to sustain you and restore your hope.
exp.22:34:
God is speaking to Jerusalem, which the prophet calls Aholibah, because she has forgotten Him and turned her back on Him. To "cast Him behind your back" means to ignore Him and treat Him with contempt. The words "indecency" and "prostitution" describe her spiritual unfaithfulness, which means chasing after idols. That is why God says she must now bear the consequences of that conduct.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. In chapter 23, Samaria (Aholah) and Jerusalem (Aholibah) are presented as two unfaithful sisters. Samaria had already fallen, and Jerusalem, instead of learning from this, followed the same path. The language is harsh, but it shows the pain of a broken covenant.

For today: when I notice that God has been pushed to the background, I can return to Him without delay. A simple practice is to begin the day by speaking with God before attending to anything else.
exp.13:5:
God tells the people of Israel, through Ezekiel: "Repent and turn away from your idols; turn your faces away from all your abominations." To "turn away" means changing direction, and "abominations" are practices that God detests.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some leaders of the people came to consult God, but they carried idols in their hearts. God answers them that it is not enough to appear faithful; first they must truly return to Him. His call is an invitation to restore the relationship.

Today we can ask ourselves what thing occupies in our heart the place that belongs to God: money, success, the opinion of others, or something else. Before asking Him for direction, let us prepare our heart, acknowledge that thing before Him, and decide to turn away from it with His help.
exp.26:30:
This verse describes very intense signs of mourning. "They will shave their heads for you" means they will cut off their hair as a sign of grief. "Wrap themselves in sackcloth" means they will dress in rough cloth worn to show mourning. "They will weep over you with anguish of soul and bitter mourning" describes crying out in lament, full of deep sorrow.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a funeral song about Tyre, a seafaring city very rich from its trade. The sailors and the pilots, who lived by the sea and their business, mourn its fall. It is poetic language: Tyre is pictured as a great ship that is sinking. The passage shows that a nation's pride and wealth are not safe before God.

For today: do not put your security in money, success, or prestige, because all of that can disappear. Trust instead in God, who always endures, and use what you have with humility and generosity.
exp.41:5:
The verse says that the chambers of this temple building were arranged in three stories, and unlike the courts, they had no pillars. Because of this, the upper rooms were set back further than the lower and middle floors. The galleries, or passages, took up part of the space, so the upper floors were narrower. The phrase about the building being seen from the ground likely refers to the fact that the difference in width could be noticed from the base of the building.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, describes a vision that God gave him during the exile in Babylon. A guide shows him the new temple and its chambers, with exact measurements, chambers that were used by the priests. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic message of hope and restoration.

For today: God cares about the details and wants His presence to be holy and orderly. We can ask Him to bring order into our lives, even in small things, so that we may live near Him with reverence and hope.
exp.41:11:
This verse says that the chambers on the south side of the temple had a door in front of the walkway, next to the wall that runs eastward, through which people entered. It explains that "south" refers to the southern side, and that the walkway was the path running alongside the building. The south chambers matched those on the north.

Ezekiel recounts a vision of the temple that a guide shows him while the people live in exile in Babylon. The guide explains that these chambers were holy: there the priests ate the offerings and changed their clothes before going back out to the people. Interpreters disagree about whether this temple would be built literally or whether it is symbolic.

For today: God cares that what is holy be treated with respect and order. Before serving others, we can pause for a moment to pray and prepare ourselves with a clean and humble heart.
exp.31:0:
This verse marks the moment when God speaks to Ezekiel again. It says that it happened in the twelfth year, on the first day of the twelfth month. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to me" means "I received a message from God." It is only the introduction to a new prophecy.

The one speaking is the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon along with other Jews. He tells that God gave him a message, and in the verses that follow that message is a lament against Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Many understand that the date corresponds to about twelve years after the deportation of King Jehoiachin, although scholars do not always agree on the exact calculation.

For today: God speaks at specific moments and does not forget history. You can trust that He sees the pride of the powerful and cares for His people. Take time to listen to His Word with attention.
exp.36:3:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to speak to some dry bones as if they could hear. "Prophesy" here means to announce what God says. "Hear" means "listen," and "LORD" is the name of God. The command seems absurd, because bones do not hear, but God asks that his word be spoken to them.

God is speaking, showing Ezekiel a vision of a valley full of bones. According to the same chapter, those bones represent Israel, a discouraged people in exile who felt they had lost all hope. God wants to teach that he can give them back their life and restore them.

For today: when a situation seems hopeless, whether in your family, your faith, or your spirit, do not just stand there looking at the dryness. Read and declare the word of God with faith, and ask him to do what you cannot do.
exp.7:3:
It says that Ezekiel saw there the glory of God, that is, his radiant and majestic presence. It was like the vision he had seen before "in the plain," probably by the river Chebar (chapters 1 to 3).

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, tells what God showed him in a vision: he was carried to Jerusalem. There the glory of God was still present, yet the people practiced idolatry in the very temple. God shows him these abominations to explain why judgment would come.

For today: God is holy and near, even when we have turned away. We can sincerely ask him whether there is something in our lives that we have put in his place, and return to him with humility.
exp.16:19:
God says he will throw his net over the king, the way a hunter catches an animal, and the king will be trapped in the snare. He will be brought to Babylon, and there God will execute judgment on him for the treason he committed against God, which means breaking his word and failing to keep a solemn commitment by rebelling against God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He is referring to King Zedekiah of Judah, who had sworn loyalty to the king of Babylon in God's name and then broke that oath by seeking help from Egypt. For God, breaking that oath was a way of despising his own name.

For today: When we give our word, God takes it seriously. Try to keep your promises, at work, in your family, and in the church, and if you fail, acknowledge it with humility and ask for forgiveness.
exp.46:14:
This describes the northern border of the promised land. The line begins at the Great Sea, which is the Mediterranean Sea, and runs by way of Hethlon through Lebo-hamath until it reaches Zedad. The verse uses "boundary" for the edge or limit of the land. These are places in the north of Israel, and today it is not known with certainty where all of them were.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In a vision of restoration, the Lord marks the limits of the land he will divide among the twelve tribes. He reminds them that he swore to give it to their fathers. That promise still stands, even though the people have gone through exile. Scholars disagree about whether this vision should be understood literally or symbolically.

For today: God keeps his promises in detail, even in what seems small. You can trust that he is faithful to you, and you can thank him for what he has given you.
exp.27:8:
It says the king of Tyre thought himself a god, but when the enemy comes to kill him, it will be seen that he is only a man. The question is a mockery: will you still say "I am a god" in the presence of the ones who take your life?

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The king of Tyre, proud of his wisdom and his riches, had set himself in God's place. God announces that he will bring foreign peoples, strong and cruel, to humble him. In the hands of those who wound him, he will be shown to be nothing more than a man.

For today: pride deceives us and makes us believe we control everything. We can remember that we are creatures, that we depend on God every day, and ask him for humility so that we do not trust only in our talent, money, or success.
exp.44:19:
It says that on the seventh day of the first month the ceremony of cleansing the temple should be repeated. This time it is for anyone who strays unintentionally or in ignorance, that is, for those who sinned without meaning to, through carelessness, or because they were led down the wrong path. Making atonement means cleansing or covering guilt through a sacrifice.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of the future temple and worship (chapters 40 to 48). Before this verse, on the first day, the sanctuary was purified with the blood of a young bull. This second purification includes sins committed unintentionally. Interpreters differ on whether this vision describes something literal, symbolic, or yet to be fulfilled; the Bible does not fully clarify this.

For today: God is also concerned with our hidden or unintentional faults. We can pray with humility, "Search me, Lord," and trust that his forgiveness reaches us too.
exp.38:17:
This verse says that birds and wild animals will be invited to a great feast. They will eat the flesh of powerful warriors and drink the blood of the leaders of the earth, as though those leaders were rams, lambs, goats, and bulls. Those animals are pictures of the strong men being defeated. Bashan was a region known for its fine livestock, and the phrase "fattened animals of Bashan" points to the best and richest animals of that land.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces the total defeat of Gog and his armies, who would attack Israel. Many understand these images as strong symbolic language to show that God judges those who rise against his people. Interpreters differ on whether this is fulfilled in a historical event or in a future time.

For today: we can rest in the fact that God is just and has the final word. Faced with the violence and pride of the powerful, trust that He governs, and leave judgment in his hands.
exp.37:6:
God speaks to Gog and tells him: "Get ready; prepare yourself, you and all your company gathered around you." He also says, "you will be their guard," meaning that Gog is to be their protector and leader.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He announces that a great alliance of nations will attack Israel, a people gathered again in their land. The tone is ironic: God himself directs the scene, and those who think they are strong are in fact under his control. Scholars debate whether this passage refers to historical events, to something in the future, or to a symbol of evil rising against God's people.

For today: even when evil seems organized and powerful, it does not have the final word. Today you can rest in the knowledge that God governs history, and pray with confidence when you feel fear for the world or for your own life.
exp.26:33:
Tyre, the great seafaring city, is told that the seas will shatter her, down in the depths of the waters. Her merchandise will go down with her, and so will the people who were part of her trade: the sailors, merchants and partners who sailed with her. The word "lamentations" in the original refers to sad funeral songs, and the same idea of sorrow runs through this section.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is living in exile in Babylon. This chapter is a poetic lament over Tyre, famous for its wealth and its trade. Using the image of a sunken ship, it announces that her pride and her power will not save her. Many read the sinking as a picture of total collapse; exactly how it happened is understood in different ways.

For today: wealth and success can disappear quickly. It is worth asking where we are placing our security. We can work with effort and honesty, but our trust belongs in God, not in what we have.
exp.13:18:
This verse speaks of a third judgment: a plague, or deadly disease, that God would send upon a land. "Pour out my wrath upon it through bloodshed" means a punishment that brings death, and "cutting off" means removing or destroying, as one cuts down a tree. It would affect both people and animals.

God speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, to the exiles of Judah in Babylon. The leaders of the people kept idols in their hearts and yet still sought God. He warns that when a people becomes corrupt, not even the prayers of righteous men like Noah, Daniel, and Job would save others; only they themselves would be saved. Commentators debate why he mentions Daniel, but the central message is clear.

Today: the faith of others, though valuable, does not replace my own relationship with God. Let us examine whether there is anything we love more than Him, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.21:21:
This verse compares Jerusalem to silver placed in a furnace. Just as fire melts metal, God says his people will be melted within the city, meaning they will go through a harsh judgment. "I have poured out my wrath" means that God would let his punishment fall upon them. The result would be that they would recognize that the LORD is the one who acts.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the time when Jerusalem was heading toward its fall. Shortly before, God describes Israel as dross, that is, worthless residue left when metals are melted down. The people were full of violence, injustice and idolatry, and God announces the consequences.

For today: let us not take sin or God's patience lightly. If the Lord corrects us, let us humble ourselves quickly and return to him, before our hearts grow hard.
exp.2:9:
God tells Ezekiel to first take in what He is going to say to him. "Son of man" is a way of addressing him as a frail human being. "Listen carefully to all the words I speak to you" means to hear closely, and "take them to heart" means to keep and ponder them deep within.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who was among the exiles in Babylon. Just before, God promises to strengthen him so that he would not fear a people who refused to listen. Then He commands him to go to the exiles and speak to them, whether or not they listen. First he had to take the message in himself.

For today: before speaking of God to others, set aside time to read the Bible and reflect on it calmly, letting it first change your own heart.
exp.20:13:
God tells Ezekiel to deliver a message and to strike his hands together, a gesture that shows strong emotion. The sword is to strike two times, even three, meaning it will hit again and again with full force. It is a sword that slays, a sword of great slaughter closing in from every side. Its reach extends into the innermost places, so that no one will be able to escape.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. The people and their leaders had rejected God, and judgment would come by the sword of Babylon. Interpreters explain the gesture of the hands and the repeated striking of the sword in different ways, but the general meaning is a severe and certain judgment.

For today: God speaks seriously about sin, but he also gives warnings so that we will return to him. Today we can listen to his voice with humility and correct our course before it is too late.
exp.25:6:
God announces that he is going to bring Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, against the city of Tyre. He comes from the north, and he is called "king of kings" because he ruled over other kings. He arrives with a full army: horses, chariots, cavalry, a great company of troops, and many people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a wealthy city, proud of its trade, and it had rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem (Ezekiel 26:2). God declares that he will judge that pride and that lack of compassion. Babylon would be the instrument of that judgment.

For today: God rules over the nations and the powerful, even when they do not acknowledge him. For that reason it is wise to avoid pride and not to rejoice in the misfortune of others. We can trust that God is just and that he is in control.
exp.11:14:
This verse says that God will make the people come to know who he is. This will happen when he disperses them among the nations and scatters them throughout the countries. The word "scatter" means to throw or spread out in every direction. Here "disperse" means to distribute across the land. The "nations" are the peoples and foreign lands.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The message announces judgment on Jerusalem and its king, who would be captured and taken to Babylon. Many understand this to refer to King Zedekiah. The people had lived in rebellion, and God warns that the punishment would make them recognize that he is the LORD. God leaves some survivors so that they can tell what happened.

For today: sometimes we only recognize God when our plans fall apart. We do not need to wait for that moment. We can listen to him today, correct our course with humility, and trust that his discipline seeks to bring us close to him.
exp.6:5:
It says that the end is coming without fail. The phrase is repeated for emphasis: "The end has come! The end has come!" The point is that the end has risen up and is coming straight against the people, like something that stirs itself and moves toward them. "Behold, it has come!" is a warning: it is already on its way.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. He addresses the land of Israel, which had fallen into idolatry and into practices that God calls "abominations." Many understand that he announces the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. God warns that the judgment is just, since it answers to the people's ways, and that it will not be a surprise without explanation.

Today we can take God's warnings seriously and not mistake his patience for indifference. If there is something in your life that you know does not please him, do not put it off. Return to him sincerely, because his mercy remains open to whoever repents.
exp.35:12:
This verse says that God speaks to the mountains of Israel, which stand for the land itself. The neighboring nations said to the land, "You devour men and deprive your nation of its children," meaning a land that consumes its own people and leaves its nation without offspring.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The land had been left empty by war and punishment, and the enemy peoples mocked it. God promises to bring Israel back, to make the land bear fruit again, and to take away that shame. Some understand the promise as fulfilled in part by the return from exile, while others also see a future fulfillment.

Today, when someone puts a humiliating label on you because of your failures, remember that God does not define you by that. He knows how to restore and to give a new beginning. Bring your shame to Him in prayer.
exp.22:46:
The passage says that a mob will come against these women. They will be stoned and cut down with swords, their sons and daughters will be killed, and their houses will be burned. "Cut down" means to strike or kill with a blade. "The mob" refers to a crowd or an army.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The two women, Oholah and Oholibah, represent Samaria and Jerusalem, which were unfaithful to God by seeking alliances with other nations and by worshiping idols. The language is harsh and symbolic, and it announces the judgment that would come with the Babylonian invasion. The punishment follows what the law prescribed for adultery.

For today: God takes faithfulness seriously. It is worth asking ourselves what things are occupying the place that belongs to Him, and returning to Him sincerely before those things destroy us.
exp.21:17:
God tells Ezekiel that the people of Israel have become dross to him. Dross is the worthless waste that rises off a metal when it is melted and refined. Although they are all like copper, tin, iron and lead, which are common metals, in the furnace they are only the waste of silver and not silver itself. "Has become to me" means "has turned into."

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. God accuses Israel of corruption and sin, and announces that he will gather his people in Jerusalem, as someone gathers metals into a furnace, to submit them to the fire of judgment and purify them.

For today: it is not enough to look valuable on the outside. We can ask God to examine our hearts and cleanse us, humbly accepting his corrections, because his goal is that we be pure and not that we be lost.
exp.19:42:
God says that when the people return to their land, they will remember there their wrong ways and all the deeds that made them unclean before God. The word "defiled" means they were stained by their sins. The phrase "you will loathe yourselves for all the evils you have done" means they will feel shame when they see themselves honestly.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Israel, who was in exile. Earlier he reviewed the people's long rebellion. Now he promises to bring them back and accept them. This shame is not the final punishment but the fruit of his grace, for the following verse says that God acts for the sake of his name, not because of their merits.

For today: when God shows you your failures, do not run away or sink into guilt. Acknowledge them honestly, for his forgiveness and his kindness are greater than your sin.
exp.4:10:
God swears by his own life that he is going to punish Jerusalem. The reason is that the people defiled his sanctuary, the temple, with their detestable idols and abominations, that is, with the things God hates. So he declares that he himself will withdraw his favor from them, that he will not look on them with pity and will not spare them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. Before the fall of Jerusalem, the people had mixed the worship of the LORD with idolatry. The punishment was not sudden: God had warned them many times. The verses that follow describe the siege of the city, with famine, war and scattering.

For today: God takes the purity of our worship seriously. We can ask ourselves what things occupy in our hearts the place that belongs to him, and return to him soon, while there is still time to repent.
exp.40:16:
It says the guide also measured the space above the entrance to the inner sanctuary, and the walls all around the inner and outer sanctuary, spaced evenly on every side. The phrase "above the outside of the entrance" means the space directly over the doorway on the outer side. "Spaced evenly" means the measurements were taken with equal care all the way around.

Ezekiel speaks of a vision God gave him. A man who looked like bronze guides him and measures every part of a new temple. The Jewish people were in exile, and this vision showed them that God had not forgotten them and that his presence matters. Scholars disagree about whether it describes a literal future temple or a symbolic picture.

For today: God cares about details, and nothing in his house is careless. We can draw near to him with order, reverence, and attention, and trust that he also cares about the details of our lives.
exp.10:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel and points out some men to him. The phrase "plot evil" means planning wrongdoing with cunning. The second phrase, "give wicked counsel," means leading others down a mistaken path. God identifies these men as responsible for what is happening in Jerusalem.

God is speaking, and Ezekiel is in a vision, carried by the Spirit to the east gate of the temple. There he sees twenty-five men, among them two leaders of the people. According to the context that follows, they were saying that it was not a time to worry and that houses should be built, as if Jerusalem were a safe pot. God confronts them about their false sense of security.

For today: those who advise others, whether in the family, the church, or the workplace, should ask God for wisdom. Advice that soothes the conscience but ignores the truth ends up doing harm.
exp.21:14:
God says that he will scatter Jerusalem among the nations, the way someone winnows grain to separate the chaff from the wheat. The word "purge" means to cleanse thoroughly and remove what does not belong, and "uncleanness" refers to moral impurity. God promises to clear away the people's wickedness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier he had accused Jerusalem of violence, injustice, and greed. This announcement of judgment aims to remove the sin of the people. The following verse shows the purpose: that they may know that he is the LORD.

For today: let us not minimize sin or hide it. God wants to cleanse us, and sometimes that involves painful correction. We can humbly ask him to show us what we need to leave behind, and respond with sincere repentance.
exp.39:44:
The guide shows Ezekiel a room in the inner court, the one that faces south. That room is set aside for the priests who are in charge of caring for the temple. A "chamber" is a room or hall, and "south" tells us the direction the room faces. The phrase "who keep charge of the temple" means they are responsible for caring for and watching over the house.

Ezekiel is in a vision, about twenty-five years after the fall of Jerusalem. A man who looks like bronze leads him and measures the temple. Each space has a purpose. Here a distinction is made between those who care for the temple and those who serve at the altar. Scholars disagree about whether this temple would be built literally or whether it is symbolic.

For today: God values faithful service, whether visible or quiet. There are those who care for, order, and sustain the life of the church without applause. Ask yourself what task you can do steadily, as for the Lord.
exp.46:17:
Here God describes the east boundary of the land Israel would receive. The border would run between the regions of Hauran and Damascus, and between Gilead and the land of Israel, following the Jordan River to the Eastern Sea and as far as Tamar. The phrase "the border will run" describes how the line would be marked out on the ground. The "Eastern Sea" is usually understood to be the Dead Sea, although some interpret it in other ways.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision about the restoration of his people after the exile. He divides the land with clear and fair boundaries for the twelve tribes. Scholars disagree: some see here a literal fulfillment in the future, while others see a spiritual picture of the kingdom of God.

For today: God is interested in the details of our lives and keeps his promises with order. We can trust that he knows how to give us what we need and to set good limits for our lives.
exp.42:20:
This verse says that the bull offered for sin was to be taken away and burned in an appointed part of the temple area, outside the sanctuary. "Atonement" means covering or removing the guilt of sin. "According to the law of the house" means according to the rules given for the temple.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of a new temple. There it is described how the altar would be consecrated so that the people could worship again. The priests descended from Zadok would carry out the service. Scholars understand this vision in different ways: some as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of God's holiness and of restoration.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but He also provides a way of cleansing. We can come to Him with sincerity, and Christians remember that Christ offered the final sacrifice for us (Hebrews 13:11-12).
exp.15:14:
Jerusalem, pictured as a woman, stopped trusting in God and put her confidence in her own beauty and fame. Here "played the harlot" means being unfaithful, giving herself to others instead of remaining faithful to her husband. Her fame led her to throw herself at anyone who came along. In the BSB, her favors were lavished on everyone who passed by, and her beauty was theirs for the asking.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of a wife who was rescued, adorned, and enriched by her husband, but who used those gifts to betray him. It is a way of showing how Jerusalem abandoned God for idols and alliances with other nations, forgetting that her beauty and prosperity came from Him.

Today we can ask ourselves what blessings, talents, or achievements make us feel secure. Everything good comes from God. Let us thank Him and use His gifts to honor Him, not to trust in ourselves.
exp.22:44:
The passage says that righteous men will sentence Aholah and Aholibah to the punishment given to those who commit adultery and those who shed blood. The two sisters are being judged for both, which is why God accuses them of being adulteresses who have blood on their hands.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he uses the story of two sisters, Aholah and Aholibah, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem. They had given themselves to other nations and to their idols, forgetting their covenant with God. Some understand the "righteous men" to be nations that God would use as an instrument of judgment, though the text gives no further detail.

For today: God expects total faithfulness, not a divided heart. Today we can ask ourselves what things we are giving to the place that belongs to Him alone, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.17:16:
He says that the son who withholds his hand from harming the poor, who takes no interest or usury, and who keeps God's ordinances and follows His statutes, will not die for his father's iniquity. He will surely live. "Withholding his hand from harming the poor" means not mistreating them. Taking interest or usury from someone who needs help is the wrong being described. Keeping God's ordinances and following His statutes is what is meant here.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. They were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their ancestors. God answers that each person is accountable for his own life. Some interpret "die" as physical death, and others as separation from God; the text allows both ideas to be seen.

For today: do not live tied to the mistakes of your family. With God's help you can choose another path, treating those in need with justice and generosity.
exp.38:15:
The verse says there will be a city named Hamonah, which means "multitude," and that in this way the land will be cleansed. The cleansing refers to burying the dead so that the country is not left in a state of defilement. Hamonah recalls the valley of Hamon-gog, where the dead would be buried.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He had already announced the defeat of Gog, an enemy who would attack Israel. After that victory, the people would have to spend months purifying the land. Scholars interpret this passage in several ways: some see it as literal and future, others as symbolic language of God's final triumph.

For today: God is interested in cleansing and restoring completely, not halfway. We can ask him to help us remove from our lives, with patience and steadiness, whatever contaminates us.
exp.13:10:
God says he wants Israel to stop straying away from him and stop defiling themselves with all their rebellions. His ultimate goal is to restore the relationship, so that they will be his people and he will be his God. To "stray" means to wander off the path and lose one's way. To "defile" means to make oneself unclean, impure through sin.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people are in exile. Some leaders and elders had idols in their hearts, yet they came seeking a word from God while still holding on to their sin. God says he will judge both the false prophets and those who seek them out. The phrase about God deceiving the prophet is difficult; many understand it to mean that God allows, or gives over, to deception the one who has already chosen error. His judgment aims to correct and cleanse.

Today: even when God corrects, his purpose is to draw us near to him. Examine what things occupy your heart, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.6:9:
It says that the day of God's judgment is here. "Doom has gone out" means the sentence has been sent forth, so the moment has already arrived. "The rod has budded" refers to the rod of punishment, or the power that carries out the judgment, and it now shows that it is ready. "Arrogance has bloomed" means that the people's pride has grown and produced its results. Scholars do not fully agree on what the rod is: some think of Babylon, others of the wickedness of the people themselves.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. He announces that Jerusalem will be judged for its idolatry, its violence, and its arrogance, after a long time of refusing to change.

For today: pride can seem harmless while it grows, but in the end it bears bad fruit. Today you can ask God to show you where you find it hard to recognize your mistakes, and to decide to humble yourself and return to Him in time.
exp.44:15:
This verse says that all the people of the land must take part in giving an offering for the prince of Israel. The word "must" means it was not optional: the whole people had to participate. The contribution included goods such as oil, grain, and animals from the flock.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision about a new temple and a new way of life for Israel. With these contributions, the prince could cover the sacrifices and the festivals on behalf of everyone. In this way, worship was a shared responsibility. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways: some see it as literal, others as symbolic or future.

For today: worship and service to God should not rest on just one person. Ask yourself how you can contribute faithfully, with your time, your gifts, or your resources, to support your community of faith.
exp.41:17:
He says the man who was guiding Ezekiel measured the south side of the temple area, and it came out to five hundred cubits long. The word "south" appears directly in the verse, so no translation of "midday" is needed. The measuring tool in this vision was a rod used as a ruler. In this vision, with a cubit of roughly 18 inches, the whole side would be about 750 feet long, which is roughly 230 meters.

Ezekiel describes a vision he received in exile, when the temple in Jerusalem had been destroyed. A heavenly guide measures the whole enclosure: east and north, south and west, and all of them come out the same. The text says the wall served to separate the holy from the common. Scholars disagree about whether this is a literal future temple or a symbolic picture of God's presence.

For today: God is a God of order and holiness. We can set healthy boundaries to protect what is sacred in our lives, such as time with God, and not let everything else crowd it out.
exp.31:6:
When God brings an end to the pharaoh of Egypt, the sky will go dark. The stars will lose their brightness, the sun will be hidden behind clouds, and the moon will not give its light.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament against the pharaoh, who was regarded as a powerful monster in the Nile. The darkness is poetic language, used in the Bible to speak of divine judgment. Many read it as imagery and not as a literal event; others also see an echo of the plagues of Egypt.

For today: no human power, however great it may seem, stands above God. We can trust that He does justice, and we should avoid putting our security in money, prestige, or power.
exp.32:10:
God swears by his own life that he takes no pleasure when a wicked person dies. What he wants is for the wicked person to turn from their ways and live. A "wicked" person is one who lives without honoring God; to "turn" means to come around and go back the other way. Then God calls his people with urgency: "Turn! Turn from your evil ways!" and asks with grief: "For why should you die?"

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls a watchman, a sentinel who warns of danger. The people were in exile and were saying, "Our sins are wasting us away; how can we live?", almost without hope. God answers that there is a way forward: repentance. The verses that follow show that neither past goodness nor past wickedness decides everything, but the direction in which a person walks today.

For today: if you feel that your mistakes can no longer be remedied, God invites you to return to him now. Pray with sincerity and take one concrete step of change today.
exp.27:15:
God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament against the king of Tyre. The king is told that his great trade filled him with violence, and that he sinned. Because of this, God drove him in disgrace from the holy mountain and banished him from among the fiery stones. "Trade" means commerce or business. "Guardian cherub" describes a being of high rank who guarded the presence of God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament against the king of Tyre, a city rich from its commerce. Many believe the language also alludes to Satan; others think it is simply a poetic image of the king's pride. Christians have understood it in both ways.

For today: riches and success can make us proud and dishonest. Today, ask God whether there is some business, profit, or achievement that is occupying the place that belongs to Him alone.
exp.42:26:
At the end of those seven days, starting on the eighth day, the priests are to offer your burnt offerings (offerings that were completely burned up for God) and your peace offerings (offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving) on the altar. Then God declares that He will accept you.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, within his vision of a new temple. First the altar had to be purified for seven days and set apart as holy. After that, the people could worship with confidence. Interpreters differ on whether this vision describes a literal future temple or is a symbolic picture of God's presence with his people.

For today: God does not accept us because of what we do, but because He himself prepares the way for us to draw near. Christians see that way fulfilled in Christ. We can pray without fear and without pretense, knowing that He receives us with pleasure.
exp.35:31:
God tells the people of Israel that he will act not because they deserve it. He wants them to understand this clearly. He calls on them to feel shame and disgrace for their wrongful ways. The phrase "let it be known" is here rendered as "let it be known to you." The word "iniquities" refers to acts of wickedness or injustice, but the verse itself speaks simply of "your ways."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to a people living in exile because they had abandoned him. Before and after this verse, he promises to bring them back to their land, make it fruitful, and rebuild the cities. Here he makes clear that he will do this for his own sake and for his name, not because Israel has earned it. His grace comes first; repentance follows.

Today we can remember that God's forgiveness and blessings are a gift, not a payment. This leads us to honestly acknowledge our failings, without excuses, but also without despair, trusting in his mercy.
exp.21:15:
The verse says that Jerusalem will be like someone who has defiled themselves in full view of the nations, and that this public shame will be part of how the people come to know God. The reader's wording "defiled yourself in the eyes of the nations" points to the same picture of disgrace in front of the other peoples, so the image of a shameful possession taken in public stays in the background. The Hebrew here is difficult, and scholars have understood it in several ways, but in the end the outcome is clear: they will know that God is the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem, which had filled itself with violence, idolatry, and injustice. Just before this verse, God announces that he will scatter her among the nations to put an end to her uncleanness, that is, her sin. The punishment aims at the people coming to recognize who God is.

For today: God does not let us ignore the consequences of our decisions, but his goal is that we come to know him. If today you are going through a correction or a loss, ask him humbly what he wants to teach you, and seek him.
exp.12:22:
This verse says that God will put an end to the false visions and divination of certain women who were prophesying lies. The BSB says "false visions" and "practice divination." Those phrases describe what they did: they claimed to receive messages from God that were not true, and they used divination to try to find out hidden things. God promises to rescue his people from their hands, and that by this they will know that he is the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He confronts false prophetesses who deceived the people: they discouraged the righteous with lies and encouraged the wicked to keep living in their evil ways. The "veils" mentioned earlier are a difficult term; some believe they were bands or cloths used in their practices, although their exact meaning is uncertain.

For today: do not follow someone who tells you only what you want to hear. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and trust that God defends those who are being deceived.
exp.22:7:
Oholah (Samaria, the kingdom of Israel) never gave up the prostitution she began in Egypt. There, in her youth, men slept with her, caressed her virgin bosom, and poured out their lust upon her. "Youth" refers to her early years; the caressing of her breasts speaks of abuse and forced intimacy; and the "prostitution" here is an image of idolatry and alliances with other nations.

God speaks through Ezekiel, using a parable of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem). With very harsh language, he wants to show that Israel gave itself over to Egypt and Assyria, trusting in them and in their idols instead of trusting in him. Many understand that Egypt is mentioned as a pattern of unfaithfulness from an early time.

For today: examine the things you place your trust in apart from God, whether money, approval, or old habits. Bring them to him honestly and ask for his help to truly let them go.
exp.15:57:
It says that Jerusalem, pictured as an unfaithful wife, now bears the weight of her great wickedness and her detestable deeds. The word "lewdness" refers to a very great wickedness, and "abominations" are things that God utterly loathes, above all idolatry. The phrase "You will bear the consequences" shows that the results of her actions are coming upon her.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16 He compares Jerusalem to a wife whom He cared for, but who was unfaithful to Him. Before, she considered herself better than Sodom; now her sin has been exposed, and other peoples despise her. Even so, the verses that follow show that God will remember His covenant and establish an everlasting one.

For today: it is not healthy to hide or justify our faults. We can acknowledge them honestly before God, knowing that His judgment is not His final word, because He is faithful and offers forgiveness and restoration.
exp.18:1:
It says that God tells Ezekiel to sing a lament, a sad song. It presents a mother lioness who lay down among the young lions and reared her cubs there. The word "lament" means a song of mourning, and the question "What was your mother?" is asked as a way of mourning what she has become.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. The song refers to the princes or kings of Judah. The lioness is usually understood as Judah or its royal line, although some see it differently. The cubs are kings who, surrounded by violence, learned to imitate it and ended up falling.

For today: what surrounds us shapes us. It is worth reviewing which environments, friendships and habits are shaping our family, and seeking God so that we raise our children in wisdom and not in the hardness of the world.
exp.47:26:
Next to the territory of Zebulun, the verse says, another strip of land would go to the tribe of Gad. That strip runs from east to west, from the eastern side to the Mediterranean Sea. "Bordering" means lying alongside or marking a boundary. Gad is the last tribe named in this southern list.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes during the exile. In the final chapters of the book, God shows a vision of the land divided into equal strips among the tribes, with the Lord at the center. Interpreters differ on whether this vision will be fulfilled literally or is symbolic. Either way, it gave hope of restoration to a people in exile.

God takes care that every family has its place. We can trust that He forgets no one, and give thanks for what He has given us, without envying what belongs to others.
exp.7:9:
He says that Ezekiel went in and looked, and that carved all around the wall were every kind of crawling creature and detestable beast, along with all the idols of the house of Israel. "Detestable" means something that God hates. The word translated "crawling creature" refers to animals that move along the ground.

God speaks to Ezekiel in a vision, around 592 B.C., while the prophet was in Babylon. He shows him what was happening in secret inside the temple in Jerusalem. Seventy elders were worshiping in hiding, thinking that God did not see them. God was showing them their sin to explain why judgment would come.

For today: God sees what we do in private. We can ask him to examine our heart, confess what is hidden, and let him cleanse us, instead of living with a faith that is only for show.
exp.34:4:
It says that God judges Edom, called here "the mountain of Seir," for two reasons: it harbored an ancient hatred, and it delivered the Israelites over to the sword, that is, to violence, in the time of their disaster at the final stage of their punishment. The verse of "you have scattered" is that Edom dispersed them. The phrase about "the final stage of their punishment" refers to the day of their ruin.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom was a neighbor of Israel and descended from Esau, brother of Jacob. When Jerusalem fell, Edom did not help but took advantage. God responds by defending his wounded people and showing that he sees the injustice.

For today: do not hold on to resentment or rejoice in the pain of others. When someone suffers, offer them help and comfort, and leave justice in God's hands.
exp.44:6:
This verse says the prince will have his own portion of land on both sides of the district set apart for the sanctuary and of the city's allotted plot. That land stretches from west to east, from one end to the other. The word "separated" refers to the portion set apart for God, and "allotted land" refers to a parcel assigned to a particular use.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a vision about the restoration of Israel. He divides the land in an orderly way: first the sanctuary, then the Levites, the city, and the prince. The verses that follow explain the reason: that the princes should stop oppressing the people, because they now have their own land. Interpreters disagree about whether this vision is to be read literally, symbolically, or as referring to the future.

For today: whoever has authority or resources should be content with what God has given them and use their position to serve with justice, never to take advantage of others.
exp.25:7:
Ezekiel 26:8 says that the army of Babylon will kill with the sword the towns on the mainland that belonged to Tyre. Those towns are called the city's "daughters." The verse then describes the siege itself: the attackers will set up siege works against the city, build a ramp up to its walls, and raise their shields to protect themselves as they advance.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a proud city, rich from trade, and it rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking of its own profit. God announces judgment and uses Nebuchadnezzar as his instrument. Historians debate how exactly this prophecy was fulfilled: Nebuchadnezzar besieged the city for years, and other parts were fulfilled later.

For today: let us not place our security in money, success, or human defenses. Whoever rejoices in another's misfortune and trusts only in themselves falls easily. Better to live with humility and compassion, trusting in God.
exp.18:9:
Israel's mother was like a healthy vine, planted beside the water. Because she had water in abundance, she bore fruit and put out many branches. The branches mentioned here are the young shoots. The Berean Standard Bible speaks of "your vineyard," which suggests the vine grew in a cultivated place, and it describes the water as abundant.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a lament about the princes of Judah. The "mother" most likely represents Judah or Jerusalem, and the young lions of the earlier chapters are her kings, who were taken captive to Babylon. The passage recalls a former prosperity to show how much was lost.

For today: what we receive from God, such as blessings, family, or gifts, is not something to boast about or take for granted. A vine grows by the water it receives. Let us remain close to God with gratitude and humility, for all fruit comes from Him.
exp.16:17:
He despised the oath and broke the covenant he had made, even though he "gave his hand in pledge," that is, he had promised with a solemn gesture of commitment. Because he did all of these things, God declares that he will not escape.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He is referring to Zedekiah, king of Judah, who swore loyalty to Babylon but rebelled and sought help from Egypt. God says that the oath, made in his name, was also God's own, and that is why the betrayal was so serious.

Today it reminds us that our word matters. Keeping what we have promised, in marriage, at work, or with friends, is a way of honoring God. If we have failed, we can come to him with sincerity and ask for forgiveness.
exp.33:16:
God speaks to his people, whom he calls "my flock," and announces that he himself will judge between one sheep and another. The strong males of the flock are the "rams," and the "goats" are the male goats. God distinguishes between one and the other within the same flock.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile in Babylon. Earlier he had rebuked the shepherds of Israel, that is, its leaders, who took advantage of the people. Now God promises to care for his flock and also to correct the strong who trample on the weak, as the verses that follow show.

For today: God sees how we treat the weakest. If I have strength, influence, or resources, I can ask myself whether I use them to care for others or to take advantage of them. Today I can help someone who is tired or in need.
exp.43:28:
They shall eat the grain offerings, the sin offerings, and the guilt offerings. Everything in Israel devoted to the LORD will belong to them.

It says the priests would eat from the offerings that the people brought to the temple: the grain offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering. Also, everything in Israel devoted to the LORD would belong to them, that is, whatever was set apart for God. The sin offering is the offering made to cover guilt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of a restored temple. The Levitical priests, descendants of Zadok, would receive no land, because God himself would be their inheritance. For this reason the people supported them with the offerings. Interpreters disagree about whether this vision will be fulfilled literally or is symbolic.
