For today: those who serve God deserve support, and all of us can learn to give with gratitude. In addition, this reminds us that our greatest security lies not in what we possess, but in God himself.
exp.34:6:
God says that he will leave Mount Seir, the region of Edom, turned into a desolate waste and empty of people. The verse speaks of total destruction, and an empty land is one with no one living in it. The words about cutting off those who come and go mean that no one will be able to travel in or out of that land, because there will be no visitors and no life.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom, a descendant of Esau, had held an old hostility against Israel, and took advantage of Israel's fall, when Israel was at its lowest point. That is why God announces this judgment: Edom did not turn away from violence, and now it will receive it. In the end, God says that in this way they will know that he is the LORD.

For today: let us not rejoice in the pain of others or take advantage of their downfall. Let us ask God for a compassionate heart, one that helps those who suffer and leaves justice in God's hands.
exp.27:5:
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: this verse opens the announcement of a judgment. God gives the reason for what follows: the ruler of Tyre regarded his own heart as the heart of a god. Here "heart" means his way of thinking and his pride.

The Lord GOD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing the prince or king of Tyre, a city rich through trade. His wisdom brought him riches, and the riches filled him with arrogance. The verses that follow announce that powerful foreigners would come against him. Some scholars see here only a human ruler; others think the text also points to something more.

For today: what we have, whether talents or money, is a gift from God. Give thanks to God for it and ask him for humility so that you do not regard yourself as the owner of your life.
exp.30:7:
No tree in the garden of God could be compared to this huge tree. The cedars could not rival it, and the cypresses could not match its branches, nor could the plane trees equal its boughs. Its beauty stood above every other tree in that garden.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and addresses the pharaoh of Egypt. He uses the image of a magnificent tree, and the text compares it to Assyria. God shows that all greatness comes from Him, and that pride brings a fall, as the passage goes on to show.

For today: if you have talents, success, or influence, remember that they are a gift from God. Use them to bless others, like that tree that gave shade and shelter, and not to boast. Humility keeps you steady.
exp.11:10:
The prophet Ezekiel is said to be a sign to the people. What he did, packing his belongings and going out as someone leaving into exile, is what will happen to them. "Exile" means being taken away as captives to another land. The words about what will be done to them mean they will truly go through it.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. The people were rebellious and did not believe Jerusalem would be judged. So God commanded him to show the coming exile through visible actions. The prince is the ruler of Jerusalem; the verses that follow announce that he will be captured and taken to Babylon. Many understand this to refer to King Zedekiah.

For today: when God warns us, it is wise to listen in time and not to mock or delay. His warning is a sign of patience, for it gives us the opportunity to return to Him before the consequences arrive.
exp.36:17:
This verse says that when the people see Ezekiel holding the two sticks joined together, they will ask him what it means. In other words, the sign would stir curiosity and open the way to explain the message. "Your people" are his fellow Israelites, and "won't you explain to us what you mean by these" asks what he is trying to tell them by this.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles. He commands him to perform a symbolic action: to join two sticks, one for Judah and another for Israel (also called Joseph or Ephraim), the northern kingdom. God wanted to show that one day he would gather his divided people into a single nation under his hand.

For today: God can use what we do, and not only what we say, to stir questions in others. Let us live with unity, forgiveness and peace, and be ready to explain with humility why we do so.
exp.15:35:
God speaks to Jerusalem, whom He portrays as an unfaithful wife. Her shame and her exposure are her sin: she poured out her wealth and exposed her nakedness through her unfaithfulness with her lovers, meaning the nations she made alliances with. Her detestable idols were also part of this, and she even gave her own children to them as sacrifices.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The whole of chapter 16 uses the image of a marriage: God cared for Jerusalem, and she betrayed Him with other nations and gods. The verses that follow announce judgment for that unfaithfulness.

For today: examine what you give your trust to that belongs only to God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Bring them to Him honestly, because He forgives and restores those who return to Him.
exp.11:18:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to "the people of the land," meaning the people who remained in the land with him. The message is that those living in Jerusalem and in the land of Israel will eat their bread with anxiety and drink their water in dread. Their land will be stripped of everything in it. The cause is the violence of all who live there.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Earlier, God asked him to eat with trembling as a visible sign. Through this he announced that Jerusalem would be besieged and destroyed because of its sin. The message was meant to awaken the people, who did not believe that judgment would come.

For today: let us not ignore God's warnings by assuming that everything will simply stay the same. Today we can examine our hearts, confess what is wrong, and return to Him with confidence, for His correction seeks that we know Him.
exp.20:9:
The verse describes a sword that has been sharpened for slaughter and polished until it flashes like lightning. The question "Should we rejoice?" sounds like a pained question, as if the one speaking cannot bring himself to celebrate. The last part of the verse is hard to render, and readers and scholars understand it in more than one way. It seems to say that this sword rejects every stick or staff, as if no other rod of authority could stand against it.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. He announces that judgment is coming upon his people and their rulers because of their continued rebellion. The sword is ready to act, and many connect it with Babylon.

Today we can take God's warning seriously without hardening our hearts. If He corrects us, let us return to Him soon with humility.
exp.25:20:
God says he will make you an object of horror, a ruin so great that it amazes and frightens everyone. He says you will be no more. People will search for you, but you will never be found again.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich and proud city, and it rejoiced when Jerusalem fell, thinking it would gain more trade. God announces his judgment. The verses before this one use the image of the sea covering her. Some scholars see here a gradual destruction, and others see poetic and exaggerated language, because the region of Tyre remained inhabited afterward.

For today: do not put your security in money, success, or power, because none of these is firm. If you feel proud, ask God for a humble and grateful heart, one that trusts in him and cares for others.
exp.20:30:
God says he will pour out his anger on the people, breathing the fire of his fury against them. He will hand them over to brutal men who are skilled in destruction. It is a very harsh sentence of judgment.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, and the message is directed to the Ammonites, who were rejoicing at the fall of Jerusalem. Some scholars think the text also refers to Jerusalem itself. False prophecies had given empty confidence, and God responds with justice because wickedness had reached its limit.

For today: do not cling to comfortable messages that keep silent about the truth. Examine your life with humility, and if there is anything crooked in it, return to God before the consequences arrive.
exp.32:26:
God, using a solemn oath ("As I live"), announces a specific punishment. Those who live among the ruins will fall by the sword. Those who are out in the open field will be given to wild animals to be devoured. Those who hide in strongholds and caves will die of plague. No one will escape, wherever they are.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people who remained in the land after the fall of Jerusalem. They believed God would give them the land, as he had promised to Abraham. But they lived with violence, idolatry, and immorality. God answers that they cannot claim his promises while they reject his way.

For today: it is not enough to say "I belong to God" while we live as we please. Ask the Lord to show you something you should change, and obey him today with humility.
exp.10:10:
God says that the city will not be a pot that keeps its leaders safe, as if they were the meat cooking inside it. A pot is a large cooking vessel, and the leaders are picturing the city as a pot that keeps them protected. God says that will not happen, and he will judge them even to the edges of the land of Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people are in exile in Babylon. Some leaders of Jerusalem were saying that the city's walls would protect them (v. 3). God answers that this is not so, because they followed the customs of the neighboring nations and not his commands. Many scholars connect this judgment with the execution of leaders at Riblah, but that is understood in different ways.

For today: let us not trust in places, positions, or appearances to feel secure. Our true protection is found in obeying God and in trusting his mercy.
exp.47:10:
This verse says that the holy portion of land is for the priests descended from Zadok. God calls them consecrated, that is, set apart for himself. "Who kept My charge" means that they faithfully carried out their service and his commands. When the Israelites went astray, they did not, unlike the Levites, who did go astray.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a vision of the future: the land divided up and a sanctuary in the center. This holy portion rewards the faithfulness of the Zadokites. The Levites receive their own place apart, alongside them. Scholars disagree about whether this vision should be understood literally, symbolically, or as something still to be fulfilled.

For today: God sees and values constant faithfulness, especially when many around us turn away. Ask him to help you follow him with firmness, even if you are one of the few who do.
exp.12:2:
God says woe, which means that pain and judgment are coming upon the prophets who are "foolish," meaning those who lack wisdom. These men follow their own spirit: they speak what comes out of their own minds and desires, not what God has told them. And they have seen nothing: they received no true vision from Him.

The Lord God speaks through Ezekiel, whom He addresses as "son of man." He tells him to speak against the prophets of Israel who make up messages out of their own hearts. The verses that follow compare them to foxes among ruins: they sought their own gain and did not protect the people or defend the walls of faith when danger came on the day of the Lord.

Today we can compare what we hear, even from leaders we like, with what the Bible says. And if we speak on God's behalf, let us do it with humility, without presenting our own ideas as if they were His voice.
exp.36:25:
God promises to make a covenant of peace with his people, a binding agreement of well-being and reconciliation that will be everlasting. He says he will establish them, meaning he will set them firmly in their land, and that he will multiply them. He also promises to set his sanctuary, his holy dwelling place, among them forever.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to a people exiled in Babylon, discouraged and divided. Shortly before, in the vision of the dry bones, God had promised to restore them. Here he announces unity under a king from the line of David. How the promise is fulfilled is understood in several ways.

Today we can trust that God seeks to dwell near his people and to give them lasting peace. When you feel far away or without hope, pray and remember that his nearness does not depend on your strength, but on his faithfulness.
exp.27:23:
The verse says that Israel will no longer be pricked or hurt by the nations around it. A "pricking brier" is a thorn that wounds, and a "painful thorn" is a source of constant pain. To treat someone "with contempt" means to look down on them and show them disrespect. God promises that these neighbors will no longer be a constant source of pain for Israel, and that they will come to know that He is the Lord GOD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. First He announces judgment against Sidon, a neighboring city that harassed Israel. Then He promises to gather His scattered people so they may live in their land in safety. The text gives no further details about how this would happen; some read it as a hope for the return from exile, and others also see it as a promise still to be fulfilled.

For today: when contempt or injustice wounds you, remember that God sees and defends His people. You can rest in the knowledge that He has the last word, and entrust your pain to Him with confidence.
exp.3:11:
God tells Ezekiel to prepare bread from barley and bake it over dried human excrement used as fuel. He must do all of this in plain view of the people, that is, right in front of them.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Through this symbolic act, together with the scanty rations of the previous verse, he announces the siege of Jerusalem and the unclean food Israel would have to eat among the nations. Ezekiel protests, and afterward the text tells that God allowed him to use cow dung instead (v. 15).

For today: God takes sin seriously, and sometimes his message is uncomfortable. Let us ask for humility to hear his correction in time, knowing that his aim is to bring us back to himself.
exp.19:14:
He says that God swore an oath in the wilderness, raising his hand as he did so. He swore that Israel would not enter the land he had given them, a land flowing with milk and honey, the glory of all lands.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the elders of Israel, who were in exile. He reminds them of their history: even after being freed from Egypt, the people rebelled, profaned the Sabbaths, and followed their idols. God shows them that their present situation has deep roots. Even so, the text that follows says that God forgave them and did not destroy them.

For today: God's blessings should not be taken for granted. Today we can examine whether we obey him wholeheartedly or whether we still follow other "idols." And we can trust that his mercy continues to give us the opportunity to return.
exp.46:4:
He says that the man guiding Ezekiel measured off another thousand cubits, and now the water was too deep to cross on foot. It had risen so high that the only way across was to swim. "River" is the word used for the stream here, and "swim" means to move through the water by swimming.

Ezekiel speaks of a vision that God gave him. A guide with a measuring cord leads him along a river that flows out from the temple. At each stretch the water rises: first to the ankles, then to the knees, then to the waist, and now to a depth where he must swim. Many understand this as a picture of the life and blessing that come from God's presence, though it has been interpreted in various ways.

For today: God invites us not to stay on the shore or in the shallows. We can move forward step by step in prayer, in the Word, and in trust in Him, letting go of control and allowing ourselves to be held up by His grace.
exp.5:10:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to make strong gestures: clap your hands, stomp your feet, and cry out "Alas!" over the wicked abominations of Israel. "Stomp your feet" means "stomp hard." The "abominations" are the detestable acts of worshiping idols. The message is that the people will fall to three blows: the sword, famine, and plague.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people had turned away from God to follow idols, and He describes this as unfaithfulness, like a broken marriage. The punishment is not whim: God says that a heart which has drifted away grieves Him, and He wants them to know that He is the Lord.

For today: God takes our faithfulness seriously because He loves us. It is worth asking ourselves what things occupy the place that belongs to Him, and turning back to Him with sincerity.
exp.15:24:
It says that Jerusalem, pictured as a woman, built her high shrines at the head of every street. She degraded the beauty God had given her and offered herself to every passerby. "At the head of every street" points to the start of the roads, the places where traffic gathered. "Unfaithfulness" here means being untrue to God, above all through idol worship and alliances with other nations.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout chapter 16 he presents Jerusalem as a young girl whom he rescued, cared for, and adorned. She, however, used those gifts to pursue other gods and other nations. God confronts her to call her to acknowledge her sin.

For today: what God has given us, such as talents, blessings, or faith, must not be placed at the service of other things that seek our heart. Think about what "shrines" you are building in your life, and return humbly to God, who remains faithful.
exp.13:8:
It says that if a prophet is enticed to speak a message, God himself is the one who enticed him: "it was I the LORD who enticed him." Then he will stretch out his hand against that prophet and destroy him, that is, cut him off completely from among his people Israel.

God speaks through Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Some elders of Israel had idols in their hearts and yet still came to seek a word from God. God says he will answer according to the condition of that heart. Interpreters explain "enticed" in various ways: as a judgment in which God allows the deception to take effect, or as strong language about his sovereignty. The text does not say that God is a liar. Both the one who asks and the prophet bear their guilt.

For today: before seeking direction from God, examine what occupies your heart. Ask him to remove whatever competes with him, and test every teaching by Scripture.
exp.11:25:
This verse says that a new word from God came to Ezekiel. The phrase "Furthermore, the word of the LORD came to me" marks the point where God begins speaking to him once more.

Ezekiel is the one speaking, writing down what God tells him. He lived among the exiles of Israel in Babylon. People mocked his warnings, thinking the judgment would take a long time or would never come. This verse introduces God's answer to that mockery, right after saying that there would be no more false visions.

For today: God still speaks through his Word, and obedience should not be put off by thinking "there will be time later." Today you can open the Bible with simple attention, ask God to speak to you, and respond without delay to something specific you already know he is asking of you.
exp.22:2:
They say that the two sisters, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem, were unfaithful from their youth, while they were in Egypt. "Played" here means giving themselves to others instead of being faithful. "Youth" refers to their early years. The images of breasts fondled and virgin bosoms caressed speak of abuse and of a purity lost early on.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel and uses a harsh parable to show the story of Israel. There was one people, divided into two kingdoms. God reminds them that they turned away from him from their beginnings, when they mixed themselves with idolatry and Egyptian alliances. Scholars debate how much historical detail lies behind this image.

For today: it is not enough to say that we belong to God; we must look at the things to which we give our hearts. Today we can ask him to show us the things we trust in more than him, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.33:14:
God promises that he himself will care for his people, like a shepherd who tends his sheep. To "tend" them means to lead them to food and look after them. The place where the sheep rest and feel safe is where God says he will make them lie down. So God says: I will tend them, and I will give them a place to rest.

The Lord GOD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The shepherds of Israel, that is, its leaders, had neglected and mistreated the people, and the sheep were scattered. For this reason God decides to act himself, to gather them and bring them back to their land.

For today: when you feel tired, lost, or without direction, remember that God does not leave you alone. Turn to him in prayer and seek his rest, trusting that he himself cares for you and guides you.
exp.15:61:
He says that God himself will establish, or make firm, his covenant with Jerusalem, the unfaithful people he is addressing. "I will establish" means to make something sure and secure. The result will be that she "will know" that he is the LORD, meaning she will truly know him through his faithfulness and his forgiveness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The whole of chapter 16 describes Jerusalem as a wife who abandoned her Lord. Even so, at the end God promises to remember his covenant and confirm it, not because she deserves it, but out of his grace. The verses around it say that she will feel shame when she remembers her sin.

For today: when you fail, do not run from God or sink into guilt. Acknowledge your wrong with humility and trust that his faithfulness is firmer than yours. His forgiveness leads us to know him better.
exp.22:42:
This verse speaks of a woman who has grown old in her unfaithfulness. God describes her as one who has long been given over to adultery, and her persistence in it is the sad center of the passage. The Berean Standard Bible renders the verse with a sharp phrase: those who pursue her are to treat her as a prostitute, because that is all she has become. The image shows how far her unfaithfulness has gone and how fully it has shaped her.

God speaks through Ezekiel. In this chapter, Aholah and Aholibah represent Samaria and Jerusalem, who turned away from God to seek alliances and idols from other nations. The language is deliberately blunt and vivid to show how serious their unfaithfulness was. Some interpreters see here a sad persistence in sin, and others a warning of judgment.

For today: bad habits, if not confronted, become custom and harden us. Today you can return to God sincerely, before sin becomes your normal way of living.
exp.6:6:
This verse says that the time of God's judgment is already coming. The phrase "those who live in the land" refers to the people who lived in the land of Israel. The word "doom" points to the coming judgment itself. The reference to "panic on the mountains" describes fear and confusion spreading across the hills, where people had gathered for celebrations and where false worship also took place.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. God announces that Jerusalem and Judah will fall because of their idolatry and injustices. The people had ignored many warnings. God warns clearly, so that they will know that He is the Lord.

Today we can take God's patience seriously and not mistake it for indifference. If He shows us something we must correct, let us do it today, with humility and repentance, without waiting for the consequences to arrive.
exp.11:19:
God says that the cities where people live will be destroyed and the land will become empty and desolate. When this happens, the people will know that he is the LORD. "Laid waste" means reduced to ruins.

God speaks and gives this message to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Ezekiel was to act as if he were eating with fear, to show what would come upon Jerusalem. The text says the cause was the wickedness of its inhabitants. God gave the warning so that they would understand that He is serious.

Today we can learn not to take God's warnings lightly. If He shows us something we need to correct, it is a sign of His care. You can pray today with humility and ask Him, "LORD, what should I change?" and obey promptly.
exp.23:14:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to me" means that a message from God came to him. It is a phrase the prophet uses several times to announce that he is going to receive an important command or message.

Ezekiel speaks, writing down what God said to him. It comes after a harsh message of judgment against Jerusalem for its sin. Now God is preparing to give the prophet a painful instruction: the death of his wife, whom he was to mourn without the usual mourning, as a sign for the people.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before we act or judge what we are living through, we can stop and listen to him with humility, even when the message is hard. Obeying him, even with pain, is a way of trusting him.
exp.29:0:
God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel once more. The phrase "The word of the LORD came to me, saying," is how this translation introduces a new message, and "the LORD" is the name for God used here. This opening is repeated throughout the book to mark the start of a new message.

Ezekiel was a priest who lived in exile in Babylon, and God called him to speak on his behalf. Here a new message begins, directed against Egypt and its allies, as the verses that follow and the rest of the chapter show. God is the one speaking, and Ezekiel only passes on what he receives. The verses that follow announce the day of the LORD, a time of judgment.

For today: God still speaks, today mainly through his Word. Before we give our opinion or make a decision, we can set aside a moment each day to read the Bible carefully and ask him to speak to us.
exp.19:34:
It says that God will bring his people into the "wilderness of the nations," a place set apart from the surrounding nations. There, "where I will enter into judgment with you face to face" means he will deal with them directly, personally, with no go-betweens and no room for excuses.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. The elders of Israel had come to consult him, but the people were still attached to their idols. God promises to bring them out from among the nations and compares this to what happened in the wilderness after they left Egypt. Interpreters debate whether the "wilderness of the nations" is a literal place or an image of a time of testing and purification. Its purpose is to restore, not to destroy.

God sometimes draws us away from the noise to speak to us clearly and without disguise. If you feel a season of solitude or correction, do not run away: it may be his way of cleansing you and drawing you near to him. Come with sincerity and listen to him.
exp.35:23:
God promises that he will take his people from among the nations where they had been scattered. He will gather them out of all the countries and bring them back into their own land. The word "nations" refers to foreign peoples, and "countries" refers to the lands where the people had been dispersed.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who wrote while Israel was in exile because of its disobedience. The people had damaged the good name of God among the nations. God makes clear that he acts for the holiness of his name and out of faithfulness to his promise, not because Israel deserves it. After this promise comes cleansing and a new heart.

For today: if you feel far from God or lost, remember that he takes the initiative to rescue and restore us by pure grace. You can return to him with confidence and ask him for a new heart.
exp.21:22:
This verse is an introductory phrase. "And the word of the LORD came to me" means: "God spoke to me." With these words, Ezekiel makes clear that what follows does not come from his own opinion, but from God.

Ezekiel is a prophet who lives among the exiles of Judah, in Babylon. Earlier, God had announced that Jerusalem would be like a furnace where silver is melted. Now a new message begins, which explains why that judgment is coming: the injustice of the leaders, the prophets, and the people. In other words, God does not punish without reason, but first states clearly what is going wrong.

Today we can learn to hear the word of God with seriousness, without softening it. Before we set ourselves to judge others, it is good to ask God: "Is there anything in me that needs to be corrected?"
exp.38:7:
He says that what God had announced is as good as certain. "Yes, it is coming, and it will surely happen" speaks of something still in the future, yet it is described with the confidence of a settled fact. "This is the day of which I have spoken" refers to the day of judgment on Gog and his army, which God had described earlier.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, to a people living in exile and discouragement. He promises that a great enemy, called Gog of the land of Magog, will come against Israel and be defeated. Interpreters differ: some see it as a historical event, others as a vision of the last times, others as a symbol. In every case, the message is that God keeps his word and defends his holy name.

For today: when God's promises seem to take a long time, we can rest in the fact that he is faithful. What he has said, he will do in his time, and we can trust him with peace.
exp.34:10:
God swears by himself that he will deal with Edom in the same way Edom dealt with Israel. The phrases "according to your anger" and "according to your jealousy" mean that Edom will receive the kind of treatment it showed. "Hatred" refers to the grudge held in the heart. "I will make Myself known among them" means that, in judging them, God will reveal himself as just and present.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel against Mount Seir, that is, Edom, a nation neighboring Israel. Edom held an old grudge and wanted to take the lands of Israel and Judah when they were wounded. God heard their words of mockery and scorn, and he answers by defending his people.

Today, this verse reminds us that God hears what we say and sees what we keep in our hearts. If we have been hurt, we can leave justice in his hands. And if we hold on to resentment, it is wise to ask him to remove it before it harms us.
exp.15:34:
This verse is a call to attention. God tells Jerusalem, whom he calls "prostitute," to hear his word. The phrase "hear the word of the LORD" marks the point where God moves from describing the fault to announcing the consequences.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout this chapter he presents Jerusalem as a woman whom he cared for and blessed, but who was unfaithful to him. Sexual unfaithfulness is an image of idolatry and of alliances with other nations. God confronts her firmly, because she paid her lovers instead of being faithful to him.

For today: when God corrects us, it is good to listen with humility and not harden our hearts. His correction seeks to bring us back to him, who loves us and waits for our return.
exp.2:8:
God tells Ezekiel that he will make his forehead like a diamond, harder than flint (a very hard stone). He asks him not to be afraid of the people or dismayed at their presence, even though they are a rebellious house, meaning a people who resist obeying.

God is speaking, having just called Ezekiel as a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. He warns that the people will not listen to him, because in truth they do not want to listen to God. For this reason he strengthens him so that he will remain faithful, even though they reject him.

For today: when God asks you to speak or live the truth with love and people resist, do not depend on their approval. Ask God for firmness, and remember that being faithful to him matters more than being accepted.
exp.46:22:
Ezekiel 47:23 says that foreigners living among the people of Israel will also receive a plot of land as an inheritance. Each one will receive it in the tribe where he is living. A stranger who settles in a place is given land there, just as the people of that tribe are.

God Himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, in the final vision of the book about the restoration of Israel and the division of the land. It is remarkable that foreigners whose children were born there are treated as native-born, that is, as part of the people. Some see here a picture of God's kindness toward all nations; others read it more literally. Both readings recognize His generosity.

For today: God invites us to make room for newcomers, whether immigrants or people new to the church. We can offer them not only help, but a true place among us.
exp.27:24:
God says that one day he will gather his people Israel from the nations where they have been scattered. When he does, he will show that he is holy, meaning pure and worthy of honor, in the sight of all the nations. Israel will live again in its own land, the land God gave to his servant Jacob.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier he had announced judgment on Sidon, a neighboring city that had mistreated Israel. Now he turns to a promise of restoration. Some believers understand that it was already fulfilled in part with the return from exile; others also see a future fulfillment.

For today: even when we feel that everything is broken or far away, God keeps what he promises. We can wait on him with patience, trusting that he knows how to gather and restore what seemed lost.
exp.15:31:
This verse says that Jerusalem is like a married woman who is unfaithful to her husband and takes other men in place of him. The word "strangers" means people who are not her husband. The verse describes someone who is unfaithful within marriage.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of a marriage to show how the people of Israel turned away from Him and sought other gods and alliances with other nations. It is strong language, meant to awaken the conscience of the people and call them to repentance.

For today: ask yourself what things are occupying the place that only God should have in your heart, such as money, fame, or a relationship. Bring them to God in prayer with honesty, and ask Him for help to return to Him with all your heart.
exp.7:4:
God tells Ezekiel to look toward the north. There, near the Altar Gate, at the entrance, the prophet sees an idol that provokes God's jealousy.

God speaks, showing Ezekiel in a vision what was happening in Jerusalem. Although the prophet was in Babylon, the vision takes him to the temple. There he sees that the people were worshiping idols in the most sacred place. God shows him this to explain why judgment would come. It is not known for certain which idol it was.

Today we can ask ourselves whether there is something we have placed in the place that belongs only to God. These can be good things, like work or money, that become too important. Let us ask him to show us those areas with sincerity and give him first place again.
exp.28:18:
Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: God announces that he will give Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Babylon will carry off the land's wealth, seize its spoil, and remove its plunder. This will be the payment for his army.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the twenty-seventh year of the exile (around 571 B.C.). Babylon had besieged Tyre for a long time, and its soldiers were worn out without receiving any plunder. God says that Egypt will be the reward for that effort. Scholars debate how much of this was fulfilled and in what way, since the historical information is limited.

For today: God rules even over powerful kings and nations, though they do not acknowledge him. We can trust that he continues to guide history and our circumstances, even when everything seems confusing.
exp.1:4:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to Israel, whether they listen or refuse to listen. The word "whether" here is used in the sense of "whether or not," so the point is that the people may listen or they may not. The important part is that, whether they listen or refuse, they will know that a prophet has been among them.

God speaks, calling Ezekiel "son of man," which simply means a human being. He is sent to a people who have rebelled again and again, with parents and children alike being stubborn. Ezekiel lives among the exiles in Babylon. His task is not to make them believe him, but to be faithful in saying, "Thus says the Lord GOD."

For today: our duty is to be faithful in sharing God's truth with love, even when others do not respond. The results do not depend on us but on God. Let us speak with sincerity and trust Him.
exp.39:24:
It says that this gate and its portico had windows all around, like the windows of the other gates that had already been measured. It was fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about 45 to 50 centimeters. The word "portico" refers to a covered porch or entry hall at the front of the gateway.

Ezekiel recounts a vision that God gave him, in which a guide takes him through a new temple and measures everything carefully. The Jewish people were exiled in Babylon and the temple had been destroyed. These exact measurements showed them that God had an orderly plan. Scholars disagree about whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both.

For today: God is a God of order and of care for details. If today you find yourself in a time of ruin or waiting, trust that he has not forgotten his people and continues building with purpose.
exp.30:14:
He says that when this great tree was brought down to Sheol, the realm of the dead, God caused mourning throughout creation. The phrase "I caused mourning" means that God brought about grief. The deep waters are described as covered, and the rivers and abundant waters are described as held back, and Lebanon is made to mourn while all the trees of the field faint because of it. The trees "fainted" means they grew weak, like someone who has lost their strength.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he compares the Pharaoh of Egypt to a very tall cedar of Lebanon, and he warns him with the example of Assyria, another proud nation that had already fallen. It is poetic language: nature weeps as if it were a funeral. Some read it only as an image of the fall of an empire.

For today: power and success do not make us untouchable. God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. Ask him to help you live with humility and not to trust in your own greatness.
exp.30:10:
God says he will hand this great tree over to a ruler from among the nations. That ruler is a foreign power, and the verse says he will deal with the tree according to its wickedness. God states plainly that he has banished it.

The Lord GOD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He compares Assyria, or according to others the pharaoh of Egypt, to a very tall and beautiful cedar. It grew proud, and for that reason God brings it low. Scholars disagree about exactly who is meant, but the message is clear: no human power is safe from the judgment of God.

Everything we have, whether beauty, talent, or success, comes from God. If we fill ourselves with pride, we move away from Him. Today we can thank Him with humility for what we have received.
exp.22:4:
Oholah, who represents Samaria, was unfaithful to God while she still belonged to him. "Prostituted herself" here does not refer only to sexual sin, but to abandoning God to give herself to others. "Lusted after" means she was consumed with a passionate desire for them. The Assyrians were the powerful neighboring nation, warriors she sought security and attraction in.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the image of two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem, to show that his people sought political alliances and foreign gods instead of trusting him. It is strong language, meant to shake consciences and reveal the pain of a faithful God before betrayal.

For today: examine the things in which you seek security or worth outside of God, such as money, the approval of others, or success. Return to trusting him first.
exp.37:2:
God tells Ezekiel to declare to Gog: "Behold, I am against you." Gog is called "chief prince of Meshech and Tubal."

The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who wrote during Israel's exile in Babylon. God announces judgment against Gog, a leader from distant lands, and his great army. Exactly who Gog and Magog are is understood in several ways: some see real nations of that time, others a symbol of the forces that oppose God.

For today: even when evil seems powerful and threatening, God remains the Lord of history. You can rest in the knowledge that he cares for his people and has the final word. Today, give him your fears and trust in his justice.
exp.38:24:
God announces that he will now restore the captive descendants of Jacob, that is, the people of Israel. He will have compassion on the whole nation of Israel and will defend his holy name with passionate commitment. "Restoring Jacob from captivity" means bringing the exiles home again and returning them to their former situation. Here, "I will be jealous" means fiercely protecting what belongs to him out of deep love.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Shortly before, he explained that Israel was taken into captivity because of their sin and rebellion. Now he promises to restore them. God acts not only out of compassion for them, but also so that his name will be honored among the nations.

For today: although our failures have real consequences, God does not tire of offering restoration. If you have drifted away, you can return with confidence, acknowledging your mistake honestly and knowing that his mercy is greater than your past.
exp.22:33:
It says that Jerusalem (Aholibah) will drink the cup of punishment to the very end, just as her sister Samaria did. The cup stands for God's judgment: she will drink all of it, and she will even break the pieces of the jar. "You will tear your breasts" is a very strong image of pain and despair.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout the chapter, Samaria and Jerusalem appear as two sisters who were unfaithful to God, seeking alliances and foreign gods. Judgment comes because they forgot Him and turned their backs on Him.

For today: God warns us out of love before the consequences arrive. If today we notice that we have set Him aside, we can return to Him with humility, for He forgives those who repent.
exp.35:7:
God speaks to the mountains of Israel as if they could hear him. He tells them that they will produce branches and bear fruit again, and that this fruit will be for his people Israel. Here "branches" refers to the limbs of the trees, and the phrase "will soon come home" means that the return of the people is close at hand.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel was in exile, its land lay desolate, and the neighboring nations mocked it. God promises to restore the land, bring his people back to it, and rebuild the ruined cities. Interpreters debate whether this was fulfilled only in the return from exile or whether it also points to a future fulfillment.

For today: when your life feels barren or in ruins, remember that God knows how to restore. Trust his promise, and while you wait, prepare yourself to bear fruit and to bless others.
exp.6:8:
God says that this time he will not look on them with pity and will not spare them. He will punish them for their ways and for the detestable practices among them, the things God loathes, such as idolatry and injustice. Those practices will come back on the people themselves. The verse ends by saying that they will know it is the LORD who strikes the blow, meaning that the punishment is his action.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the people of Judah, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem. After a long time of warnings, they kept on in idolatry and violence. The judgment is not an outburst without reason, but the result of rejecting God again and again.

For today: let us not confuse God's patience with indifference. If there is something we know displeases him, today is a good day to acknowledge it and turn back to him, who continues to offer forgiveness to whoever repents.
exp.26:10:
It says that men of Arvad and Helech manned Tyre's walls all around, and that the men of Gammad were in its towers. They hung their shields around the walls, and so they made the city more beautiful. The "helmets" and "galleys" mentioned elsewhere in the passage are the same kinds of items, and the Gammadims are not certain: some believe they were a people, others think the word refers to guards or to a place.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and laments over Tyre, a wealthy and proud seaport city. The text describes its beauty like that of a great ship, built with the help of many nations. This praise prepares the announcement of its fall, because its trust was in its wealth and its power.

For today: everything that seems strong and beautiful, such as money, success, or prestige, can disappear. It is better to trust in God, who does not change, and to use what we have with humility and gratitude.
exp.36:4:
God speaks to Ezekiel and tells him to say to some dry bones: "I will cause breath to enter you, and you will come to life."

God, the Lord, speaks in a vision that Ezekiel had. The bones represent the people of Israel, who were exiled in Babylon and felt they had no hope (Ezekiel 37:11). God promises to restore them to life and bring them back. Many also see here an image of spiritual renewal, though the text focuses on Israel.

For today: if there are areas of your life that feel dry or without a way out, do not stop talking with God about them. He can bring life where it seems impossible. Trust in His Word, even when you cannot see how.
exp.32:20:
Ezekiel recounts that, in the twelfth year of their exile in Babylon, a fugitive who had escaped from Jerusalem came to him with a report. A fugitive is someone who has fled from danger. "The city has been taken" means the city was overrun and defeated.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a prophet who was exiled along with his people. For years he had warned that Jerusalem would fall, but many did not believe him. This news confirms that his words came from God. The verses that follow say that God opened his mouth so that he could speak again. Some manuscripts and scholars debate the exact date, but the meaning remains the same.

For today: God keeps what he says. We should not wait for the consequences to arrive before listening to him. Today we can respond to his Word with humility, turn back to him, and trust that his mercy is still open.
exp.17:26:
It says that if a wicked person turns away from his evil and begins to do what is just and right, he will save his life. "Wickedness" means living without respect for God and doing what is wrong. "Doing what is just and right" means acting uprightly and dealing fairly with others. "His life" refers to his whole life.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. They were saying that God's way was not fair, as if they were paying for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person is accountable for his own life, and that He offers forgiveness to whoever repents.

It is never too late to change. If today you recognize something you are doing wrong, stop blaming others or your past, ask God for forgiveness, and take a concrete step of justice, such as apologizing or correcting an unfair dealing.
exp.24:2:
God tells Ezekiel to deliver a message to the Ammonites. They shouted "Aha!", an expression of mockery and delight at the misfortune of others. They rejoiced because the sanctuary was profaned, the land of Israel was laid waste, and the house of Judah went into exile. "Hear" means "listen."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Ammon was a neighboring people of Israel, and God judges them for rejoicing when Judah fell. The verses that follow announce that peoples from the east would take their land.

For today: God notices how we react to the pain of others. Even when someone has failed or is suffering the consequences of their mistakes, we should not mock or rejoice. Instead, let us pray, help, and show compassion.
exp.20:22:
The people of Jerusalem will consider the king of Babylon's omen to be false, because they feel safe behind the oaths and promises they have made. But "he" will draw their attention to their guilt so that they are seized and taken captive. To be taken means to be caught or captured. Some think "he" is the king of Babylon, while others think it is God; the next verse points more toward God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Babylon is moving closer to Jerusalem, and God even uses the king's pagan practice of omen-reading to carry out his judgment. The people trusted in human agreements and did not turn back to God. Some believe this refers to the oath of loyalty that Zedekiah swore to Babylon and then broke.

For today: do not rely on your own human guarantees or on what others promise you. Instead, examine your heart honestly and return to God before the consequences arrive.
exp.1:3:
God tells Ezekiel that he is sending him to a people who are obstinate and stubborn. That is, they are defiant and unyielding, with hearts set against change and no desire to turn back. Ezekiel is to say to them, "This is what the Lord GOD says," meaning that his message is not his own but comes from God.

The one speaking is God himself, after his Spirit lifted Ezekiel up, since Ezekiel had fallen face down before his glory. Ezekiel was a priest who lived in exile, and God calls him as a prophet to a people who had rebelled against him for generations. From the start, God warns him that the people may not listen.

For today: God asks us for faithfulness, not results. We can share his Word with humility and love, without changing it, and leave each person's response in his hands.
exp.2:26:
God tells Ezekiel that there will be times when he will be left unable to speak, but when God gives him a message, He will open his mouth. Then Ezekiel is to tell the people, "This is what the Lord GOD says." The words "Whoever listens, let him listen; and whoever refuses, let him refuse" mean that anyone who is willing to hear should listen, and anyone who chooses to refuse may do so. The reason is that the people are a "rebellious house," that is, a stubborn nation.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. Earlier, the Lord had announced that he would be bound and would remain silent. Thus, Ezekiel would speak only when God gave him words. His message did not depend on his own opinion. Some understand this as a sign for the people, and others as a real but limited silence.

Today we can speak of God faithfully and simply, without forcing anyone. Our task is to share his truth with love; the response of each person is up to God.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that Ezekiel heard the wheels being called "the whirling wheels." The phrase is the one the translation gives for the wheels, so the sense of the name is open to interpretation and is understood in several ways.

Ezekiel, a priest and prophet, recounts a vision of God while in exile. The cherubim and the wheels full of eyes accompany the glory of God. Shortly afterward, that glory leaves the temple in Jerusalem, as a sign of judgment for the sin of the people. The detail that the wheels are named and addressed suggests that they move under God's authority.

For today: even when life seems to spin out of control, nothing moves outside of God's authority. You can rest in the fact that He sees everything, and entrust to Him today what you do not understand.
exp.26:13:
This verse says that the men of Beth-togarmah brought horses, war horses, and mules to the market of Tyre to exchange them for goods. "War horses" here means horses used in battle. The phrase "for your wares" means that they did business there, trading their animals for the goods that Tyre had to offer.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and raises a lament over Tyre, a city made rich by sea trade. The list of nations and products shows how great and prosperous it was. Beth-togarmah was probably in the region of Anatolia, north of Israel, though its exact location is debated. The purpose of the list is to show Tyre's pride before announcing its fall.

For today: wealth and success are not wrong in themselves, but they can make us proud. Thank God for what you have and use it with humility and generosity, remembering that everything comes from Him.
exp.25:1:
It says that Tyre, a great trading city, rejoiced when Jerusalem fell. The word "Aha!" expresses mockery and satisfaction, like saying "how good!" Jerusalem is described as the gate to the nations, that is, a place through which trade and people passed. Tyre thought that, with Jerusalem broken, its own gains would grow: "I will be filled," while Jerusalem lay in ruins.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, called "son of man." This takes place shortly after Jerusalem's fall before Babylon. God does not overlook the fact that Tyre mocked and sought gain from the pain of others, and for this reason he announces his judgment in the verses that follow.

Today we can examine our hearts: do I rejoice when others are doing badly, or when their fall benefits me? God calls us to compassion, not to the selfish profit of another's suffering.
exp.23:1:
God asks Ezekiel to write down the exact date of that day. "Son of man" is the way God addresses the prophet. "Jerusalem" is the city, and the king of Babylon has laid siege to it, that is, surrounded it with his army.

God is speaking, and Ezekiel is in exile in Babylon. The exiles believed that Jerusalem would never fall. That is why God marks the exact day the siege began: on that very day, far away, the announced judgment was being fulfilled. In this way it became clear that God had spoken and that his words were true. Many understand that this day corresponds to January of 588 B.C., although the exact calculation is debated.

God does what he says, both his warnings and his promises. Today we can listen to him with humility and not put it off, trusting that his word is firm.
exp.25:18:
This verse says that God will turn the city of Tyre into a ruined and empty place, like those deserted cities where no one lives anymore. The verb here means to make one thing into another, and the word for "desolate" describes a place left in ruins. The picture of the deep rising up and the mighty waters covering the city suggests that the sea itself will overwhelm it, as if the city were buried beneath the waves.

God Himself speaks here, through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich and powerful city that depended on sea trade. Earlier in this chapter, its pride is described, along with how it rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem. Some scholars see the fulfillment across several historical stages, not in a single event.

For today: power and wealth are not a safe refuge. We can ask ourselves where we place our trust, and ask God to give us humility to depend on Him and not on what we have.
exp.0:6:
Their legs were straight, with no bends or bent joints, and the soles of their feet were like the hooves of a calf, a young bull. Their feet also gleamed like polished bronze. The word "gleaming" means shining with a soft, bright light, as metal does when it has been rubbed until it shines.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. He describes a vision of God that he had by the river Chebar. These beings support the divine throne. Interpreters explain the details in several ways: some see strength and firmness; others see service. The text does not explain them, so it is wise to be cautious.

For today: God shows himself powerful and steady even when everything seems to be falling apart. If your life feels unstable, remember that God is still on his throne, and you can walk with confidence, moving straight toward what he asks of you.
exp.40:13:
This verse gives one more measurement of the temple that Ezekiel sees in his vision: the width of the temple courtyard on the east, including the front of the temple, measured one hundred cubits. A cubit was roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the fingers, about 45 to 50 centimeters. The courtyard here is an open area set apart beside the temple. Its exact use is not known with certainty.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, receives this vision from God. A guide leads him, measuring every part of the temple. Chapters 40 to 48 show a temple that is orderly and symmetrical. Scholars interpret it in different ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbol of God's presence with his people.

For today: God cares about order and about details. We can devote the small things of daily life to him with care, because he dwells among his people.
exp.28:6:
It says that Egypt is like a weak reed. When Israel took hold of it with their hands to lean on it, the reed splintered and tore their shoulders. When they leaned on it, it broke and wrenched their backs.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, addressing the pharaoh of Egypt, who is compared to a great monster of the river. Judah was seeking help in Egypt against Babylon, instead of trusting in God. Egypt could not hold them up, and God judged it for its pride, for it said: "My river is my own."

Today we can ask ourselves what we lean on most: money, people, status, or our own strength. All of these can fail. It is good to use help and good resources, but our final trust must be in God, who does not break and does not let us fall.
exp.44:7:
It says the land set apart in the vision will be the prince's possession in Israel. And it promises that the princes will no longer oppress my people. Instead, they will give the rest of the land to the house of Israel, according to their tribes. The word "oppress" here means to treat others harshly and unjustly, and "possession" is the share of property that is received.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision about the restoration of Israel, with a temple, a city, and a land divided in an orderly way. The leaders had previously abused the people, and for that reason the following verse orders them to stop the violence and practice justice. Interpreters differ on whether this vision is fulfilled in a literal or symbolic way.

For today: if you have authority, whether at home, at work, or in the church, use it to care for others and not to take advantage of them. God is concerned with justice and honesty.
exp.4:15:
God says He will send famine against the people like deadly arrows that bring ruin. As the famine grows worse, He will cut off their food supply, as if He were snapping their supply of bread in two. "Harmful" here means damaging and deadly. The arrows are the famine itself.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem. The people had turned away from His laws and worshiped idols, and because of this God announces judgment. This happens before the city falls to Babylon. He had already warned of these consequences in the law of Moses, and here He confirms His word: "I, the LORD, have spoken."

For today: let us not place our final trust in provision, work, or money, but in God, who gives us everything. If He corrects us, let us listen and return to Him with humility.
exp.22:22:
This verse lists the lovers who will come against Aholibah: the Babylonians and all the Chaldeans, the men of Pekod, Shoa, and Koa, and the Assyrians with them. They are described as desirable young men, governors and commanders, officers and men of renown, all mounted on horses. "Desirable" means appealing, and "young men" refers to their youth. "Governors and commanders" points to officials and military leaders.

God speaks through Ezekiel. Using the image of two sisters, Aholah (Samaria) and Aholibah (Jerusalem), he denounces his people for being unfaithful to him by seeking alliances with other nations instead of trusting him. Those who attracted them will become the instruments of their punishment. Interpreters see Babylon here as the nation that would come to judge Judah.

For today: what draws us away from God often looks bright, but it can end up hurting us. Examine the things you place your trust in, and return to God, who is faithful.
exp.21:24:
The verse says that the princes of Jerusalem have joined together in a plot, like a roaring lion tearing apart its prey. "They devour the people" means they destroyed lives; "they seize the treasures and precious things" refers to goods and possessions taken for themselves; and their abuses left many women widowed.

God speaks, telling Ezekiel to accuse Jerusalem shortly before its fall to Babylon. The leaders of the people, prophets, priests and princes, used their position for their own gain instead of caring for the people. That is why the judgment was just.

For today: if you have any influence, whether in the church, at work or in the family, use it to serve and protect others, not to get ahead. Ask God to examine your heart and give you integrity.
exp.19:5:
He says that God, on that day, made a solemn oath: he would bring Israel out of Egypt into a land that he himself had searched out for them. Swearing an oath was a gesture of firm promise. The phrase about a land flowing with milk and honey describes a fertile and abundant land. Calling it the glory of all lands shows God's affection for his gift. The phrase "searched out" means that God had looked over and chosen the land in advance.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is with the elders of Israel in exile. God reminds them of their history: from Egypt he was faithful, but the people fell into idolatry. With this he shows them that their present situation is not due to any lack of goodness on God's part.

For today: God keeps what he promises and prepares what is best for us. Trust in his goodness, and do not let any modern idolatry take the place that belongs to him.
exp.29:13:
It says that God will punish several important cities of Egypt. The phrase "I will lay waste" means to leave in ruins, and the word "Pathros" names the region of Upper Egypt, "Zoan" was a city in the Nile Delta, and "Thebes" is the city known in the text as "No." The phrase "execute judgment" means that God will bring his justice upon them.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. Egypt was a proud power, with idols and princes who felt secure. God announces that no fortress or false god will be able to save them. Many understand that Babylon would be the instrument of this judgment, although the text speaks of "foreigners."

For today: do not put your security in power, money, or prestige, for all of these can fall. Trust in the living God, who governs the nations and is just. Ask him today what you have put in the place of him.
exp.46:13:
It says the land will be divided into equal shares among the tribes. God says that he swore with an uplifted hand, that is, he made a solemn oath, to give this land to Israel's forefathers. So this land will come to them as an inheritance.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a vision of restoration for his people after the exile. Before this comes the image of the river that flows out from the sanctuary and gives life. Then the boundaries of the land are marked out. Interpreters differ: some see a literal fulfillment for Israel, others a spiritual picture of God's final blessing.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when a long time passes. We can trust his word in our hopes, and also be just and generous, without favoritism, with what he gives us.
exp.43:7:
It says that the people did not take proper care of the holy things that God had entrusted to them. Instead of serving faithfully themselves, they handed the work of looking after God's sanctuary over to other people.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision of the new temple. He rebukes Israel because they let in foreigners without wholehearted commitment to serve in the sanctuary, and in this way their house was dishonored. Some scholars see here a call to purity in worship; others debate how this vision of the temple will be fulfilled.

For today: God asks us to care sincerely for what He has entrusted to us, without leaving it all in the hands of others. Ask yourself what spiritual responsibility you need to take on personally.
exp.34:9:
This verse shows what Edom, represented by Mount Seir, was saying. Edom declared that the "two nations" and "two countries" would belong to them, and that they would take possession of them. Most readers understand these to be Israel and Judah, the northern and southern kingdoms. Edom spoke as if the LORD was not there, as if He would not act. The words "even though the LORD was there" show that God was present in that land and that His presence did not stop them from speaking this way.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Edom had long shown hostility toward Israel and wanted to profit from Israel's fall by seizing its land. God answers that He has heard these words and that He will judge that greed and that pride.

Today, we should not rejoice in the misfortune of others or hope to gain from it. God sees what we say and what we think. We can ask Him for a humble heart, one that helps and does not covet.
exp.38:16:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel to call out to the birds and the wild animals and invite them to a great feast on the mountains of Israel. The feast is the defeat of Israel's enemies, which God calls a sacrifice, and the birds and animals will eat flesh and drink blood.

The Lord God speaks to Ezekiel with strong, vivid language. This is part of the prophecy about Gog, a leader who would attack Israel. Scholars understand it in different ways: some read it as a literal future event, while others see it as a picture of God's final judgment against evil. Either way, God has the last word.

For today, we can take comfort that God will bring justice. Instead of seeking revenge, let us trust Him and keep doing good.
exp.32:22:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel again. The opening phrase of the verse, "Then the word of the LORD came to me," marks the start of a new message.

Ezekiel was a prophet exiled in Babylon. A survivor had just arrived with the news that Jerusalem had fallen, just as Ezekiel had announced. God had restored his speech, and now he gives him a message for those who had been left in the land and believed it belonged to them, even though they lived in injustice and idolatry.

For today: God still speaks through his Word, and it is wise to listen with humility, especially when he corrects us. Before claiming blessings, let us ask ourselves whether we are living in obedience and justice.
exp.24:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. The phrase "Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying" is the verse's way of saying, in plain terms: "I received a message from God." Ezekiel uses this wording to mark the beginning of a new message. There is no content yet here, only the introduction.

Ezekiel speaks as a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. With this verse a new section of the book opens: messages against the nations that bordered Israel. The first message, according to the verses that follow, is aimed at Ammon, which rejoiced when Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed. God does not ignore that mockery.

For today: God keeps speaking and hopes we will listen closely. Before we speak or react, we can pause to hear his word in the Bible. This passage also reminds us that God sees how we treat those who suffer, and it invites us not to take pleasure in other people's pain.
exp.26:14:
Dedan was a people of traders who did business with Tyre. Many coastlands, that is, distant lands along the sea, were the places where Tyre sold its goods. They paid Tyre with ivory tusks and with ebony, a dark, fine wood.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He is mourning the fall of Tyre, a city rich and proud because of its trade. The long list of peoples who did business with it shows how famous and powerful it was. But the chapter announces that all that wealth would not save it from God's judgment.

Today: Money and success can grow a great deal, but they are not a secure foundation. Use what you have with gratitude and generosity, and trust first in God, who does not change.
exp.36:16:
God tells Ezekiel to join the two sticks, one with the name of Judah and the other with the name of Joseph or Ephraim, until they become one. The instruction "join them together" means to bring them together as one. The words "so that they become one in your hand" mean that, when he holds them, they will look like a single stick.

Ezekiel speaks to a people in exile and divided. For centuries, the northern kingdom (Israel or Ephraim) and the southern kingdom (Judah) had been separated. God uses this action as a sign to prompt people to ask questions, so that he can explain his promise: one day he will gather them and they will be one people under his hand.

For today: if God promises to join what was broken, we too can seek reconciliation. Think of a divided relationship, in your family or in your church, and take a humble step toward peace today, trusting that God knows how to heal what seems impossible.
exp.6:3:
God says that he will not look on his people with pity, nor will he spare them. He will punish them for their ways and for the detestable practices among them. Their wrongdoing will not be hidden or excused, but will be out in the open in their midst. In the end they will know that he is the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. He announces judgment on Israel for years of idolatry and injustice. This is not a sudden outburst of anger: the people had repeatedly rejected his warnings. Some understand the statement that he will not spare them as the end of his patience after a long time of calls to repentance.

For today: our choices have consequences, and God calls us to turn back to him before it is too late. Today you can honestly examine a habit you know does not please him, and ask him for forgiveness and help to change.
exp.47:5:
This verse says that, alongside the territory of Ephraim, another strip of land was set aside for the tribe of Reuben. The portion runs from east to west, reaching across the full width of the land, all the way to the Mediterranean Sea. A "border" is a boundary or edge, and a "portion" is the share assigned.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who writes during the exile in Babylon. In this final vision, it describes how the land would be divided among the tribes, with even strips and the sanctuary at the center. Scholars understand this vision in different ways: some see it as a literal promise, others as a symbolic picture of God's restoration.

For today: God cares that each person has their place, and that He is at the center. We can ask ourselves whether, in our lives, our families, and our church, we are giving God that central place.
exp.14:6:
God says that he will set himself against the inhabitants of Jerusalem. To set one's face against someone means to confront them with judgment. Though they may have escaped one fire, another fire will consume them. In this way they will recognize that God is the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. He compares Jerusalem to the wood of a vine, which is of no use for making anything and is only valuable if it bears fruit. Because the people did not bear the fruit of faithfulness and rebelled against God (unfaithfulness means betraying or seriously breaking a covenant), God announces his judgment.

For today: God expects a life that bears the fruit of obedience and trust in him. We can honestly examine where we have turned away, and return to him sincerely, before pride hardens us.
exp.43:23:
In any dispute, the priests will serve as judges, and they must judge according to God's ordinances, not according to their own opinions. They must also keep God's laws and statutes concerning all his appointed feasts, and they must keep his Sabbaths holy.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of a new temple. In this passage he describes how the Levitical priests of the family of Zadok must live: teaching the people the difference between what is holy and what is common, and setting an example of obedience. Scholars interpret this vision in different ways, and there is no complete agreement.

For today: if God has given you some responsibility over others, as a parent, leader, or teacher, seek to decide with justice according to his Word, not according to your convenience, and live out yourself what you teach.
exp.17:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. "Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying" means that a message from God came to him. It is an opening phrase that announces that what follows is not the prophet's own ideas, but what God wants to say.

Ezekiel was a priest who lived in exile in Babylon with other Israelites. Many of them believed they were suffering for the sins of their ancestors and not because of their own choices. God gives Ezekiel a message to correct that way of thinking, and in the verses that follow he does so with a popular proverb.

For today: before listening to God, it helps to stop blaming others for our situation. His word invites us to look honestly at our own lives, and to receive his correction with humility and hope.
exp.24:9:
God says he will hand the land of Ammon over to the people of the East, the desert peoples to the east, probably nomadic tribes, along with Moab, to possess as their inheritance. As a result, Ammon would no longer be remembered among the nations. The verse speaks of giving the land and possessing it, and "the nations" means the peoples of the world.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile of Judah in Babylon. Ammon and Moab mocked Judah when it fell, saying it was just like any other people. God responds by defending his people and judging that contempt. Scholars generally agree that this is a historical judgment, though they do not all agree on exactly how it was fulfilled.

For today: God sees the mockery and pride that rejoice in the pain of others. Let us learn not to celebrate anyone's downfall, but to show compassion, and to trust that God cares for those who suffer.
exp.33:24:
God promises to make a covenant of peace with his people, meaning a firm commitment to protect them and give them calm and security. He will rid the land of wild animals, meaning dangerous beasts. Because of this, his people will be able to live in the wilderness securely, which means safe and free from fear, and even sleep peacefully in the forest.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier, he has criticized the bad shepherds of Israel, who abused the sheep. Now he promises a faithful shepherd, called David. Many Christians see here a reference to Jesus, a descendant of David. Some interpreters understand the beasts literally, and others as a symbol of enemies and threats.

For today: if Christ is your shepherd, you can rest in his care even in places that seem dangerous. Speak to him about your fears tonight and hand them over to him before you sleep.
exp.19:21:
God says that he held back his punishment. "I withheld My hand" means that he stopped himself from carrying out judgment and did not destroy them. He did this for the sake of his name, so that it would not be profaned, that is, dishonored or treated with contempt, in the eyes of the nations who had seen him bring Israel out of Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He reminds the leaders of Israel that their rebellion goes back a long way, all the way to the wilderness. Even so, God did not finish them off, because his reputation was tied to his people. The verses that follow show that discipline came anyway, later on.

For today: our hope does not rest on how good we are, but on God's faithfulness to his own name. His patience with you is not permission to keep doing the same things, but an invitation to return to him and to live in a way that honors him before those who watch you.
exp.2:19:
Ezekiel 3:20 says that if a person who has been living righteously turns away from what is good and commits evil, and God puts a stumbling block in his path, that person will die. If no one warned him, he will die in his sin, and the good things he did earlier will not be remembered. The watchman who failed to warn him will be held responsible for his blood.

God is speaking to Ezekiel, whom he appointed as a watchman over Israel during the exile in Babylon. His task was to warn faithfully, both the wicked and the righteous. If he gave the warning, he fulfilled his responsibility, even if the people did not listen. Scholars debate how to understand "he will die," whether it refers to physical death or spiritual death.

For today: if you see someone close to you turning away from God, do not stay silent out of fear or comfort. Speak to them with love, humility, and truth, and leave the outcome in God's hands.
exp.11:2:
God tells Ezekiel to pack his bags as if he were leaving for exile, and to set out from his home in broad daylight, where everyone can see him. Packing bags for the road refers to the things a person takes along on a long journey. The phrase "as they watch" means right in front of their eyes. The phrase "perhaps they will understand" means they might respond and take notice.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet among the exiles in Babylon. The people did not want to listen or believe that Jerusalem would be taken into captivity. That is why God uses a visible action, a prophetic sign, as a message that can be seen and not only heard. Even so, the hope that they might "perhaps understand" shows his patience.

For today: God still wants us to listen to him. Ask him for an attentive and teachable heart, and let your life, not only your words, speak with honesty and clarity.
exp.38:2:
It says God will take away Gog's main weapon. The bow in the left hand and the arrows in the right hand show a warrior ready to fight. God declares that He will strike the bow from his hand and knock the arrows down, leaving him without power and without defense. The verse uses a word that scholars understand in different ways, so its exact meaning in the original remains open to some debate.
