The Lord God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Gog appears as a leader of enemy nations who will attack Israel. The prophecy announces that God Himself will step in and defeat them. Scholars disagree about whether Gog refers to historical events, a future event, or a symbol of evil.

For today: when you feel you are facing something stronger than you, remember that God rules over all human power. Trust in Him, pray, and rest in the knowledge that justice and protection ultimately belong to Him.
exp.20:15:
The passage gives a command to the sword of judgment: "Slash to the right; set your blade to the left, wherever your blade is directed." The sword is pictured as something that goes where it is sent, cutting in whichever direction it is aimed.

God is speaking, and he has asked Ezekiel to announce judgment on Jerusalem and its people for their rebellion. The sword is usually understood as the army of Babylon, although the text presents it as an instrument of God. Some think God is speaking to the sword, others that he is addressing the prophet; the general sense is that the judgment is not by chance, but is directed.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also is in control and sets limits on his judgment. Today we can come to him with humility, trust in his justice, and let him correct our heart in time.
exp.27:2:
God says to the prince of Tyre: "Behold, you are wiser than Daniel; no secret is hidden from you!" Many read this as mockery: the ruler believed he was the wisest of all. The word "Behold" here is a call to pay attention, to look and take notice.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The ruler of Tyre, a rich and powerful city, had filled himself with pride and even compared himself to God. Daniel was famous for his wisdom, although some scholars debate whether Ezekiel means the Daniel of Babylon or an older righteous man. The central point is that God confronts his arrogance.

For today: intelligence, success, and money are gifts, not reasons to feel superior. Ask God for humility and acknowledge that all wisdom comes from Him.
exp.24:13:
God says he will punish Edom, and that he will do it through his people Israel. The words "vengeance," "anger," and "wrath" speak of a just judgment from God, not of a human outburst. In the end, Edom will know that this punishment comes from God himself. "Then they will know" means they will recognize it through what actually happens.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, around the time Jerusalem fell to Babylon. Edom, a neighboring nation descended from Esau, had held a grudge and took revenge on Judah with cruelty in its time of weakness. God responds to that wickedness. Scholars debate how and when this prophecy was exactly fulfilled.

For today: do not take revenge on your own, and do not hold on to old grudges. Leave judgment to God, because he sees every injustice and is the only one who judges with perfect justice. Trust in him and seek peace.
exp.13:3:
God tells Ezekiel to warn the people of Israel who set up idols in their hearts, meaning they inwardly value and serve them, even while they come to ask the prophet for guidance. A wicked stumbling block placed before their face is whatever leads them into sin. God says he will answer such a person according to their great idolatry, which points to a severe response, one of judgment, that matches their divided heart.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to some of the elders of Israel who were living in exile. They appeared to be seeking God, but their hearts remained devoted to other gods. God is not satisfied with a religion that is only outward appearance; he wants them to truly turn back to him, as shown by the call to repentance.

Today we can ask ourselves what, in secret, holds the place of God in our hearts. Before asking him for anything, it is good to be honest, let go of that idol, and return to him with all our heart.
exp.20:17:
Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying. This sentence is a short formula that appears again and again in Ezekiel. "Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying" means that God spoke to Ezekiel once more. It is like saying: "A message from the LORD came to me."

The one speaking is God, and he gives the prophet a new message. Before this, God had announced judgment using the image of a sword. Now a new instruction begins: Ezekiel is to draw two roads along which the king of Babylon could advance, toward Rabbah of the Ammonites or toward Jerusalem. This shows that God works even within human decisions and political pressures.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before deciding something important, seek to hear him with humility, by reading the Bible and praying, rather than trusting only your own judgment.
exp.24:16:
God says he will punish the Philistines with force. The word "vengeance" here means a just punishment, not a hateful payback. "Furious reproof" describes a harsh correction, given with holy anger. The purpose is that they will come to recognize that the LORD is God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The Philistines had acted with spite and had attacked Israel out of long-standing hostility. God judges them for that wickedness. This message is part of a series of words against Israel's neighboring nations.

For today: let us not hold on to old grudges or look for a way to get even. God sees every injustice and is the one who judges with righteousness. We can hand our wounds over to him, forgive, and trust that he will do what is right, as Romans 12:19 teaches.
exp.0:24:
When the living creatures stood still, they lowered their wings, and then a voice came from above them, from the expanse, which is a kind of firm, shining vault or platform over their heads. "Lowered" means that they folded down or relaxed their wings. "Came" is what the verse says.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. He recounts a vision of the glory of God. First there is a loud noise of wings; then stillness and a voice. After that a throne appears. Many understand that God shows himself close to his people, even in exile, and is about to speak to them. The details of the vision are interpreted in various ways.

For today: before hearing God, it is good to pause. Find a moment of stillness, without hurry or noise, to listen for his voice in the Bible and in prayer.
exp.20:29:
God asks whether he will return the sword to its sheath. "Return" means to put it back, and "sheath" is the case that holds the blade. The implied answer is no: the judgment is not finished. God says he will judge Ammon in the place where it was created, in the land of its origin.

God speaks through Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man." Ammon mocked the fall of Judah, and its false prophets promised that it would be safe. God answers that this comforting deception will not save it. Some scholars think the verse is addressed to the sword and others that it is addressed to Ammon, so the text is not entirely clear on that point.

For today: do not trust in words that only reassure you. Seek God's truth, and do not mock the suffering of others.
exp.17:17:
This verse speaks about the father in the previous example. He practiced extortion, robbed his brother, and did what was wrong among his people. For this reason, God says, that father will die for his own iniquity. "Wrong" means harm or injustice, and "robbed" means that he took what belonged to his brother, which is the same idea as the wording of the verse itself.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. They were repeating a saying: that the children paid for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person answers for himself. The righteous son would not be punished for his unjust father, and the unjust father would be judged for what he himself did.

For today: do not use your family's history as an excuse for wrongdoing, and do not live tied to the guilt of others. God invites you to seek justice, to be honest, and to treat others well, starting today.
exp.28:13:
God says he will restore the Egyptians who were taken captive and scattered. He will bring them back to Pathros, the region of southern Egypt, which was their land of origin. The phrase "I will restore" points to returning people to a former condition, and "a lowly kingdom" describes a humble kingdom without greatness.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Egypt had been proud and unreliable for Israel, which at times sought its help instead of trusting in God. For this reason God announces judgment, but also a limited restoration. The forty years can be understood literally or as a symbolic period; scholars interpret them in different ways.

For today: God corrects pride, but he can also restore in humility. If today you trust your money, your strength, or your connections more than God, ask him to teach you to depend on him. His discipline is not always the end of the story.
exp.30:11:
It says a huge and proud tree will be brought down. Foreigners, "the most ruthless of the nations," will cut it down and leave it lying there. Its branches will fall on the mountains and in every valley, and its broken boughs will lie scattered across all the earth's ravines. The peoples who used to rest in its shadow will leave it and abandon it.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, and directs this message to the pharaoh of Egypt. He compares him to a very tall tree, like Assyria. God judges him because his heart was filled with pride. Many understand that Babylon would be the instrument of this judgment.

For today: power, success, and fame are neither secure nor eternal. If I start to trust in what I have and look down on others, it is wise to remember that God opposes the proud. We can ask him for a humble heart and use our influence to serve.
exp.18:7:
This verse says that the nations around him gathered their forces and came against the young lion, that is, the king the chapter is about. They spread a net over him, as hunters do with wild animals, and he was trapped in the pit they had dug. The phrase about being trapped simply means he was caught and taken captive. The provinces mentioned are the surrounding regions.

God speaks through Ezekiel in a lament over the princes of Israel. Many understand that this young lion is Jehoahaz or Jehoiachin, kings of Judah who were carried into captivity, although the text does not give a name and this is debated. The song shows that his violence and pride ended in defeat and exile.

For today: what we sow with our power or our character sooner or later reaches us. Let us ask God for humility to use well whatever authority we have, caring for others instead of taking advantage of them.
exp.6:25:
Disasters will come one after another, and bad news will keep following. In their distress, the people will look for a word from God through a prophet, but they will not receive one. Instruction from the priests will be lost, and the elders will have no counsel to give. "Disaster" means destruction or calamity; "news" is information, and here it is almost always bad.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Jerusalem for the people's idolatry and violence. They had ignored God for a long time, and now, in the crisis, their leaders could not guide them. Interpreters understand this silence as part of the judgment itself.

For today: let us not wait for a crisis to seek God. If we read his Word and obey it now, we will have direction and peace when difficult times arrive.
exp.22:8:
This verse says that God handed Aholah, a symbolic woman, over into the hands of her lovers, the Assyrians, whom she lusted after. "Lovers" refers to those she sought out instead of remaining faithful; "lusted for" describes a desire that took hold of her and drove her choices.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this allegory, Aholah represents Samaria, the northern kingdom of Israel, and Aholibah represents Jerusalem. The adulterous acts symbolize unfaithfulness to God: seeking political alliances and foreign idols. When Assyria conquered Samaria, God presents this as the consequence of that choice.

For today: whatever we put in place of God, whether success, money, or approval, ends up controlling us and hurting us. Today you could identify what you are trusting in more than God, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.6:7:
God says he is about to punish his people, and that it will happen soon. The words translated "soon" in the reader's version mean "very soon" or "right away." The phrases "pour out My wrath" and "vent My anger" are strong ways of saying that his anger will be fully expressed. "I will judge you according to your ways" means the punishment will match the people's conduct. The "abominations" are detestable practices, above all idolatry.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He addresses Israel, the land of Judah, which had turned away from him. The text presents this as a judgment already announced: the end is coming. Interpreters connect it with the fall of Jerusalem, which took place in 586 BC.

Today we can take seriously that God sees our lives and is not indifferent to evil. It is wise to examine our ways with humility and turn back to him while there is still time, trusting that he welcomes those who repent.
exp.45:4:
Along with each ram offered, the prince was to bring one ephah of grain offering. With the lambs, he gave as much as he was able, according to his generosity. In addition, a hin of oil was added for each ephah. An ephah was a measure of dry goods, roughly 20 to 40 liters by estimates, and a hin was a measure of liquids, much smaller.

God speaks through Ezekiel in the vision of the new temple (chapters 40 to 48). There he gives rules for worship, the Sabbath, and the new moon. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as a literal future temple, others as a symbolic picture of God's presence with his restored people.

For today: worshiping God includes order, but also a generous heart. Think about what you can give this week, according to your means, with joy and without pressure.
exp.27:18:
All the nations who know you are appalled over you. You have come to a horrible end and will be no more.

This verse says that all the nations who knew the king of Tyre will be appalled at his downfall. His end will be a horrible one, filled with dread and horror. "You have come to a horrible end and will be no more" announces that his power and glory will disappear completely.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He is judging the king of Tyre, a rich trading city. The king took pride in his beauty and wisdom, and used them badly through injustice and corrupt dealings. Some see here only a human king; others think the language also alludes to Satan. Interpreters do not agree.

For today: success, talent, and wealth are gifts from God, not reasons to think ourselves superior. Let us ask him for a humble heart, one that uses what it has to serve honestly and not to exalt itself.
exp.22:15:
She saw the Chaldean men painted on the wall, and at the sight of them she lusted for them. Then she sent messengers to them in Chaldea. The Chaldeans are the Babylonians.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the story of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem), as a picture of an unfaithful people. Oholibah sought alliances and foreign gods instead of trusting the LORD. The "lusted" here describes spiritual and political unfaithfulness. Scholars agree on this, although they debate some historical details.

For today: what we gaze at persistently can awaken desires that pull us away from God. Be careful what you let in through your eyes and your heart, and when you feel drawn to something that separates you from Him, stop and ask Him again to be your greatest treasure.
exp.35:6:
God says that he has lifted up his hand, which means he has sworn a solemn oath. He promises that the nations around Israel will bear the consequences of their own reproach. The reproach in this verse is the insult and dishonor they heaped on Israel, and now they will have to endure it themselves.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel at a time when the people were in exile and their land lay desolate. Nations such as Edom mocked Israel and wanted to take that land for themselves. God responds with a fierce, firm love that defends his people. Then he promises that the mountains of Israel will once again bear fruit.

For today: when you feel humiliated or unjustly treated, you can trust that God sees and that his justice is certain. Give him your pain, refrain from seeking revenge, and wait on his faithfulness.
exp.6:23:
He says that God will bring the most wicked of nations to take possession of their houses. He will also end the pride of the mighty, and the places they regarded as holy will be profaned. "Profaned" means treated without respect, as if they were not holy.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, shortly before the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. The people were full of violence and injustice, and they also trusted in the temple as if it would protect them. God shows that judgment is serious, and that religion without obedience does not save.

For today: let us not trust in our reputation, our religious customs, or our possessions. Let us examine the heart, put aside pride, and seek God with humility and sincere obedience.
exp.16:10:
This verse says: "Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying." The word "came" here introduces the new message. It is a transition that announces God is about to speak to Ezekiel again.

The prophet Ezekiel is speaking, and he is in exile in Babylon. He has just told a parable about a vine that does not prosper, and now God gives him a new message to explain it. The verses that follow make clear that the parable refers to the king of Judah and his alliance with Babylon, which he later broke. The people did not want to understand, so God calls them a "rebellious house."

For today: God does not leave his messages half-finished, but helps us understand them. We can come to the Bible with an open heart, asking him to explain what we do not understand and being willing to obey what he shows us.
exp.33:22:
God promises to appoint over his people one shepherd who will care for them and feed them. "To appoint" means to put someone in place to lead, and "to feed" means to lead the flock to eat and to look after it. He calls him "My servant David," and says twice that he will feed them and be their shepherd.

The passage comes from the prophet Ezekiel, during Israel's exile. Earlier he had condemned the leaders who took advantage of the people, like strong sheep that shove the weak ones aside. David had died centuries before, so many understand this name to point to a future descendant of his. Christians see in it Jesus, the Good Shepherd; others read it as a king who would restore the people.

For today: when you feel lost or mistreated, remember that God provides a Shepherd who cares for you. And if you have any influence over others, care for them tenderly, without pushing the weak aside.
exp.32:28:
God says that when the land is left a desolate waste, the people will come to know who he is. The cause is the abominations they have committed, meaning the detestable things they did, such as idolatry, violence, and injustice.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel after Jerusalem had already fallen (Ezekiel 33:21). Those who remained in the ruins of Judah were still confident and had not turned back to God. He tells them that his judgment is real and that his words will come true.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we only hear the Word of God with pleasure or whether we truly obey it. Right now you can choose one concrete action that God is asking of you and put it into practice with humility.
exp.32:24:
God asks this with irony: how do they expect to keep the land if they eat meat with the blood still in it, lift their eyes to their idols, and shed blood? To "lift up their eyes to the idols" means to place their trust and desire in them. The question makes clear that the answer is no.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to those who remained among the ruins of Israel after the fall of Jerusalem. They boasted: "Abraham was only one man and he received the land; we are many, so the land is even more rightly ours." God answers them that the land is not secured by numbers, but by living faithfully to Him.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we expect God's blessings while living as we please. His grace invites us to return to Him with sincerity, not to rely on our privileges or inheritance.
exp.26:17:
1) What it says: Damascus traded with Tyre because Tyre made a great many products and had great wealth in goods. Damascus brought wine from Helbon and wool from Zahar to Tyre. The word "merchant" refers to someone who trades. The "products" are the goods that Tyre made or produced. Helbon was a place known for its wine, although scholars are not sure of its exact location. The wool is described as coming from Zahar, though the exact place is also uncertain.

2) Context: God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He asks him to sing a lament over Tyre, a city rich from its sea trade. This list of nations shows how great and proud Tyre was, before the announcement of its fall.

3) For today: Riches and success can seem secure, but they are not a firm foundation. Be thankful for what you have, work with integrity, and place your trust in God, not in your possessions.
exp.38:0:
God commands Ezekiel, whom He calls "son of man," a human being, to prophesy, meaning to speak on God's behalf. The message is aimed at Gog. God declares: "Behold, I am against you." The phrase "chief prince of Meshech and Tubal" can be understood as the main leader of Meshech and Tubal.

The Lord GOD speaks, in a prophecy given to the prophet Ezekiel for the people of Israel. Gog appears as a leader who attacks God's people. Scholars disagree about who he is: some see real nations, others a symbol of evil in the last times. What is clear is that God opposes whoever oppresses His people.

For today: when evil seems very powerful, remember that God is greater than any power. You can rest in Him and pray with confidence.
exp.40:24:
The verse says that the doors of the temple were decorated with carvings of cherubim and palm trees, matching the carvings on the walls. It also says there was a wooden canopy outside, on the front of the entrance porch. "Carved" means cut or shaped into the wood or stone.

Ezekiel was a priest and prophet who had been taken into exile in Babylon. God gave him a vision of a new temple, measured with great care. This encouraged a people who had lost their homeland to believe that God was still with them and that they would be restored. Scholars disagree about whether this temple should be understood literally, symbolically, or as something still to come.

For today: the cherubim and palm trees remind us that God is holy, but He also invites us to live in His presence with life and hope. We can set aside a quiet moment each day to draw near to Him with reverence and gratitude, without hurry.
exp.22:20:
Ezekiel 23:21 says that Aholibah, a name for Jerusalem, called to mind again the indecency of her youth. The key word is "youth," because it points to the earlier years of Israel's unfaithfulness. "Revisited" means she returned to those memories with longing. The picture of the Egyptians caressing her bosom and pressing her young breasts is frank, sensual language, describing how she had given herself to Egypt in improper and shameful relationships.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the vivid image of two unfaithful sisters to show that Judah sought foreign alliances and idols instead of trusting in Him. Egypt was one of those temptations. Then comes judgment: the very allies she had chased would turn against her.

For today: when we feel nostalgia for a past that hurt us, let us remember where it led us. Better to bring those desires to God and seek in Him our security and rest.
exp.33:9:
It says that God himself sets himself against the shepherds who failed. "Behold, I am against the shepherds" means "here I am, against the shepherds." God will demand the flock from them, will remove them from tending the flock, and will deliver his flock from their mouths, so that the flock is no longer food for them. To feed the flock means to care for and nourish it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during Israel's exile in Babylon. The "shepherds" were the leaders of the people, especially the rulers. Instead of caring for the people, they sought their own gain, and the people were scattered and left unprotected. God responds by defending his sheep and promising to care for them himself.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, in the family, the church, or at work, ask yourself whether you are serving or only seeking your own advantage. And if you have been hurt by bad leaders, remember that God sees and cares for his own.
exp.2:11:
Then the Spirit lifted Ezekiel up, and behind him he heard a great rumbling sound. The voice said: "Blessed be the glory of the LORD in His dwelling place!" The phrase about the Spirit lifting him is the same idea as the verse above, which reads "lifted me up." The word "rumbling" here names the same great, strong noise described in the verse above.

Ezekiel speaks here, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. He had just seen the glory of God and received the task of speaking to his people, though perhaps they would not want to listen. Before sending him, God shows him his greatness. It is not known with certainty who speaks these words; some think they are the living creatures or angels, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: before doing what God asks of you, stop to praise him. Remembering who God is gives you strength and encouragement to obey, even when the task is difficult.
exp.28:14:
This verse says that Egypt will be a lowly kingdom, lower than the others. It will never again rise above the nations, because God himself will make it smaller. The phrase about ruling means to dominate or give orders over others, so the sentence means that God will bring it about that Egypt can no longer rule over the nations.

Here God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during Israel's exile in Babylon. Egypt had been proud and was also a false source of security for Israel, which sought its help instead of trusting God. God promises to restore Egypt after forty years, but without its former greatness. Scholars debate exactly how and when this was fulfilled.

For today: trusting in power, money or prestige is always fragile. God brings down the proud, but he also offers restoration. Today we can place our security in him and not in things that pass away.
exp.27:21:
God speaks to Ezekiel and commands him to declare a message against the city of Sidon. He says that he is against her, and that he will be glorified within her, meaning he will be honored and recognized as great. When he carries out his judgments, his just punishments, Sidon will know that he is the LORD.

"Demonstrate My holiness through her" means that he will show his holiness, which is his perfect purity and separateness from all that is wrong.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Sidon was a neighboring city of Israel, and the following passage says that it had been a thorn and a terror to Israel, for it had despised them. God promises justice and relief for his people. The text does not detail every historical event, so it is not wise to add more.

For today: God sees unjust treatment and is not indifferent. We can trust him instead of taking revenge, and live in such a way that his holiness is seen in us.
exp.16:18:
God says, swearing by his own life, that the king of Judah despised the oath he had made in God's name and broke the covenant. Therefore, God will bring the consequences of that sin down upon the king's own head. The phrase "I will bring down upon his head" means that God will repay him with the punishment he deserves.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Zedekiah, king of Judah, had sworn loyalty to Babylon before God, but he rebelled and sought help from Egypt. God regards that oath as something serious, even though it was made to a foreign king.

For today: our word matters to God. If we promise something, at work, in the family, or in the church, let us try to keep it with honesty. And if we fail, we can ask him for forgiveness and for help to be faithful.
exp.26:0:
Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying. This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. "Then the word of the LORD came to me" is the opening phrase of a new message, and what God will say comes in the verses that follow.

The one speaking is God, and the one listening is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon. With this verse begins a chapter devoted to Tyre, a rich and proud city that traded by sea. God instructs Ezekiel to raise a lament, that is, a funeral song, because it announces the fall of that city, which boasted of its beauty and its power.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before trusting in our riches or achievements, it is wise to stop and listen to him with humility.
exp.15:19:
God says that Jerusalem took the sons and daughters she had borne to Him and sacrificed them as food to idols. Their children were given up to be consumed by fire. The word "prostitution" describes spiritual unfaithfulness, a turning away from God to other gods. The final question shows grief: was all that unfaithfulness not enough?

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout the chapter, Jerusalem is like a wife whom God cared for, clothed, and fed from her humble beginnings. She used those same gifts to worship idols. Sacrificing children was a pagan practice that God forbade.

For today: everything we have comes from God, and we can put it in the wrong place. Ask yourself which things, such as success or money, receive the best of your time and your heart, and place them again under God's care.
exp.7:16:
God asks Ezekiel, "Have you seen this, son of man?" Then he says that what Judah was doing was not a small matter. On top of the wrongs they were committing there, they had filled the land with violence and kept provoking his anger again and again. "Look, they are even putting the branch to their nose" is a difficult phrase. It is understood as something that offends God. Some scholars think it refers to an insulting gesture, but no one can say this for certain.

God speaks in a vision that shows the prophet what was happening in Jerusalem. Shortly before, twenty-five men, with their backs to the temple, were worshiping the sun, something God had forbidden. Judah joined social injustice with idolatry, and God sees them together.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith in the temple or the church is supported by a just life at home and at work. God is not pleased with a worship that exists alongside injustice and with routines that dishonor him.
exp.35:8:
God says to the mountains of Israel: "Look, I am on your side, and I will turn toward you." The phrase "I am on your side" means "I am for you." "Plowed" means turned over by a plow, and "sown" means that seed will be scattered on them. In other words, the land will be worked again and will bear fruit.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Israel was in exile, and its land had been left in ruins and mocked by the neighboring nations. God promises to restore the land and his people, so that they will live there again and the land will bear fruit once more.

For today: when you feel that your life is like dry or abandoned ground, remember that God can turn toward you. Bring Him your ruins honestly and let Him work them again. Restoration is usually a patient process, like a field being prepared before it bears fruit.
exp.29:9:
God announces that he is going to bring an end to the hordes of Egypt, that is, its great population, wealth and power. To do this he will use Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. The phrase "I will put an end to" means that this power will be brought to a stop.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. Egypt was a proud nation that trusted in its own strength and had been a deceptive support for Judah. God shows that he rules over all nations and that he can use even a king who does not know him to carry out his judgment. Scholars recognize this prophecy within the Babylonian campaigns against Egypt, although the historical details are debated.

Today we can remember that no human power is secure: not money, not fame, not allies. It is wise to place our trust in God, who continues to govern history.
exp.15:28:
It says that Jerusalem, compared to an unfaithful woman, kept increasing her unfaithfulness toward God. She did this by extending her promiscuity to Chaldea, the land of merchants, which is Babylon. Here "promiscuity" means idolatry and alliances with other nations, not only sexual sin. Yet even with all of this, she was not satisfied. Despite all her searching outside of God, she never became content.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he tells the story of Jerusalem as a girl whom He rescued, cared for, and adorned. She, however, turned to idols and to neighboring nations. God shows her her sin in order to call her to acknowledge it. Some understand the references to Chaldea as religious and political influences; the text uses it as a strong image.

For today: when we look for satisfaction in things that are not God, such as money, success, or approval, it is never enough. Today you can ask yourself what you are pursuing to fill your emptiness, and bring it to God in prayer.
exp.40:25:
The verse describes the temple building as having beveled windows and palm trees carved on the sidewalls of the portico. It also says the side rooms of the temple had canopies. The word "beveled" is the one the verse uses for the windows. The meaning of the canopies is hard to pin down, and scholars understand them in several ways.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, a priest who was living in exile in Babylon. In a vision, a guide shows him and measures a new temple. God wanted to encourage his wounded people, reminding them that one day he would dwell among them again. Scholars disagree about whether this temple is literal or symbolic.

For today: God cares even about the details of where he dwells. Today the New Testament says that our body is a temple of the Holy Spirit. Ask yourself: what small detail of my life can I care for today to honor God?
exp.2:23:
The verse tells us that the Spirit entered Ezekiel, set him on his feet, and spoke to him. He was told to go into his house and shut himself inside.

God is the speaker. Ezekiel had fallen on his face when he saw the glory of the Lord in the plain. Now God lifts him up and sends him home. The verses that follow explain that the people were rebellious, and that Ezekiel would be restricted and would speak only when God gave him a message. Interpreters debate whether all of this was literal or symbolic, but the sense is clear: his silence was part of the message.

When God shows us something great, He sometimes asks us for stillness before we speak. Learn to wait for His voice, and let Him sustain you when you feel without strength.
exp.7:11:
God asks Ezekiel whether he has seen what the elders of Israel are doing in the darkness, each at the shrine of his own idol. They are saying, "The LORD does not see us; the LORD has forsaken the land." The phrase "in the darkness" speaks of what is hidden, and "shrine" refers to a private place set apart for worship.

God speaks in a vision shown to Ezekiel, a prophet in exile, about what was happening in the temple in Jerusalem. Seventy elders were worshiping images in hiding. God shows them their sin and explains why judgment is coming. They believed that God was far away or was not paying attention.

For today: God also sees what we do when we are alone. Instead of hiding something that pulls us away from him, we can confess it honestly, ask for his forgiveness, and ask for his help to change.
exp.43:1:
God tells Ezekiel that the east gate of the sanctuary must remain shut. No one will be able to open it or go through it, because the Lord, the God of Israel, has entered through that gate. "This gate is to remain shut" is the start of the message, and "no one" here means any person at all.

The Lord speaks in a vision of the temple that Ezekiel receives during the exile. In chapter 43 the glory of God returned to the temple through that east gate. The gate remains closed as a sign that the place through which God entered is holy. The text goes on to mention the prince, who will be allowed to eat there before God. Interpreters explain this vision in several ways, and not all of them agree.

For today: let us value what God has set apart. Let us draw near to Him with reverence, remembering that His presence is a holy gift and not something ordinary.
exp.37:22:
God says that He Himself will be magnified and recognized as holy before many nations. Being "sanctified" means that His holiness, that is, His greatness and purity, will be displayed for all to see. The words "I will reveal Myself in the sight of many nations" mean that He will make Himself visible before many peoples. The final result is that they will know that He is the LORD.

God is speaking through the prophet Ezekiel. He has just described judgment on Gog and his allies, who come against Israel, with sword, plague, heavy rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur. Scholars interpret Gog in several ways (a historical enemy, a future enemy, or a symbol of evil), and there is no full agreement. What is clear is the purpose: that God be recognized.

For today: even when the world seems dominated by evil, we can trust that God has the last word. Today we can live with calm and honor Him in our everyday lives.
exp.22:3:
Ezekiel 23:4 names two sisters, Oholah, the older, and Oholibah, her sister. God says they became his and gave birth to sons and daughters. Then the verse explains the symbol: Oholah stands for Samaria, and Oholibah stands for Jerusalem.

The one speaking is God, and he is speaking to the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the picture of two sisters to show how the kingdoms of Israel (Samaria) and Judah (Jerusalem) were unfaithful to him, turning to other gods and foreign alliances. The language is harsh on purpose, so that the people would see how serious their sin was. The names sound alike in Hebrew, and their meanings are explained in several ways.

God does not overlook it when we give to others the place that belongs only to him. Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security, and return to trusting him.
exp.33:23:
It says that God himself will be the God of his people, and that "my servant David" will be a prince among them. "Prince" here means ruler or leader. It ends with "I, the LORD, have spoken," which works like a seal: what has been said is firm and sure.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during Israel's exile. Earlier he had condemned the unfaithful shepherds who mistreated the sheep. Now he promises to rescue them. David died centuries before, so "David" is understood as a future king of his line. Christians see in this Jesus, the Good Shepherd, though others read it differently.

For today: when leaders fail you or you feel lost, remember that God remains your Shepherd. Trust his guidance and seek to follow Jesus, who cares for his people faithfully.
exp.16:14:
It says that the king of Judah rebelled against the king of Babylon by sending envoys to Egypt to ask for horses and a large army. Then God asks, with a tone of reproach: Will he flourish? Will the one who does such things escape? Can he break a covenant and yet escape? A covenant is a firm promise or agreement, and envoys are official messengers sent on behalf of a ruler.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was exiled in Babylon. King Zedekiah had sworn loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar, but he broke that oath and sought help from Egypt. God reminds him that a promise made in his name is serious, and that trusting in human power would not save him.

For today: keep your word, even when it is hard, and do not look for deceptive shortcuts. When you feel fear or pressure, instead of relying only on human resources, go first to God with honesty and ask him for wisdom to act with integrity.
exp.0:16:
This verse says that the wheels Ezekiel saw beside the living creatures could move in any of the four directions without pivoting as they moved. The phrase "four directions" here means the four points of the compass. In other words, they moved in any direction without needing to change how they faced.

Ezekiel was a priest living in exile in Babylon. He describes a vision of God's glory that he received by the river Chebar. The wheels, with eyes all around them, accompany the living creatures. Interpreters understand them in several ways, but many see in them the presence and power of God, who is not limited to a single place.

For today: God is not bound to one place or one circumstance. Even when your life takes unexpected turns, He remains with you and knows where it is going. You can trust that He is with you in every direction.
exp.26:35:
Those who trade among the nations will hiss over Tyre, that is, they will make a sound of astonishment or scorn when they see her fall. A "horrible end" is a dreadful fate that causes shock and dismay. The city will be destroyed and will no longer exist.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a city rich and powerful through its sea trade. Earlier, the text describes her as a great ship full of riches that sinks. It says that Tyre filled herself with pride because of her wealth. Some understand the "will be no more" as a final blow to her power of that time.

For today: riches and success can be lost quickly. If we place our trust in money or prestige, we become fragile. We can be thankful for what we have, live with humility, and trust in God more than in our possessions.
exp.21:0:
It says that God spoke to Ezekiel. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to me" is a way of saying "the LORD spoke to me," and this formula is repeated throughout this book to mark that a new message is beginning. What follows does not come from the prophet's own opinion, but from what God tells him.

The speaker is the LORD, and the receiver is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. This message is about Jerusalem, which is called "the city that sheds blood." God confronts it for its violence and its idolatry. This brief phrase sets the stage: what follows is a serious accusation, but given with the purpose of truth and of a call to return to God.

For today: before we speak, it is wise to listen to God. We can open the Bible with humility and ask him to show us the truth, even when it is uncomfortable, so that he corrects our hearts and not only points out the mistakes of others.
exp.33:7:
God makes a solemn promise with an oath: "As surely as I live," that is, by his own living existence. He says his flock has been left without a shepherd and has become prey and food for every wild beast. The shepherds did not search for his flock; instead, they fed only themselves.

Here the Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the exile of the people in Babylon. The "shepherds" were the leaders of Israel, above all the kings, and also other officials. God accuses them because they used their position for their own benefit and neglected the people.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, in the church, in the family, or at work, ask yourself whether you are serving or only serving yourself. Look carefully after those whom God has placed in your charge.
exp.8:5:
God commands certain executioners to punish Jerusalem without exception: old men, young men and maidens, women and children. Only those who have the mark on their foreheads are spared. The judgment begins "at my sanctuary," that is, at the temple, and the first to fall are the elders who were standing in front of it.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel in a vision, a few years before Jerusalem fell to Babylon. The people, even their religious leaders, had filled the temple with idolatry and the city with violence. The mark protects those who grieved over these wrongs. Ezekiel, seeing this, pleads for the rest of Israel.

God takes sin seriously, especially among those who claim to serve him. We can ask him to give us a heart that feels pain over evil, and not one that grows used to it.
exp.37:13:
God tells Ezekiel to deliver a clear message to Gog. When Israel is dwelling securely, that is, living in confidence and safety, Gog will take notice. The question "will you not take notice of this?" is a way of saying that Gog will certainly see it and recognize his opportunity there.

The Lord God is the one speaking through Ezekiel. Gog is the leader of a great northern coalition who intends to plunder Israel when he sees the nation at rest. Scholars interpret this passage in several ways: as future events, as a symbol of evil's attack against God's people, or as both. What is certain is that God knows what is coming and directs it to display his holiness.

Although at times it may feel that evil advances without control, God sees everything and continues to govern. We can rest in him and remain faithful, without letting fear overcome us.
exp.6:11:
The time has come, and the day has arrived. Ezekiel says the moment of judgment is already here, not far off. The phrase "the day has arrived" means that the day is right on top of them. "Let the buyer not rejoice" means that no one should be glad, and "the whole multitude" refers to all the people of the nation. Neither the buyer nor the seller should carry on as usual, because God's wrath falls on everyone.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. He announces judgment on Judah and Jerusalem for their violence, their pride, and their idolatry. Many understand this to refer to the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. Buying and selling will no longer matter, because everything will be lost.

For today: let us not set our hearts on material things, which pass away. Let us live with humility and return to God in time, without assuming that there will always be another opportunity tomorrow.
exp.18:11:
It says the vine, once strong and fruitful, was uprooted in anger and cast down to the ground. The east wind, a hot and dry wind from the east, dried up its fruit. Its strong branches were stripped off and withered, and the fire consumed them. "But" here signals a sharp turn from what came before, and the "strong branches" are the firm, sturdy stems that once held the vine's strength.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and commands him to raise a lament, that is, a funeral song, over the princes of Judah. The vine is usually understood as Judah or its royal dynasty, and the "mother" as Jerusalem or the house of David. Scholars debate which kings are meant, but the message is clear: the kingdom lost its power and ended in exile.

For today: privileges and blessings do not replace a life rooted in God. Ask yourself what source you are drinking from, and nurture your relationship with Him before the drought arrives.
exp.42:10:
God tells Ezekiel that if the people feel shame for what they have done, he should make known to them the design of the temple: its layout, its exits and entrances, its full design, and all its rules and laws. The word for "design" in the original points to a plan or blueprint. The rest of the phrase describes how everything is arranged. Ezekiel is to write it down in their sight so that they can follow its complete design faithfully and carry out its rules.

God speaks to Ezekiel, a prophet who was among the exiles in Babylon. God promises to dwell among his people again, but first he wants a repentant heart. The vision of the temple shows God's holiness. Interpreters differ: some see it as a literal temple in the future, and others see it as a symbolic picture of God's presence.

For today: sincere shame over sin is not the end, but the beginning of drawing near to God. If you recognize a failure, bring it before him and ask him for help to live according to his Word.
exp.35:28:
It says that God himself will cleanse his people from their uncleanness, that is, from everything that made them unclean before him: sin and idolatry. It also promises that he will summon the grain and make it plentiful, so that there will be enough food and no famine will come upon them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the Israelites exiled in Babylon. They had suffered the consequences of their disobedience. God promises to restore them, to give them a new heart and his Spirit, and to bring them back to their land. First comes inner cleansing, and then provision.

For today: God cares for our heart and also for our daily needs. You can ask him to cleanse you from whatever keeps you from him, and trust that he will take care of you, though in his own way and in his own time.
exp.19:2:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to the elders of Israel. They had come to inquire of the Lord, that is, to ask for a word or direction from him. But God answers with a pointed question: "Have you come to inquire of Me?" He swears by his own life that he will not be consulted by them.

Ezekiel was among the exiles in Babylon. Some of the elders sat down in front of him, waiting for a word from God. But God knew their hearts: his people had lived in rebellion and idolatry. So before answering them, he confronts them with their history of unfaithfulness, as the following context shows.

For today: we cannot come to God only to ask for help while we keep unconfessed sins. Before asking for guidance, it is good to examine the heart and return to him with sincerity. He receives with grace those who truly repent.
exp.15:38:
God says he will hand Jerusalem over to her lovers, the nations she once relied on. They will level her mounds and tear down her lofty shrines, the places where she worshiped idols. They will also strip off her clothes, take her fine jewelry, and leave her naked and bare.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter He compares Jerusalem to a woman He cared for and dressed, but who was unfaithful to Him by seeking idols and alliances with other nations. Those nations she turned to would become the instrument of judgment. Many understand this as a reference to Jerusalem's fall to Babylon.

For today: What we put in place of God does not protect us, and sooner or later it leaves us exposed. Today you can ask yourself what you trust more than Him, and return to God with sincerity. His judgment aims to lead to repentance.
exp.19:40:
God promises that he will accept Israel as a pleasing aroma. This will happen when he brings them out from the peoples and gathers them from the lands where they have been scattered. In this way, God will show his holiness through them in the sight of the nations. "I will show My holiness through you" means that God will be recognized as holy.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. Earlier, God rebukes Israel for their idolatry and disobedience. But here he promises to restore his people to their land, so that they will worship him truly again. Interpreters apply this to the return from exile, and some also to a future restoration.

Today we can remember that God does not give up on us when we turn away. His forgiveness seeks to restore us, and a changed life can show others who he is. If you have wandered away, you can return with confidence.
exp.15:22:
Ezekiel 16:23 says that, after all of Jerusalem's wickedness, God cries out in grief: "Woe! Woe to you!" It is like a sentence full of pain, interrupted by a cry. The phrase "in addition to all your other wickedness" points to sin that keeps piling up, and the verse does not stop there. The thought continues in the verses that follow, where even more sin is described.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he compares Jerusalem to an abandoned girl whom He rescued, cared for, and adorned. She, however, was unfaithful to Him with idols and with other nations. The "woe" is not only anger; it also shows sorrow and a warning before judgment.

For today: when God corrects us, He does not do so with coldness, but with a Father's pain. If today you have drifted away from Him, remember where He brought you from and return with humility. His warning seeks your return, not only that you feel condemned.
exp.21:11:
The verse says that in Jerusalem people accepted bribes in order to kill innocent people, lent money at excessive interest, and extorted their neighbors. All of this happened because they had forgotten God.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. He is accusing Jerusalem of serious wrongs: injustice, sexual abuse, violence, and greed. The verse points to the root of the problem: forgetting God. When they stopped keeping him in mind, they stopped seeing people as valuable and used them for their own gain.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, in our work, our businesses, or our debts, we treat others justly. Remembering that God sees us helps us earn our living honestly and not take advantage of those in need.
exp.2:21:
God laid his hand upon Ezekiel, meaning he took hold of him with his power and presence. He told him to get up and go out into the plain, because there he was going to speak with him.

Here the Lord speaks with Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. God had just appointed him as a watchman, someone who warns of danger, and explained how heavy that task is. Now he calls him aside to speak with him in private. Afterward, Ezekiel sees the glory of God, falls face down on the ground, and the Spirit lifts him up.

For today: if God entrusts us with something important, first we need to set ourselves apart to listen to him. Finding a moment of quiet, without noise or hurry, prepares us to speak to others with humility, truth, and love.
exp.39:30:
The verse describes the gate of the outer court on the north side of the temple that Ezekiel sees. Its portico faced the outer court, and its side pillars were decorated with palm trees. Eight steps led up to it. The portico is probably an entrance hall or porch. Some details of the Hebrew wording are uncertain.

Ezekiel speaks, recounting a vision God gave him during the exile in Babylon. A guide who looked like a man leads him through the temple and measures it with a measuring rod. These measurements showed an orderly, holy place, already restored, to encourage a discouraged people. Scholars disagree about whether it is a literal future temple or a symbolic picture.

For today: approaching God is not something done carelessly. The steps and the palm trees remind us that He deserves reverence and order. We can prepare ourselves calmly before praying or going to church, and remember that God cares even for the details of His house and of our lives.
exp.29:22:
This verse says that God will scatter the Egyptians among the nations. The verse's word "disperse" means to spread out or send in many directions, and the phrase about scattering "throughout the lands" means to send them far apart, the way seed is thrown across a field. "Nations" here means the peoples of the earth, and "lands" means various countries.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during Israel's exile in Babylon. Egypt had been a false hope of help for Judah, and God announces its fall. Pharaoh's "broken arm" symbolizes the breaking of his military power. Babylon appears as the instrument of God's judgment. How this scattering was exactly fulfilled is something scholars debate.

For today: let us not place our ultimate security in human powers, whether money, governments, or people. Only God is a firm refuge. Ask yourself what you are trusting in more than in Him.
exp.17:14:
This verse describes the son who decides not to follow his father's bad example. He does not eat at the mountain shrines, so he does not take part in the meals and offerings at the pagan places of worship on the high hills. He does not look to the idols of Israel, meaning he does not give them his trust or worship. And he does not defile his neighbor's wife, meaning he does not commit adultery.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The people in exile were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their parents. God answers that each person is accountable for their own choices. The righteous son will not be condemned for his father's wickedness, and this shows that there is always room to change.

For today: your family past does not define you. Even if you grew up with bad examples, you can choose faithfulness to God, respect for others, and care for your relationships. Ask God for help to begin a new path.
exp.25:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel in the twelfth year, on the first day of the eleventh month. The phrase "came to me" simply means that the word of the LORD reached the prophet, and "saying" introduces the message that follows. It is a plain way of opening a new message: God took the initiative and spoke.

The one speaking is God, and the one who listens is the prophet Ezekiel. The verse dates the message to the twelfth year, counted from the exile, and gives the month and the day. The next verse shows that God is going to speak against Tyre, a city that rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem because it expected to profit from it.

For today: God sees what happens in the world and also how we react to the suffering of others. We can ask ourselves whether we rejoice when someone falls, or whether we accompany them with compassion. Listening to God's word helps us look at others the way He looks at them.
exp.47:27:
This verse describes the southern border of the portion of Gad, the last tribe in the list. It runs from Tamar to the waters of Meribath-kadesh, then along the Brook of Egypt, and out to the Great Sea, the Mediterranean. The phrase "the southern border" in the verse names the south side of the land.

God speaks through Ezekiel, who receives this vision during the exile in Babylon. It is part of the vision of the future division of the land, with the tribes arranged from north to south. It is understood in several ways: as a promise of restoration for Israel, or as a symbolic picture of God's order. Scholars do not fully agree.

For today: God cares for every detail and forgets no one, not even in a list of borders. We can trust that he has a place prepared and a purpose for our lives, even when we are in times of waiting.
exp.42:14:
This verse describes the highest part of the altar: a hearth four cubits high, with four horns rising upward from it. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of the forearm. Here it is the "long cubit," meaning an ordinary cubit plus a handbreadth, the width of the hand.

Ezekiel recounts a vision of a new temple, and a heavenly guide gives him its measurements. This takes place after the exile, when the people had lost the temple. The horns of the altar were a symbol of refuge and atonement. Scholars interpret the temple in various ways: some see it as something literal and future, others as a symbol of God's presence.

For today: God cares about the details of worship and wants us to draw near to Him with reverence. Today we can come with confidence to Christ, our refuge and perfect sacrifice.
exp.33:2:
This verse says that Israel's shepherds took advantage of the flock: they ate the fat, wore the wool, and butchered the fattened sheep, but they did not care for the sheep. Feeding and caring for the flock is what the shepherds were supposed to do. To butcher is to slaughter an animal for food.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. The "shepherds" were the leaders of Israel, especially the kings and rulers. God rebukes them because they used their position for their own benefit and not to serve the people, who were left wounded and scattered. Then God promises to care for His flock Himself.

Anyone who has some responsibility over others, whether in the church, at work, or in the family, should ask themselves: am I serving, or am I being served? Caring for others with humility and attention is the true way to lead.
exp.7:8:
Then God said to Ezekiel, "Go in and see the wicked abominations they are committing here." God tells the prophet to go through the opening he has found in the wall and look for himself at what the people are doing inside. The words spoken are God's own speech to the prophet, and the practices described are deeply offensive to God, especially idolatry. God wants Ezekiel to see these things with his own eyes.

God speaks in a vision that Ezekiel has while he is in Babylon, where he is carried in spirit to the temple in Jerusalem. The Lord shows him that the people and their leaders practice false worship in secret while appearing to be faithful. Many understand this as the reason for the judgment that would come upon the city.

For today: God sees what we do in hidden places. We can ask ourselves what things we keep out of sight, and what we give the place that belongs only to God. Instead of pretending, we can confess it honestly and ask him to cleanse us and guide us.
exp.14:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. The phrase "came to me, saying" means that a message from the LORD came to me. It is the simple way the book announces that what follows is not the prophet's own ideas, but what God wants to say.

Ezekiel was a priest who lived in exile in Babylon, along with other Jews taken captive. Here God begins a new message addressed to the people. The verses that follow compare Jerusalem to the wood of the vine, which is of little use except for bearing fruit. For that reason, this verse works as an introduction.

For today: before we look for what God wants to tell us, it is good to stop and listen. We can read the Bible calmly and ask, "Lord, speak to me," ready to receive even what is hard for us to hear.
exp.5:11:
Ezekiel 6:12 says that no one in Israel would escape God's judgment. Whoever was far off would die of the plague; whoever was near would fall by the sword; and whoever remained would die of famine. Here "fury" means God's righteous anger, and "vent" means He would pour it out fully on them.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived among the exiles in Babylon. The people had filled the land with idols and with altars on the mountains. God warns that the punishment would come so that they would recognize that He is the LORD. Even in judgment, His aim was that they would know Him.

For today: let us not take sin or God's warnings lightly. If there is something in your life that takes the place that only He deserves, do not wait for the consequences to show you it; return to Him today with humility, knowing that He forgives those who repent.
exp.31:19:
It says Egypt will fall among those who die by the sword. The sword is appointed, so she is already marked for war and destruction. Then the command is given to drag her away, along with all her multitudes, to the same end.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, whom he calls "son of man." He asks him to sing a funeral lament over Egypt, a powerful and proud nation. According to the text, God announces that this power will not save her. The image used is that of going down to the grave together with other nations already defeated. Many read this as poetic language about God's judgment.

For today: let us not trust in power, fame, or success, because everything is temporary. Let us place our security in God and live with humility.
exp.47:0:
This verse begins to divide the land among the tribes of Israel. Dan receives a strip at the far north, running along the road to Hethlon, reaching Lebo-hamath, Hazar-enan and the border of Damascus. "Border" means the edge or boundary line. The "sides" are the two edges of the strip, running from east to west. The "sea" refers to the Mediterranean.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in the last vision of the book. After the destruction of Jerusalem, the people live in exile. God shows them a restored land, with a temple and an orderly division of the territory. Scholars disagree about whether this vision will be fulfilled literally, whether it is symbolic, or whether it points to the final restoration that God promises.

For today: God cares for every detail and forgets no one. Even when you feel that your life is out of place, you can trust that he has prepared a place for you and keeps his promises.
exp.46:11:
It says that along both banks of the river, fruit trees of every kind will grow. Their leaves will not wither, and their fruit will never run out. They will bear fruit every month, because the water that feeds them flows from the sanctuary, that is, from the temple. The fruit will be used for food and the leaves for healing.

God shows the prophet Ezekiel a vision of a river that flows out of the temple and brings life wherever it goes. The people of Israel, who were in exile and needed hope of restoration, receive this. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some see it as a promise for Israel, others as a spiritual symbol. Revelation 22:2 uses a similar image.

Today we can remember that life and healing come from the presence of God. Set aside time each day for prayer and for the Bible, and ask him to fill you so that you can be food and comfort for others.
exp.16:1:
God speaks to Ezekiel and calls him "son of man", a way of saying "human being". He tells him to pose a riddle, that is, a puzzle, and to speak a parable, a story with a hidden message, to the house of Israel.

The LORD speaks. Ezekiel is living in exile in Babylon, alongside other Jews taken captive. God will use the story of the eagle, the cedar and the topmost shoot to show what happened to the kings of Judah and the political decisions of the people. Many understand that the eagle represents Babylon, but the following text explains this in more detail.

Today: God sometimes speaks to us in images so that we will think and recognize our mistakes. Let us listen with humility, without becoming defensive, and let his word correct and guide us.
exp.22:35:
God tells Ezekiel to act as a judge. The question "Will you pass judgment?" means: "Do it now." He is to bring charges against Oholah and Oholibah and make them face their sins openly, declaring their abominations to them.

The Lord speaks to the prophet Ezekiel during the exile. Oholah and Oholibah are two sisters who represent Samaria and Jerusalem, the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. God uses this vivid picture to show that his people were unfaithful to him, chasing idols and alliances instead of trusting him.

God does not stay silent in the face of sin, but he exposes it in truth to call his people back to himself. Today we can ask him to show us the areas where we have turned our backs on him, and respond with humility and repentance, without excuses.
exp.13:22:
God says that the exiles who arrive in Babylon will be comforted when they see how the survivors of Jerusalem live. The phrase "they shall comfort you" is rewritten here as "you will be comforted." When they see the survivors' conduct and actions, they will understand that God did not act without reason in all that he did against the city.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was among the exiles in Babylon. Jerusalem had fallen into idolatry and injustice, and God announces judgment. Even so, he leaves a remnant that comes out of the city. Their conduct would show that the punishment was just. Some scholars see comfort here because God was not arbitrary; others stress that God preserves a small group.

For today: when we do not understand our pain, we can trust that God is just and good, and that he does not act without cause. He also keeps hope for his people.
exp.42:25:
During seven days the priests are to make atonement for the altar and cleanse it, so that it is consecrated for use. To "make atonement" means to cover sin in order to repair the wrong. The verse says the altar is consecrated, and it describes the priests making atonement for it and cleansing it.

God speaks through Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple. Before the altar is used for regular worship, it must be set apart for God through a ceremony lasting seven days. Scholars interpret this vision in various ways: some see it as literal and others as symbolic.

For today: before serving God, we need to approach him with humility and a clean heart. We can ask him for forgiveness and offer him our time and our strength to serve him.
exp.27:19:
Ezekiel 28:20 says, "Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying." The word "came" means that the message arrived or was received, and it is a formula Ezekiel uses to introduce a new message from God.

The one speaking is Ezekiel, the prophet, who says he received the word of God. He has just finished the message against the king of Tyre, and now he begins a new one against Sidon, another neighboring city. God announces that he will judge the pride and injustice of the nations, and that they will know that he is the LORD.

God does not stay silent before wickedness, but he does not act in secret either: he speaks and warns. Today we can approach the Bible with attention, knowing that God still speaks to us through his word. Listening with humility helps us correct our course in time.
exp.34:8:
It says God will leave Edom, the mountain of Seir, completely ruined. "A perpetual desolation" means a ruin that lasts forever, and "your cities will not be inhabited" means its towns will stand empty. In the end, everyone will recognize that the Lord is the Lord.

Here God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. The mountain of Seir is the region of Edom, the descendants of Esau. According to the text, Edom held an old hostility against Israel and wanted to take over its lands, as if God were not present there. For this reason the Lord announces judgment. Scholars debate how this was fulfilled in history, but the central message is clear.

For today: let us not hold grudges or envy toward others, nor think that God does not see what we do. Rather, let us ask him for a forgiving heart, and trust that he does justice.
exp.15:42:
God says to Jerusalem that she did not remember the days of her youth, when He cared for her and rescued her. Instead of being thankful, she angered Him. For this reason God will bring the result of her own actions down upon her own head. The word for youth in this passage refers to the time when she was young. Bringing the deeds upon the head means she will receive the consequences of what she has done. Moreover, she did not even stop to consider her abominations, meaning her detestable practices.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Throughout this chapter, Jerusalem is portrayed as a young woman rescued by God who later became unfaithful to Him, above all through idolatry and alliances with other nations. The judgment comes because of that ingratitude and lack of repentance.

For today: remembering with gratitude what God has done in your life guards you against pride and forgetfulness. Take a moment this week to write down and give thanks for how God has cared for you.
exp.33:19:
It says that God himself, the Lord GOD, will act personally. He will judge between the fat sheep, who are the strong and well-fed, and the lean sheep, who are the weak and mistreated. The verse speaks of the sheep, not cattle, and the picture is of a shepherd who sees how the flock treats one another.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, during the people's exile in Babylon. In this chapter he rebukes the shepherds of Israel, that is, their leaders, who took advantage of the flock instead of caring for it. Some of the strong sheep also pushed the weak ones aside. For this reason God promises to defend the mistreated and to be the one who establishes justice.

For today: if you have some place of influence, in the home, the church or at work, use it to care for the weakest and not to gain advantage. And if you feel trampled, remember that God sees and promises to bring justice.
exp.47:3:
The passage describes the land being divided into long strips that run from east to west. Next to the territory of Naphtali lies another strip, that of Manasseh. A "border" is the boundary or edge of a territory. "The sea" is the Mediterranean Sea, to the west. "One portion" means one more share of the land given to another tribe.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, near the end of the book. He is describing a vision of the land restored for Israel, with an orderly division among the tribes and a temple at the center. Many interpret it in different ways: as a promise for Israel, as a spiritual picture, or as something yet to be fulfilled. What is clear is that it shows God cares for each tribe and each family.

God forgets no one, and He gives each person a place. Today we can trust that He also has a place and a purpose for you, and live thankful for what He gives us.
exp.22:38:
This verse says that the people sacrificed their children to their idols and that same day entered God's temple as if nothing had happened. "Profaning it" means making it unclean, making it impure. "The sanctuary" is the temple, the holy place. God points out the contradiction: one hand offered to the idols while the other claimed to worship him.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapter 23 he uses the story of two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, who represent Samaria and Jerusalem. With that image he denounces their unfaithfulness: they made alliances with other nations and worshiped false gods. This verse shows that their sin reached the temple itself.

For today: God is not content with a Sunday-only religion. We can ask ourselves whether our daily life, at work, at home, and in what we love, agrees with what we say at church.
exp.47:13:
The passage says that the portion of land set apart for the Levites could not be sold, exchanged, or handed over to someone else. Exchanging means trading one thing for another, and handing it over means giving it away to another person. The "best part of the land" refers to what is first and finest in what the land yields, set apart for God. It was holy, meaning dedicated to the LORD.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a vision about the restored people and the new division of the land, along with the temple and the city. This holy portion lay at the center, for the service of God. Scholars debate whether this is to be fulfilled literally or symbolically, and it is fair to acknowledge that there are several interpretations.

Today we can ask ourselves what the first and best things we set aside for God are: time, money, or attention. What we dedicate to him should not be bargained away or traded according to our convenience.
exp.6:18:
They will throw their silver into the streets, and their gold will seem unclean, as if it were worthless. When God's judgment comes, that money will not be able to save them, and it will not satisfy their hunger or fill their stomachs. The gold became a stumbling block that brought their iniquity, that is, it led them into sin.

Here God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, before the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon. He announces the day of the Lord's wrath against a people who had become filled with pride and idolatry. According to the following verse, they even used their jewels and precious metals to make images of their idols.

For today: money cannot give us lasting security or fill the soul. We can ask ourselves whether our riches help us do good or whether they have become a stumbling block. Let us trust God first and use what we have with generosity and humility.
exp.3:14:
God tells Ezekiel that, instead of using human excrement, he may use cow dung to bake his bread. The verse of the word for dung and the phrase about preparing the bread is set aside here, since the verse uses the plain words "cow dung" and "bake," which need no explanation.

God speaks with Ezekiel, who represents through his actions the siege of Jerusalem. Earlier, God had commanded him to bake the bread over human excrement to show that the people would eat unclean bread in exile. Ezekiel protested because he had always guarded his purity. God accepts his plea and grants a change, though the message of judgment still stands.

For today: God listens patiently to our sincere objections and can show mercy even when he asks us to do difficult things. We can speak to him honestly in prayer.
exp.15:13:
Ezekiel 16:14 says that Jerusalem's fame spread among the nations because of her beauty. That beauty was flawless, but it did not come from her own merit. God says it was the splendor he bestowed on her.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In this chapter he describes Jerusalem as an abandoned infant whom he rescued, cared for, and adorned, and with whom he entered into a covenant, as in a marriage. All of this prepares the accusation that follows: she forgot who had given her everything, trusted in her own beauty, and gave herself to idolatry, which the text calls "harlotry."

For today: everything good we have, such as talents, successes, or a good reputation, is a gift from God. If we remember this, we live with gratitude and humility, and we do not turn away from him out of pride.
exp.8:0:
Then I heard Him call out in a loud voice, calling for the executioners of the city to come near, each one with a weapon of destruction in hand. Here, the people summoned are not guests or casual visitors. They are the ones assigned to come and carry out a punishment, and each one had a weapon of destruction in his hand.

The one speaking is God, and Ezekiel hears him in a vision. This takes place while the prophet is living in exile in Babylon. God shows him that Jerusalem will be judged for its idolatry and injustice, described in the previous chapter. The verses that follow speak of six men and of another dressed in linen, who marks the faithful. Scholars interpret these figures in various ways, and the text does not explain them fully.

God is patient, but he is also just and takes sin seriously. Today we can take advantage of his patience to turn back to him with humility and sincerity, without putting off what he asks us to change.
exp.26:4:
They say the builders of Tyre made this "ship" from the finest materials. The planking is the boards that form the hull. They built it with cypress from Senir, another name for Mount Hermon. For the mast they took a cedar from Lebanon, known for its strength and quality.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who is commanded to raise a lament over Tyre. The trading city is presented as a magnificent ship. Tyre boasted of its beauty, and the image shows its wealth and pride. Later in the chapter that great ship sinks, and so its fall is announced.

Whatever beautiful things we have, whether money, talents or success, can make us feel secure without God. Today we can give thanks for what He has given us, use it with humility, and remember that our true security is in God, not in what we boast of.
exp.17:3:
God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles of Israel.
