They kept repeating a saying: the parents ate sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge, meaning that the children pay for the sins of their parents. With this they seemed to excuse themselves, as if they were not to blame. God rejects that saying and affirms that each person answers for himself or herself before Him. Some understand that dying refers mainly to the present consequences of sin, and others also to spiritual death.

Today we cannot blame our family or our past for our mistakes. Even if we inherit wounds, God invites us to repent and begin again, with the certainty that we belong to Him.
exp.38:14:
As they pass through the land, anyone who sees a human bone will set up a pillar next to it, marking the spot until the gravediggers carry it away to be buried in the Valley of Hamon-gog. The name "Hamon-gog" means something like "the multitude of Gog."

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier he announced the defeat of Gog, an enemy who attacks Israel. After the victory, the people must clear the land of corpses, because under Israel's law contact with death made a person unclean. Many understand this literally, and others as a symbol of the complete purification God will bring. Interpreters do not agree.

For today: God cares about what is clean and orderly. If we see something damaged around us, let us not ignore it. We can help with patience, step by step, until it is restored.
exp.10:18:
God promises to change his people from the inside. The "inner parts" are the deepest part of a person. A "heart of stone" is a hard heart that neither listens nor obeys; a "heart of flesh" is a tender heart that responds to God.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to the exiles in Babylon. Jerusalem had fallen into idolatry, and God promises to gather them and return the land to them. But returning to the place is not enough; they need an inner change to walk in his statutes and truly be his people.

For today: we cannot fix our hearts on our own. Ask God sincerely to soften the areas where you have become hard, such as forgiveness or obedience, and open yourself to whatever he shows you in his Word.
exp.19:4:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to the elders of Israel and remind them of the day he chose his people. The phrase "I swore an oath" makes clear that God made a solemn promise to the descendants of Jacob. God made himself known to them in the land of Egypt, and with a raised hand he declared to them: "I am the LORD your God."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Some elders had come to seek his counsel, but God answers that he will not attend to them, because first they must face their history of unfaithfulness. That is why he begins by recalling how everything started: with his choosing and his promise.

For today: before asking something of God, it is good to remember who he is and how faithful he has been to us. That helps us come near with sincerity and humility, ready to correct what we need to change.
exp.39:34:
In this verse, a guide leads Ezekiel to the north gate of the temple and measures it. The gate has the same measurements as the others. The sentence "Then he brought me to the north gate and measured it" tells us that the guide took Ezekiel there and measured it, so it is simply rendered as "then he led me." The clause about the measurements means that this gate had the same size and design as the others.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he received while Israel was in exile. A man shows him a new temple, step by step, and measures it as they go. Some believe it is a literal future temple, others that it is a symbol of God's presence and holiness. The Bible does not fully explain this, and Christians interpret it in different ways.

For today: God is a God of order and care, and He leaves nothing to chance. If He is concerned with every detail of His house, He is also concerned with the details of your life. You can trust that His plan is orderly and faithful, even when you cannot see the whole of it.
exp.22:18:
It says that Oholibah (Jerusalem, the younger sister) did not stop, but sinned even more. The word "promiscuity" here means spiritual unfaithfulness, and "the days of her youth" refers to her early years. She kept recalling those days in Egypt, and those memories pushed her to keep seeking other lovers.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the story of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Judah), to show how his people abandoned God and gave themselves to alliances and gods of other nations, such as Egypt and Babylon. The language is harsh because it is meant to show God's grief over betrayal and to lead the people to see their sin.

For today: let us be careful about what we bring to mind. Remembering with desire a past that drew us away from God can lead us to repeat it. Better to remember his faithfulness and return to him.
exp.43:5:
God commands Ezekiel to speak plainly to the people of Israel, whom he calls "rebellious." The message is that God has had enough of their detestable practices, the things that offended him.

The Lord speaks in a vision of the new temple, just after Ezekiel sees the glory of God fill the house. God is about to give rules about who may serve in the sanctuary, and first he recalls how the people had defiled that place, letting in foreigners of uncommitted heart and neglecting their covenant.

For today: God calls us to say "enough" to what we know displeases him. We can come near to Him with sincerity, acknowledge our failures, and return to Him from the heart, not merely in appearance.
exp.27:3:
The verse says that the prince of Tyre used his wisdom and understanding, and by them he gained great wealth. "Wisdom" means good judgment in managing things, and "understanding" refers to his skill at making sound decisions. "Treasuries" are the places where he stored his goods, and "amassed" means that he gathered up gold and silver.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a city made rich by its trade at sea. Its ruler thought of himself as almost a god because of his wisdom and success. God does not say that riches are evil, but that pride made him forget he was only a man. The verses that follow show that his wealth led his heart to become proud.

We can be thankful for our abilities and make good use of them, but without thinking we own everything. Everything we have, whether talent or money, is a gift from God, and humility keeps us grounded.
exp.16:3:
It says the eagle plucked off the topmost shoot of the cedar, carried it to a land of merchants, and planted it in a city of traders. The topmost shoot is the fresh, young growth at the very top of the tree; the words "carried" and "planted" simply mean that the eagle took the branch away and placed it in that city.

God asks Ezekiel to tell a parable to Israel. Many understand that the eagle is the king of Babylon, and that the shoot taken away is King Jehoiachin, carried into exile with other leaders of Judah. The "land of merchants" would be Babylon. God uses this image to show the people why they suffered that fall and what would happen next.

For today: even when we lose what seemed secure, such as a job or a sense of safety, God still governs. We can ask Him for wisdom to trust Him and not only human powers.
exp.46:16:
This passage sets out the northern boundary of the land that God promises to his people. It begins at the Sea, runs to Hazar-enan, and then follows the northern border of Damascus with the territory of Hamath lying to the north. A boundary is a line that marks where a territory ends.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who describes a vision of restoration after the exile. God shows how the land will be divided among the tribes. Scholars do not agree on the exact location of some of these places, nor on whether this vision is to be fulfilled literally or spiritually.

For today: God is a God of order and concrete promises. He cares for the details of our lives and keeps what he says. We can trust that he has a place and a purpose for each of us.
exp.42:22:
When you have finished the purification of the altar, you are to present a young, unblemished bull and an unblemished ram from the flock. This verse says that once the ceremony of purifying the altar with sin offerings is complete, a young bull and a ram, both without fault, must be offered. "Atone" means to cleanse or cover guilt. "Blemish" means a stain or flaw. The animals are offered as part of the altar's dedication.

God speaks to Ezekiel in a vision of the new temple. After the exile, the people needed to understand that God is holy and that people must approach him with reverence. These rites dedicate the altar over seven days. Interpreters differ on whether this will be fulfilled literally or is a symbolic picture of restored worship.

For today: come to God with sincerity and respect. Christians believe that Jesus is the perfect sacrifice, so we can pray with confidence, without hiding our failures.
exp.19:9:
He says that God brought Israel out of Egypt and led them into the wilderness. The words "I brought them out" and "led them" are the verse's own wording, so this is a brief fact, but a very important one: God took the initiative to rescue his people.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who addresses the leaders of Israel who are in exile. God reminds them of their history to show that his people rebelled from the beginning, even in Egypt, since they kept following their idols. Even so, God rescued them for the sake of his name, that is, out of faithfulness to himself and not because of anything they deserved.

For today: God rescues us by his grace, not because we deserve it. If you feel unworthy today or have failed, remember his faithfulness and respond with gratitude, letting go of whatever has taken his place in your heart.
exp.25:19:
God tells the city of Tyre that he will bring it down into the pit, the place of the dead, along with the people of antiquity. The people of antiquity are people from very ancient times. Tyre will be placed in the lowest parts of the earth, among ancient ruins, and will no longer be inhabited. Then God says he will make glory appear in the land of the living, pointing to a restoration of his people.

The Lord GOD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. Tyre was a rich and proud trading city, which rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem, thinking of its own gain. God announces his judgment. Scholars understand in different ways how this prophecy was fulfilled in history, and some see in it several stages.

For today: power and wealth are not secure if we forget God. We can ask him for a humble heart, one that does not rejoice in the misfortune of others and that trusts in him, not in what we have.
exp.43:25:
It says that a priest who had become defiled by touching a dead body, such as when he buried a close relative, could not return to service right away. First he had to be purified, and afterward he had to count off seven days for himself. The phrase "he must count off seven days for himself" means that the days would be counted before he returned to his duties.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in his vision of the new temple. He is giving rules to the priests descended from Zadok. Because they served in a holy place, they had to guard their purity. The law of Moses also required seven days of purification after touching a dead body (Numbers 19). Then the priest would offer a sin offering before returning to the sanctuary.

For today: God values our seeking him with a prepared heart. After a failure or a loss, we should not rush. We can give ourselves time to heal, repent, and return to God with sincerity.
exp.43:13:
God says that he will appoint these Levites to take charge of the temple. They will look after all its work and everything that has to be done inside it.

The Berean wording makes the job clear: they are appointed to keep charge of the work for the temple. This means they are given responsibility for guarding and carrying out its duties.

The Lord GOD speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. These Levites had served before the idols and caused Israel to stumble, so God takes away their place in the priesthood. They will not be allowed to come near the most holy things, but they are not left without a place: they will have lesser tasks of service. The sons of Zadok, who were faithful, will serve as priests. In this way God's justice and mercy are shown together.

God can restore someone who has failed, even though there are consequences. If we have failed, we can serve with humility wherever He opens the door for us, without bitterness.
exp.18:6:
This young lion, who represents a king of Judah, became violent. The text uses the sense of "broke down" and "devastated" for what he did, and it calls the sound of his roaring the cause of the land's fear. His attacks on the strongholds and cities of others brought ruin across the land.

Ezekiel sings this lament over the princes of Israel, using the image of a lioness and her cubs. He is in exile, and he explains why the dynasty of David fell. It is not certain which king this is: many think of Jehoiachin, and others of Zedekiah. What is clear is that he ended up a prisoner in Babylon.

For today: power without justice ends up destroying others and oneself. If you have authority, at home, at work, or in the church, ask God to use it to care for people and not to crush them.
exp.36:15:
God tells Ezekiel to take two sticks, or pieces of wood. On one he is to write "Belonging to Judah and to the Israelites associated with him," and on the other "Belonging to Joseph—the stick of Ephraim—and to all the house of Israel associated with him." Here "stick" means a rod or a piece of wood, and "associated with him" refers to the tribes joined to each one.

The Lord speaks, and Ezekiel lives among the exiles. After the vision of the dry bones coming back to life, God announces a restoration. The kingdom had been divided in two: Judah to the south and Israel, with Ephraim as its leader, to the north. This gesture prepares the promise to bring them back together.

For today: God heals divisions that seem impossible. We can ask him to help us seek unity with other believers, without waiting for the other person to take the first step.
exp.13:1:
It says that, after some elders of Israel came to visit Ezekiel, the word of the LORD came to him. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to me" in the verse above means that God Himself acted and gave him a message for those men.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks here; he was living among the exiles in Babylon. The elders were leaders of the people, and they came, probably, to seek a word from God. But God sees beyond their visit: He notices that their hearts are divided by idols, and so He answers them with a warning.

For today: before seeking an answer from God, it is good to ask ourselves what things hold first place in our hearts. God does not only look at what we do on the outside; He desires a sincere heart that is devoted to Him.
exp.4:13:
God tells Jerusalem that he will leave her in ruins and in disgrace. A "ruin" is an empty, destroyed place. "Disgrace" means dishonor or mockery. A "passerby" is anyone who goes along the road. Everyone who passes by will see her fall.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who lived in exile in Babylon. Jerusalem had fallen into idolatry and disobedience, and had despised the covenant with God. For this reason he announces a severe judgment: famine, sword, and scattering. The text says that God speaks "in his zeal," meaning that it grieves him that his people abandon him. His purpose is that they will know that he is the Lord.

For today: let us not take God's correction lightly. If he shows us something crooked in our lives, it is better to repent quickly and return to him with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.9:11:
This verse describes the cherubim and their wheels. Their entire bodies, including their backs, hands, and wings, as well as their four wheels, were full of eyes all around.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, a priest exiled in Babylon. He recounts a vision in which he sees the glory of God leaving the temple in Jerusalem because of the sin of the people. Eyes can speak of complete sight; many think they point to the total knowledge of God, although the text does not explain this clearly.

For today: nothing is hidden from God, and that is a comfort. He sees our struggles, our injustices and our pain. He also invites us to live with sincerity before Him, trusting that His gaze is that of a holy and faithful God.
exp.2:20:
If Ezekiel warns a righteous person not to sin, and that person does not sin because he heeded the warning, he will indeed live. Ezekiel will have saved himself from guilt.

God speaks to Ezekiel, whom he appointed as a watchman, that is, a lookout for the people of Israel, who were living in exile in Babylon. His task was to warn them of the danger of sin. The previous verses show that if he did not warn them, he would bear responsibility. Here the positive side is shown: if he warns and the person listens, all turns out well.

For today: if, with love and humility, you see someone moving away from the good path, do not stay silent. Speak with respect and without judging, and let God do his work in that person. Your faithfulness counts, even though you do not control the response.
exp.37:14:
Gog will come from his place in the far north, bringing many peoples with him. They all ride on horses, forming a huge horde and a mighty army. The phrase about riding horses simply tells us that they are mounted on horses. The "far north" points to the most distant parts of the north.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel and addresses Gog directly. Israel is living in peace, and God announces that a huge army will attack it. The verses that follow say that God himself allows this in order to show his holiness before the nations. Interpreters disagree: some see a past historical event, some a future event, and others a symbolic picture of the final conflict between evil and God.

For today: even when the powers of the world seem enormous, God remains in control. We can rest in him and not let fear of the news take control of us.
exp.18:13:
The passage says that a fire came out from its main branch and consumed its fruit, so that no strong branch remained fit to serve as a ruler's scepter, a staff of authority for governing. "To rule" here means to dominate or reign. A lament is a sad song of mourning. The text declares that this is a lament and that it will be used as one from now on.

God commands Ezekiel to raise this lament over the princes of Judah. The vine represents the house of David, uprooted and carried off into exile in Babylon. The fire that comes from the branch itself is usually understood as the guilt of the rulers themselves, perhaps King Zedekiah. Scholars debate exactly whom each image refers to.

For today: whoever holds authority can destroy what they are meant to protect when they act with pride or injustice. Let us ask God for humility to lead with integrity in our family, our work, or our church.
exp.47:33:
This verse describes the west side of the city that Ezekiel sees in his vision. It is 4,500 cubits long and has three gates, named for the tribes of Gad, Asher, and Naphtali, three of the twelve tribes of Israel.

The prophet Ezekiel speaks, recounting what God showed him. Israel was in exile and had lost its city and its temple. This vision, at the end of the book, gave them hope: God would restore his people. Christians interpret it in various ways, either as a promise for Israel or as an image of God's presence with his people. The city's final name is "The LORD Is There."

For today: each tribe had its own gate, so everyone had a place in the city. God reminds us that every person among his people is welcome and has their place before him.
exp.22:12:
God says that he saw that Oholibah, just like her sister Oholah, had defiled herself, that is, she had made herself morally impure. The two of them took the same path of unfaithfulness. Here, the idea of unfaithfulness refers to turning away from God, not only sexual sin.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile. He uses the image of two sisters, who represent Samaria (Oholah) and Jerusalem (Oholibah). Both looked for alliances and gods of other nations, such as Assyria and Babylon, instead of trusting in Him. Jerusalem did not learn from Samaria's punishment.

For today: it is easy to repeat the mistakes we see in others and think it will never happen to us. Let us learn from the falls of others, examine what we place our trust in, and return to God with sincerity.
exp.21:12:
God says that he "strikes his hands together," bringing his palms into a clap. In that time this was a strong gesture that showed anger, indignation, or a firm decision to act. The "unjust gain" is money gotten through dishonest means, and "the blood you have shed in your midst" refers to the murders and violence within Jerusalem.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel while the people lived in sin: injustice, immorality, abuse of their neighbors, and forgetfulness of God. For this reason he announces that judgment will come and that the people will be scattered.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we seek gain at the expense of others, even in ways that seem ordinary or accepted. God sees injustice and calls us to live with honesty, compassion, and respect, remembering that he is the one who holds us accountable.
exp.22:10:
This verse says that Oholibah, the younger sister, saw what had happened to her sister Oholah. But instead of learning from it, she gave herself to her lust and prostitution even more than her sister did. Her unfaithfulness was more depraved than her sister's, and her sins were worse.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. He uses the story of two sisters as a picture: Oholah represents Samaria (Israel) and Oholibah represents Jerusalem (Judah). Both allied themselves with Assyria and with its idols instead of remaining faithful to God. Samaria had already been punished, and Jerusalem should have taken it as a warning.

For today: let us learn from the mistakes of others before repeating them. If we see someone suffering because they have turned away from God, it is an opportunity to examine our own hearts and return to Him in time.
exp.20:2:
God tells Ezekiel to speak to the land of Israel, and the message is severe: "I am against you." God says he will draw his sword from its sheath, meaning he will bring it out to carry out judgment, and that he will cut off both the righteous and the wicked.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was living in exile in Babylon. The people had kept turning to idols and acting unjustly, and God announces judgment on Jerusalem. That the righteous would also be struck is understood in several ways: the judgment would fall on the whole nation, and the righteous would suffer along with everyone else, though not because they were guilty as the wicked were.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also calls us to live faithfully in the midst of a society that is turning away from him. We can pray for our surroundings and return to God with humility.
exp.23:6:
It says that Jerusalem, called the "city of blood," has blood shed within her. That blood was not hidden: it was poured out on the bare rock, an exposed stone open to view. They did not pour it on the ground to cover it with dust, as was done to hide blood.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile in Babylon. With the image of a boiling pot, He denounces the violence and injustice of Jerusalem. According to Leviticus 17:13, spilled blood was to be covered with earth. Here, by being left uncovered, the crime is in plain view and cries out for justice. Interpreters explain the detail of the rock in various ways, but the central message is clear.

For today: God sees what we try to hide. If we have harmed someone, the best course is to acknowledge it, ask forgiveness, and make amends where possible, rather than covering it up.
exp.36:9:
He says that Ezekiel obeyed what God had commanded him. He spoke as he was told, and the breath entered the bodies that had been lifeless before. Then they came to life, stood up on their feet, and became a vast army. The word for "breath" here can also mean "wind" or "spirit," and in Hebrew it is the same word (ruach). To "prophesy" means to speak on God's behalf.

God shows Ezekiel a vision of dry bones. He then explains them right away: they are Israel, a people discouraged by the exile in Babylon, who said they had lost all hope. God promises to restore their life and bring them back to their land. Many understand this as a national restoration; some also see a sign of the future resurrection.

For today: when a situation seems hopeless, do not stay in discouragement. Obey what God shows you, pray, and trust that He can give new life where today you see only weariness or loss.
exp.20:3:
He says that God will draw out his sword, that is, his judgment, and that it will reach everyone in the land: the righteous and the wicked. "Cut off" means to remove or strike down, "north" is the direction the sword points, and "everyone" refers to every person. From south to north, no one would be left out.

The LORD speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who was living among the exiles in Babylon. God announces judgment on Jerusalem and Judah for their persistent sin. That the righteous would also fall is hard to understand. Some think the righteous would share in the consequences of a national calamity; others think the text speaks in general terms. The passage does not fully explain it.

For today: let us take God's warning seriously and not grow comfortable with the sin around us. Let us ask him to give us a humble heart, and trust in his justice and mercy even when we do not understand everything.
exp.9:5:
God gave a command to the man dressed in linen: take fire from within the wheelwork, from among the cherubim. The man obeyed, went in, and stood beside a wheel. The phrase "man clothed in linen" refers to a man dressed in linen.

Ezekiel recounts a vision he had during the exile. God speaks from his throne, surrounded by cherubim, and is about to judge Jerusalem. The fire this man takes is later used as a sign of that judgment. Some believe the fire represents purification and others destruction; the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: God acts with holiness and order, and his servants obey his word calmly. We can ask him for a heart willing to obey, even when we do not understand everything he does.
exp.23:24:
God tells Ezekiel that a day is coming when he will take away from the people their stronghold, their pride and joy, the desire of their eyes that lifted their souls, and their sons and daughters as well. The "stronghold" refers to the temple, which was their pride and their security. "The desire of their eyes" is what they loved most. The sentence is left unfinished and is completed in the next verse.

The Lord speaks to Ezekiel, who is among the exiles in Babylon. God had just announced the fall of Jerusalem and the death of Ezekiel's wife, which was a sign of the loss of the temple. Ezekiel was not to mourn publicly. The people would not be able to weep openly either, because the calamity would come because of their own sins.

For today: examine what your security depends on. Everything good we have is a gift from God, but only He should be our firm foundation.
exp.19:44:
This verse says: "Now the word of the LORD came to me, saying." The phrase "came to me" is the verse's own wording, so you can see it for yourself. Ezekiel announces that God is speaking to him again and that a new message is about to be given.

The one speaking is Ezekiel, a prophet who lived among the exiles in Babylon. With this phrase, which is repeated many times in the book, he marks the start of a new prophecy. Earlier, God had promised to restore Israel for the sake of his name and not because of their merits. Now the message shifts to judgment: the image of a forest that will be burned appears. Some scholars connect it with Jerusalem and Judah, although it is interpreted in different ways.

For today: God still speaks through his Word. Before reading the Bible, we can pray and ask him for an attentive heart, ready to listen both to what comforts and to what corrects.
exp.17:8:
This verse says that the person who follows God's statutes and faithfully keeps his ordinances is counted righteous, and therefore will live. "Statutes" are God's instructions; "ordinances" are his righteous standards; "faithfully keeps" means living out his commands with honesty and loyalty.

God himself speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, who was writing to the exiles in Babylon. They were saying that they were suffering for the sins of their fathers. God answers that each person is accountable for his own life. This verse closes the description of a righteous man: he helps the poor, does not oppress, does not rob, and judges with uprightness. Then comes the example of his son, who does not live this way.

For today: faith shows itself in everyday life. This week, look for one concrete way to act with honesty or to help someone in need, without excusing yourself by what others have done.
exp.16:0:
This verse says that God spoke to Ezekiel. The phrase "Now the word of the LORD came to me, saying," is the familiar way the prophet introduces a new message.

The one speaking is the LORD, and he is addressing Ezekiel, a prophet who lived in exile in Babylon together with other Israelites. This verse opens a new message. As the following passage shows, God will ask him to tell a parable about eagles and a cedar, directed to the house of Israel. The full meaning is explained later in the chapter.

For today: before we speak or make a decision, it is good to pause and listen to God. We can read his Word with attention and humility, knowing that he wants to speak to us and guide us, even when circumstances are difficult.
exp.22:29:
This verse gives the reason for the punishment announced: Jerusalem, pictured here as a woman, has prostituted herself with the nations, meaning she was unfaithful to God by seeking alliances with pagan peoples. Her defilement with their idols means she took on their false gods and became unclean before God.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel. In chapter 23 he tells the story of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem). Samaria had already fallen into the hands of Assyria because of her unfaithfulness. Oholibah saw that, but she followed the same path. For this reason God hands her over to the peoples she once admired and later despised.

For today: God calls us not to give our hearts to things that take his place, such as money, fame, or influence. Ask yourself today: what am I trusting in more than in God? Return to him with sincerity.
exp.27:0:
This verse is an introductory formula. It tells us that a message from God came to Ezekiel. The sentence "And the word of the LORD came to me, saying," is the reader's guide here, so the wording should be followed closely. The key point is that the message does not come from the prophet himself, but from the LORD, the God of Israel.

The one speaking is God, and Ezekiel is the messenger. This verse opens a new message, addressed to the ruler of Tyre, a rich and powerful city by the sea. According to the text that follows, God confronts him because his heart has been lifted up with pride and he has considered himself to be a god.

For today: before we speak or judge, it is wise to listen to God in his Word. And if we receive success or power, let us remember that everything is a gift and that we are still people who depend on him.
exp.0:5:
It says that each of the four living beings Ezekiel saw had four faces and four wings. The word "faces" refers to the faces, and the word "living beings" in the earlier context refers to living creatures, not ordinary animals. They had a form similar to that of a man, but with extraordinary features.

Ezekiel speaks as a priest and prophet who was exiled in Babylon with his people. He recounts a vision of God's glory that he received by the river Chebar. Scholars interpret the meaning of the four faces and the wings in various ways, so it is wise to be cautious. What is clear is that the vision showed God as majestic, present, and active, even far from the temple in Jerusalem.

For today: even if you feel far from your home, your church, or what you once knew, God is not limited to one place. Today you can worship him and pray to him with confidence wherever you are.
exp.11:0:
This verse says that God spoke to the prophet Ezekiel. "Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying," means that God's message came to Ezekiel. The word "saying" announces that the message follows right away. It is a common way in this book to mark that God takes the initiative to speak.

Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon along with the people of Judah, speaks here. God gives him a new message. According to what follows, the people heard and saw, but did not want to respond. For that reason God asks Ezekiel to represent it with a visible action, so that perhaps they would react.

For today: God still speaks, above all through his Word. Before asking him for anything, take a moment to listen. Read the Bible carefully and with a willingness to obey what you understand.
exp.2:22:
Ezekiel obeys God's command: he gets up and goes out into the field. There he finds the glory of the LORD, that is, the bright and powerful presence of God, just as he had seen it by the River Kebar. When he sees it, he falls facedown on the ground.

The phrase "got up" in the verse describes Ezekiel standing and heading out, and "behold" calls the reader's attention to what he suddenly sees.

The speaker is Ezekiel, a priest who lived in exile in Babylon. God had just called him as a watchman to warn his people. Before sending him out, God summons him to the field to speak with him. The vision of the glory reminds him who is sending him. The River Kebar is a canal near Babylon, where he had already seen that glory (chapter 1).

For today: before speaking on God's behalf or taking on a difficult task, first seek to be alone with Him. Obey His call and spend time in His presence, with humility and reverence, to receive strength and direction.
exp.31:13:
He says God will let the waters of Egypt settle, meaning they will become calm and still, and that its rivers will flow slowly and smoothly, like oil. Before, those waters were stirred up by the feet of men and animals. Now they will be clear and quiet, because no crowd will be left to stir them.

God himself speaks, through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament against Pharaoh and Egypt. Egypt depended on the Nile and felt powerful. God announces that this pride will fall through judgment, and that everything will fall silent. Some understand the image as a symbol of desolation; the text gives no further details.

For today: power and human pride are not secure. We can trust in God, not in our achievements, and live with humility.
exp.38:1:
God tells Gog that he will turn him around, drive him along, and bring him up from the far north to attack the mountains of Israel. The Hebrew behind the phrase that describes the leader's destruction is hard to pin down, and scholars read it in different ways, so the exact sense of that part of the verse remains open.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Ezekiel. He tells Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog, a leader from the northern nations who will come against Israel. Christians understand this passage in different ways: some see it as a future event, others as a symbolic picture of the final confrontation against God's people. What is clear in the verse is that God directs the entire scene.

When the world seems out of control, remember that God still governs history. Hand over your fears to him today and trust in his care.
exp.39:29:
The verse says that the porticoes around the inner court were twenty-five cubits long and five cubits deep. These were likely porches or open galleries, and a cubit was an ancient measure of roughly half a meter, so they would be about twelve meters long and two and a half meters deep. Some scholars think the words describe covered spaces beside the entrance.

Ezekiel, a priest exiled in Babylon, recounts a vision he received. A guide who looks like a man takes him through a future temple and measures each part carefully. Here he is shown the inner court, at the south gate. Interpreters differ on whether this temple is literal, symbolic, or both, and on when it would be fulfilled.

For today: God pays attention to details and cares that his people approach him with order and reverence. When you pray or gather with others, do not take it lightly. Prepare your heart with respect and gratitude.
exp.2:12:
Ezekiel reports that he heard the sound of the wings of the living creatures brushing against one another, and the sound of the wheels beside them, and all of it together was a great rumbling sound. The "animals" mentioned here are the living creatures he saw in his vision of God's glory.

Ezekiel speaks as a prophet among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. God had just sent him to speak to them, whether or not they would listen. Then the Spirit lifted him up, and those sounds accompanied the movement of God's glory. Ezekiel was deeply moved, and the verses that follow say that he felt bitter and astonished.

For today: God is great and cannot be contained by our small ideas. Before speaking or serving, take a moment to stop, listen, and acknowledge who He is. His calling is fulfilled with reverence and obedience, even when we do not know how others will respond.
exp.29:10:
This verse says that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and his army, described as the most ruthless of the nations, will be brought in to lay Egypt waste. The verse's phrase about drawing swords means taking them out of their scabbards. Filling the land means covering it. The image is of a land covered with the dead from war.

God himself speaks here, through the prophet Ezekiel. Egypt had been a proud power, with its idols and with allies who trusted in it. God announces judgment on that pride and that idolatry. The verses that follow show that God directs history, for he says: "I, the LORD, have spoken." The Babylonians are an instrument in his hand, though that does not excuse their cruelty.

For today: do not place your security in what seems strong, such as money, power or influence. All of that passes away. Trust in God, who is just and rules over every nation.
exp.39:39:
It says that, on the outer side of the stairs, beside the entrance of the north gate of the temple, there were two tables. On the other side, also beside the entrance, there were two more. The word for "stairs" refers to the steps leading up to the gate. These tables were used to prepare the sacrifices, such as the burnt offering and the sin offering.

Ezekiel recounts a vision that God gave him during the exile in Babylon. A guide, holding a measuring rod, shows him a new temple in detail. Interpreters differ: some see it as a literal temple in the future, others as a symbol of God's presence with his restored people. The details aim to show order and holiness.

God cares about the way we draw near to him. Today we can give God an orderly place in our lives, with times of prayer and reading, remembering that Christ has already made the sacrifice for our sins.
exp.2:15:
It says that seven days passed, and then God spoke to Ezekiel. The phrase "the word of the LORD came to me" means that God broke the silence and gave him a message.

Ezekiel was a priest exiled in Babylon. He had seen a vision of the glory of God and received his call as a prophet. Then he came to Tel-abib, by the river Chebar, where other exiles lived, and he stayed there seven days, stunned and silent. Afterward God told him that He had made him a watchman, one who warns of danger, to warn Israel.

God does not always answer right away, and sometimes He asks us to wait and take in what we have lived through. If you feel confused or overwhelmed, do not be troubled by the silence. Stay close to God, pray, and keep watching for His guidance, because He speaks in His own time.
exp.21:4:
It says that people near and far, from all the surrounding nations, will mock Jerusalem. The phrase "infamous city" points to a city whose name is ruined and whose reputation is spoiled. The phrase "full of turmoil" speaks of great disorder and confusion within the city.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem. She shed innocent blood and filled herself with idols. The verses that follow show that her leaders abused their power, despised parents, and oppressed the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow. Therefore God announces that this sin would bring public shame and chaos.

For today: our secret decisions end up affecting our witness and others. Let us ask God to help us live with justice and to care for the most vulnerable, so that our lives honor his name.
exp.36:21:
God promises that he will bring his people together as one nation in the mountains of Israel. One king will rule over all of them, and they will no longer be two separate nations or divided into two kingdoms.

The phrase "one king will rule over all of them" means that a single king will govern everyone. The word "will" points to a future promise that God himself will carry out.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel during the exile. Earlier, the kingdom of Israel had been split into two: Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Ezekiel took two sticks, one for each part, and joined them together in his hand as a sign. God promises to gather and cleanse his people. Many Christians see in this a promise that points to Christ, a descendant of David, although there are different interpretations.

For today: God is a God who reconciles what is divided. Ask him to help you seek peace and unity in your family or your church, beginning with forgiving someone.
exp.32:29:
God tells the prophet Ezekiel that his people are talking about him near the city walls and in the doorways of their houses. One speaks to another, each saying to his brother, "Come and hear the message that has come from the LORD!" The word that is rendered here as "talking against" can be understood as talking about him with curiosity or with mockery; scholars read it in different ways.

God speaks to Ezekiel, who was already among the exiles in Babylon. He had announced the fall of Jerusalem and the desolation of the land, and those words had come true. Even so, the people saw his preaching as an interesting show, not as a serious call.

Today we can hear sermons, read the Bible, or listen to Christian songs only for enjoyment or out of habit. Let us ask God for a willing heart, and let us choose today one teaching that we can put into practice.
exp.26:15:
It says that Aram (Syria) traded with Tyre because Tyre produced a great many goods. In return, Aram gave Tyre turquoise, purple cloth, embroidered work, fine linen, coral, and rubies. Some of these items are hard to identify with certainty, and the stone rendered as turquoise may refer to a different kind of gem. "Customer" here means a buyer who trades with Tyre.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel in a lament over Tyre, a very rich seafaring city. This list of nations shows the vast network of trade that made Tyre great. But the chapter prepares the announcement of its fall: its wealth and pride would not save it from God's judgment.

Today we can ask ourselves what we trust in most: what we own, or God. Enjoying our work and possessions is not wrong, but they must not take God's place in our hearts. Let us ask him to teach us to be thankful, generous, and humble.
exp.2:24:
God tells Ezekiel that they will tie him with ropes and bind him, so that he cannot go out among the people. The ropes are cords used to tie him up, and being bound means he is held in place and unable to move freely. "Son of man" is the way God addresses Ezekiel, a reminder that he is a human being.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, who lives among the exiles in Babylon. God commands him to shut himself up in his house and be unable to speak, because the people are a rebellious house. Scholars debate whether the ropes were physical bonds or an image of the restrictions the people would place on him; the text does not make this clear. His silence would be a sign to them.

For today: sometimes God leads us into times of limitation or silence that we do not understand. We can trust that he keeps speaking in his own time and obey him even when we cannot see the purpose, knowing that he will open our mouths when the time is right.
exp.18:10:
It says the vine, which represents the mother of the prince, grew with strength. It had firm branches, so good that they were used to make scepters, that is, staffs of authority for rulers. It rose very high among the foliage and could be seen from afar, with many branches. The long shoots of the vine are the tendrils that spread out from its stem.

God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, in a lament over the princes of Israel. The vine probably represents Judah or its royal dynasty, and its branches are the kings. Some think of specific kings, but the text does not make this entirely clear. The following verses show that this greatness ended in judgment and exile.

For today: blessings, success, and influence are no guarantee of security if we forget God. Let us be thankful for what he gives us, use what we have with humility, and remember that our strength comes from remaining in him.

sum.0: Ezekiel, a priest exiled by the Kebar River, sees the heavens opened and a great storm with fire. In it appear four living beings with several faces and wings, wheels full of eyes, and, above all, a throne of sapphire. There he sees a figure with the appearance of a man, surrounded by radiance, which is the glory of Jehovah, and he falls face down to the ground.
sum.6: In Ezekiel 7, God announces that the end has come for Israel because of its wickedness, its violence, and its idolatry. Neither gold nor silver will save them, and war, famine, and plague will come. No one will find peace or counsel, and so they will know that he is the LORD.
sum.10: In a vision, God shows Ezekiel the leaders of Jerusalem who give bad advice and fill the city with the dead, and He announces judgment on them. Then Pelatiah dies. God promises to gather the scattered people, give them a new heart, and be their God. After that, His glory leaves the city, and Ezekiel tells the exiles everything.
sum.11: God tells Ezekiel to act out the part of someone going into exile: he is to bring out his belongings by day, dig a hole through the wall, and leave at night with his face covered. This is a sign that the prince of Jerusalem and the people will be taken away as captives. God also says that he will not delay any longer in fulfilling his word.
sum.9: Ezekiel sees the cherubim and the wheels full of eyes again, with a sapphire throne above them. God commands the man dressed in linen to take burning coals and scatter them over the city. The glory of the LORD moves away from the threshold of the temple and stops at the east gate, showing that God is withdrawing from Jerusalem.
sum.2: God gives Ezekiel a scroll to eat, sweet as honey, and sends him to speak to a stubborn people. He gives him a hardened resolve so that he will not be afraid. He appoints him as a watchman, responsible for warning both the wicked and the righteous. Then he tells him that he will be shut in and unable to speak until God opens his mouth again.
sum.7: In a vision, God takes the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem and shows him the idolatry the people are practicing, even inside the temple: images, elders secretly burning incense, women weeping for Tammuz, and men worshiping the sun. Because of this, God announces that he will act in anger and will show no pity.
sum.5: God tells Ezekiel to prophesy against the mountains of Israel, where the people were worshiping idols. He announces judgment by sword, famine, and plague, with their altars destroyed and their cities left desolate. But he promises that some will survive. Among the nations they will remember God, they will feel ashamed of their unfaithfulness, and they will know that he is the LORD.
sum.3: God tells Ezekiel to act out a sign showing the siege of Jerusalem: he draws the city on a clay tablet, lies on one side for many days bearing the wickedness of Israel and Judah, and eats only a small ration of bread and water. In this way he announces that the people will suffer hunger and distress because of their sin.
sum.8: God summons six executioners and a man dressed in linen to judge Jerusalem for its wickedness and violence. First, he marks the foreheads of those who grieve over all the detestable things being done, and they are protected, while the judgment begins at the sanctuary. Ezekiel pleads in distress, and the man in linen reports that he has carried out the command.
sum.1: God raises Ezekiel to his feet, gives him his Spirit, and sends him to speak to the Israelites, a rebellious and stubborn people, whether they listen or not. He tells him not to be afraid and not to rebel as they do, but to open his mouth and take in what God gives him. Then he sees a scroll written on both sides with laments and woes.
sum.4: God tells Ezekiel to shave off his hair and beard and divide it into three parts. This is a sign of what will happen to Jerusalem: some will die by fire, some will die by the sword, and others will be scattered. Jerusalem was placed at the center of the nations, but she rebelled and behaved worse than they did. Because of this, God will judge her with famine, disease, and war, so that they will know that he has spoken.
sum.32: God appoints Ezekiel as a watchman to warn Israel, and he tells him that He does not want the wicked to die, but to turn from their ways and live. Each person will be judged according to their own way, yet the people still refuse to obey. When the news arrives that Jerusalem has fallen, God announces judgment on the land and declares that they will know a prophet had been among them.
sum.19: Some elders of Israel come to consult God, but he refuses to answer them and reviews the history of their rebellion. From Egypt, through the wilderness and into the promised land, Israel kept following idols, and God acted for the sake of his name. He promises to judge them, gather them, and restore them. The passage ends with a prophecy of fire against the forest of the south.
sum.43: Ezekiel sees the east gate of the sanctuary shut, because the Lord entered through it, and only the prince may sit there to eat bread before God. Then God rebukes Israel for letting in foreigners who were not committed to him, and he assigns the unfaithful Levites to lesser tasks. The priests who were descendants of Zadok, who remained faithful, will serve close to God under rules of holiness.
sum.39: In a vision, fourteen years after the fall of Jerusalem, God takes Ezekiel to a very high mountain in Israel, where a man with a measuring reed shows him a temple. The man measures in detail the gates, the courtyards, the tables for the sacrifices, and the chambers for the priests and singers, and he tells Ezekiel to report everything to Israel.
sum.21: God sends Ezekiel to denounce Jerusalem for its violence, its idolatry, and its injustice against the weak. Just as dross is melted down in a furnace, so the people will be gathered and purified under the fire of his anger. The leaders, prophets, and priests have failed, and God found no one who would stand in the gap.
sum.36: God takes Ezekiel to a valley full of dry bones, and as he prophesies, the bones come back to life and form a great army. This is a sign that God will restore Israel, which had lost hope and been scattered. Then, using two sticks joined together, God promises to gather Judah and Israel into one nation, cleanse them, give them a shepherd named David, and live among them in an everlasting covenant of peace.
sum.35: God promises to restore the mountains of Israel, which had been humiliated by the nations, and to fill the land again with people, crops, and cities. Israel had defiled the land and God's name with its sin and idolatry, and that is why it was scattered. But God will act for the sake of his holy name: he will gather his people, cleanse them, and give them a new heart and his Spirit.
sum.18: Ezekiel chants a lament over the princes of Israel. He compares their mother to a lioness whose two cubs, now grown into lions, were captured: one was taken to Egypt and the other to Babylon. He then compares her to a strong vine that was uprooted and planted in the wilderness, and fire consumed its branches. It is a funeral song mourning the fall of the kings.
sum.25: God announces judgment against Tyre, which rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem because it expected to profit from it. He will send Nebuchadnezzar and many nations to destroy her walls and riches, and the city will be left like a bare, smooth rock. The islands will tremble at her fall, and everyone will know that God is the Lord.
sum.16: God tells a parable about eagles and a vine. Babylon carried off the king of Judah, but that king broke his oath and sought help from Egypt, so he will not escape judgment. In the end, God promises to plant a shoot on the high mountain of Israel, and it will become a magnificent cedar where everyone will find shelter.
sum.37: God tells Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog, a leader from the north who will gather many nations to attack Israel, a people living in confidence and without walls. God Himself will bring him in and destroy him with earthquake, sword, plague and fire. In this way the nations will know that He is the LORD, holy and great.
sum.13: Some elders of Israel came to consult Ezekiel, but God said they had idols in their hearts and called them to turn away from those idols. He then explained that even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in the land, they would only save their own lives, not the lives of their sons and daughters, when the four judgments came upon Jerusalem. Even so, a remnant would be left behind to bring comfort to the people.
sum.40: In this vision, a guide takes Ezekiel through the temple, measuring the entrance, the Holy Place, the Most Holy Place, and the chambers that surround the building. The walls were carved with cherubim and palm trees, and there was a wooden altar called "the table before the LORD." Everything shows order, holiness, and the presence of God.
sum.28: God announces judgment against Pharaoh, who thought he owned the Nile, and Egypt will be left desolate for about forty years because it was a "broken reed" to Israel. Afterward God will restore it, but as a humble kingdom. He also gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment, and promises to strengthen Israel.
sum.33: God rebukes the shepherds of Israel, who looked after themselves and mistreated the sheep, and promises to take the flock away from them. He himself will search for his people, rescue them, and care for them. He will judge between the strong sheep and the weak ones, and he will set his servant David over them as shepherd. He will give them peace, blessing, and safety.
sum.42: The glory of God returns from the east and fills the temple. God promises to live with Israel forever, if they give up their sins and idolatry. Ezekiel is to show the plan of the temple to the people, and the measurements of the altar and the offerings to purify it over seven days are given.
sum.31: God asks Ezekiel to sing a lament over Pharaoh, whom he compares to a river monster that will be caught, and he announces that Babylon's sword will destroy Egypt. Then Egypt is sent down to the place of the dead, along with other nations that spread terror. In this way God shows that no proud power escapes his judgment.
sum.14: God asks Ezekiel what good the wood of a vine is. It is useless for making anything, and even less so after it has been burned. The people of Jerusalem will be the same: God will turn against them, fire will consume them, and the land will be left desolate because of their unfaithfulness.
sum.29: Through Ezekiel, God announces that a day of judgment is coming upon Egypt and its allies. Babylon, under King Nebuchadnezzar, will be the sword that destroys its cities, its idols, and its power. God will break the arm of Pharaoh, and in this way the Egyptians will know that Jehovah is the Lord.
sum.30: God tells Pharaoh to compare himself with Assyria, a huge and beautiful cedar that gave shade to many nations. But Assyria's heart grew proud, so God handed it over to a powerful nation, which cut it down. The same fate awaits Pharaoh: pride ends in downfall and death.
sum.27: God condemns the prince of Tyre for thinking himself a god because of his wisdom and wealth, and announces that foreigners will bring him down. Then he laments over the king of Tyre, whose beauty and pride led him to sin and fall. Finally, he judges Sidon and promises Israel that they will return to their land and live in safety.
sum.41: In this vision, a guide leads Ezekiel through the outer courtyard and shows him chambers on several levels, to the north and south of the temple. He explains that they are holy: there the priests eat the offerings and change their clothes before going out to the people. Then the whole enclosure is measured, and its wall separates what is holy from what is common.
sum.17: God corrects the saying that children pay for their parents' sins: each person answers for their own life. The righteous person who turns away from God will die, and the wicked person who repents will live. God does not desire the death of anyone, and he calls Israel to turn back to him and receive a new heart.
sum.15: God shows Jerusalem as an abandoned infant girl whom He rescued, cared for, and adorned. But she trusted in her own beauty, gave herself to idols and to alliances with foreign nations, and even sacrificed her children. Because of this, she will be judged and shamed, worse than Sodom and Samaria. Even so, God promises to remember His covenant and restore her with mercy.
sum.44: God commands that a holy portion of the land be set apart for the sanctuary, the priests, the Levites, the city, and the prince. He tells the princes to stop using violence and to use honest weights and measures. He also sets out offerings and festivals, including the Passover, to make atonement for the people's sins.
sum.20: God tells Ezekiel that his sword of judgment will fall on Jerusalem and the whole land of Israel, without distinguishing between the righteous and the wicked, and the prophet must groan as a sign of anguish. The king of Babylon consults his divinations and decides to attack Jerusalem. God removes the crown from the wicked prince, and he will also judge Ammon.
sum.22: God uses the story of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem), to show how his people were unfaithful to him with Egypt, Assyria and Babylon, and with their idols. Samaria was handed over to her Assyrian lovers, and Jerusalem, who did not learn from her sister, would receive the same punishment. In this way God intends to put an end to that wickedness, so that they will know that he is the Lord.
sum.45: In this vision from Ezekiel, God gives rules for worship in the temple: when the eastern gate is opened, what offerings the prince presents, and the daily sacrifice of a lamb each morning. He also commands that the prince must not take land away from the people, and the places where the sacrifices are cooked are shown.
sum.47: Ezekiel describes how the land will be divided among the tribes of Israel, in strips running from east to west. In the center there is a holy portion set apart for the sanctuary, the priests, the Levites, the city, and the prince. The city will have twelve gates bearing the names of the tribes, and it will be called "The LORD Is There."
sum.38: God promises to destroy Gog and his armies on the mountains of Israel. Israel will burn their weapons and bury the bodies to cleanse the land. In this way the nations will know that God is holy and just. Then God will bring his people back, have mercy on them, and pour out his Spirit upon them.
sum.23: God shows Ezekiel the parable of a pot set over a fire. It stands for Jerusalem, a city full of blood and filth that will be burned in judgment. Then his wife dies suddenly, and God forbids him to mourn. This is meant as a sign that Israel will lose the temple and its sons and daughters and will be left without comfort. When the news arrives, Ezekiel will speak again.
sum.24: In Ezekiel 25, God announces judgment against Ammon, Moab, Edom, and the Philistines, because they mocked Judah and Israel in their disaster, or took revenge against them. In this way it teaches that God sees pride and cruelty, and that he acts so that everyone will know that he is the LORD.
sum.26: God told Ezekiel to sing a lament over Tyre, the seafaring city that boasted of its perfect beauty. Tyre is described as a great ship, built with fine materials and made rich through its trade with many peoples. But a storm will sink it, and everyone will mourn its fall.
sum.34: God commands Ezekiel to prophesy against Mount Seir, that is, Edom, because it held an ancient hatred against Israel, handed Israel over to the sword in its time of distress, and wanted to take over its land. God heard their mockery and promises to leave it desolate. In this way it teaches that God sees wickedness and defends his people.
sum.12: God tells Ezekiel to speak against the prophets and prophetesses of Israel who were making up messages from their own hearts and saying "God says this" when God had not spoken. They were offering false peace, like a badly plastered wall that will collapse when the storm hits. God promises to judge them and to rescue his people from their deceptions.
sum.46: In a vision, Ezekiel sees a river flowing out from the temple, and the farther it goes, the deeper it becomes. Wherever it reaches, it brings life and healing, and trees grow along its banks with fruit and leaves used for medicine. Then God marks out the boundaries of the land and commands that it be divided among the tribes, including the foreigners who live among them.
